title_key: the impact of ai assistance on the academic writing self efficacy of undergraduates with different writing abilities|gong
title: The Impact of AI Assistance on the Academic Writing Self-Efficacy of Undergraduates with Different Writing Abilities
abstract: Against digital education background, generative AI has become common writing assistance for undergraduates. Existing studies mainly focus on second-language writing and ignore stratified comparisons across learners, while the dual effects of AI on academic writing self-efficacy remain understudied. Based on self-efficacy theory, this paper distributes questionnaires and divides respondents into three proficiency groups by CET-4 scores. Descriptive statistics, group difference tests and correlation analysis are adopted for empirical analysis. The results reveal prevalent AI over-dependence despite its polishing functions. Participants’ writing self-efficacy stays at medium-upper level yet hampered by writing anxiety. AI delivers short-term confidence promotion but impairs independent writing competence in the long run, with stronger influences on low-proficiency students. This stratified dual-path framework offers empirical references for standardized AI application in university writing teaching.
venue: Journal of Education and Educational Research

title_key: leveraging agentic coding for interactive education in electrical engineering|sawicki
title: Leveraging Agentic Coding for Interactive Education in Electrical Engineering
abstract: Large language models enable the automated synthesis of interactive educational software beyond conversational tutoring. This paper presents an authoring methodology using agentic coding (an autonomous, tool-augmented workflow based on the Reason-and-Act (ReAct) paradigm) to generate standalone, browser-based simulation modules for electrical engineering curricula. It was applied across three undergraduate courses, using three distinct agentic development environments: a transient commutation simulator for second-order RLC circuits (circuit theory), an eddy-current induction laboratory (electromagnetism), and an interactive benchmark of iterative linear solvers (numerical methods). We formalize a pipeline built on (1) strict decoupling of pedagogical specification from implementation, (2) formal mathematical notation constraints, (3) singlepass holistic generation to prevent context window degradation, (4) human-in-the-loop validation gates, and (5) prompt-level regeneration rather than conversational code patching. Recurring failure modes: notation drift, context saturation, feature creep, and physically invalid simulations ("vibe physics"); are analyzed together with their mitigations, and an independent analytical audit of two generated modules is reported. Modules are synthesized in 5–10 minutes over 3–5 specification iterations, shifting instructor effort from manual programming to requirements engineering and domain verification.
venue: 2026 27th International Conference on Computational Problems of Electrical Engineering (CPEE)

title_key: generative artificial intelligence in secondary education educational value motivation and ethical perceptions of students|bartovcak
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Secondary Education: Educational Value, Motivation, and Ethical Perceptions of Students
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is becoming increasingly integrated into educational processes, particularly among secondary school students, where it is used to support learning, complete academic assignments, and develop a variety of skills. The aim of this study is to analyse how secondary school students perceive the educational value of generative artificial intelligence and to examine the role of motivation, sense of security, and ethical concerns in shaping that perception. The study was conducted on a sample of 281 secondary school students (Economics and Administrative Officer programmes) using a structured online questionnaire. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and regression models. The results indicate that students most strongly recognise the contribution of generative artificial intelligence to the development of creativity and the adaptation of learning to individual needs, while its contribution to the development of critical thinking and teamwork was rated more moderately. Hypothesis testing revealed a statistically significant association between motivation for learning, sense of security, and ethical concerns with the perception of the educational value of GAI, albeit in unexpected directions. Students who reported a weaker motivational effect of GAI and a lower sense of security when using it tended to perceive GAI as a more educationally valuable tool. However, the mechanisms underlying these relationships require further investigation. At the same time, ethical concerns proved to be a weak but significant positive predictor of perceived educational value, suggesting an ambivalent relationship between students and this technology. The findings underscore the importance of pedagogically guided and ethically grounded integration of generative artificial intelligence into secondary education.
venue: Symposium on Intelligent Systems and Informatics

title_key: paradigm reconstruction and practical pathways of ai enabled physical chemistry teaching|ning
title: Paradigm Reconstruction and Practical Pathways of AI-Enabled Physical Chemistry Teaching
abstract: Physical chemistry is a core course for chemistry‑related majors. Its teaching faces problems such as abstract concepts, complicated mathematical deductions, and disconnection between theory and practice, making it difficult to improve teaching quality. Generative artificial intelligence offers new solutions to these teaching difficulties. This paper proposes strategies to reduce cognitive barriers, reshape classroom models, and optimize evaluations. Besides, it also puts forward risk prevention measures for “cognitive outsourcing” and “AI hallucinations”. This research holds that the essence of AI-enabled physical chemistry teaching lies in realizing the paradigm shift from unified content supply to the construction of an educational ecosystem through technology, and its effectiveness depends on consistently prioritizing the cultivation of students’ higher‑order thinking abilities.

title_key: use and perceptions of artificial intelligence tools among clinical medical students in selected nigerian universities a multi institutional survey|nwankwo
title: Use and Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence Tools among Clinical Medical Students in Selected Nigerian Universities: A Multi-Institutional Survey.
abstract:
BACKGROUND
AI tools are increasingly used in medical education for learning, clinical reasoning, and examination preparation, but there is limited data from Nigeria.


AIM
To examine AI use and attitudes among Nigerian medical students to inform policy.


METHODS
A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among medical students in three Nigerian medical schools from December 2025 to February 2026. The questionnaire covered demographics, awareness, and use of AI tools, perceived benefits and risks, attitudes toward integration, and barriers to adoption. Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Descriptive statistics and Chi-square tests were used to analyze data.


RESULTS
A total of 328 responses were received. Respondents demonstrated generally positive attitudes toward AI use, although concerns regarding accuracy, academic integrity, and regulation were identified. 53.8% were males, (70.8%) aged 20-24, (55.7%) fourth-year students, and (43.1%) from the University of Nigeria. Smartphones (94.5%) and ChatGPT (98.2%) were mostly used. AI was useful for understanding difficult concepts (92.9%), self-directed learning (83.1%), and saving study time (81.2%). Concerns included misinformation (75.1%), academic dishonesty (60.7%), and reduced critical thinking (47.4%). Barriers included subscriptions (71.4%), poor connectivity (69.2%), and high data costs (66.8%). There was no statistically significant association between AI use and level of study ( P = 0.78), age group ( P = 0.12), and gender ( P = 0.82).


CONCLUSION
AI tools are widely adopted by medical students in Nigeria without clear guidelines for use, despite concerns regarding accuracy, dependence, and academic integrity. Curricula integration, along with clear guidelines and training, is recommended for responsible use.
authors: ["E. Nwankwo", "I. Chukwu", "D. Malachy", "I. Obianyo", "CC Amah", "JO Ugwu", "Ephraim Nwangwu", "UO Ezomike", "CB Eke"]

title_key: motivations and gratifications in generative ai adoption a survey based uses and gratifications study of media and communication students at the university of gujrat pakistan|sarwar
title: Motivations and Gratifications in Generative AI Adoption: A Survey-Based Uses and Gratifications Study of Media and Communication Students at the University of Gujrat, Pakistan
abstract: In Pakistan, AI tools, including ChatGPT which are used as generative AI tools, have changed academic practice in higher education, but the motivations of students are under-researched. This quantitative survey uses the Uses and Gratifications Theory (UGT) to investigate generative AI usage by media and communication students in the University of Gujrat (UOG) in meeting academic needs, such as cognitive (content creation, research), tension-release (meeting deadlines), and personal integrative (learn media production) gratifications. A survey was conducted on 250 students of UOG who have been on the media-related programs using a structured questionnaire. The SPSS descriptive statistics demonstrated moderate awareness of AI (40.8%), dominating self-taught adoption (40.0%), and the frequency of usage being high (59.2% per week/day), with ChatGPT (30.0%), and virtual assistants (21.6%), prevailing in writing, brainstorming, and plagiarism. Integration was not even across the board as advanced tools (e.g., machine learning platforms, 4.0%) were barely utilized. Results are positive in favor of UGT, which demonstrates active selection of AI in terms of utilitarian and hedonic gratifications, but indicates shortcomings in formal training and ethical consciousness. Implications consist in the introduction of AI literacy in media curricula in order to maximize gratifications, and reduce the risks of dependency. This paper builds upon UGT to generative AI within Pakistani media education providing information on the fair implementation in resourceconstrained contexts.

title_key: beyond the score uptick foundational proficiency cognitive agency and ai era learning in indonesias pisa 2025|judijanto
title: Beyond the Score Uptick: Foundational Proficiency, Cognitive Agency, and AI-Era Learning in Indonesia’s PISA 2025
abstract: Indonesia’s PISA 2025 results present a paradox. Reading and science scores increased nominally from 2022, educational participation among 15-year-olds expanded substantially, and several indicators of curiosity, perseverance, teacher support, and self-regulation appear favourable. Yet the OECD concludes that average performance in mathematics, reading, and science did not change significantly from 2022, while proficiency remains critically low. Only 17% of Indonesian students reached at least Level 2 in mathematics, 27% in reading, and 37% in science. This qualitative literature review synthesises PISA 2025 evidence with recent peer-reviewed literature published predominantly between 2020 and 2026 to reinterpret Indonesia’s performance through an access–learning–cognition–digital ecology framework. The review identifies five interacting challenges: an access–quality paradox; a foundational-proficiency deficit, particularly in mathematics; a gap between teacher support and cognitive activation; socioeconomic and school-level constraints; and an emerging digital-learning paradox in which extensive device and generative-AI use can either augment or substitute for productive cognitive effort. The analysis argues that neither international ranking nor nominal score changes provide an adequate diagnosis. Indonesia’s next educational challenge is to convert expanded schooling, supportive learning environments, and digital access into deeper reading, mathematical modelling, scientific reasoning, self-regulated learning, and epistemically responsible AI use. Policy implications emphasise diagnostic remediation, cognitively demanding instruction, disciplined technology integration, AI literacy, family engagement, and proficiency-based monitoring
venue: Multitech Journal of Science and Technology

title_key: code commits and complexity in the genai era a longitudinal study of team based capstone projects|shakil
title: Code, Commits, and Complexity in the GenAI Era: A Longitudinal Study of Team-Based Capstone Projects
abstract: Generative AI tools are now widely available to students, but little is known about how team-based project codebases have changed since they appeared. This matters when project courses use repository activity as evidence of progress and learning. Existing studies have largely examined self-reports, controlled tasks, or short individual assignments, leaving open questions around how student codebases evolve in authentic project settings. We present a ten-semester analysis of N=260 capstone team repositories from 2021 to 2025, spanning pre- and post-AI cohorts. We examine three dimensions: code size (lines of code), code characteristics (comment density, error-handling density, and cyclomatic complexity), and development behaviour (commit volume, edit size, and commit frequency). We find that end-of-semester codebases roughly triple, from about 3.4 KLOC in 2021--2023 to about 10 KLOC in 2024--2025. Code characteristics show a clear decoupling: cyclomatic complexity and error-handling density increase, while comment density does not. Later cohorts commit far more often and in greater volume, but individual commit sizes are largely unchanged, suggesting a shift in development rhythm rather than edit granularity. Most changes appear from 2024 onwards and are not uniformly monotonic. We did not directly observe AI use, so we report these as changes that coincide with increased GenAI availability rather than as effects of AI use. Our findings highlight the need to reconsider how student-produced artefacts are used and assessed in project courses.

title_key: reimagining the role of a medical teacher in the era of artificial intelligence|mughal
title: Reimagining the Role of a Medical Teacher in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
abstract:
For the past three decades, the "Twelve Roles of the Medical Teacher" has been the key framework to determine the competencies required to be effective in the practice of medical teaching. It identifies twelve specific roles in six categories i.e. Information Provider, Role Model, Facilitator, Assessor, Planner, Resource Developer. 1 In Pakistan, it remains the key driver of almost all faculty development programs, including the short six-month Certificate in Health Professions Education (CHPE) and more comprehensive two-year Master in Health Professions Education (MHPE) programs. However, currently, there is a shift in Health Professions Education due to the rise of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the explosion of big data which raises the question: are these traditional roles still sufficient? 
Contemporary literature clearly suggests that they are not. 2,3 The pace at which medical knowledge expands today far exceeds the capacity of traditional teaching tools, such as textbooks. Thus, the role of the health professions educator is moving away from being a deliverer of information and toward becoming a developer of digital platforms curated according to learners’ needs.

title_key: the influence of ai facilitated personalised education on improving student academic performance|han
title: The Influence of AI-Facilitated Personalised Education on Improving Student Academic Performance
abstract: AI has revolutionised the landscape of personalised learning, empowering learning systems to analyse learner data, tailor learning paths, provide feedback, suggest learning materials, and pinpoint learning challenges. This paper aims at answering the main question: What is the association between AI-facilitated personalisation and students' academic achievement, and what are the implementation conditions that influence this association? This paper introduces a systematic, evidence-based review that integrates findings from peer-reviewed systematic reviews, scoping reviews, meta-analyses, and selected empirical research in the fields of artificial intelligence in education, adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, personalised recommendations, and digitally-delivered feedback. The findings suggest that personalised adaptive learning is linked with higher academic achievement in a significant number of the studies examined. A 2024 scoping review of 69 studies found that 41 studies (59%) showed improvements in student academic achievement and 25 studies (36%) showed improvements in students' engagement. A 125 study synthesis from the systematic review in the education sectors in 2025 found that adaptive learning, machine learning, natural language processing, recommendation systems, intelligent tutoring, and generative AI are key technical methods to personalisation. There were 29 empirical studies chosen for a 2025 meta-analysis of AI and academic outcomes, and 99 effect sizes from 32 RCTs used in a separate meta-analysis for the effects of AI for personalised STEM education. This suggests that, alongside automation, academic benefits for AI depend on adaptive feedback in instruction, diagnostic assessment, appropriate sequencing in instruction, control by the learner, involvement of the teacher, and pedagogical alignment. The paper presents a conceptual model that connects the concepts of AI-assisted Learner Profiling, Adaptive Content, Feedback, Engagement, Self-regulation, and Academic Achievement. The analysis also highlights data privacy, unequal access, algorithmic limitations, educator readiness, and over-reliance on automated outputs as conditions that need to be protected within institutional contexts. The results encourage a human-centred approach in which AI is used as an adaptive teaching layer, not to replace teachers.The topics include, but are not limited to, the following: artificial intelligence, personalised education, adaptive learning, academic performance, intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, student engagement, educational technology.

title_key: prompt engineering as an extension of information literacy implications for library instruction programmes|adewojo
title: Prompt engineering as an extension of information literacy: Implications for library instruction programmes
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now a routine information tool for students and knowledge workers, and the quality of what they obtain depends in part on how they instruct it. This article argues that prompt engineering is best understood as an extension of information literacy, and that library and information professionals should lead its teaching in partnership with other units. Using conceptual analysis, it maps prompt competencies onto the six frames of the ACRL Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education and, unlike earlier mappings, identifies where the analogy fails. The mapping holds for question formulation, evaluation and refinement. It fails where a language model generates text and does not retrieve documents, where its sources cannot be inspected, and where it fabricates citations. Those failures are the strongest argument for librarian involvement, because they call for verification skills that prompt technique alone does not supply. The article proposes an instructional design in four strands, including one for workplace settings, sets out how each can be assessed, and considers equity of access to instruction. It also addresses two objections: that prompt engineering is a transient skill, and that librarians are not yet prepared to teach it. The argument is conceptual and requires empirical evaluation.

title_key: human or machine efl students trust calibration in ai generated english content a study at the faculty of languages surman|altarabulsi
title: Human or Machine? EFL Students’ Trust Calibration in AI-Generated English Content:A Study at the Faculty of Languages, Surman
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by university EFL students for language learning and academic tasks, yet fluent output may be inaccurate. This study examined self-reported trust and verification practices and students’ judgments of selected AI-generated English content among undergraduates at the Faculty of Languages, Surman, University of Sabratha. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was applied to questionnaire responses from 38 students. The instrument included background questions, ten five-point Likert items, five evaluation tasks with confidence and verification-intention responses, and an optional open-ended item. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, and Spearman’s rank correlations were used. Mean self-reported trust was 3.36/5 and verification was 3.74/5. Students correctly judged 62.1% of task responses under the primary answer key. Use frequency was not significantly associated with trust (ρ = .279, p = .090), whereas verification was associated with accuracy (ρ = .473, p = .003), as was confidence (ρ = .648, p < .001). Findings are preliminary given the small sample, modest trust-scale internal consistency, and ambiguity in one evaluation item. In exploratory HC3 regression, confidence remained associated with accuracy (β = .51, p = .005), while reported verification did not uniquely reach p < .05 after confidence was included (p = .063). After Holm correction across 28 exploratory pairs, only confidence–accuracy and awareness–adaptive-trust correlations remained significant. The study highlights the value of teaching verification and interpreting trust relative to output reliability.

title_key: ai bias in special education|laconner
title: AI Bias in Special Education
abstract: Despite the rapid deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) to support K–12 educators in improving their practice, serious concerns remain unanswered about large-language model (LLM) output. This is especially true in special education, where educators report little training in disability theory, leading them to consult with AI systems without the background knowledge needed for objective analysis of the chatbot responses. To address this issue, we conducted a qualitative content analysis of the transcripts of responses from five major LLMs (Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, OpenAI ChatGPT, Perplexity Sonar, and xAI Grok) to common questions from early-career educators. We found an overreliance in the chatbot output on the Medical Model of disability, as well as almost no engagement with the Human Rights Model. We also found a wide variability between the different LLMs, as well as internal variability within each LLM based on the wording of the prompt. We conclude by calling for explicit instruction on disability theory in teacher preservice programs to support critical engagement by teachers with AI tools, as well as improved LLM models that consider multiple models of disability. This article makes a practical contribution to special education practice by identifying imbalanced AI output and suggesting ways to minimize the negative impacts that may result from using these tools.

title_key: from static to dynamic parameter manipulation as adaptive ddl scaffolding in creative writing with generative ai|yu
title: From Static to Dynamic: Parameter Manipulation as Adaptive DDL Scaffolding in Creative Writing with Generative AI
abstract: Abstract Generative AI tools now pervade university classrooms, yet the field lacks empirical understanding of how technical AI configurations translate into adaptive Data-driven Learning (DDL) scaffolding. This gap is crucial in creative writing, where excessive structure can suppress authorship and insufficient support can stall exploration. This study investigates how large language model (LLM) parameter configuration functions as a pedagogical design lever for DDL scaffolding in poetry writing classrooms. Across a three-phase mixed-methods study with 30 university creative writing learners (a 2 × 2 factorial experiment, an offline classroom workshop, and an online classroom workshop), two parameter settings, temperature and top-p, reliably reshaped the distribution of three pre-coded interaction types: Constraint Repair (Type A), Exemplar Giving (Type B), and Surprise Harvest (Type C). Moving from a structured to an exploratory setting, Type C rose roughly seven-fold in Phase 1, with the same direction of effect in the two subsequent classroom phases. Triangulating chat logs, reflection templates, and panel transcripts, Type B was voted most helpful but linked to diminished authorship, while Type C was associated with the highest authorship and satisfaction. We position parameter literacy as a necessary instructor competence for adaptive AI scaffolding.
venue: Digital Studies in Language and Literature

title_key: an ai generative ai assisted blended learning intervention for nursing undergraduates a quasi experimental study of attitudes toward ai ai literacy and autonomous learning competency|lan
title: An AI/generative AI-assisted blended learning intervention for nursing undergraduates: a quasi-experimental study of attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency
abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping healthcare, highlighting the need for nursing graduates to develop relevant competencies. However, structured AI education remains limited in nursing programs, and evidence on the effects of AI-focused teaching interventions remains scarce.
 
 
 
 A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study was conducted among 142 undergraduate nursing students at a university in southwestern Zhejiang, China. Seventy-two students participated in a 10-week AI/generative AI (GenAI)-assisted blended learning course comprising 12 h of self-paced online learning and 6 h of hands-on workshops, while 70 students received standard instruction. Attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency were assessed before and immediately after the intervention using validated instruments. Post-test outcomes were compared using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for the corresponding baseline score, previous AI training experience, frequency of AI use, and digital literacy.
 
 
 
 
 In the intervention group, AI literacy increased significantly from 55.67 ± 9.84 to 65.01 ± 8.81 (
 P
  < 0.001), as did attitudes toward AI, which increased from 48.07 ± 6.77 to 51.72 ± 9.90 (
 P
  = 0.049). Neither outcome changed significantly in the control group. After adjustment for covariates, the intervention group had significantly higher post-test scores for AI literacy (adjusted mean difference = 11.01, 95% CI 8.55–13.47;
 P
  < 0.001) and attitudes toward AI (adjusted mean difference = 4.60, 95% CI 1.98–7.21;
 P
  < 0.001). Autonomous learning competency changed little in the intervention group (
 P
  = 0.578) but declined significantly in the control group (
 P
  < 0.001). The adjusted post-test difference also favored the intervention group (adjusted mean difference = 10.94, 95% CI 7.44–14.43;
 P
  < 0.001).
 
 
 
 
 AI/GenAI-assisted blended teaching was associated with higher AI literacy and more favorable attitudes toward AI, while autonomous learning competency remained relatively stable in the intervention group but declined in the control group. Structured AI education integrating conceptual learning, practical application, and responsible AI use may be a valuable addition to undergraduate nursing education.
authors: ["Xue-Fen Lan", "Ya-Xuan Luo", "Shun-Fei Lu", "Yu-Feng Wu", "Xian-Qi Gao", "Li-Juan Xu", "Qing-Yan Tao", "Min Li", "Min-Hua Chen"]

title_key: a pedagogically guided llm framework for scaffolding human ai cocreation and preserving learners agency and creativity|haq
title: A pedagogically guided LLM framework for scaffolding human-AI cocreation and preserving learners'agency and creativity
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate alternatives, elaborate ideas and supply rationales, overlapping with cognitive work learners are expected to perform. However, human-AI cocreation still lacks a mechanism for determining how AI can scaffold learners'creative decision-making. This study develops a cognitive-pedagogical framework for deriving the behaviour of a pedagogically constrained LLM from an educator-approved specification of each activity in a cocreative process in project-based learning. The creative-process phase supplies the activity's purpose, typical processes and pedagogical conditions; the active section of a creative technique specifies how the group works on its ideas. For each task, an educator approves four fields: a cognitive and metacognitive objective, a pedagogical objective, the task and group artefact as context, and the learner-owned product. The objective identifies the creative operations and decisions about progress, focus, criteria and next steps that remain with the group. Four translation rules derive permitted support, timing, feedback scope and prohibitions. The framework is illustrated with Viacocrea's six phases and two activities: Plan Brainstorming and a constructed Build activity using PPCo (Pluses, Potentials, Concerns, Overcoming concerns). In the proposed workflow, a controller applies the approved specification to student requests and feedback offers. Prompt engineering and approved pedagogical guidance retrieved through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) inform a draft, which is checked for form, pedagogical function and safety before delivery. The worked examples illustrate how support can differ between activities while its constraints remain traceable to educator decisions. The framework offers educators and researchers a reusable way to derive LLM support from creative activities while preserving learners'agency and creativity.

title_key: towards comparative comprehension in cs1 an exploratory study using structured code comparisons|eagal
title: Towards Comparative Comprehension in CS1: An Exploratory Study using Structured Code Comparisons
abstract: Software developers routinely evaluate code alternatives during code review, refactoring, debugging, maintenance, and when adapting examples from online resources or AI-generated suggestions. This skill, known as comparative comprehension, is fundamental yet difficult: developers must compare different implementations and reason about correctness and task alignment. Its importance is increasing as Generative AI tools produce plausible alternative solutions requiring critical evaluation. Despite its growing role in professional software development, CS1 instruction continues to emphasize producing working code over evaluating competing solutions. As a result, an increasingly important skill in programming practice may remain underdeveloped in CS1 instruction. We explore how structured code comparison activities support comparative comprehension in CS1 students transitioning from Snap! to Python. Drawing on work in mathematics education, we designed instructional activities that ask students to analyze alternative implementations, explain differences in program behavior, and justify solution choices. We evaluated these activities through a pilot study using pre- and post-tests and students’ responses to comparison prompts. While we did not observe statistically significant improvements across quantitative measures, our findings reveal patterns in how novice programmers engage with code comparisons. Students frequently relied on surface-level syntactic differences and struggled to reason about program behavior, particularly when comparisons contained multiple differences. These structured code comparisons also exposed misconceptions and false carryover that traditional code-writing tasks often failed to reveal. Our findings highlight both the challenges and opportunities of supporting comparative comprehension through structured comparison activities, particularly in terms of timing, scaffolding, and comparison design.
venue: Proceedings of the 26th Koli Calling International Conference on Computing Education Research

title_key: effect of the eduphys ai tutor on the learning achievement of undergraduate physics students at federal university dutsinma katsina state nigeria|salihu
title: Effect of the EduPhys AI Tutor on the Learning Achievement of Undergraduate Physics Students at Federal University Dutsinma, Katsina State, Nigeria.
abstract: This exploratory pilot study evaluated the association between engagement with the EduPhys AI Tutor and the learning achievement of undergraduate physics students at Federal University Dutsin-Ma, Katsina State, Nigeria. Physics education in Sub-Saharan Africa faces challenges related to abstract conceptual demands, mathematical rigor, and high student-to-lecturer ratios. To address these instructional barriers, the EduPhys AI Tutor was developed to provide micro-prompting feedback, adaptive problem-solving support, and automated diagnostic assistance. Utilizing a single-group pre-test/post-test exploratory quantitative design, an intact cohort of 18 undergraduate Physics Education students engaged with the system across selected mechanics topics. Learning achievement was evaluated using a 20-item researcher-developed Physics Achievement Test (PAT), validated by expert reviewers with a high Kuder-Richardson 20 (KR-20) reliability coefficient of 0.87. Normality of difference scores was established prior to parametric testing (W=0.954,p=.492). A paired-samples t-test revealed a statistically significant increase from pre-test scores (M=13.61,SD=1.577) to post-test scores (M=17.44,SD=1.338), with a mean difference of 3.833 points (t(17)=7.295,p<.001). The paired-sample effect size (dz=1.72) indicated a substantial score gain within the cohort. While these findings offer encouraging preliminary evidence of the tutor's pedagogical utility in resource-constrained settings, the lack of a control group precludes direct causal attribution. Further large-scale quasi-experimental studies incorporating control groups are recommended to validate these results across broader institutional contexts.
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science

title_key: integrating generative ai and large language models into software engineering curricula challenges and opportunities|wang
title: Integrating Generative AI and Large Language Models into Software Engineering Curricula: Challenges and Opportunities
abstract: The rapid evolution of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs)—such as GitHub Copilot and advanced conversational agents—has fundamentally transformed the software engineering (SE) industry. Modern software development is increasingly characterized by AI-assisted coding, automated requirement extraction, and intelligent testing. However, higher education institutions face profound pedagogical challenges as traditional curricula struggle to keep pace with these technological disruptions. This paper examines the multifaceted impact of GenAI on software engineering education, identifies core challenges including academic integrity, assessment obsolescence, and over-reliance on automated tools, and proposes a comprehensive curriculum reform framework. By restructuring course contents, fostering critical evaluation skills, and shifting evaluation metrics toward human-AI collaboration and code review, educational institutions can effectively bridge the gap between academia and industry.

title_key: generative ai empowered contextual educational games as facilitators of elementary school students computational thinking tendencies|zhou
title: Generative AI empowered contextual educational games as facilitators of elementary school students' computational thinking tendencies
abstract: Abstract Computational thinking (CT) is a critical skill for the 21st century. To enhance students' engagement in CT‐related learning activities, educational games are considered an effective tool, especially for younger students. However, the absence of individualized feedback may limit their potential. To address this challenge, a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)‐empowered contextual gaming environment was developed. A quasi‐experimental study was conducted with two intact fifth‐grade classes at an elementary school in eastern China. After controlling for pretest scores, the experimental group showed a modest but statistically significant advantage in self‐reported CT tendencies compared with the control group, whereas no significant between‐group difference was found in algorithmic knowledge. Students in the experimental group valued the opportunity to ask questions of GenAI‐powered non‐player characters (NPCs). The qualitative findings suggest that GenAI primarily functioned as motivational and cognitive scaffolding by encouraging inquiry, supporting problem clarification and sustaining engagement, rather than as a direct mechanism for improving algorithmic knowledge during the short intervention. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because CT tendencies were measured through self‐report, the intervention lasted 3 instructional weeks, and the sample was drawn from a single school. The study therefore provides preliminary evidence regarding the potential of GenAI‐supported contextual games to foster CT‐related tendencies and inquiry behaviours among elementary school students. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Game‐based learning (GBL) has been shown to support student development, particularly in enhancing primary school students' CT‐related tendencies and problem‐solving orientations. Generative AI (GenAI) has the potential to support personalized learning support within a GBL environment to facilitate learning. What this paper adds After adjustment for pretest scores, students in the GenAI‐enhanced condition showed a modest but statistically significant advantage in self‐reported CT tendencies compared with those in the conventional GBL condition. Interaction with GenAI‐powered NPCs in a GBL environment can stimulate students' inquiry, engagement and problem‐solving awareness. Implications for practice and/or policy: This study highlights the importance of engaging students in exploration, dialogue, reflection and repeated practice for fostering CT tendencies. Role‐playing contextual educational games, when integrated with GenAI, can effectively nurture students' CT tendencies while sustaining their motivation and engagement.

title_key: uptake and day level patterns of instructor provided and other generative ai chatbot use in an undergraduate medical research methodology course a cross sectional survey with retrospective day level assessment|tanasugarn
title: Uptake and day-level patterns of instructor-provided and other generative AI chatbot use in an undergraduate medical research methodology course: a cross-sectional survey with retrospective day-level assessment
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence chatbots are increasingly used by medical students. Educational programs are also beginning to provide course-specific chatbots, but little is known about how students incorporate these tools into their existing AI practices. This study quantified uptake of an instructor-provided chatbot and characterized retrospective day-level patterns of chatbot engagement during an undergraduate course. We conducted a survey among medical students enrolled in a 6-day research-methodology course. Students retrospectively reported their daily use and duration of use of the instructor-provided chatbot and other self-selected chatbots. Uptake of the instructor-provided chatbot was described using alternative frequency thresholds ranging from use on at least one to at least four course days. Daily chatbot-use states, intensity, and overlapping use were described. Satisfaction and open-ended feedback were assessed among students who had used the instructor-provided chatbot. We further explored factors associated with daily use of any AI chatbot using repeated measures analysis. Eighty-nine students were included. Thirty-one students (34.83%) used the instructor-provided chatbot on at least one course day, while 17 (19.10%) used it on at least two days, 11 (12.36%) on at least three days, and eight (8.99%) on at least four days. Daily use of any AI chatbot ranged from 61.80% to 87.64% across the course period and was driven primarily by self-selected chatbots. Student-level patterns showed that engagement with the instructor-provided chatbot was concentrated among a relatively small subgroup, whereas self-selected chatbot use was more widespread and sustained. In exploration analysis, daily AI chatbot use was lower during the weekend and was positively associated with more frequent prior AI use for non-medical purposes. Higher mean overall satisfaction was observed among repeated users than among one-time users, although the trend in overall satisfaction did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.064). Open-ended feedback indicated a need for clearer guidance regarding the chatbot’s scope, information sources, prompting, and limitations. Uptake of the instructor-provided chatbot was selective and usually occurred alongside other chatbots rather than in isolation. Course-specific AI tools may therefore be more readily incorporated when their distinct role is clearly communicated and aligned with students’ existing AI practices. Assessing frequency, intensity, timing, and overlapping use provides a more informative account of self-reported AI engagement than ever-use measures alone.
authors: ["Lokachet Tanasugarn", "Ngamphol Soonthornworasiri", "Nichapat Petchin", "Manatsanan Phonananrat", "Tanaporn Panyaniphon", "Saranath Lawpoolsri"]

title_key: human tutoring generative ai tutoring and independent internet search a randomised betweensubjects experiment on students responses to academic challenge|ennion
title: Human tutoring, generative AI tutoring and independent internet search: A randomised between‐subjects experiment on students' responses to academic challenge
abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

title_key: ai assistant for physiology and physical well being of students|gowda
title: AI Assistant for Physiology and Physical Well-Being of Students
abstract: Students in higher education often contend with erratic sleep, little exercise, poorly balanced diets and mounting academic pressure, yet most campuses provide no continuous, individualised support for these daily habits. This paper describes the design of an artificial-intelligence assistant that promotes the physiological and physical well-being of students. The system collects brief daily self-reports and optional wearable readings, turns them into six sub-scores tied to published health guidelines, and combines these into a transparent wellness index from 0 to 100. A hybrid decision layer, made up of explicit rules, a machine-learning risk classifier and a retrieval-grounded conversational module, generates tailored advice, while a safety guard forwards signs of serious distress to human counsellors rather than replying automatically. We present the layered architecture, the scoring equations, the recommendation logic, the data model, the privacy controls and a protocol for a pilot evaluation. The framework is modular, explainable and cheap to deploy in an engineering-college setting.

title_key: learning chemistry with generative artificial intelligence a phenomenological study of secondary school students experiences in bayelsa state nigeria|amangele
title: Learning Chemistry with Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Phenomenological Study of Secondary School Students’ Experiences in Bayelsa State, Nigeria
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence offers new opportunities for supporting Chemistry learning, but accessible explanations may not translate into independent conceptual understanding. This paper examined experiences of understanding Chemistry concepts, perceptions of usefulness and challenges associated with generative artificial intelligence within a secondary school context in Bayelsa State, Nigeria. A qualitative analysis informed by an interpretative phenomenological approach was undertaken using ten participants. Analysis involved examining individual accounts, identifying experiential meanings and comparing patterns across cases. The accounts portrayed conceptual understanding as developing through manageable explanations, recognition of errors, comparison with other resources, and independent practice. However, apparent clarity sometimes coexisted with difficulties applying knowledge to unfamiliar problems. Perceived usefulness centred on repeated clarification without embarrassment, support outside classroom instruction, revision activities and alternative explanations. Challenges included shared devices, data costs, unreliable connectivity, unfamiliar terminology, uncertainty about response accuracy, difficulty formulating questions and the temptation to copy solutions. The analysis suggests that generative artificial intelligence may serve as a supplementary resource when combined with teacher guidance, textbooks, practical demonstrations, and independent problem-solving. Faculty of Education, Niger Delta University, Wilberforce Island, Bayelsa State
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATION AND EVALUATION

title_key: design of a generative ai based prompt for object oriented programming education for high school students|choi
title: Design of a Generative AI-Based Prompt for Object-Oriented Programming Education for High School Students
abstract: This study developed an educational prompt utilizing generative AI to support object-oriented programming education, which was newly introduced at the high school level in the 2022 revised informatics curriculum. The prompt was designed around the stepwise transformation process from unstructured programming code to procedural programming and ultimately to object-oriented programming. The designed prompt was executed repeatedly across three programming topics, and semantic similarity was analyzed using CodeBERT-based cosine similarity. The results demonstrated that the semantic similarity among codes generated within the same step was stably maintained under repeated execution. Furthermore, each step’s code consistently addressed the same problem even as the programming paradigm transitioned across steps. This study suggests the potential of generative AI-based object-oriented programming education that leverages the conceptual continuity of programming paradigms.
venue: The Journal of Korean Association of Computer Education

title_key: rethinking assessment and academic integrity in the era of generative artificial intelligence empirical findings from a computer science school|ghomari
title: Rethinking Assessment and Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence: Empirical Findings from a Computer Science School
abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) demands urgent empirical investigation into its role in undergraduate studies. This study examines the transformative impact of these tools in higher education (HE) in Algeria. The primary objective is to investigate how students at the National School of Computer Science (ESI) in Algiers use GenAI tools. The research also aims to provide evidence-based recommendations for Algerian HE institutions on academic integrity and pedagogical adaptation. Using a case study methodology, the research combined a GenAI use survey of 74 students with an educational experiment involving 12 teams in November 2023. The findings reveal a high adoption rate: 94.44% of students use GenAI, and 73.61% report daily use. GenAI serves as a powerful ancillary educational tool that shifts focus from content memorisation to competency application. In the experimental phase, 100% of teams relied on GenAI tools to execute the core cognitive and text-generation tasks. However, several groups integrated conventional auxiliary software to support their final visual deliverables. However, the quality of interaction remains narrow. Practical implications for HE institutions in Algeria suggest that teachers and trainers must restructure tutorials and practical work to favour complex, collaborative problem-solving. Additionally, institutions should prioritise formative over summative assessment and implement comprehensive AI literacy training to safeguard academic integrity.
venue: AI Computer Science and Robotics Technology

title_key: formation of adaptive engineering competencies ai tutor as an activator of cognitive synthesis|
title: Formation of Adaptive Engineering Competencies: Ai Tutor as an Activator of Cognitive Synthesis
abstract: Research objective. The integration of artificial intelligence-based systems into engineering education faces terminological ambiguity: conditional logic automation platforms are positioned by developers as genuine intelligent agents, which hinders the objective selection of educational technologies and creates the risk of substituting pedagogical development with technological imitation. The aim of this paper is to develop a criteria-based verification framework that distinguishes conditional logic automation systems from agents capable of initiating the synthesis of engineering and management heuristics that are absent from educational materials, and to describe the mechanism for forming adaptive expertise — a competency that is ahead of the requirements of Federal State Educational Standards. Materials and methods. A functional analysis of educational system architectures based on artificial intelligence, described in peer-reviewed domestic and international sources from 2024 –2026, was conducted. The theoretical and methodological foundation comprised the concepts of adaptive expertise, metacognitive regulation, and expansive learning. Three qualitative criteria with observable markers were formulated to verify the system’s ability to initiate heuristic synthesis: differentiation of error types, generation of non-canonical scenarios, and activation of heuristic synthesis. Expert calibration of the criteria was performed using the sequential evaluation method with the participation of 14 experts — practitioners in engineering and management disciplines (Kendall’s coefficient of concordance W = 0.74, p < 0.01). Demonstrative pilot testing of the methodology was carried out on a sample of master’s students in engineering disciplines (38 learners) solving a logistics problem with infrastructure constraints. Results. It was established that the vast majority of platforms labeled as “AI tutors” operate on static conditional rules and fail to initiate the construction of new algorithmic strategies. For the first time, the concept of “activation of cognitive synthesis” is introduced as an operationally measurable characteristic of an intelligent agent, tied to three observable markers. The key paradigm shift in assessment consists in transitioning from formal academic performance to recording the learner’s ability to go beyond a known algorithm. Pilot data (accuracy of error type recognition 89%, proportion of unique scenarios 63%, and proportion of master’s students who developed specialized heuristics 12.5%) are illustrative and confirm the fundamental fixability of heuristic synthesis in interaction protocols. A new paradigm of pedagogical roles is proposed: the teacher as a real-sector strategist, the intelligent system as an activator of cognitive synthesis. Conclusion. The developed toolkit resolves terminological ambiguity in the evaluation of artificial intelligence-based educational technologies and establishes a foundation for comparable verification of digital platforms in the industry. The transformation of pedagogical roles ensures the formation of adaptive expertise — a competency that is absent in the current Federal State Educational Standards but critically important for engineering activities under conditions of infrastructure uncertainty. The methodology is addressed to methodologists and teachers of engineering and management disciplines, enabling evidence-based decisions when selecting digital tools based on observable markers rather than marketing formulations. The threshold values are of a project nature and require further empirical calibration on extended samples.

title_key: exploration of a paradigm for building llm knowledge corpora for computer science courses computer architecture as an example|guofeng
title: Exploration of a Paradigm for Building LLM Knowledge Corpora for Computer Science Courses: Computer Architecture as an Example
abstract: Artificial intelligence is driving a new wave of educational transformation and profoundly reshaping knowledge acquisition, course teaching, and learning assessment. Computer science courses are both an important foundation for the development of artificial intelligence and a key category requiring adaptation as large language models are introduced into discipline-specific education. Compared with general-purpose question answering, computer science courses are characterized by complex knowledge hierarchies, tightly interconnected concepts, explicit computational reasoning, and substantial practical requirements. Building knowledge corpora tailored to computer science courses is therefore an important foundation for the deeper integration of artificial intelligence into course instruction. Taking the Computer Architecture course as an example, an approach is systematically discussed a method how to constructing LLM knowledge corpora for computer science courses, focusing on four main stages: establishing a chain-of-thought reasoning framework, building a course knowledge corpus, conducting domain model training, and generating questions and answers. By organizing the course knowledge system, knowledge-point reasoning trees, question-type structures, and reasoning procedures, course knowledge is transformed into training data with an explicit structure and clearly defined relationships. The paper further examines the value of such data for question answering, test-paper generation, and online tutoring, providing a practical reference for the construction of LLM knowledge corpora for computer science courses.

title_key: exploring undergraduate students experiences with chatgpt in thesis writing a phenomenological study|deviyanti
title: Exploring undergraduate students' experiences with ChatGPT in thesis writing: a phenomenological study
abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence, particularly ChatGPT, has profoundly transformed academic writing practices in higher education. This phenomenological study explores the lived experiences of final-year undergraduate students at the Faculty of Teacher Training and Education (FKIP), Lampung University, in utilizing ChatGPT during their thesis writing process. Employing Van Manen's hermeneutic phenomenological approach, this research involved 15 participants selected through purposive sampling across four departments: English Education, Economics Education, Biology Education, and Mathematics Education. Data were collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews, two-week reflective journals, and document analysis of ChatGPT interactions and thesis drafts. Thematic analysis following Moustakas's phenomenological framework revealed five essential themes: ChatGPT as a cognitive partner in the writing process, enhanced time efficiency and academic productivity, negotiation between technological assistance and originality, ChatGPT as a stimulus for autonomous learning and self-reflection, and limitations in validity, references, and factual accuracy. Findings indicate that students position ChatGPT not merely as a mechanical tool but as an intellectual companion that facilitates idea generation, conceptual clarification, and structural organization while maintaining awareness of ethical boundaries and academic integrity concerns. The study demonstrates that ChatGPT usage represents an epistemological transition toward AI-assisted learner autonomy, where students actively negotiate the roles of technology, supervisors, and themselves in academic learning and writing processes. However, concerns about cognitive dependency, fabricated citations, and the erosion of critical thinking skills persist. This research contributes to developing a conceptual framework for responsible AI integration in academic contexts and provides evidence-based recommendations for institutional policy formulation, curriculum development in AI literacy, and pedagogical strategies for supervisors. The findings suggest that rather than threatening academic integrity, ChatGPT presents an epistemic and moral challenge requiring judicious use, critical digital literacy, and institutional guidance to harness its benefits while preserving the fundamental values of scholarly honesty and intellectual autonomy.

title_key: integration of diffusion innovation theory in tvet for improving students adoption of ai chatbots in nigerian universities|georg
title: Integration of Diffusion Innovation Theory in TVET for Improving Students’ Adoption of AI-Chatbots in Nigerian Universities
abstract: This study examined the integration of diffusion innovation theory in Technical Vocational Education and Training (TVET) for improving students’ adoption of Artificial Intelligence chatbots in Federal universities in South East geopolitical zone, Nigeria. Three research questions, three hypotheses and descriptive survey research design was used to guide the study. The population of the study was one hundred and eighty-nine (189) final year TVET students which consisted of 86 and 103 students in MOUAU and UNN respectively. A sample size of ninety-seven (97) students comprising of 46 and 51 students in Michael Okpara University of Agriculture, Umudike (MOUAU) and University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN) respectively were randomly selected for the study. A 30-item questionnaire consisting of four sections and 5- point rating scale used for data collection was faced validated by three experts. Cronbach alpha statistics was used to determine the reliability coefficient of the instrument which yielded overall reliability index of .76 comprising of .75, .73 and .81 for Section B, C and D respectively indicating that the instrument was reliable. The research questions were answered using Mean and Standard Deviation while independent t- test was used to test the hypotheses at .05 level of significance. The findings of the study showed that compatibility, trialability and relative advantage have very high influence on TVET students' adoption of AI-chatbots for learning in Universities in South-East, Nigeria. The study recommended that universities should organize training programs that emphasize the compatibility, trialability and relative advantage of AIChatbots with University goals and values for students. These training programmes should showcase case studies highlighting the benefits of chatbots in education such as improved accessibility to resources, faster response times, and personalized assistance, thus motivating students to adopt the technology.
venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
