title_key: performance of chatgpt 4 deepseek r1 and gemini 2 0 in undergraduate dental implantology education a comparative study|wei
title: Performance of ChatGPT-4, DeepSeek-R1, and Gemini-2.0 in undergraduate dental implantology education: a comparative study
abstract: Existing guidance on the application of artificial intelligence in implantology education was mostly based on clinical cases or scenarios, making them more suitable for postgraduate or continuing education. To date, no study has evaluated the capability and quality of large language models’ (LLMs) responses to foundational implantology education, considering both core textbook knowledge and open-ended literature research. This study aims to compare the performance of different LLMs in answering professional implantology questions. Fifty multiple-choice questions (MCQs) including four knowledge sections and 10 open-ended questions (OEQs) for undergraduate dental implantology education were prepared. Each question was presented to three models (including ChatGPT-4.0, DeepSeek-R1, and Gemini-2.0) three times for three consecutive weeks. MCQ responses were evaluated by calculating accuracy rates. OEQs responses were blindly evaluated for accuracy, completeness, and relevance based on a three-point Likert scale. Generalized Estimating Equations, Kruskal-Wallis H test, and Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparison were used for statistical analysis (α = 0.05). LLM type significantly influenced performance on both MCQs and OEQs ( p < 0.05). For MCQs, the overall accuracy rate ranked as: ChatGPT-4 (84.67%) > DeepSeek-R1 (83.78%) > Gemini-2.0 (78.44%). For OEQs, the total score ranked as: Gemini-2.0 (1.63 ± 0.29) > DeepSeek-R1 (1.57 ± 0.36) > ChatGPT-4 (1.53 ± 0.30). Significant differences were observed in accuracy across different knowledge sections within the same LLM ( p < 0.001). The testing time only significantly affected OEQs, with Gemini-2.0 exhibiting a consistent weekly score increase ( p < 0.001). In MCQs, ChatGPT-4 outperformed both DeepSeek-R1 and Gemini-2.0; however, the opposite trend was observed for OEQs. Nevertheless, none of the three models demonstrated sufficient reliability for independent use in professional implantology education within the present study framework, highlighting the necessity of expert oversight. Developing domain-specific AI programs for dental implantology may help improve accuracy and consistency.

title_key: aiotutor design and evaluation of a scaffolded ai tutoring intervention with a teacher review pipeline for embedded iot laboratory education|guo
title: AIoTutor: Design and Evaluation of a Scaffolded AI Tutoring Intervention with a Teacher Review Pipeline for Embedded IoT Laboratory Education
abstract: Embedded Internet of Things (IoT) laboratory courses face two persistent challenges: novice students bear excessive extraneous cognitive load in cross-layer hardware–software fault diagnosis, and teachers’ tacit troubleshooting pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) cannot be systematically preserved. This paper presents AIoTutor, a four-layer scaffolded generative artificial intelligence tutoring intervention grounded in cognitive load theory, the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework, and self-regulated learning theory, centered on a mandatory teacher knowledge-review pipeline. A four-group sequential ablation quasi-experiment with 96 engineering undergraduates compared the full intervention against raw large language model support, unreviewed knowledge base support, and traditional instruction. Compared with traditional instruction, the full intervention was associated with higher post-test conceptual mastery (78.42 vs. 66.96, p < 0.001), 42.9% lower perceived cognitive load (4.61 vs. 8.08), larger self-regulated learning gains (3.54 vs. 0.83), and an 82.7% reduction in repetitive teacher troubleshooting workload (14 vs. 81 interventions). A delayed transfer test with novel faults showed the highest independent fault-location rate under the full intervention (58.3%, 52.1%, 39.6%, and 29.2% for G1, G3, G2, and G4); because transfer observations are nested within students, these results are treated as exploratory, with only the full-intervention versus control contrast reaching significance (mixed-effects model, p = 0.028). Blind-rated answer-quality analysis showed that teacher revision primarily improved pedagogical rather than technical dimensions, a pattern interpreted as preliminary associative evidence given the sequential design.

title_key: assessing the impact of chatgpt supported personalized instruction on academic achievement a pilot experimental study in education|hilali
title: Assessing the Impact of ChatGPT-Supported Personalized Instruction on Academic Achievement: A Pilot Experimental Study in Education
abstract: In higher education, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is being leveraged to facilitate personalized learning, adaptive instruction, and real-time feedback. The present study examined the effectiveness of a structured instructional model using ChatGPT in an undergraduate program in Information Systems at Sultan Qaboos University, Oman. A quasi-experimental pre-test - post-test design with control and experimental groups was used. This intervention consisted of a four-stage prompt system that included instruction, individualized explanations, customized learning activities, and formative feedback. The findings showed that the mean scores increased from 15.87 (pre-test) to 17.30 (post-test). Both groups improved significantly from pre-test to post-test (p. 001). The experimental (ChatGPT) group showed a numerically larger gain than the control group (+1.86 vs. +1.06 points, $\mathrm{d}=0.48)$, but a Group × Time analysis found this difference was not statistically significant $(\mathrm{p}=.20)$, so the study did not find conclusive evidence that ChatGPT produced greater learning gains than the comparison condition. These findings showed a positive pattern suggesting that learning outcomes could be improved with the help of a structured incorporation of ChatGPT. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously as it is a pilot study and uses small sample size with limited intervention period.
venue: 2026 IEEE 13th International Conference on E-Learning in Industrial Electronics (ICELIE)

title_key: curriculum aligned analysis of assessment feedback a retrieval augmented large language model approach for revealing fine grained student error patterns in higher education|hua
title: Curriculum-aligned analysis of assessment feedback: a retrieval-augmented large language model approach for revealing fine-grained student error patterns in higher education
abstract: Assessment feedback in higher education provides fine-grained evidence about students’ specific errors but remains underutilized as a data source for teaching improvement. This study proposes a method based on a large language model (LLM) that transforms unstructured feedback into curriculum-aligned error analysis in three steps, deriving an error taxonomy from the feedback, mapping each piece to curriculum content by retrieval-augmented generation, and aggregating the annotations into error patterns with quantified cohort coverage. The method was applied to 6072 pieces of feedback across four cohorts (2022–2025) of an undergraduate engineering course. The feedback resolved into recurring, curriculum-aligned error patterns, dominated by missing content and justification, clustered in identifiable modules and weeks, and more than half recurring across cohorts. The resulting annotations achieved 89.1% agreement with human judgment, substantially higher than the 74.7% obtained when an expert-designed taxonomy was applied to the same data. In a focus group, the teaching team confirmed the patterns against their marking experience, proposed course revisions from them, and set the bound that they serve as a reference and not as a direct measure of teaching quality. The study reports a process account of this team’s use of curriculum-aligned error analytics, built on sensemaking and pedagogical response. The analysis turns feedback written for students into evidence on the teaching that preceded it, by which a teaching team can check the alignment between intended outcomes, teaching, and assessment in students’ actual work, reflect on its own practice, and improve its teaching across cohorts.
authors: ["Lin-Xin Hua", "Jia Xu", "Li-Rui Guo", "Nan Zheng", "Qing-Tan Shen", "Di-Lang Tan", "Ye Lu"]
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

title_key: structured chatgpt assisted writing instruction and academic writing performance among jordanian efl university students experimental findings and associations with critical thinking self regulated learning and academic motivation|wardat
title: Structured ChatGPT-Assisted Writing Instruction and Academic Writing Performance Among Jordanian EFL University Students: Experimental Findings and Associations with Critical Thinking, Self-Regulated Learning, and Academic Motivation
abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence in teaching English as a foreign language (EFL) writing is becoming prevalent, though there is still a gap between writing performance and cognitive and motivational variables. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study, incorporating an individually randomized pre-test/post-test controlled comparison, explored the impact of an eight-week intervention program based on ChatGPT for EFL writing on 300 Jordanian university EFL learners. The subjects were randomly assigned to experimental (n = 150) and control (n = 150) groups following purposive sampling. Writing performance was tested using independent-samples t-tests and ANCOVA, and the relationships between ChatGPT-based learning, critical thinking, self-regulated learning, academic motivation, and writing performance were measured using PLS-SEM. The experimental group demonstrated significantly better post-test performance compared to the control group. There were positive correlations between ChatGPT-based learning and writing performance (β = 0.237), critical thinking (β = 0.456), self-regulated learning (β = 0.341), and academic motivation (β = 0.270) (p < 0.001). The qualitative results emphasized better feedback utilization, revision, autonomy, motivation, and responsible AI usage.

title_key: reconfiguracion del docente universitario de matematicas dentro del escenario de la ia generativa|hernandez
title: RECONFIGURACIÓN DEL DOCENTE UNIVERSITARIO DE MATEMÁTICAS DENTRO DEL ESCENARIO DE LA IA GENERATIVA
abstract:
This section examines the impact of generative AI on university mathematics education. Tools such as Wolfram Alpha, ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini demonstrate technological progress in procedural problem-solving, forcing a reconfiguration of the teaching role: the professor transitions from an algorithm provider to a designer of didactic experiences and a mediator between natural and formal language, leveraging AI errors to foster mathematical argumentation. Drawing on Freire and Faundez's pedagogy of the question, the key competence lies in teaching students to query technology while maintaining conceptual rigor. The literature review highlights benefits like personalized learning, dynamic content generation, and immediate feedback, but also warns of risks such as technological dependence, diminished critical thinking, and dehumanization without adequate mediation. Finally, studies indicate that AI strengthens autonomous learning within constructivist frameworks and underscore the need for future research on its impact on performance, teaching competencies, formative assessment, and hybrid didactic models.

Keywords: generative ai, mathematics education, teaching role, ontosemiotic approach, critical thinking, didactics

title_key: comparative effects of generative ai assisted and teacher guided problem solving approaches on senior secondary school students achievement and problem solving skills in stoichiometry in anambra state|anekwe
title: Comparative Effects of Generative AI-Assisted and Teacher-Guided Problem-Solving Approaches on Senior Secondary School Students’ Achievement and Problem-Solving Skills in Stoichiometry in Anambra State
abstract:
Stoichiometry is a key concept in Chemistry that involves conceptual understanding, quantitative 
reasoning and sequential problem solving. In secondary school Chemistry, generative artificial 
intelligence (GenAI) can enable interactive explanations and immediate feedback, but its 
effectiveness compared with teacher-guided problem-solving needs empirical research. This study 
examined the comparative effects of GenAI-assisted and teacher-guided problem-solving 
approaches on students’ achievement and problem-solving skills in stoichiometry in Onitsha and 
Otuocha education zones, Anambra State. The study population was 5,274 SS2 Chemistry students. 
A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest, non-equivalent control-group design was used. A sample 
of 495 SS2 Chemistry students (260 females and 245 males) was selected through multi-stage 
sampling. Data were collected with the Stoichiometry Achievement Test (SAT) and the 
Stoichiometry Problem-Solving Skills Test (SPST), which were validated; reliability was 0.84 (KR
20) for SAT and 0.82 (Cronbach’s alpha) for SPST. Research questions were answered using 
regression analysis, and hypotheses were tested using regression ANOVA at the 0.05 significance 
level. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) compared posttest performance while controlling for 
pretest scores. The GenAI-assisted group obtained an adjusted achievement mean of 54.89, 
compared with 52.32 for the teacher-guided group, F(1,117) = 4.86, p = .029, partial η² = .040. 
For problem-solving skills, the adjusted means were 55.54 and 51.64, F(1,117) = 8.15, p = .005, 
partial η² = .065. These illustrative results suggest modest advantages for structured GenAI
assisted problem-solving. The study framework highlights the importance of controlled 
comparisons, independent assessment, and responsible AI integration in Chemistry Education.
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF CHEMISTRY AND CHEMICAL PROCESSES

title_key: artificial intelligence as a learning tool its influence on students academic performance and learning engagement|poblador
title: Artificial Intelligence as a Learning Tool: Its Influence on Students Academic Performance and Learning Engagement
abstract: This study examined the use of ChatGPT as a learning tool, students’ academic performance, and learning engagement in English reading comprehension. Specifically, it sought to describe the respondents’ profiles, frequency and duration of ChatGPT use, purposes of using the tool, academic performance, and levels of behavioral, emotional, cognitive, and agentic engagement. It also aimed to determine the relationships between ChatGPT use and academic performance, ChatGPT use and learning engagement, and academic performance and learning engagement. A correlational research design was employed to examine the relationships among the study variables. The intended respondents were 200 students from the participating schools. A researcher-made questionnaire was proposed to gather information regarding students’ use of ChatGPT and learning engagement, while academic performance was to be determined using authorized school records for the specified grading period, subject to appropriate permission. Descriptive statistics and an appropriate correlation coefficient were identified as the statistical tools for analyzing the data. The study was also intended to provide a basis for developing a Proposed Instructional Guide for the Responsible Use of ChatGPT in English Reading Comprehension. The proposed guide emphasizes purposeful AI use, vocabulary development, identification of main ideas and supporting details, interpretation of texts, critical evaluation of AI-generated responses, academic integrity, and independent learning. The study recognizes that ChatGPT may provide supplementary explanations and reading support, but its responses require verification and should not replace students’ own comprehension and critical thinking. Since the research design is correlational, any identified relationships would not establish cause and effect. The findings may provide information that teachers and school administrators can consider when developing responsible approaches to AI-assisted English instruction. The final conclusions and recommendations should be based on the actual collected data and statistical results.

title_key: learning on the record the observabilityauthenticity paradox in ai era stem assessment|nakamura
title: Learning on the record: the observability–authenticity paradox in AI-era STEM assessment
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence tutors produce detailed records of how learners question, reason, and revise, and these interaction traces are increasingly available to teachers and institutions. This commentary examines what happens to the evidential value of interaction traces when they are used to assess learning in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education. I describe an Observability–Authenticity Paradox: the features that make interaction traces informative, such as exploration, expressed uncertainty, and error, are the features that learners have most reason to suppress or manage once they expect the traces to be evaluated. In terms of argument-based validity, such reactivity to evaluation weakens the extrapolation from interaction observed under evaluative conditions to learning activity that takes place without evaluation; it can also reduce the exploration on which learning depends. The threat is greatest when traces generated during learning are used for grading or credentialing without learners knowing when and how, and when inferences rest on behaviors that learners can choose to display or withhold. I distinguish this situation from teachers’ ongoing formative monitoring, consider whether assessment could instead reward productive failure, and explain why differential reactivity is a fairness issue in the measurement sense. I conclude by proposing three design principles (declared, episodic, and learner-owned assessment) and illustrating them with STEM tasks, drawing examples mainly from science education.

title_key: from covid to genai tracing long term changes of students help seeking behaviors in a cs2 course|gao
title: From Covid to GenAI: Tracing Long-term Changes of Students' Help-seeking Behaviors in a CS2 Course
abstract: In recent years, computer science (CS) education has undergone rapid change, first due to the shift to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic, and more recently with the rise of generative AI (GenAI) tools. These changes have impacted how students seek help in their computing classes. Although many studies have examined student help-seeking behavior, most focus on a single semester and do not capture how these behaviors and attitudes evolve over time. This study presents a multi-year analysis of help-seeking patterns and student perspectives in a CS2 course, using data from multiple offerings (Fall 2020 - Fall 2025). We observe a noticeable decline in both office hours and online post forum usage after Spring 2023, along with negative shifts in students' attitudes in recent semesters, when GenAI tools became readily available. By tracing how help-seeking behaviors have changed over time, this work highlights the influence of broader educational and technological shifts. Our findings suggest that as learning environments continue to evolve, course support must adapt to better meet students' changing needs. With the continuing influence from GenAI, instructors should guide students on when, and when not, to use GenAI, particularly for help-seeking, and emphasize the importance of higher-level strategic feedback from human support.
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.1

title_key: efektivitas media pembelajaran interaktif berbasis kasus berbantuan generative ai terhadap kemampuan berpikir kritis mahasiswa magister administrasi pendidikan|suyanto
title: EFEKTIVITAS MEDIA PEMBELAJARAN INTERAKTIF BERBASIS KASUS BERBANTUAN GENERATIVE AI TERHADAP KEMAMPUAN BERPIKIR KRITIS MAHASISWA MAGISTER ADMINISTRASI PENDIDIKAN
abstract:
ABSTRACT
Critical thinking is essential for Educational Administration students to examine educational issues, evaluate information, and make evidence-based decisions. Developing this competency requires learning activities that connect conceptual understanding with the analysis of real-world problems. This study aimed to analyze the effectiveness of case-based learning media assisted by Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) in improving the critical thinking skills of Educational Administration students. The study employed a quantitative approach using a quasi-experimental method with a Nonequivalent Control Group Design. The participants consisted of 50 students divided into an experimental group and a control group, with 25 students in each group. The experimental group used case-based learning media assisted by Generative AI, whereas the control group received instruction using regular learning media. Data were collected through critical thinking tests administered before and after the learning intervention and analyzed using descriptive statistics, assumption tests, and an independent samples t-test. Based on the simulation results, the experimental group achieved a mean posttest score of 77.97, while the control group obtained 65.82. The difference was statistically significant (t(48) = 4.331; p < 0.001), with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.23). These simulation results indicate that integrating contextual cases with Generative AI has the potential to support the development of students’ critical thinking skills through problem analysis, information evaluation, and evidence-based recommendation formulation.
ABSTRAK
Kemampuan berpikir kritis diperlukan oleh mahasiswa Administrasi Pendidikan untuk menelaah persoalan pendidikan, mengevaluasi informasi, dan menentukan keputusan berdasarkan bukti. Pengembangan kompetensi tersebut membutuhkan pembelajaran yang menghubungkan pemahaman konseptual dengan analisis permasalahan nyata. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis efektivitas media pembelajaran berbasis kasus berbantuan Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) terhadap kemampuan berpikir kritis mahasiswa Administrasi Pendidikan. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan metode kuasi-eksperimen melalui desain Nonequivalent Control Group Design. Partisipan terdiri atas 50 mahasiswa yang dibagi menjadi kelompok eksperimen dan kontrol, masing-masing 25 orang. Kelompok eksperimen menggunakan media berbasis kasus berbantuan Generative AI, sedangkan kelompok kontrol mengikuti pembelajaran dengan media reguler. Data diperoleh melalui tes kemampuan berpikir kritis sebelum dan sesudah pembelajaran, kemudian dianalisis menggunakan statistik deskriptif, uji asumsi, dan independent samples t-test. Berdasarkan hasil simulasi, kelompok eksperimen memperoleh rata-rata posttest 77,97, sedangkan kelompok kontrol mencapai 65,82. Perbedaan tersebut signifikan secara statistik (t(48) = 4,331; p < 0,001), dengan ukuran efek Cohen’s d = 1,23. Hasil simulasi mengindikasikan bahwa integrasi kasus kontekstual dan Generative AI berpotensi mendukung pengembangan kemampuan berpikir kritis melalui kegiatan analisis, evaluasi informasi, dan perumusan rekomendasi berbasis bukti.
venue: EDUTECH Jurnal Inovasi Pendidikan Berbantuan Teknologi

title_key: automated educational content summarization using textrank algorithm in e learning management systems|s
title: Automated Educational Content Summarization Using TextRank Algorithm in E-Learning Management Systems
abstract: The accelerating volume of digital educational content hosted on institutional learning management systems (LMS) has produced a structural mismatch between content provision and content engagement: Moodle's 2024 global usage analytics report documents a mean course reading completion rate of 48% across 330 million active users—a figure that operationalises the cognitive overload challenge of modern LMS-hosted instruction and establishes the magnitude of the content reduction problem that automated summarisation addresses. TextRank (Mihalcea and Tarau, 2004), a graph-based extractive summarisation algorithm that applies PageRank random-walk scoring to a sentence similarity graph constructed from the source document, offers a uniquely appropriate solution for institutional LMS deployment: it requires no training data, operates without external API dependencies, processes documents in 0.84 seconds at zero marginal cost, and produces summaries whose pedagogical coherence is rated 4.12 out of 5 by domain expert evaluators—within 0.06 points of GPT-4's 4.18 despite a 5.71-fold speed advantage and USD 0.042 per-document cost saving. This study evaluates TextRank against four comparison methods (LSA, LexRank, BERT-Ext, GPT-4) across a corpus of 12,840 educational documents drawn from six LMS platforms (Canvas: 3,840; Moodle: 3,200; Blackboard: 2,400; Google Classroom: 1,600; Microsoft Teams Education: 1,000; Schoology: 800), spanning three academic disciplines (STEM: 4,840 documents; Humanities: 3,640; Business: 4,360) and four document types (lecture slides: 4,280; textbook chapters: 3,640; course notes: 2,840; video transcripts: 2,080). The TextRank configuration employs a TF-IDF cosine similarity sentence graph, damping factor d = 0.85, convergence threshold $\varepsilon=0.0001$, sentence window size 4, and a 28.4% target compression ratio validated through pilot evaluation on 1,284 held-out documents. TextRank achieves ROUGE-1 = 0.484, ROUGE-2 = 0.248, and ROUGE-L = 0.412 on the evaluation subset-below BERT-Ext (ROUGE-1: 0.512) and GPT-4 (0.528) but superior on every operational deployment dimension. Deployment across the six LMS platforms serving 24,800 students over 36 months demonstrates a 24.5 percentage point improvement in content engagement rate (40.9% to 65.4%) and an 18.4% reduction in mean study time per learning objective, with student satisfaction of 4.24/5 and instructor satisfaction of 4.08/5.
authors: ["Sujatha S", "N. K. Tursunov", "Doaa Falah Razzaq", "Nabiev Bosit Sobirovich", "D. Kalidoss"]
venue: 2026 1st International Conference on Sustainable Solutions in Engineering Technologies and Earth Science (ICSSETES)

title_key: antidistillation is cheap lightweight distillation resistance via stylistic corruption|ngo
title: Antidistillation is Cheap: Lightweight Distillation-Resistance via Stylistic Corruption
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective paradigm for transferring capabilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller, more specialized student models. In commercial deployment where frontier models are restricted behind black-box APIs, sequence-level distillation remains a potent vector for competitors to clone proprietary capabilities at a fraction of the development cost. Existing defenses mostly rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which increases computational overhead and real-time inference latency. In this work, we propose a lightweight defense that dynamically injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations upon malicious queries. This framework offers exceptional flexibility, allowing hosts to customize target defensive styles and dynamically blend them to maximize stylistic variance. Crucially, this inference-time intervention preserves semantic utility and fluency during malicious queries, misleading adversaries into believing that they are extracting pristine teacher outputs, while standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework successfully disrupts student learning, achieving substantial anti-distillation performance while incurring negligible overhead and preserving text naturalness. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/distill-resist-38C6/.

title_key: generative artificial intelligence in high school science education a systematic review of learning outcomes pedagogical strategies and critical thinking development|cargason
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in High School Science Education: A Systematic Review of Learning Outcomes, Pedagogical Strategies, and Critical Thinking Development
abstract:
Background and Aim: Evidence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary science education remains limited. This systematic review examined students’ conceptual understanding and engagement, teachers’ pedagogical strategies and challenges, and students’ critical thinking and scientific inquiry.
Materials and Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, ERIC, Scopus, and Lens.org were searched for peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026. Two authors independently screened 187 unique records (Cohen’s κ = .78), identifying 20 eligible studies. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Framework synthesis integrated findings, informed by Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK).
Results: Seven studies assessed AI capabilities rather than classroom implementation. Only two compared learning outcomes across conditions; none employed a randomized controlled design. Student perceptions and engagement were generally positive, whereas learning outcomes were mixed. A chatbot supporting self-regulated learning outperformed a rule-based chatbot, but ChatGPT-4o yielded smaller gains than peer collaboration. Teachers reported concerns regarding content accuracy, assessment reliability, and instructional readiness. Generative AI matched or exceeded student performance on structured examinations but demonstrated lower grading reliability than human assessors. Evidence concerning critical thinking was particularly limited. Richer reasoning was reported with dialogue-oriented tools or teacher guidance, whereas answer-seeking use of general-purpose tools was associated with weaker reasoning.
Conclusion: Pedagogical structuring was recurrently associated with productive AI use, although causal inference remains limited. A provisional model warrants empirical testing. Priorities include structured tasks, science-specific teacher development, human assessment oversight, explicit AI literacy instruction, school governance, and controlled comparisons of structured and unstructured use across secondary science classrooms.
authors: ["Aniza C. Cargason", "Shaniz F. Dumam-ag", "J. Amol", "Samcedar M. Dirampatun", "Matthew Sabasales"]
venue: Journal of Education and Learning Reviews

title_key: personalized feedback based on artificial intelligence in higher education impact on the quality of assignment performance|usyk
title: Personalized Feedback Based on Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Impact on the Quality of Assignment Performance
abstract:
Purpose.
 
 To evaluate whether integrating generative AI into formative assessment (rubric-based feedback on course texts + an analytical progress dashboard) can improve academic performance and selfregulation of student learning in a blended course.
 
 
 
 Methodology and methods.
 
 This study presents a replicable quasi
 experimental study. Design: An 8-week intervention with assignment to study groups (N=312, undergraduate, 1st and 2nd years; 156 - control, 156 - intervention). The control group received traditional teacher feedback; the intervention group received structured AI feedback on the rubric with mandatory teacher moderation and individualized learning analytics in the LMS. Outcome measures: writing scores (0–100; double-blind assessment, ICC (2,1)=0.94 on 20% of items), self-regulation of learning (12 items, 1–5;
 α
 =0.88
 
 –
 
 0.89),
 
 cognitive
 load (1–9), engagement (min/week), and teacher efforts.
 
 
 
 Results.
 
 Controlling for the pretest, the intervention was associated with a 4.46-point increase in the final writing score (95% C.I. 3.25–5.68; p<0.001; Hedges’ g=0.84) and a 0.41-point increase in 
 self-regulation (95% C.I. 0.22–0.60; p<0.001; g=0.50). Cognitive load was lower by 0.73 points (95% C.I. -1.01…-0.45; p<0.001; g=
 –
 0.60), and engagement was higher by 22.26 minutes/week (95% C.I. 6.12–38.39; p=0.007; g=0.32). Average teacher efforts per feedback cycle was lower in the intervention (7.07±2.44 min) compared to the control (18.28±4.02 min; p<0.001).
 
 
 
 Conclusions.
 
 The combination of rubric-based AI feedback, teacher moderation, and learning analytics is a promising didactic tool for scaling up formative assessment: it improves the quality of academic writing and regulatory competencies while reducing subjective teacher workload and efforts. The methodological value of this paper is its demonstration of a full analysis cycle (protocol → data → hypothesis testing), which can be replicated and applied to data from a specific educational program.

title_key: a pedagogical authoring platform for ai enhanced educational role playing games in requirements engineering|correa
title: A Pedagogical Authoring Platform for AI-Enhanced Educational Role-Playing Games in Requirements Engineering
abstract: Requirements Engineering (RE) education requires students to develop technical competencies and interpersonal skills through realistic learning experiences. Although numerous educational games have demonstrated the potential of game-based learning for RE education, existing approaches are typically implemented as standalone applications designed for predefined educational scenarios. This paper proposes an AI-enhanced authoring platform that enables instructors to create customized educational Role-Playing Games (RPGs) for RE without requiring expertise in game development. The platform adopts a pedagogical authoring model in which instructors configure knowledge topics, Bloom-based learning objectives, narrative structures, non-player characters, and assessment strategies. During gameplay, Large Language Models integrated with Retrieval-Augmented Generation support adaptive dialogue generation and AI-assisted formative assessment. A conceptual demonstration illustrates the authoring of an educational RPG covering RE activities, including stakeholder interviews, requirements specification, software modeling, and formative assessment. The proposed approach provides a reusable authoring environment that combines educational design, generative artificial intelligence, and game technologies to facilitate the development of adaptive educational RPGs for RE education.
venue: Anais do II Workshop sobre Engenharia de Software para Desenvolvimento de Jogos (SE4Games 2026)

title_key: integrating slides mathematics and simulation in one page genai assisted html learning objects for engineering courses|dao
title: Integrating Slides, Mathematics, and Simulation in One Page: GenAI-Assisted HTML Learning Objects for Engineering Courses
abstract: Engineering courses spread their materials across slides (PPTX), typeset notes (LaTeX/PDF), and MATLAB, leaving students to connect them. We describe an instructor-in-the-loop workflow in which generative AI (GenAI) converts these assets into single-file HTML learning objects that combine presentation, mathematics, visualization, simulation, and assessment; a page is released only after its simulations pass numerical verification. Six open demonstrators implement 18 tasks from six engineering courses. In the eight tasks with quantitative cross-checks, every quantity met its tolerance at default settings (1\%, or 2\% for the finite-difference time-domain simulation) and agreed with a separate Python re-computation and a value-blinded MATLAB re-computation run by a colleague not involved in development; the checks also flagged under-resolved settings. In a perception survey, students (19 after post-hoc screening of 28 responses) reported that the pages linked equations with simulation, and 74\% preferred them to separate files, but usability was marginal (System Usability Scale 56.8). Twelve lecturers rated the approach as useful (item means 4.25--4.58) but were hesitant to adopt it; their median ratings on a 12-criterion capability rubric agreed moderately with the first author's ($\kappa_w=0.60$; individual median 0.31). The results show technical feasibility and preliminary positive perceptions; learning outcomes were not measured.

title_key: who or what are they prompting how cs students conceptualize and use llms|chandrashekar
title: Who (or what) are they prompting? How CS students conceptualize and use LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by students in computing courses. Yet computing education research has not fully examined how teaching and inclusion of LLMs shape students'conceptualization and understanding of LLMs, and how these factors relate to their subsequent use. Although prior work has examined prompting strategies and AI literacy, the relationships among students'conceptualizations of LLMs, their understanding of LLM mechanisms, and their prompting behavior remain underexplored. We studied these relationships in a post CS1 course that introduces students to the various CS subfields. We adapted the course to teach and allow the usage of LLMs. We administered an end-of-course survey, using open-ended items to elicit students'representations of LLMs and their explanations of how LLMs work, alongside closed-response measures of prompting style and prompt count (N=283 students consented and provided codable responses). Using qualitative coding, we categorized students'understanding of how LLMs work into four ordinal knowledge levels based on the Structure of Observed Learning Outcomes (SOLO) taxonomy and coded their metaphoric conceptualizations along two dimensions: persona type and relational role. Our results show that students most often conceptualized LLMs as human assistants, and context-rich prompting was the preferred style. The study contributes a two-dimensional characterization of students'LLM metaphoric representation and exploratory analyses also identified associations among these constructs showing how understanding these systems relates to their usage.

title_key: qualitative study on digital classrooms equal futures artificial intelligence powered digital pedagogy for closing the gender digital divide in stem|terhemba
title: Qualitative Study on Digital Classrooms, Equal Futures: Artificial Intelligence-Powered Digital Pedagogy for Closing the Gender Digital Divide in STEM
abstract: The increase in Artificial Intelligence (AI), online learning platforms and virtual instructional technologies is definitely defining the possibilities for Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) education. However, benefits of digital change are not equally shared. Girls and women still face difficulties regarding access to devices and connectivity, affordability, digital skills, confidence, gender stereotypes, safety and limited representation in STEM learning and careers. These differences are critical in Nigeria, where increase in digital education and AI creates opportunity to strengthen STEM participation but somewhat risks reproducing ongoing gender differences if technology is introduced without an explicit inclusion agenda. This paper investigates how AI-enhanced online and virtual STEM instruction can help to closing the gender digital divide, with attention to tertiary education and teacher education in Nigerian universities and colleges of education. The paper conceptualises AI-powered digital pedagogy as more than the use of generative AI tools; it incorporates adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, virtual laboratories, automated feedback, AI-assisted content creation, collaborative platforms and AI literacy. The paper adds that these technologies cane enhance accessibility, personalisation, feedback, participation and exposure to female STEM role models when they are fixed within gender-responsive pedagogy. However, AI can also reproduce gender bias, widen disparities through unequal shared access, compromise privacy and create new forms of exclusion. A gender-responsive AI digital pedagogy framework is further proposed, organised around six principles: equitable shared access, inclusive design, personalised learning, agency and voice, human-centred teacher support, and ethical accountability. The paper ends with recommendations for Nigerian tertiary institutions, teacher-education programmes, lecturers, policymakers and technology providers. It suffices that the objective should not merely place girls in digital classrooms, but to redesign digital classrooms so that girls can participate, belong, succeed and eventually lead in STEM.
venue: Federal University Gusau Faculty of Education Journal

title_key: exploring efl writing assessment in omani higher education a comparative study of large language models and human raters|youzbashi
title: Exploring EFL Writing Assessment in Omani Higher Education: A Comparative Study of Large Language Models and Human Raters
abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of three automated assessors—ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini—in evaluating English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing tasks across four foundation levels. The design was quantitative and comparative. It compared human ratings with AI-generated scores for two types of writing tasks. The evaluation was based on a rubric covering Task Achievement, Coherence and Cohesion, Grammar, and Lexical Resource. The participants were 36 EFL learners enrolled in the General Foundation Program at the University of Technology and Applied Sciences, Oman. Writing scores were analyzed using SPSS to identify differences between human and AI writing assessments. Results indicate that ChatGPT and DeepSeek closely align with human ratings at lower proficiency levels (Levels 1 and 2). However, discrepancies emerged at Level 4, especially in Coherence and Cohesion, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and Lexical Resource. Gemini showed limited reliability and inconsistent alignment across all levels. The findings suggest that automated tools can support the assessment of simpler writing tasks. However, human raters remain essential for evaluating more complex language use. The study recommends optimizing AI scoring systems to enhance their ability to handle advanced language features and ensure fairness in high-stakes writing assessments.
venue: Journal of Language Teaching and Research

title_key: the problem with problem solving how can intro sequence cs students develop problem solving skills in the age of ai|sizemore
title: The Problem with Problem Solving: How Can Intro-Sequence CS Students Develop Problem-Solving Skills in the Age of AI?
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are rapidly being adopted in undergraduate computer science (CS) education, fundamentally changing how students approach introductory programming. Moreover, GenAI tools can now easily solve most problems at this level. As more students rely on these tools, educators have raised concerns that overreliance and inappropriate use may hinder student development. More broadly, widespread access to GenAI requires rethinking what students should learn, how they learn it, and how learning should be assessed. Of particular interest is how students can develop programming problem-solving skills while using GenAI responsibly. Programming problem-solving is a foundational skill that enables students to translate problem statements into effective programs. This Birds of a Feather session invites instructors and researchers to come together to discuss how GenAI is reshaping programming problem-solving in introductory computer science. After a brief overview of existing perspectives, participants will contribute ideas to open questions through a collaborative activity before joining small-group discussions. Discussions will explore topics such as problem-solving steps, learning objectives, assignment structures, and assessment methods in introductory-sequence computer science courses. The goal of the session is not to identify a single solution, but to surface diverse experiences, identify common challenges, and build connections among educators navigating similar questions across institutions and contexts. Participants will leave with new perspectives, practical ideas to explore in their own courses, and connections with colleagues who share similar interests in preparing students to become effective problem solvers in the age of AI.
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.2

title_key: the effect of generative ai supported learning on students epistemic confidence examining the role of critical thinking disposition|bilal
title: The Effect of Generative AI-Supported Learning on Students’ Epistemic Confidence: Examining the Role of Critical Thinking Disposition
abstract: The increasing use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education has created new opportunities for academic learning while raising questions about students' confidence in evaluating and understanding knowledge. This study examines the effect of Generative AI-supported learning on students' epistemic confidence and investigates the moderating role of critical thinking disposition among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed, and primary data were obtained from 335 undergraduate and postgraduate students with experience of using Generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, for academic purposes. Data were collected through a structured, self-administered questionnaire distributed using Google Forms and a convenience sampling technique. The collected responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach's Alpha, Pearson correlation, multiple linear regression, and Hayes' PROCESS Macro Model 1 with 5,000 bootstrap samples. The proposed results indicate a positive and significant relationship between Generative AI-supported learning and students' epistemic confidence (r = 0.624, p < 0.01). Multiple regression analysis suggests that Generative AI-supported learning (β = 0.421, p < 0.001) and critical thinking disposition (β = 0.341, p < 0.001) jointly explain 47.7% of the variance in students' epistemic confidence (R² = 0.477). Furthermore, moderation analysis indicates a positive interaction between Generative AI-supported learning and critical thinking disposition (B = 0.158, p < 0.001), suggesting that critical thinking disposition strengthens the relationship between AI-supported learning and epistemic confidence. The study highlights the importance of integrating Generative AI tools with critical thinking practices to promote informed academic judgments, responsible technology use, and meaningful learning experiences in higher education. It further emphasizes that students should evaluate and verify AI-generated information rather than accept it without critical examination. The findings may guide educators and universities in developing effective AI literacy strategies that support independent thinking and evidence-based learning. This research also contributes to educational psychology by extending understanding of how students' critical thinking disposition may shape their confidence in academic knowledge when using emerging AI technologies.

title_key: the effect of trust in generative ai on critical thinking the mediating role of ai over reliance|matsumoto
title: The Effect of Trust in Generative AI on Critical Thinking: The Mediating Role of AI Over-Reliance
abstract: Trust is necessary for productive use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), yet excessive trust can shift cognitive work from the learner to the system. This study tests whether AI over-reliance mediates the relationship between trust in GenAI and critical-thinking disposition. We conduct a reproducible secondary mediation analysis using a public dataset of 2,614 Bangladeshi university students and construct-level statistics reported in its companion conference study. Trust in AI was strongly associated with cognitive dependence (r = .707). Using standardized ordinary least-squares mediation reconstructed from the published correlation matrix, the trust→dependence path was a = .707; the dependence→critical-thinking path controlling for trust was b = .150; the direct trust→critical-thinking path was c′ = .242; and the indirect effect was ab = .106 (delta-method SE = .018, z = 5.78, 95% CI [.070, .142]). The total trust–critical-thinking association was c = .348, so 30.5% of the observed association was carried through cognitive dependence. Importantly, the indirect path is positive in this self-report dataset, which does not support a simple “more dependence means less critical thinking” account. We interpret this pattern as a calibration paradox: high-trust students may simultaneously report stronger critical-thinking tendencies and stronger reliance, while behavioral studies can still show performance costs from uncritical acceptance. The paper contributes a dual-pathway framework that distinguishes trust, dependence, and verification quality, and derives design implications for GenAI-supported learning.
venue: SOCIAL AND MANAGEMENT SCIENCES RESEARCH JOURNAL

title_key: admission without answers label free certification and experience learning for llm based optimization modeling|lian
title: Admission Without Answers: Label-Free Certification and Experience Learning for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
abstract: Agents that learn from experience improve at optimization modeling by storing solved trajectories and reusing them as skills. A wrong trajectory that enters the library can be retrieved for many later problems, and a stream of new problems carries no ground-truth answers that could keep it out. Existing learners admit trajectories by matching known optima, and label-free substitutes such as execution success or agreement at one instance admit wrong models. We introduce AdmitOR, a label-free admission gate. It generates models from three model families and solves each on the stated problem and on instances with resampled parameters. It keeps the largest group of models whose optimal values agree on every instance and that spans more than one family. A threshold fitted on solver-verified problems maps this agreement to acceptance, abstention, or escalation, with a finite-sample bound on the false-discovery rate of accepted values. Inside a recent skill learner, AdmitOR raises admission precision from 0.871 under majority vote to 0.927. Its library is the smallest of the four compared and has the highest macro accuracy on five benchmarks. An ablation traces the gain to an accepted value external to the learner. One program from the learner's own model already raises precision to 0.923, and agreement across families raises it further. With one candidate per family, resampling can withhold a certificate but cannot change its value, and the values it withholds are wrong far more often than those it keeps, on the stream and on the solver-verified calibration set. The false-discovery bound holds on the calibration set but not on the benchmark stream. An audit traces every false certificate to a benchmark text that omits or rounds the numbers needed to reproduce the labeled answer, or to a label error. A label-free check of the extracted numbers against the text flags most omitted-number cases.

title_key: augmenting students academic achievements in quadratic equations through access and usage of generativeai symbolab in akwa ibom state|akpan
title: Augmenting Students’ Academic Achievements in Quadratic Equations through Access and Usage of GenerativeAI-SymboLab in Akwa Ibom State
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is expanding opportunities for digital support in mathematics education. This study examined the relationships between students’ access to and use of Symbolab and academic achievement in quadratic equations in Uyo Local Government Area. A mixed-methods research design involved 110 Senior Secondary II mathematics students drawn from intact classes in two schools. Data were collected using the Symbolab Generative AI Questionnaire (SGenAIQ) and the Quadratic Equation Achievement Test (QEAT). Reliability coefficients estimated using the Kuder–Richardson 21 formula were .78 for the SGenAIQ and .72 for the QEAT. Data were analyzed using linear regression. The findings indicated statistically significant positive associations between students’ access to Symbolab and achievement, and between their use of Symbolab and achievement, after controlling for gender. Access and use had reported contributions to achievement of 62% and 66%, respectively. These findings suggest that access to and use of Symbolab are relevant to students’ achievement in quadratic equations, providing evidence to inform the integration of AI tools into mathematics instruction. The study recommends that educational stakeholders improve the availability, accessibility, and affordability of these tools and that mathematics teachers incorporate Symbolab as an instructional resource to support learning.
venue: African Multidisciplinary Journal of Sciences and Artificial Intelligence

title_key: enhancing student learning in operating systems and computer architecture via genai infused pedagogical interventions|essenmacher
title: Enhancing Student Learning in Operating Systems and Computer Architecture via GenAI-Infused Pedagogical Interventions
abstract: System-level courses in computing disciplines are often challenging for students and researchers have been proposing a variety of interventions with and without generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to aid students enrolled in these courses. The non-GenAI interventions have been extensively explored for years and as a result the emerging research scene is now focused on the GenAI interventions which are showing promise. Many GenAI interventions are showcasing its effectiveness in introductory level programming courses as well as in other computer science courses including system-level courses. The literature, however, shows only a few well-known topics such as system-level programming in C (using pointers as an example). The other major topics of system-level courses have yet to be showcased at scale. The main motivation of this research will be centered around the design and deployment of GenAI-based interventions for system-level courses with a specific target of more diverse content topics to be covered. To study the impact of such efforts, the quasi-experimental design will be used in ''Introduction to Computer Architecture'' and ''Introduction to Operating Systems and Networking'' core undergraduate courses. The overall goal of this study is to design, implement, and analyze effective GenAI-based approaches in system-level computing courses.
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.2

title_key: fine tuned large language models for theory aligned social science content analysis evidence from collaborative learning discourse|shin
title: Fine-Tuned Large Language Models for Theory-Aligned Social Science Content Analysis: Evidence From Collaborative Learning Discourse
abstract: Theory-based content analysis is central to social science research, but coding context-dependent interactional discourse remains difficult to scale. This study examines whether fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) can support theory-aligned, episode-level coding of complex social interaction, using socially shared metacognitive regulation (SSMR) in collaborative learning discourse as a demanding empirical case. Using a human-coded dataset of 2,372 discourse episodes from undergraduate collaborative problem-solving, we adapted the large language model content analysis (LACA) framework through an AI-aligned codebook, prompt design, and supervised fine-tuning. Prompt-only and fine-tuned models were compared across episode-level classification and multilayer SSMR coding. Fine-tuned models substantially improved agreement with human coding and predictive performance relative to prompt-only baselines. Performance was strongest for episode-level classification and several higher-support coding layers, whereas errors remained concentrated in sparse, boundary-prone, and highly interpretive categories requiring social-intent reconstruction and temporally unfolding context. The findings extend recent work on LLM-assisted qualitative and content analysis by showing both the promise and limits of supervised, theory-aligned automation for multilayer social interaction coding. Overall, the study supports a human-centered approach to LLM-assisted content analysis, in which automated coding can support more stable coding tasks while human expertise remains essential for ambiguous, boundary-prone, and interpretively demanding judgments.

title_key: effect of application based learning using generative artificial intelligence on information literacy of first year medical students in yunnan province|tian
title: Effect of Application-Based Learning Using Generative Artificial Intelligence on Information Literacy of First-Year Medical Students in Yunnan Province
abstract:
Background and Aims: This experimental research aimed to 1) compare students’ information literacy before and after learning through Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence, 2) compare students’ information literacy after learning through Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence with the determined criterion set at 70%, and 3) assess students’ satisfaction after learning through Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence.
Methodology: The research instruments were lesson plans, students’ information literacy test, and a satisfaction questionnaire. The appropriateness of the lesson plans overall was at a very high level (M=4.62, SD=0.49). The students’ information literacy test had an IOC between 0.67–1.00, item difficulty (p=0.43-0.60), item discrimination (r=0.25-0.50), and KR20 equal to 0.76. The students’ satisfaction questionnaire had an IOC between 0.67 and 1.00 and a reliability index of 0.85. The statistics used to analyze data were mean, standard deviation, t-test for dependent samples, and t-test for one sample.
Results: 1) students’ information literacy after learning through Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence was higher than before at statistically significant level of .01 (t29=18.53, p=.000), 2) students’ information literacy was higher than the determined criterion of 70% at a significance level of .01 (t29=6.00, p=.000) and 3) students’ satisfaction after learning through Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence overall was at a high level (M=4.14, SD= 0.85).
Conclusion: The knowledge gained from the research is that a six-step learning management system using Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence (ABL-GAI), which represents an innovative instructional framework that systematically integrates human-AI co-creation into information literacy education. The most significant steps for enhancing students’ information literacy are step 4: Practice the skills + GAI, and step 5: Apply & create + GAI. Furthermore, this method has been shown to boost students' interest in learning and enhance their proficiency in core information literacy competencies, including information definition & planning, seeking & access, analysis, synthesis & communication, and reflection & self-evaluation.

title_key: the modern stage of integrating artificial intelligence in students autonomous work challenges and solutions|chikileva
title: The Modern Stage of Integrating Artificial Intelligence in Students’ Autonomous Work: Challenges and Solutions
abstract:
The purpose of the study
 
 is to develop a model for integrating artificial intelligence in students’ autonomous work at non-linguistic universities, based on the principles of pedagogical management, academic integrity, and individual learning routes. To achieve this aim, the following objectives were set: assessing the effectiveness of using artificial intelligence tools for developing linguistic competence, fostering a critical attitude toward the results produced by artificial
 intelligence, identifying key factors that facilitate or hinder this process, 
 selecting promising directions for the use of artificial intelligence, and evaluating potential risks.
 
 
 
 Materials and methods.
 
 The study employed the following methods: an analysis of domestic and foreign scholarly publications and practical research on the subject, a Likert-scale questionnaire survey, quantitative content analysis, qualitative analysis to identify emerging issues and formulate solutions, graphical processing and semantic interpretation of the obtained results. Statistical analysis of the survey 
 data
 
 was
 
 conducted,
 
 followed
 
 by
 
 graphical
 
 presentation
 
 of
 
 the
 
 findings.
 
 The
 
 research
 
 materials
 
 comprised
 
 the
 
 results
 
 of
 
 a
 
 survey
 
 of
 
 the
 
 students
 conducted at the Financial University under the Government of the Russian Federation and Moscow Polytechnic University.
 
 
 
 Results.
 
 The results of the study are presented in the form of an author-developed model for integrating artificial intelligence in students’ autonomous work at non-linguistic universities. The proposed model positions artificial intelligence as an element of the educational environment used to develop linguistic, digital, and metacognitive competencies. It comprises the following interrelated components: diagnostic, design, executive, reflective, and evaluative. This model enables pedagogically managed integration of generative artificial intelligence in students’ autonomous work in a foreign language and allows to use the potential of AI for developing language competencies without diminishing the level of learners’ autonomy. The implementation of the model contributes to the formation of critical thinking skills, digital literacy, reflection, and responsible use of AI technologies in both academic and professional contexts. The outcomes of the study include a classification of current trends in the use of artificial intelligence tools in foreign language education, 
 a systematization of effective tools for use in autonomous foreign language study, and the identification of vectors for controlling the respective contributions of learners and artificial intelligence to the co-created language product.
 
 
 
 Conclusion.
 
 The study convincingly demonstrates that the primary advantage of using artificial intelligence in autonomous foreign language work is in significant time savings and better quality of completed assignments. This underscores the role of artificial intelligence as a tool that optimizes the learning process, enabling students to receive prompt feedback and focus on more complex tasks. The authors conclude that it is necessary to preserve the role of the lecturer as one of the key participants in the educational process. Based on the data obtained, it appears feasible to conduct an experimental
 foreign language teaching program using specific artificial intelligence tools in order to determine the respective contributions of AI and students to the jointly created language product.

title_key: generative ai use in indonesian language learning a descriptive survey of university students|jafar
title: Generative AI Use in Indonesian Language Learning: A Descriptive Survey of University Students
abstract: Despite considerable research attention to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, empirical evidence on its use in Indonesian language courses remains limited, particularly studies integrating usage, perceptions, opportunities, challenges, AI literacy, and ethics. This study aimed to describe these six dimensions among first-year university students. A quantitative descriptive survey involved 69 students from two parallel classes. Data were collected using a 30-item questionnaire (Cronbach’s α = .752–.873) and analyzed using descriptive statistics, categorical interpretation, and supplementary nonparametric comparisons. The findings showed that 87.0% of students had used GenAI, primarily Gemini and ChatGPT. Perceptions (M = 3.79), opportunities (M = 3.70), and ethical awareness (M = 3.82) were high, whereas challenges (M = 3.37), AI literacy (M = 3.27), and usage intensity (M = 2.88) were moderate. Users scored higher than non-users on perceptions, opportunities, and AI literacy; however, among users, AI literacy was not associated with frequency or duration of use. These findings suggest that students’ acceptance of GenAI exceeds their AI literacy, identifying a potential acceptance–competence gap in GenAI adoption. The study contributes a conceptual perspective on this gap and highlights the need for lecturers and institutions to integrate structured AI literacy and ethics instruction into Indonesian language courses. Further research should examine this gap using larger samples and performance-based measures.
venue: International Journal of Humanities, Education, and Social Sciences

title_key: examining the relationship between digital leadership and employee innovation behaviour in hybrid work environments a quantitative investigation|ahmed
title: Examining the Relationship Between Digital Leadership and Employee Innovation Behaviour in Hybrid Work Environments: A Quantitative Investigation
abstract:
Organizations’ leadership practices have changed with the rapid development of the hybrid work model and the ways employees participate in organizational innovation-related activities. In this study, the relationship between digital leadership and employee innovation behaviour was examined using a survey-based analytical approach in hybrid workplaces. This study is concerned with the impact of digitally competent leadership on staff to develop, share and put into practice innovative ideas in virtual and physical environments. The data were collected using a structured questionnaire, which included 22 questions about digital leadership, communication, technological support, collaborative culture and innovative work behaviour among employees of the hybrid organizational structure. These findings indicate that digital leadership can positively encourage employees to generate more creative ideas and promote knowledge-sharing among employees. Digital leaders who demonstrate effective use of digital tools, clear and transparent communication, and trust building help foster employees’ participation in innovative activities. The study also finds that when shifting to the hybrid workplace, the opportunities and challenges for innovation can vary based on how well a digital coordination and organizational support framework is in place. Digital leadership is proven to have a positive impact on employee self-confidence, team problem-solving, and lifelong learning in distributed workplace. This study builds upon the current, and expanding, body of research on leadership and innovation management, by emphasizing the need for leadership abilities within a digital context of work. The study also offers implications for organizations aiming to boost employee innovation in the new hybrid model of work by applying certain strategic digital leadership practices.
