title_key: why constrained interfaces are the right default for llms in programming education|masi
title: Why Constrained Interfaces are the Right Default for LLMs in Programming Education
abstract: Free-form chat and agent-style coding interfaces such as ChatGPT Codex, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot are now the default LLM affordance in introductory programming education, yet the strongest available evidence suggests they widen attainment gaps, compound metacognitive failure for struggling novices, and trade short-term throughput for as-yet-unobserved durable learning. We take the position that constrained, scaffolded, and traceable LLM interfaces are the right design default for LLMs in programming education, and that a unifying theoretical frame for this design move already exists in canonical interaction design: the Human-Centered AI framework and the Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design. Our contribution is to articulate that bridge: we map six recurring constraint patterns from the existing constrained-LLM-UI literature onto five load-bearing Golden Rules, recasting fragmented system-level design moves as instances of a single principle, high human control with high automation, and we argue that the resulting design space is itself a visual-languages problem in which the learner's reasoning state is externalised into an inspectable interface object. We close by exposing the gaps the next research wave should address.
venue: IEEE Symposium on Visual Languages / Human-Centric Computing Languages and Environments

title_key: comparing llm approaches for automated curriculum knowledge graph generation|jhajj
title: Comparing LLM Approaches for Automated Curriculum Knowledge Graph Generation
abstract: Knowledge graphs (KG) play a crucial role in intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) by structuring curriculum content and enabling personalized learning pathways. However, manually constructing KGs is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Although recent advances in large language models (LLMs) with extended context windows offer new possibilities for automated KG generation, the optimal approach remains unclear. This paper presents an empirical comparison of four practical deployment configurations for LLM-based curriculum KG generation: (i) Long-Context using Gemini 2.0, which processes entire course syllabi within extended context windows; (ii) RAG-API using Gemini 2.0 with vector retrieval; (iii) RAG-Local using Qwen2.5-7B for on-device generation; and (iv) CAG-Local using Qwen2.5-7B with KV cache preloading. This work evaluates these approaches across 36 computer science courses at Athabasca University, comparing KG size, generation efficiency, and structural consistency. Our results show that Long-Context and RAG-API produce the largest graphs, while CAG-Local balances extraction volume against local deployment. RAG-Local produces sparser graphs, but eliminates API dependencies. These findings provide practical guidance for educators and ITS developers looking to automate the construction of curriculum KGs based on their infrastructure constraints and quality requirements.

title_key: large language model linear algebra automatic question generation|zieleman
title: Large Language Model Linear Algebra Automatic Question Generation
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become commonplace over the past few years, and students have been increasingly using Large Language Models (LLMs) in their daily lives. There has been much debate over whether LLMs can help or hinder in the education of students. LLMs will sometimes give incorrect or misleading information which cannot be discerned by a student learning new material. LLMs have been explored in the field of education as a tool to help educators, more specifically with Automatic Question Generation (AQG). Generating educational material is costly and current research shows much promise that LLMs will be able to make quality AQG a reality. There are, however, certain limitations that have been discovered among many researchers. They have conceded that acceptable quality questions have yet to be produced at a 100% consistent rate. Moreover, LLMs have difficulty producing anything other than Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs). This experiment intends on targeting one specific area of Linear Algebra. With prompt engineering and a new multi-step explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) correction pipeline technique, the overall quality of the AQG was greatly increased.

title_key: ai can do your homework now what developing a taxonomy of computing assessments that accommodate genai use|challen
title: AI Can Do Your Homework. Now What-: Developing a Taxonomy of Computing Assessments That Accommodate GenAI Use
abstract: For decades, computing instructors have given students a specification, asked them to translate it into code, and evaluated the result against the specification. Coding agents can now complete most of these assessments with only a small number of prompts. Students who use AI this way learn neither what the assessment was meant to teach nor how to collaborate with AI effectively. Meanwhile, the rapid adoption of coding agents by developers is reshaping how technology is created. Working with them multiplies individual productivity, accelerates teams, and expands what computing can build. Agentic development is an important new skill. Students must learn it. Updated assessments are needed to teach it. This working group will map how computing educators are responding. In July 2026, we organized a public workshop convening computing educators to discuss how they intended to redesign assessments in response to AI and prepared a public report from those discussions. Then, we will survey computing educators to identify assessments that have been redesigned, replaced, or deliberately preserved, along with the rationale behind each choice. Finally, we will assemble what we discover into a taxonomy that can help future computing education researchers and practitioners design assessments that resist AI delegation and assessments that teach students to direct it.
authors: ["Geoffrey Challen", "Kevin Lin", "Ranysha Ware", "Muhammad Sajjad Akbar", "Fraida Fund", "Casey Hopkins", "Oscar Karnalim", "J. McGuffee", "Shubbhi Taneja"]
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.2

title_key: a workplace based task oriented continuing professional development model for training school nurses in generative artificial intelligence|chang
title: A Workplace-Based, Task-Oriented Continuing Professional Development Model for Training School Nurses in Generative Artificial Intelligence.
abstract: School nurses need workplace-based training to use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) responsibly in practice; this study developed and preliminarily evaluated a task-oriented GenAI continuing professional development program. Using a multiphase multiple-methods preliminary evaluation guided by instructional design and self-directed learning theory, 42 school nurses from 22 counties and cities in Taiwan completed an 18-h blended program comprising prompt-scaffolded instruction, workplace assignments, an online booster session, and peer sharing. Self-directed learning and critical thinking were assessed at four time points, assignment performance was rated using task-specific rubrics, and follow-up interviews explored workplace application. No significant overall time effects were found for self-directed learning or critical thinking, although exploratory comparisons suggested increases at later assessments. Take-home assignment scores exceeded in-class scores, and participants described applying GenAI to student health data analysis, health education, and individualized communication. These preliminary findings suggest that task-oriented GenAI training warrants further evaluation in school nursing practice.

title_key: vibe coding as a pedagogical design space within programming education|allison
title: Vibe Coding as a Pedagogical Design Space Within Programming Education
abstract: The increasing use of large language models (LLMs) for code generation is reshaping how programming is practiced in educational contexts. Rather than treating this shift as a replacement for traditional programming instruction, this poster frames ''vibe coding'' as a pedagogical design space in which students learn to specify, interrogate, and validate AI-generated code. Drawing on recent work in computing education and curriculum guidance on generative AI integration, we propose a structured set of classroom activities that reposition students as evaluators and refiners of model outputs rather than solely implementers of algorithms. The design space is informed by research on LLM-supported programming education, curriculum integration efforts, and known risks such as hallucinated or insecure code generation. We outline three activity types: prompt refinement tasks, multi-model comparison exercises, and failure analysis of generated code. We further propose initial evaluation dimensions for future empirical study, including specification quality, debugging reasoning, and evaluative judgement of generated artefacts.
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.2

title_key: from vibe coding to guardrailed vibe writing for non english major efl students a conceptual framework and pedagogical proposal|pham
title: From Vibe Coding to Guardrailed Vibe Writing for Non-English-Major EFL Students: A Conceptual Framework and Pedagogical Proposal
abstract: Vibe coding is an iterative, natural-language approach to human-AI collaboration and offers new possibilities for writing pedagogy. This conceptual paper proposes a framework for applying vibe coding principles to the teaching of academic and professional writing for non-English-major students learning English as a foreign language (EFL), particularly in Vietnamese higher education. Based on a structured narrative synthesis of selected literature, and drawing on cognitive load theory, self-regulated learning, and contrastive rhetoric, the paper introduces the Guardrailed Vibe Writing (GVW) approach, which aims to reduce linguistic barriers while supporting higher-order rhetorical and critical thinking skills. The framework includes five key components: intentional prompting, AI-mediated scaffolding with human oversight, meta-languaging, documented revision, and metacognitive reflection. No learner data are reported; the proposed benefits require empirical testing. The paper also discusses potential risks associated with AI-assisted writing such as cognitive debt, voice homogenization, and academic integrity issues, and proposes pedagogical strategies to address them. The GVW framework provides practical guidance for integrating generative AI responsibly into non-English-major EFL writing instruction.
authors: ["T. V. Pham", "Vuong Thao Nguyen", "Anh Huy Phan"]
venue: International Journal of AI in Language Education

title_key: generative ai in mathematics learning a bibliometric analysis and narrative review|ismiyati
title: Generative AI in Mathematics Learning: A Bibliometric Analysis and Narrative Review
abstract: Since late 2022, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has expanded rapidly in mathematics education, yet the research field remains insufficiently mapped, and evidence of its effects on learning is inconsistent. This study mapped the development, structure, and emerging topics of research on GenAI in mathematics learning and synthesized evidence on its uses, effects, and challenges. Bibliometric analysis was combined with a narrative review. Searches for records published between 2022 and 2026 in OpenAlex, ERIC, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and Garuda yielded 1,480 records, with 1,206 unique records retained after cleaning. Descriptive and text-mining analyses examined the full corpus, while citation and keyword co-occurrence analyses were conducted in VOSviewer using 758 OpenAlex records. The findings show that 95.2% of records were published from 2024 onward, 48.6% mentioned ChatGPT, and 29.5% explicitly addressed primary or secondary education. The keyword network comprised five clusters, with AI literacy, academic integrity, and self-regulation emerging as the newest topics. The narrative synthesis indicates that GenAI can support learning when integrated into scaffolded instruction with safeguards, whereas unrestricted use as an answer source can undermine learning. These findings highlight instructional design as central to the educational value of GenAI and inform the extension of scaffolding perspectives to AI-mediated mathematics learning. The study identifies school-level experimental research and teacher preparation as priorities for advancing evidence and guiding GenAI integration.
venue: International Journal of Humanities, Education, and Social Sciences

title_key: theorising algorithmic colonialism generative ai and the threat to indigenous knowledge systems in african higher education|fomunyam
title: Theorising Algorithmic Colonialism: Generative AI and the Threat to Indigenous Knowledge Systems in African Higher Education
abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence in higher education has precipitated a new crisis of legitimacy for Indigenous Knowledge Systems. While the utility of large language models is widely touted, this paper critically interrogates the epistemological architecture of these tools, theorising algorithmic colonialism as a curricular mechanism of epistemic erasure in post-#FeesMustFall South African universities. Designed as a conceptual paper, the article extends the boundaries of knowledge by theorising peer-reviewed literature and policy frameworks between 2020 and 2025 to understand the specific threat Generative AI poses to Indigenous Knowledge Systems within African curricula. The principal analytical findings reveal that Large Language Models rely on data extractivism and linguistic hegemony, mechanisms that systematically marginalise Indigenous Knowledge Systems in favour of Western cognitive models. Drawing on decoloniality and critical digital pedagogy, the paper argues that the uncritical integration of these tools into African university curricula risks entrenching a monoculture of the mind where machine-generated consensus displaces localised, context-specific wisdom. The analysis explores the specific mechanisms through which algorithmic bias reinforces historical inequities. Consequently, the paper proposes a robust, operational framework for AI sovereignty within African higher education grounded in data trusts, Reinforcement Learning from African Feedback (RLAF), and algorithmic literacy as counter-conduct. The paper concludes that for the Fourth Industrial Revolution to be emancipatory rather than recolonising, the curriculum must explicitly teach students to audit the colonial logic embedded within the code itself.

title_key: ai powered content summarization system for coding platforms|deekshikesh
title: AI-Powered Content Summarization System for Coding Platforms
abstract:
Coding platforms are important environments for programming practice and technical interview preparation, but
learners can face difficulty understanding code, identifying errors, and progressing through problems without depending on
complete solutions. This paper presents an AI-powered browser extension designed to provide learning-oriented coding
assistance directly within supported coding platforms. The proposed system integrates four assistance modes: Explain Code, Give
Hint, Debug Code, and Ask AI. The extension extracts the coding problem statement, user-submitted code, programming
language, and other relevant context, and combines this information with the learner's request before sending it to a selected AI
model. The project report considers ChatGPT, Ollama, and Grok as possible AI-model integrations. The system is intended to
reduce context switching, provide understandable explanations, offer progressive guidance, and support interactive
programming learning. Evaluation is structured around response accuracy, relevance, response time, usability, and explanation
quality. The proposed approach emphasizes assistance that supports independent problem solving rather than simply presenting
complete solutions.
authors: ["K. B. Deekshikesh", "K. R. Kumar", "P. V. Goud", "N. M. Reddy", "O. Tharun"]
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology

title_key: sophia a student oriented proactive helper for intelligent assistance|mitsou
title: SOPHIA: A Student-Oriented Proactive Helper for Intelligent Assistance
abstract: Secondary education students often face difficulties in Self-Regulated Learning (SRL), resulting in procrastination and anxiety. Though Large Language Models (LLMs) have made it possible to build advanced chatbots for educational purposes, the current systems follow a reactive paradigm in which the system waits for the students to make the first contact. This paper proposes SOPHIA - Student-Oriented Proactive Helper for Intelligent Assistance, an AI-based system to provide a learning companion that inverts the interaction paradigm. SOPHIA utilizes a conversational LLM along with a skill-based system and memory to track the students’ context - schedule, study habits, and mood. Unlike other systems, SOPHIA initiates conversation during critical times. As an initial, simulation-based feasibility study, SOPHIA is evaluated by simulating four different student personas over 28 days. SOPHIA is found to recall 98% of the correct moments when intervention is needed, achieves a quality score of 4.39/5.0 as judged by an LLM-based judge, and shows that the precision of the system’s proactive notification can be increased from 0.68 to 0.73 through prompt engineering itself, thus reducing the number of unnecessary notifications by 30%. These results establish the technical feasibility of the proactive paradigm; validation with real students remains future work.
venue: International Conference on Software, Telecommunications and Computer Networks

title_key: characterizing university students geometric thinking through dialogues with generative artificial intelligence in geometry transformation learning|fashihah
title: Characterizing University Students’ Geometric Thinking Through Dialogues with Generative Artificial Intelligence in Geometry Transformation Learning
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a promising technology for supporting mathematical dialogue, feedback, and reasoning in mathematics education. However, research has paid limited attention to how university students’ geometric thinking develops through sustained interaction with GenAI, particularly in geometry transformation learning. This study aims to develop a Dialogic Geometric Thinking Framework that characterizes the dimensions and progression of university students’ geometric thinking during sustained dialogue with ChatGPT. A qualitative exploratory design was employed involving undergraduate mathematics education students enrolled in a Geometry Transformation course at an Indonesian public university. Data were collected from student–ChatGPT dialogue transcripts, students’ written solutions, and reflective interviews. The data were analyzed thematically using reflexive thematic analysis to identify recurring characteristics and relationships among dimensions of geometric thinking and to synthesize them into an integrated framework. The findings identified five interrelated dimensions of geometric thinking: conceptual reasoning, representational coordination, procedural justification, reflective regulation, and mathematical elaboration. These dimensions illustrate how students progressively articulate mathematical concepts, coordinate representations, justify solution procedures, evaluate their reasoning, and extend mathematical ideas during AI-mediated dialogue. The study resulted in a Dialogic Geometric Thinking Framework that provides a process-oriented perspective on the development of university students’ geometric thinking during interaction with GenAI. The framework offers an initial theoretical foundation for understanding and further investigating geometric thinking in AI-mediated mathematics learning. Keywords: geometric thinking, generative artificial intelligence, chatGPT, geometry transformation, mathematical dialogue.

title_key: ai dependency and academic self efficacy among university students a multivariable cross sectional study|alqahtani
title: AI dependency and academic self-efficacy among university students: a multivariable cross-sectional study
abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into university education, raising questions about whether frequent reliance on AI is associated with the academic confidence and performance of students. However, evidence on AI dependency and academic self-efficacy remains limited and inconsistent, particularly among university students in Saudi Arabia. This study examined the association between AI dependency and academic self-efficacy.
 
 
 
 We conducted a cross-sectional web-based survey among university students recruited from three public universities located in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, between 20 May 2026 and 15 June 2026. Participants completed measures of AI dependency, academic self-efficacy, daily AI use, and sociodemographic and academic characteristics. AI dependency was assessed using a nine-item measure adapted from the AI Dependence Scale, while academic self-efficacy was assessed using the five-item General Academic Self-Efficacy Scale. Multivariable linear regression was used to examine the association between AI dependency and academic self-efficacy, adjusting for daily AI use, gender, age group, year of study, and college.
 
 
 
 
 The analysis included 227 students: 59.9% of them were from health sciences programs, 11.5% were from engineering and technology programs, and the remaining participants were distributed across other academic fields. The AI dependency scale demonstrated high internal consistency (Cronbach's
 α
  = 0.837; McDonald's
 ω
  = 0.940) similar to the academic self-efficacy scale (Cronbach's
 α
  = 0.943; McDonald's
 ω
  = 0.945). Higher AI dependency was significantly associated with higher academic self-efficacy after adjustment for potential confounders (standardized
 β
  = 0.25; 95% CI, 0.11–0.39;
 P
  < 0.001). The overall model explained 44% of the variance in academic self-efficacy (
 R
 2
  = 0.44; adjusted
 R
 2
  = 0.40).
 
 
 
 
 Higher AI dependency was associated with greater academic self-efficacy among university students. Given the cross-sectional design, self-reported measures, and potential for common method bias, this association should not be interpreted causally. Furthermore, longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to clarify the temporal relationship between AI dependency and academic self-efficacy. Because the participants of this study were recruited from only three public universities in Riyadh and health sciences students were predominant, the findings should not be generalized directly to all university students in Saudi Arabia.

title_key: 288 generative ai usage in medical education insights from a single institutional analysis among medical students|hannon
title: 288 Generative AI Usage in Medical Education: Insights From a Single Institutional Analysis Among Medical Students
abstract:
Generative AI has drawn increasing interest among medical students and has the potential to transform study methods. This study investigates the use, satisfaction, reliability, and perceived barriers to AI among medical students.
 
 
 
 A survey was conducted among medical students to evaluate their engagement with AI tools. Data from the responses were entered into an Excel spreadsheet and analyzed.
 
 
 
 We received a total of 58 responses across all four medical school classes. Generative AI use was reported by 88% of student respondents. ChatGPT was the most used, with 84% of students using, followed by OpenEvidence (21%) and Gemini (19%). Students primarily used AI to create practice questions (69%) and generate study materials (67%). The average reliability and satisfaction scores among all students were 3.50 and 3.60, respectively. The most common reported barrier to AI use was concern about accuracy and reliability (24%), with the next being ethical concerns (19%). Regarding formal AI training, many students were unsure whether it would benefit or not (57%), while those supporting (22%) and opposed (21%) were nearly equal.
 
 
 
 Medical students reported using a variety of AI programs for different educational purposes, indicating that generative AI has become an important tool in medical education.

title_key: generative ai use and scientific literacy among 15 year olds in beijing shanghai jiangsu and zhejiang china the mediating role of academic help seeking|wu
title: Generative AI use and scientific literacy among 15-year-olds in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China: the mediating role of academic help-seeking
abstract:
Adolescents increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots for schoolwork, yet evidence on whether this use supports or undermines learning is mixed. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading and self-regulated learning, we examined whether GenAI use for schoolwork is related to scientific literacy directly and through two components of self-regulated learning, academic help-seeking and metacognitive strategy use, and whether the purpose of use matters.
 
 
 
 We analyzed the Program for International Student Assessment 2025 (PISA 2025) data from 12,191 15-year-old students in 374 schools in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China. Weighted two-level mediation models compared students within the same school, used all ten plausible values, and evaluated indirect effects with Monte Carlo confidence intervals. Results were checked against a design-based model with school fixed effects and balanced repeated replication weights.
 
 
 
 
 Students who used GenAI more often than their schoolmates reported more help-seeking (
 β
  = 0.17) and more metacognitive strategy use (
 β
  = 0.30). Help-seeking was positively associated with scientific literacy, yielding a positive indirect effect (
 β
  = 0.013, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]); the indirect effect through metacognitive strategies was smaller (
 β
  = 0.007) and was fully accounted for by science self-efficacy. The direct association between GenAI use and scientific literacy was negative (
 β
  = −0.048, about 4 PISA points), and the positive indirect effects offset about 40% of it, leaving a small negative total association (
 β
  = −0.028). Purpose mattered: among users, using GenAI “to help me learn” was associated with higher scientific literacy (+5.8 points per response category), whereas using it to summarize texts, research new topics, or draft assignments was associated with lower scores (−6.6 points). The results did not differ by gender or socioeconomic status and were identical under the design-based model.
 
 
 
 
 GenAI use for schoolwork is associated with scientific literacy through opposing pathways: a positive one through academic help-seeking and a negative direct one, and the direction of the association differs by purpose of use. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations may partly reflect which students use GenAI rather than the effects of its use.

title_key: ai awareness and personal data protection practices in bangladesh|mira
title: AI Awareness and Personal Data Protection Practices in Bangladesh
abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence creates opportunities for learning and professional work while requiring users to make decisions about sensitive information. This study examines whether self-reported AI awareness aligns with two distinct personal-data protection practices in Bangladesh: avoiding sensitive information in public AI tools and checking privacy or data-use information before sensitive tasks. A cross-sectional analysis of 385 adult respondents uses item-level distributions, paired endorsement contrasts, proportional-odds models and direct comparison of outcome-specific coefficients. The sample includes 242 law students alongside graduates, legal professionals and other respondents; it is not representative of all university students or the national population. Checking privacy information was endorsed by 284 respondents (73.8%), compared with 222 (57.7%) for avoiding sensitive input. Their within-person difference was 16.1 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval 9.6–22.6; Holm-adjusted p < .001). Self-reported understanding of privacy risks was endorsed by 275 respondents (71.4%), whereas understanding that AI services may collect, store or process user data was endorsed by 177 (46.0%). None of the eight focal awareness–practice coefficients received clear support after Holm correction; the joint comparison of associations across the two practices was inconclusive (χ²(4) = 1.83, p = .768). The findings distinguish self-reported understanding, reported protective practices and their uncertain adjusted relationships. Privacy calculus and protection motivation theory inform interpretation, but the questionnaire does not measure all components required to test either theory. Future research should document recruitment and evaluate privacy decisions through observed tasks or experiments involving specific AI services.

Keywords: AI awareness; personal data protection; privacy literacy; sensitive information; generative AI; Bangladesh; self-reported behaviour

title_key: customising chatgpt for chemistry education a domain grounded chatbot to support pharmacy students in medicinal chemistry|fookes
title: Customising ChatGPT for chemistry education: A domain-grounded chatbot to support pharmacy students in medicinal chemistry
abstract:
Background: This study develops and evaluates ChemIA, a course-specific GPT that supports pharmacy students in undergraduate Medicinal Chemistry. Customised with instructor-authored materials, it better matches the syllabus and reduces generic-model inaccuracies.   
Methods: The exploratory evaluation assessed technical performance and student perceptions. Technical performance was tested with 15 multiple-choice questions from course assessments. Across repeated interactions, ChemIA largely matched instructor-validated answers; discrepancies mainly involved information found only in images. It also handled a small set of questions based on English-translated materials. These findings indicate basic multilingual functionality in the tested conditions, not comprehensive multilingual capability. ChemIA supported course activities including quizzes, pre-class study, podcast-style content, and a pharmacological case study.
Results: Survey responses indicated that students perceived ChemIA as useful for clarifying medicinal chemistry concepts, preparing for examinations, and obtaining supplementary explanations. Students also reported greater confidence in ChemIA’s responses than in those generated by a generic GPT model. In the case-study activity, students rated ChemIA's explanations more often as very clear than those from the non-custom model.   
Conclusion: These findings offer exploratory evidence that a domain-grounded GPT can complement Medicinal Chemistry education. Its simple setup and adaptability may support similar applications in other disciplines. However, findings are limited by the exploratory design and the absence of direct measures of learning or academic performance.

title_key: the use of artificial intelligence when working with first semester students|oskolkov
title: The use of artificial intelligence when working with first-semester students
abstract: This article examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the higher education system of the Republic of Kazakhstan. The author analyzes the specifics of Kazakhstani higher education, including statutory regulations, standard curricula, and challenges associated with the lag of educational programs behind labor market demands. Drawing on practical experience in teaching “Political Science” at Caspian University, the paper presents a methodology for developing foundational AI application skills among first-year students. A step-by-step algorithm for executing practical assignments — specifically compiling a systematized bibliography and automating grading using neural networks (Gemini, ChatGPT) — is outlined. Special emphasis is placed on fostering analytical thinking, information verification skills, and the critical role of human agency when collaborating with AI tools.

title_key: chat bloom a taxonomy for classifying cognitive offloading in student ai interactions in cs education|chao
title: Chat-Bloom: A Taxonomy for Classifying Cognitive Offloading in Student-AI Interactions in CS Education
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming computer science (CS) education by providing immediate problem solving support and on-demand knowledge. However, commercial LLMs frequently deliver complete solutions, fostering overreliance and diminishing the productive struggle essential for deep learning. Neurological evidence further suggests that LLM dependence can significantly reduce brain activity, threatening long-term retention. In response, educators have begun customizing LLM-based AI assistants to deliver structured scaffolding. Despite these efforts, the effect of cognitive offloading in student–AI interactions on CS learning outcomes remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose Chat-Bloom (CB), a taxonomy that classifies the cognitive offloading level of both student prompts and AI responses. We validated CB through inter-rater reliability testing (Gwet's AC2 = 0.81) and trained machine learning (ML) models to achieve 81% classification accuracy for large-scale analysis. Applying CB to CS1 chat logs, we identify distinct interaction sequences, compare cognitive offloading patterns across AI assistants, and examine their relationship to student outcomes. These findings position CB as a practical framework for evaluating and improving AI-assisted learning in CS education.
authors: ["Leo Chao", "Christiana Cho", "Candice Lu", "Mikayla McGrath", "Troy Yeh", "Misaki Rios", "Ellie Yeh", "Sowmiyalakshmi Ganesh", "Thomas Y. Yeh"]
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.1

title_key: raqamli talim muhitida talabalar intellektual faolligini osirisning psixologik omillari|baratova
title: RAQAMLI TAʼLIM MUHITIDA TALABALAR INTELLEKTUAL FAOLLIGINI OŞIRIŞNING PSIXOLOGIK OMILLARI
abstract: The article analyses the psychological factors that shape students’ intellectual activity in the digital learning environment, including the context of widespread generative artificial intelligence, on the basis of meta-analyses, systematic reviews and empirical studies published in 2021–2026. Fourteen sources were included in a systematic narrative review and coded by factor type, outcome indicator, direction of effect and conditions. The findings show that digital tools do not activate students by themselves; intellectual activity depends on motivational (satisfaction of the needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness), regulatory (self-regulated learning, metacognition), cognitive (degree of cognitive offloading) and attentional-emotional (smartphone addiction) factors. When AI is used as a guiding tutor rather than an answer provider, higher-order thinking develops, whereas unrestricted use weakens independent thinking. An empirical research design and practical recommendations are proposed.
venue: Ta'limda Istiqbolli Izlanishlar xalqaro ilmiy metodik jurnal

title_key: students positions towards generative ai technologies strengths and challenges in higher education|kashkosh
title: Students’ Positions towards Generative AI Technologies: Strengths and Challenges in Higher Education
abstract:
The current study examined the attitudes of Arab students toward generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, focusing on their self-reported awareness of its limitations and risks, readiness to use these technologies, concerns, and recommendations for effective integration into teaching and learning. The study employed a mixed-methods design involving 337 undergraduate and postgraduate students from a teacher education college in Israel, recruited through convenience sampling. Data were collected using an online questionnaire comprising closed-ended and open-ended questions. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and independent-samples t-tests, while qualitative responses were analyzed thematically. The findings revealed an overall mean of 2.91 (SD = 0.783) for students’ self-reported awareness of GenAI limitations and risks and a mean of 3.53 (SD = 0.865) for readiness to use these technologies. Readiness was positively correlated with previous use (r = 0.408, p < 0.001), but not significantly correlated with self-reported familiarity (r = 0.031, p = 0.571). Male students reported significantly higher readiness than female students, t(335) = 2.326, p = 0.021, whereas no significant difference was found by academic level. Students’ concerns had an overall mean of 3.06 (SD = 0.872), with the potential negative effects of overreliance on generic skills emerging as the highest-rated concern. Concerns did not differ significantly by previous-use group, gender, or academic level. The qualitative findings showed that students recommended using GenAI to support research and academic tasks, integrating it into courses and learning activities, verifying the accuracy of generated information, and providing appropriate training and instructor guidance. The findings highlight the importance of a balanced and responsible approach to GenAI integration that combines practical support with critical evaluation, academic integrity, and the preservation of independent thinking. 
  
 Received: 11 August  2026 / Accepted: 24 October  2026 / Published: November  2026
venue: Journal of Educational and Social Research

title_key: development and validation of a multidimensional gen ai competence scale for pre service science teachers|mardiyanti
title: Development and Validation of a Multidimensional Gen-AI Competence Scale for Pre-Service Science Teachers
abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) into education is transforming the competencies required of future teachers and creating a need for a robust multidimensional measure of Gen-AI competency. This study developed and validated a six-dimensional framework comprising output evaluation, use appropriateness, prompting & operation, technical integration, model literacy, and responsible practice among pre-service science teachers. Data were obtained from 426 biology, chemistry, and physics education students at Universitas Jambi, Indonesia. The responses were randomly split into EFA (n = 256; 60%) and CFA (n = 170; 40%) subsamples. An initial 84-item pool was evaluated through ten experts’ judgment using CVR and CVI, resulting in 63 content-valid items. The data were suitable for factor analysis (KMO = 0.972; Bartlett’s χ² = 20430.533; df = 1,953; p < 0.001), and EFA retained 33 items across six dimensions, with factor loadings of 0.502–0.811 and Cronbach’s alpha of 0.765–0.909. CFA supported the six-dimensional structure with acceptable fit (RMSEA = 0.063, CFI = 0.913, TLI = 0.904, SRMR = 0.052). The dimensions demonstrated satisfactory reliability and convergent validity (α = 0.754–0.909; CR = 0.752–0.910; AVE = 0.505–0.611), while HTMT values of 0.586–0.874 supported discriminant validity. The resulting measure provides an empirically supported basis for profiling Gen-AI competency and strengthening teachers’ preparation for responsible Gen-AI use. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence, gen-AI competency, instrument validation, pre-service science teachers.

title_key: patterns and perceptions of generative artificial intelligence use in anatomy education a cross sectional study in australia|trung
title: Patterns and perceptions of generative artificial intelligence use in anatomy education: a cross-sectional study in Australia
abstract:
While generative artificial intelligence is transforming medical education, student-led use of AI tools for anatomy learning remains largely unexplored. This study investigated patterns and perceptions of AI usage among anatomy students to inform evidence-based integration strategies. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1,166 undergraduate students enrolled in Medicine, Allied Health, and Science programs at the University of New South Wales. The questionnaire assessed AI adoption rates, usage patterns, perceived helpfulness, and demographic associations. Quantitative data were analyzed using Chi-Square Tests, Fishers Exact Test, Moods Median Test and Analysis of Variance, while open-ended responses underwent thematic analysis.
Overall, 64.9% of students used AI for anatomy learning, with significant program-specific variations. ChatGPT was the dominant platform (68.5%), primarily used for concept explanation and answering factual questions. Despite widespread adoption, students recognized AI’s limitations for visual and spatial learning tasks, with 81.3% also using non-AI digital anatomy resources such as 3D visualization platforms. Medicine and Allied Health students demonstrated higher adoption rates and more frequent use compared to science students, reflecting curricular differences. Nearly all students (97.7%) rated AI as at least somewhat helpful, though it was perceived as less useful for anatomy than for other subjects (90.8%). This study indicated that students strategically integrate AI with traditional and digital learning tools in a complementary manner, with usage patterns shaped by curricular context rather than technology alone. These findings provide foundational data for developing targeted educational interventions that leverage AI’s strengths while addressing its limitations through hybrid learning approaches.
authors: ["James Le-Trung", "Thomas Duncan", "B. Billings", "A. Ngwenya", "Palesa Budaki", "T. Prvan", "G. \u0160trkalj"]

title_key: analyzing code provenance in llms for programming education|maity
title: Analyzing Code Provenance in LLMs for Programming Education
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasing role in programming education, challenging traditional assessment methods as they can generate fully functional code instantly. This disrupts the reliability of student submissions as indicators of learning and effort. To address this issue, code provenance is essential for tracing the origins of code and distinguishing student-authored, AI-generated, and externally sourced components. We extend the Min-K% probability approach by incorporating synthetic non-member code generation and apply it to Python code for membership inference and provenance tracking. Evaluations cover free LLMs such as GPT-2, DistilGPT-2, and DialoGPT, as well as state-of-the-art commercial models including GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Mistral, DeepSeek, and LLaMA 3.3. Before evaluating our approach on higher-education student assignments, we validate its feasibility using Stack Overflow data. The results show that free models enable more sensitive code memorization detection than commercial models. By systematically comparing these LLMs, we assess trade-offs between detection accuracy and privacy protection, taking an initial step toward effective assessment of AI-assisted programming education through combined provenance detection and process visibility.

title_key: education and employment through chatgpt student perceptions in latin america and asia|reyes
title: Education and Employment Through ChatGPT: Student Perceptions in Latin America and Asia
abstract: This article examines higher education students’ perceptions of ChatGPT in relation to skills development, anticipated labor-market transformation, and job readiness across ten countries in Latin America and Asia. The analytical sample included 3085 students for the skills-development dimension (PQ29) and 3083 for the labor-market transformation (PQ30) and skills-mismatch reduction (PQ31) dimensions. Analyses included descriptive statistics by country and discipline, adjusted general linear models, correlations, network analyses, and regional comparisons using Welch’s t tests, Cohen’s d, and covariate-adjusted models. Country-level differences remained statistically detectable after adjustment for discipline, gender, and level of study, whereas adjusted discipline-level mean differences were not statistically significant. Latin America–Asia differences were negligible for PQ29 and PQ30 and small for PQ31; after adjustment, the PQ30 regional difference was no longer statistically significant. The findings therefore describe students’ perceptions and associations, not demonstrated gains in skills, employability, or employment outcomes.

title_key: animating microbiology and immunology student tool preferences and pedagogical insights in an ai era|lloyd
title: Animating microbiology and immunology: student tool preferences and pedagogical insights in an AI era
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools have changed how undergraduate students approach written coursework, often bypassing required levels of active reading and conceptual engagement. To encourage genuine interaction with course content without resorting to high-stress invigilated exams, a low-stakes digital animation task (2% weighting) was integrated into an undergraduate microbiology and immunology course, to pilot students’ preferences on using animation tools to construct visuals. Students created a 30-s animation, illustrating dynamic biological processes, such as viral replication or phagocytosis. Pre- and post-exercise surveys evaluated students’ prior tool experience, selection criteria and software adoption. Pre-survey results showed that only 57% of students had prior animation experience – predominantly using Microsoft PowerPoint (32%). Key tool selection criteria included user-friendliness (32%), available tutorial support (18%) and zero cost (15%). Following targeted tutorial support for in-house digital tools (e.g. Adobe Express, Adobe Animate, Adobe Character Animator) and autonomy to select Adobe or other preferred tools for the task, post-survey analysis demonstrated a substantial rise in preference for Adobe Express, growing from 2 to 41%, while maintaining high levels of student engagement. Tutors observed that translating biological concepts into moving representations required greater time-on-task, research and deconstruction of study content to construct an accurate visual, thus offering an effective, AI-resistant assessment strategy for science education.
authors: ["Charmaine Lloyd", "Matteo Curcio", "Clare Dyson", "Mahsa Majzoobi", "R. Eri", "P. Apputhurai", "D. Grando"]

title_key: generative artificial intelligence in the context of stimulating cognitive interest in schoolchildren pedagogical assessments and professional expectations|prolygin
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Context of Stimulating Cognitive Interest in Schoolchildren: Pedagogical Assessments and Professional Expectations
abstract:
Introduction. International instruments (the Convention on the Rights of the Child, UN SDG 4) enshrine the child's right 
to personal development and quality education, while UNESCO documents emphasize that digital solutions, including 
generative artificial intelligence (AI), are acceptable only if they enhance student agency and preserve pedagogical 
guidance. 
The aim of the study is to identify the perceptions of teachers and future teachers regarding the pedagogical potential of 
generative AI in stimulating students' cognitive interest.
Materials and Methods. The study is based on an anonymous online survey (N=986) conducted in 2025 across 12 
regions of the Russian Federation. The sample included practicing teachers (19.5%) and students in teacher education 
programs (76.5%). The survey instrument covered questions on the structure of cognitive interest, assessment of 
academic engagement, effective ways of stimulation, and attitudes toward generative AI. Descriptive statistics, cross
tabulation, the χ² test, and correlation-regression analysis were applied.
KEYWORDS
Results. It was found that professional perceptions are dominated by an interpretation of cognitive interest through 
motivational-value (44.5%) and emotional (42.3%) components, while the activity component is significantly less 
pronounced (13.2%). A statistically significant relationship was revealed between the type of teaching experience and the 
preferred model of interest (p < 0.01). Respondents associate the potential of generative AI with enhanced visualization 
(68%) and engagement, yet they identify a key risk — the substitution of independent thinking with ready-made answers 
(45%). The main condition for pedagogically justified AI integration was named as preliminary methodological training for 
teachers (52%). Subject-specific expectations were discovered: science teachers view AI as a visualization tool (72%), 
while humanities teachers see it as a tool for interpreting contexts (65%).
Conclusion. Generative AI is perceived as a promising resource, yet one that depends on pedagogical design and 
teacher competence. Its application requires the development of subject-specific methodological models to facilitate the 
transition from situational activation to sustained cognitive independence.

title_key: unequal ai readiness why digital inequality matters for governing generative ai in african universities|steven
title: Unequal AI Readiness: Why Digital Inequality Matters for Governing Generative AI in African Universities
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is moving into African higher education faster than many universities can develop coherent rules for its use. Students and staff are already using systems such as ChatGPT and related tools for writing, research, feedback, coding, information retrieval, and problem-solving. Across African higher education, the emerging evidence points to substantial interest in GenAI alongside concerns about academic integrity, accuracy, privacy, overreliance, assessment, and institutional preparedness (Apata et al., 2026). The policy challenge is therefore no longer whether universities will encounter GenAI, but whether they can govern its use in ways that are educationally meaningful, accountable, and equitable.

title_key: content validity of a framework for problem solving competence in programming among information technology students a two round delphi study in vietnam|nguyen
title: Content Validity of a Framework for Problem-Solving Competence in Programming Among Information Technology Students: A Two-Round Delphi Study in Vietnam
abstract: Competence-based education requires that learning outcomes for information technology (IT) programs rest on a competence framework whose content has been validated by experts, yet Vietnam has no framework for problem-solving competence in programming validated through a quantitative, criterion-based procedure. This study validated the content of such a framework, comprising five competence components, twenty-one criteria, and behavioural indicators across four developmental levels, using a two-round Delphi procedure with a purposively heterogeneous, Vietnam-based panel of 23 experts drawn from programming instruction, the software industry, and educational measurement. Round 1 (21 respondents; 91.3%) elicited structured qualitative judgements that generated six documented revisions. Round 2, sent to the same fixed panel (n = 20; 87.0%; 19 also responding in Round 1), rated 169 items against three consensus criteria set in advance: an item-level content validity index (I-CVI) of at least 0.78, a median of at least 4, and an interquartile range of at most 1. Every one of the 169 items satisfied all three criteria simultaneously, the scale-level index (S-CVI/Ave) reached 0.98, and the predefined stopping rule was therefore met after two rounds; a sensitivity analysis restricted to respondents who passed an embedded attention check left this conclusion unchanged. The validated core comprises twenty-one criteria and eighty-four indicators. Two content areas that experts raised without prompting, collaboration with generative artificial intelligence and exception handling, were integrated as twelve extended indicators at the indicator layer rather than as new criteria, preserving the validated criterion structure; these twelve await separate validation. The framework supplies an evidence-based foundation for writing learning outcomes, constructing analytic rubrics, and designing project-based instruction in IT programmes.
venue: Journal Of Education And Teaching Learning (JETL)

title_key: chemmindlab an intelligent web based platform for the integrated development of computational and ai thinking|xu
title:
ChemMindLab:
An Intelligent Web-Based Platform for
the Integrated Development of Computational and AI Thinking
abstract: AI for Science (AI4S) education has become an important direction in chemistry education as artificial intelligence increasingly shapes the formulation, screening, and validation of molecular and materials problems. ChemMindLab was developed as a web-based instructional platform that uses AI4S-oriented molecular candidate-screening activities to cultivate interdisciplinary learners with both computational and AI thinking. Through two representative instructional activities, the platform introduces students to research practices resembling authentic AI4S materials discovery: comparison of quantum mechanical (QM) calculations with machine-learning-potential (MLP) predictions for a molecular structure, followed by extension to isomeric candidate-set screening. A context-aware large language model (LLM) assistant supports explanation, operational guidance, and troubleshooting. Preliminary classroom use with undergraduate and graduate chemistry students suggests that ChemMindLab can support guided activities based on the two instructional workflows.

title_key: evaluating the accuracy of large language models applied to hardware synthesis|lee
title: Evaluating the Accuracy of Large Language Models Applied to Hardware Synthesis
abstract: This paper is to investigate the reliability of ChatGPT LLM and Gemini LLM in generating the correct hardware Register transfer level (RTL) code, graphs and meeting the academic assignment requirements for VHDL and system-verilog based hardware design. By comparing the two major AI-generated code including floating point adders, integer multipliers, and posit arithmetic multipliers will provide a general aspect of which one is more accurate. The compartment results aim to evaluate ChatGPT LLM and Gemini LLM's performance accuracy (throughput, area, and power), consistency, and ability to follow design specifications. The results will help determine how effectively AI can assist students in completing digital design coursework and how much it could impact learning outcomes, productivity, and academic integrity in engineering education.
venue: Ubiquitous Computing, Electronics & Mobile Communication Conference

title_key: analysis of data with multiple representations conducted by genai and a chemistry education expert strengths and weaknesses of genais analysis|gunbatar
title:
Analysis of
Data with Multiple Representations Conducted
by GenAI and a Chemistry Education Expert: Strengths and Weaknesses
of GenAI’s Analysis
abstract: Studies examining how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) contributes to analyzing data with multiple representations (i.e., symbolic, particulate-level drawings, and written explanations) are scarce. To address the gap, this study compares the potential of GenAI with a chemistry education expert to analyze multimodal data of chemical reactions. Responses to two open-ended chemistry tasks, collected from 30 preservice teachers enrolled in undergraduate programs in chemistry and science education departments, were analyzed by ChatGPT 5.1, a large language model, and a chemistry education expert. The consistency between the expert and ChatGPT was evaluated through qualitative content analysis and thematic analyses of participants’ responses to the tasks. The findings showed that ChatGPT effectively analyzed symbolic representations and written explanations, demonstrating greater consistency with the expert’s assessment. Additionally, ChatGPT recommended novel assessment criteria that went beyond the predefined evaluation for both questions and provided individualized feedback and specific recommendations to address participants’ areas for development in chemistry content knowledge. Nevertheless, it also struggled to identify and assess particulate-level drawings in many cases, leading to reduced consistency due to perceptual errors and limitations in interpreting molecular geometry and stoichiometry. While GenAI tools show promise in assessing open-ended content in chemistry education, ChatGPT 5.1 showed limitations in analyzing the multimodal data used in this study. These findings have implications for chemistry education research and instruction, indicating that GenAI-supported assessment of multimodal chemistry responses may still require expert supervision.

title_key: from learning objectives to immersive lessons using generative ai to author stem learning experiences in mixed reality|austin
title: From Learning Objectives to Immersive Lessons: Using Generative AI to Author STEM Learning Experiences in Mixed Reality
abstract: Creating customized STEM learning experiences for virtual and mixed reality (VR/MR) environments remains challenging due to the combined demands of pedagogical design, subject-matter expertise, and immersive technology development. We address this challenge through an AI-assisted authoring framework designed to support the creation of adaptable, pedagogically grounded immersive lessons. The framework connects instructor-defined pedagogical specifications with a student-facing VR learning environment, enabling lessons that incorporate computational thinking (CT) practices and AI tutor support. We describe the design and implementation of the framework and report findings from a pilot usability study with 16 undergraduate students across two universities. Results indicate positive perceptions of usability, interactivity, immersion, and AI-supported learning, providing initial evidence of the feasibility and user acceptance of the developed VR learning experience.
authors: ["Noah Austin", "Sophia Golden", "B. G. Sorinolu", "F. J. Agbo"]
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.2

title_key: the ai curriculum we never designed what do we expect students to know about ai where were they supposed to learn it and when is it fair to assess|kamboj
title: The AI Curriculum We Never Designed: What do We Expect Students to Know About AI, Where were They Supposed to Learn It, and When is it Fair to Assess-
abstract: Across computing courses and programs, students are often expected to use AI responsibly, but ''responsible use'' can carry expectations not visible as curriculum. These may include verifying outputs, disclosing assistance, protecting data, recognizing limitations, explaining AI-assisted work, or knowing when AI should not be used. Such expectations can accumulate across instructions, policies, rubrics, and grading without a clear learning pathway. This Birds of a Feather session asks computing educators, students, and teaching assistants to examine their own contexts rather than adopt a predetermined competency list. Using facilitator-prepared public excerpts, participants will identify one AI-related capability and trace it: Where is it stated and taught? Is it verified prior knowledge, an explicit learning outcome, a course rule, a supported but unassessed capability, or a hidden expectation? Who is responsible for supporting it? Does it affect assessment? What evidence shows that students understand it? Open discussions will invite everyone to contribute and compare expectations across introductory, advanced, CS+X, and non-major settings and different LLMs. Participants will distinguish evidence and local observation from unverified expectation, considering experience, tool access, and inconsistent course policies. The central question is: if an expectation affects evaluation but its learning pathway cannot be identified, what should change? The facilitator contributes an interdisciplinary curriculum and assessment perspective, while participants supply computing-specific examples. The session will create a working map of hidden expectations, responsibility gaps, and questions to take back to students and programs.
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.2

title_key: visual aesthetic convergence and performative gaps between sustainability and biomimicry in ai generated interiors|kalay
title: Visual-Aesthetic Convergence and Performative Gaps Between Sustainability and Biomimicry in AI-Generated Interiors
abstract: Text-to-image generative artificial intelligence tools are increasingly used in interior architecture and design education, yet it remains unclear whether biomimicry and sustainability retain their distinct design intentions when visualized through such tools. This study comparatively examines biomimicry (B), sustainability (S), and combined (B + S) conditions in AI-generated interior images from 22 student projects in a Biomimicry and Space Design course, using descriptive content analysis. Visual-aesthetic similarity (VA1–VA5, Gower), biomimetic representation (B1–B4), sustainability strategies (S1–S7), and integration level (IL0–IL3) were coded as separate layers, with prompt (P-) and visual-output (V-) levels analyzed independently. The B and S outputs showed high visual-aesthetic similarity (mean Gower 0.82; 81.8% of projects scoring ≥0.80); however, biomimetic representation was strong at formal and structural levels but was verified in no project at the functional-mechanism level (V-B4). Sustainability prompt–output correspondence was 26.3% overall, 66.7% for visually assessable strategies, and 0% for strategies requiring specification or performance evidence. Combined outputs remained additive or coordinated (IL1–IL2), and none reached synergistic integration. In this course-based dataset, nature-oriented visual features were represented more readily than functional and performance-related dimensions; visual similarity is not equivalent to environmental performance, suggesting that prompt literacy and critical evaluation deserve attention in design education.

title_key: ai assisted adaptive problem based learning in a programming course its effects on students problem solving and debugging skills|anugrah
title: AI-assisted adaptive problem-based learning in a programming course: its effects on students' problem-solving and debugging skills
abstract: This study examined differences in problem-solving and debugging skills between students who participated in AI-assisted adaptive Problem-Based Learning (PBL) and those who participated in the Case Method in a programming course. A quasi-experimental nonequivalent pretest-posttest control-group design involved 69 students from the Department of Curriculum and Educational Technology, Universitas Negeri Padang. The experimental group (n = 35) followed Arends' PBL with data-informed adaptive grouping and structured use of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude during the investigation phase, while the control group (n = 34) followed the Case Method without generative AI. Multivariate analysis of covariance (MANCOVA) tested the two posttest scores while controlling for both pretest scores. The results showed a significant multivariate difference between the instructional conditions, Pillai's Trace = 0.456, F(2, 64) = 26.780, p < 0.001, partial η² = .456. Follow-up tests also showed significant differences in problem solving (partial η² = 0.335) and debugging (partial η² = 0.435). Adjusted means were higher for the experimental group on both skills. The findings suggest that an instructional package integrating PBL, adaptive grouping, and structured AI assistance has the potential to support problem-solving and debugging skills. However, because the three components were implemented simultaneously, their individual effects cannot be separated.
authors: ["Septriyan Anugrah", "Nadya Faranda", "Nofri Hendri", "Meldi Ade Kurnia Yusri"]
venue: Journal of Educational and Learning Studies

title_key: shield a trust calibrated intelligent tutor environment|leuva
title: SHIELD - A Trust Calibrated Intelligent Tutor Environment
abstract: AI tutoring systems can provide timely, personalised feedback on programming tasks at scale with increasing number of GenAI-based programming tutors successfully generating course-relevant feedback through pedagogical guardrails and course-aware retrieval. A key challenge in such systems is ensuring appropriate reliance on AI output, neither dismissing useful guidance nor accepting fluent but incorrect suggestions. Accuracy alone does not guarantee uptake, as evidence suggests that students may discount feedback they know to be AI-generated. In this paper, we frame this as a trust calibration problem; how feedback is presented and how well learners can judge when to rely on it is as consequential as the feedback itself. We present SHIELD (Secure Helper for Intelligent Education and Learning Developments), an LLM-based tutor designed through the Human-Centred AI (HCAI) theoretical lens, embedding aspects associated with Oversight, Comprehension, and Integrity as key design properties. In a preliminary exploratory study with five undergraduate students, participants generally perceived SHIELD responses as more actionable and trustworthy than feedback from a plain RAG-based baseline. These findings concern perceived trustworthiness and call for further studies to establish trust calibration and system efficacy.
authors: ["Drishtant Leuva", "Iromie Samarasekara", "M. Bandara", "Peter Athanasatos", "Yi-Wen Liao", "Yu-Chao Jiang", "Yue-Kang Li"]
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.2

title_key: transformation stem education in the age of artificial intelligence generative technologies adaptive learning digital assessment and new stem competencies|balmukanova
title: Transformation STEM Education in The Age of Artificial Intelligence: Generative Technologies, Adaptive Learning, Digital Assessment and New STEM Competencies
abstract:
The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), generative models, adaptive educational systems, and digital assessment tools has begun to significantly change the content and organization of STEM education. While previously the key issue was the creation of interdisciplinary STEM tasks integrating natural sciences, technology, engineering, and mathematics, the current era is characterized by a transition to intelligently supported and personalized educational environments.

The purpose of this analytical review is to identify the main areas of transformation in STEM education under the influence of artificial intelligence and to define new requirements for the educational process and STEM competencies. This review analyzes scientific publications on the use of AI in science teaching, generative AI in STEM, personalized and adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring systems, digital assessment, and the development of teacher and student competencies. It demonstrates that AI can enhance personalization, provide dynamic feedback, and support modeling and complex problem solving. However, the educational impact depends significantly on instructional design.

Recent meta-analytic data confirm the positive effects of AI-supported instruction and GenAI, but also demonstrate high heterogeneity in the results. The changing nature of assessment is particularly significant: traditional checking of the final answer is no longer sufficient, as generative models are capable of independently generating texts, program code, mathematical solutions, and explanations. The need for a shift to assessing the process of reasoning, design, verification, critical evaluation of AI results, and the student's ability to meaningfully use AI is substantiated. A conclusion is drawn regarding the emergence of a new model of STEM education, in which artificial intelligence is not a substitute for teachers or students, but an intelligent tool for collaborative problem solving, and AI literacy, critical thinking, verification, data management, and the ethical use of technology become integral elements of modern STEM competence.

The scientific novelty of this review lies in its approach to the transformation of STEM education, which is not viewed as a standalone implementation of AI technologies, but rather as a change in the entire architecture of STEM activities—from task setting and personalization of learning to assessment and competency structure. The article proposes a conceptual model of Human-AI Integrated STEM, in which artificial intelligence is not a substitute for students or teachers, but an intellectual component of interdisciplinary problem solving. It is further substantiated that, in today's environment, independent verification, validation, and critical assessment of AI results should be considered independent components of a new STEM competency.
venue: The American Journal of Engineering and Technology

title_key: peningkatan kapasitas guru dalam pengembangan media pembelajaran berbasis ai melalui pelatihan praktik di kabupaten administrasi kepulauan seribu|meilani
title: Peningkatan Kapasitas Guru dalam Pengembangan Media Pembelajaran Berbasis AI melalui Pelatihan Praktik di Kabupaten Administrasi Kepulauan Seribu
abstract: Introduction: Limited digital literacy among teachers in archipelagic regions has resulted in the suboptimal use of technology in the learning process. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers a strategic solution to support teachers in developing more creative and adaptive learning media. Objective: This program aims to enhance teachers’ capacity to utilize AI for the development of learning media in the Administrative Regency of Kepulauan Seribu. Methods: The program was implemented through practice-based training, workshops, reflective discussions, and mentoring for teachers from elementary to senior high school levels on Pramuka Island on August 2, 2025. The materials covered fundamental concepts of AI, the use of ChatGPT and Canva AI, and hands-on practice in developing learning media. Results: The program led to an improvement in teachers’ understanding and skills in utilizing AI, as evidenced by participants’ ability to create interactive presentation media and AI-based automated assessments. It also fostered collaboration among teachers in developing digital learning media. Conclusion: Practice-based training combined with mentoring represents a promising approach to enhancing teachers’ capacity in utilizing AI. However, the sustainability of the program requires continued infrastructure support and ongoing assistance.
authors: ["R. Meilani", "Tjutju Yuniarsih", "A. Sobandi", "Tutik Inayati", "Abi Sopyan Febrianto"]
