title_key: the effect of chatgpt use on students reflection on pancasila and citizenship education learning materials|jayadiputra
title: The Effect of ChatGPT Use on Students’ Reflection on Pancasila and Citizenship Education Learning Materials
abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) into education has created new opportunities to support reflective learning; however, empirical evidence regarding the relationship between ChatGPT use and learning reflection in Pancasila and Citizenship Education remains limited. This study examined the relationship between ChatGPT use and students' learning reflection among Grade XI students. A quantitative correlational design was employed involving 56 Grade XI students selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using validated questionnaires comprising 15 items measuring ChatGPT Use and 12 items measuring Learning Reflection. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression. The results demonstrated a positive and statistically significant relationship between ChatGPT use and learning reflection (R² = 0.813, p < 0.001). Descriptive analysis indicated that ChatGPT Use (M = 54.21, SD = 3.57) and learning reflection (M = 42.77, SD = 4.38) were classified as being in the "Good" category. These findings suggest that ChatGPT can support reflective learning when integrated into well-designed pedagogical activities under teacher guidance. This study contributes empirical evidence regarding the educational use of Generative AI in Pancasila and Citizenship Education and provides practical implications for promoting reflective and responsible learning.
venue: Journal of General Education and Humanities

title_key: generative artificial intelligence in classrooms calls for observation based rubrics alongside self report scales|demir
title: GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN CLASSROOMS CALLS FOR OBSERVATION-BASED RUBRICS ALONGSIDE SELF-REPORT SCALES
abstract:
GenAI is changing teachers' work faster than the field is changing the way it measures teachers' competence. Self-report scales inherited from the TPACK tradition will remain useful, and the development of comprehensive scales is part of the same agenda. If research relies on them alone, however, it is likely to describe teachers' perceptions of AI integration in increasing detail while saying comparatively little about the practice of integration. This paper is an attempt to draw attention to the need for observation-based, practice-oriented rubrics that can stand alongside these scales.
A research agenda follows from this argument. Observable indicators for AI-specific competencies need to be defined and subjected to expert review; rubrics need to be calibrated with anchor lessons and rater training; their reliability needs to be examined with rater-mediated psychometric models and generalizability studies; their relations with self-report scales, lesson plans and scenario-based tasks need to be investigated; and their functioning needs to be compared across pre-service and in-service teachers and across countries. It is recommended that journals welcome studies that combine self-report with observational, artifact-based, and scenario-based evidence; that teacher education programs assess pre-service teachers' AI integration in microteaching and practicum settings; and that researchers openly share validated rubrics for classroom use of GenAI.
venue: Problems of Education in the 21st Century

title_key: an industry oriented curriculum framework for graduate education in quantitative finance integrating large language models and spatio temporal wavelet networks|zhao
title: An Industry-Oriented Curriculum Framework for Graduate Education in Quantitative Finance: Integrating Large Language Models and Spatio-Temporal Wavelet Networks
abstract: The gap between the standard curriculum of quantitative finance and what is needed in practice has been increasing with the speed of financial artificial intelligence. The graduate students are being asked to be able to perform a single workflow involving structured market data, non-structured financial text, cross-asset dependence, non-stationary signal, reproducible backtesting, and deployable computing environments. This paper develops an industry-based curriculum framework which groups these needs on the basis of competency education and project based learning. The structure of the framework includes four interrelated components that include an industry-task and competency map, a three-tiered modular curriculum, a capstone multimodal forecasting project, and a feedback mechanism of revising the curriculum based on evidence. Factor research can be done using Microsoft Qlib; text representation and sentiment analysis can be performed by means of financial language models; discrete wavelet transform, Wavelet Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, graph convolutional networks and Stockformer can be used to provide progressively more complex modelling operations; Linux-based deployment will allow for reproducibility, monitoring and engineering practice. It makes the difference between the technical metrics of projects, such as Information Coefficient, ICIR, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, and the demonstration of student competence, such as the provenance of data, comparison of models, reliability of the deployment, reasoning about risk, and technical writing. The proposed curriculum design is reusable in terms of domain knowledge, modeling, engineering, and use of generative AI in responsible manner. Future multi-cohort application and outcome testing should prove its educational efficacy.
authors: ["Shang-Gui Zhao", "Qing Zhong", "Pan-Ke Qin", "Yun Xin", "Zhan-Qiang Huo", "Guo-Sheng Zhang", "Hai-Yan Li", "Ming Xu", "Jing-Wen Guo"]
venue: Innovations in Applied Engineering and Technology

title_key: a hybrid bibliometric and systematic review of generative ai in engineering education since the advent of chatgpt|tresor
title: A hybrid bibliometric and systematic review of generative AI in engineering education since the advent of ChatGPT
abstract: This review examines how engineering educators have empirically studied generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) in their courses since the November 2022 release of ChatGPT. From a 402-record Scopus corpus on AI in engineering education, a GenAI/LLM filter applied to titles, author keywords, and abstracts identified 184 candidates (142 paywalled, 42 open-access); 50 full-text records (42 open-access plus 8 institutionally acquired) constitute the synthesis base. Each record was coded on engineering sub-discipline, instructional application, and study design, paired with a bibliometric overview of citation anchors and venue distribution. Four findings dominate. First, the literature is overwhelmingly perceptual rather than experimental: only 6 of 50 records (12%) report controlled or quasi-experimental interventions, while 18 (36%) are surveys and 16 (32%) are perception or opinion pieces. Second, evidence is concentrated in software and computer engineering (n = 11, 22%), computing-adjacent settings (n = 9, 18%), and general engineering (n = 15, 30%); chemical (n = 4), mechanical (n = 4), civil (n = 3), and other sub-disciplines are thinly populated, and a sensitivity analysis excluding computing records leaves the principal findings unaffected. Third, application activity centres on assessment and grading (66%), perceptions and acceptance (62%), and ethics and integrity (28%), while safety and accreditation, both central to engineering as a profession, each appear in a single record. Fourth, the specific model version studied is unreported in the majority of records, and reporting practice has not improved across the review window. The six controlled studies are synthesised in detail and a framework for assessment redesign is proposed. It is argued that the most urgent contribution this review can make is to render visible the field’s methodological composition, and implications are drawn for educators, program leaders, accreditation bodies, and researchers. Not applicable.

title_key: toward understanding collaboration and learning in llm supported pair programming|hridi
title: Toward Understanding Collaboration and Learning in LLM-Supported Pair Programming
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in programming courses to generate code, explain concepts, and support debugging. In pair programming, their use creates a new form of collaboration in which students must coordinate not only with one another but also with an AI system. Although pair programming is widely adopted in computing education, instructors often have limited visibility into how students divide work, negotiate solutions, and develop shared understanding, particularly when generative AI tools are involved. Existing evaluations typically emphasize final code quality, grades, or students' perceptions, offering limited insight into how dialogue, programming actions, and LLM use interact and evolve over time. This paper presents a multimodal framework for studying semester-long LLM-supported pair programming in undergraduate programming courses. The framework integrates three data sources: video-based dialogue transcripts, programming activity logs, and LLM interaction logs. Dialogue and LLM exchanges are qualitatively coded, while programming logs are converted into labeled action sequences. Sequence pattern mining is then used to identify recurring collaboration, programming, and LLM-use trajectories. Cross-modal analysis examines how these trajectories align at the week and semester levels, and how the resulting patterns relate to course grades and other available learning outcomes. By making these interaction processes more visible, the study aims to identify recurring patterns of LLM-supported collaboration and generate evidence for instructors that can inform the design of pair-programming activities.
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.2

title_key: llms and the homogenization of teaching|tan
title: LLMs and the Homogenization of Teaching
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to lack diversity in open-ended text generation, a limitation that is especially consequential in education, where homogeneity can narrow the kinds of thinking and disciplinary work students are invited to do. We study diversity in two educational generation tasks: math items and essay feedback. We compare frontier and open-weight models with human-authored reference distributions using lexical, semantic, and domain-grounded measures. For math, we examine the mathematical activities students are asked to perform; for feedback, we examine the revision work requested and the rhetorical strategies used to communicate it. We evaluate direct prompting, two diversity prompting methods, and post-training. Across both tasks, directly prompted model outputs are markedly less diverse than human-authored content--78% higher on lexical (Self-BLEU) and 51% higher on semantic (embedding) similarity--and represent a narrower range of instructional forms. Diversity prompting and post-training increase variation largely through surface features without broadening the instructional repertoire. Models inherit and amplify the most normative routines of human instruction. Overcoming mode collapse in education will require richer instructional data and investment in teachers'creative capacity and professional judgment.

title_key: generative ai as scaffolding for operations research education framework classroom evaluation and design principles|armas
title: Generative AI as Scaffolding for Operations Research Education: Framework, Classroom Evaluation, and Design Principles
abstract:
Operations research (OR) education requires students to progress through a demanding sequence of cognitive transitions, from problem framing and mathematical formulation to computational implementation, validation, and interpretation, yet scalable instructional support for these transitions remains limited. This article proposes a task-centered framework that maps generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) support functions to the main bottlenecks of OR learning and specifies the instructor role needed at each stage. We illustrate the framework through six use cases, organized by implementation complexity and evaluated in terms of pedagogical role and risks. We then evaluate one classroom implementation in depth: a study in which 66 master’s students used a customized GPT companion to implement and solve a quadratic multiknapsack case in Python and Pyomo. Mixed-methods evidence from pre-post surveys, regression and mediation analyses, a compact path model, and qualitative coding shows that the intervention worked through manageability rather than task ease. Confidence gains were large and concentrated in the computational stages of OR modeling ([Formula: see text] overall). The findings suggest that GenAI is most valuable in OR education not when it removes difficulty, but when it makes difficult modeling and implementation tasks manageable enough for students to engage, persist, and learn.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/ited.2025.0167 .

title_key: generative ai interaction patterns cognitive autonomy and delegation initial versus final semesters in stem higher education|vazquez
title: Generative AI interaction patterns, cognitive autonomy, and delegation: Initial versus final semesters in STEM higher education
abstract: The intensive use of generative AI tools in higher education raises questions about their impact on students' cognitive autonomy. This study compares students' interaction with these tools and examines factors potentially associated with differences in cognitive autonomy between students in the early semesters (2nd to 4th) and final semesters (8th to 10th) of STEM programs. Using a cross-sectional comparative mixed-methods design, cognitive autonomy is assessed with the self-regulation subscale of the Motivated Learning Strategies Questionnaire (MSLQ) and a prompt coding system measuring complexity, critical iteration, and cognitive delegation. Semi-structured interviews identified factors associated with the observed differences between groups. A sample of 188 STEM students participated (116 in early and 72 in final semesters). The results reveal distinct profiles of interaction with AI according to academic progress, with a delegative prompt profile predominating among early-semester students (75.9 %) compared to final-semester students (19.4 %), and a higher overall interaction-autonomy index among the latter (d = 3.92). These findings are consistent with an association, rather than a causal or developmental effect, given the cross-sectional design, between academic trajectory and a more critical, epistemically reflective use of this technology. The results indicate potential risks of technological dependence and a possible weakening of autonomous thinking among students with less disciplinary maturity.

title_key: immersive and interactive technologies in computer science education a systematic review|zabir
title: Immersive and Interactive Technologies in Computer Science Education: A Systematic Review
abstract: As computer science (CS) education evolves, emerging technologies — including virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), artificial intelligence (AI), gamification, and mobile learning — are increas- ingly reshaping instructional practices and learning environments. This systematic literature review synthesizes empirical findings from 75 peer-reviewed studies to critically evaluate the pedagogi- cal value, effectiveness, and implementation challenges associated with integrating these technologies into CS classrooms. Drawing on thematic analysis across five research questions, this review examines how immersive environments foster deeper conceptual understanding, how AI-driven tutoring systems enable adaptive and personalized learning experiences, and how game-based and mobile learning tools enhance student engagement and intrinsic motivation. Key themes emerging from the literature include the benefits of interactivity, accessibility, and learner-centered per- sonalization, alongside persistent barriers such as infrastructural limitations, cost constraints, and insufficient instructor professional development. The review further highlights how blended learning models and social technologies support flexible, student-centered pedagogical approaches, while identifying critical gaps in longitu- dinal evidence, standardized assessment frameworks, and equitable access across diverse learner populations. To address these gaps, this paper presents a structured set of future research directions spanning longitudinal effectiveness, K–12 applications, inclusive design, ethical governance, and the emerging convergence of im- mersive environments with large language models. The insights offered are intended to inform educators, researchers, and policy- makers seeking to advance evidence-based, scalable, and inclusive technology integration in CS education.
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.1

title_key: from answer seeking to reasoning a request protocol for sustainable integration of generative ai in engineering graphics education|li
title: From Answer-Seeking to Reasoning: A Request Protocol for Sustainable Integration of Generative AI in Engineering Graphics Education
abstract: Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) emphasizes inclusive and equitable quality education and lifelong learning opportunities for all. Within this broader framework, the sustainable integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in engineering education raises a specific question: whether students can retain and apply the competencies developed during AI-supported learning when the tool is no longer used. Generative AI can provide learning support beyond limited classroom hours, but it can also perform the cognitive operations that students are expected to master. Using an engineering graphics course, this study compared three strategies of AI use for their effects on how long student competence lasts. The three strategies were no AI, unrestricted AI use, and a request protocol. Under the protocol, students may ask questions about work they have already produced, but they may not ask for the answer. Competence was measured four times under an instruction not to use the tool, and the last measurement fell four weeks after the course ended. The ranking changed after withdrawal. Immediately after instruction, the unrestricted group scored highest before adjustment, but the adjusted between-group differences were not significant. At the delayed test the protocol group held the largest advantage of any contrast and the unrestricted group fell to last. Both adjusted differences were significant at p < 0.001. The advantage was largest among students who started lowest and was no longer distinguishable from zero above a baseline score of 64.95. The difference between the two tool conditions sat in classification rather than drafting. Curve-type misjudgment was about six times as frequent in the unrestricted condition as under the protocol, while the drafting conventions did not differ detectably at the end of term. Protocol adherence acted as a graded skill rather than a compliance record and tracked delayed competence (r = 0.63, n = 33). In this 48 h foundation course, regulating what students asked, not how much they used the tool, was associated with competence that persisted after withdrawal.

title_key: exploring preservice teachers use of ai generated media in genre based english teaching for young learners|emilia
title: Exploring preservice teachers’ use of AI-generated media in genre-based English teaching for young learners
abstract: Generative AI (GAI) offers opportunities to create personalized, multimodal teaching materials, yet integrating it into English instruction for young learners requires careful consideration of developmental, pedagogical, and ethical factors. This study examines how pre-service teachers designed and integrated AI-generated media into a Genre-Based Approach (GBA) for teaching English to young learners. This study employed a qualitative case study design. Data were collected over sixteen meetings in which students learned to create and integrate AI-generated media into the GBA, two focus group discussions, AI-generated media artifacts, and lesson plans developed by 15 pre-service teachers enrolled in two courses: English for Young Learners Material Development and English for Young Learners Course Design. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify patterns in pedagogical and ethical considerations and how participants integrated AI-generated media across the stages of the GBA. The findings show that the participants considered both pedagogical and ethical factors when creating generative AI-based learning media. Pedagogically, they ensured that the media were age-appropriate, aligned with learning objectives, relevant to learners' cultural contexts, and complemented by hands-on learning activities. Ethically, they showed growing awareness of responsible AI use by considering issues such as overreliance on AI, plagiarism, and learner safeguarding. The AI-generated media were primarily integrated by the pre-service teacher students in GBA during the Building Knowledge of the Field, Modeling, and Joint Construction stages. In the Independent Construction stage, AI-generated media were not used. GAI can enhance engagement and scaffolded learning when used as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for teacher-led instruction. Teacher education programs should provide guidance on ethical AI use and pedagogical alignment to optimize benefits while mitigating risks.
authors: ["Emi Emilia", "Susan Santika", "Aditya Randika", "Dian Tjondronegoro", "Yustina Nita Sulistami"]

title_key: feeling easier working harder cognitive load in ai assisted code comprehension|white
title: Feeling Easier, Working Harder: Cognitive Load in AI-Assisted Code Comprehension
abstract: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers'real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants'perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.
authors: ["Maryangela White", "Maximilian Rose", "M. Buckman", "Amy McDonnell", "Francisco Ortega", "Bianca Trinkenreich"]

title_key: digital learning ecosystems in continuing education diagnosis of teachers digital competence for transformation and sustain ability|martinez
title: Digital Learning Ecosystems in Continuing Education. Diagnosis of Teachers' Digital Competence For Transformation And Sustain-Ability
abstract: Virtual continuing education requires teachers to possess high-level digital skills to develop quality educational resources, as mentioned in     [1] and    [2] . The objective of the study is to evaluate teachers' digital competence in a Continuing Education Center in order to identify strengths and areas for improvement in the construction of relevant and sustainable digital learning ecosystems    [3] . The methodology is mixed, with a predominantly descriptive-quantitative approach. [4] A questionnaire based on the DigCompEdu framework was applied to 76 teachers and 116 students, with the addition of qualitative components. The results indicated an intermediate level of digital competence, along with gaps in areas such as the use, creation, and management of digital content, pedagogy involving cutting-edge technologies such as generative AI, and the use of inclusive active methodologies    [5] . These findings support the importance of specific and ongoing training programs to strengthen educators’ digital skills, enhance pedagogical innovation, and maximize the effectiveness of educational resources. The assessment is linked to the evaluation of educators’ digital competence aimed at educational transformation, thus fostering the development of a high-quality and sustainable virtual continuing education system [6, 7].
authors: ["C. Castillo Mart\u00ednez", "Sonia Casilllas Mart\u00edn", "Lena Ivannova Ruiz-Rojas"]

title_key: fostering social responsibility in schoolchildren when teaching python programming using a neural network|kurganova
title: Fostering social responsibility in schoolchildren when teaching Python programming using a neural network
abstract: The article examines the potential of integrating generative artificial intelligence technologies into the school informatics curriculum — specifically during Python programming instruction — to foster social responsibility among students. Using the example of neural network usage in Python programming, the study provides a detailed analysis of three components of social responsibility: the cognitive (knowledge-based), the emotional-value, and the behavioral (action-oriented) components. Drawing on contemporary pedagogical and psychological research, the article substantiates the need to move beyond students' "blind trust" in AI technologies. The neural networks used in programming are listed. A lesson plan is presented that includes practical Python programming tasks designed to address the cognitive, emotional-value, and behavioral components of social responsibility. Particular emphasis is placed on developing skills in critical code verification, academic integrity, and understanding the legal and regulatory aspects of AI technology use. The article is intended for informatics teachers and specialists in digital education methodology.

title_key: current practices and emerging trends of the teaching assistant role in computing education|chao
title: Current Practices and Emerging Trends of the Teaching Assistant Role in Computing Education
abstract: Teaching assistants (TAs) play a central role in computing education, supporting instruction and student learning. However, the COVID-19 pandemic and the rise of Generative AI have significantly reshaped this landscape, raising questions about how TA roles are evolving and how training programs should adapt. This working group investigates teaching assistants in computing education, focusing on their roles, training, and practices in a post-pandemic, AI-enabled context. We will conduct a systematic literature review of TA-related research, complemented by a scoping review of publicly available TA training resources and a cross-institutional qualitative study using surveys and focus-group interviews with instructional faculty and teaching assistants. Through this work, we aim to identify how TA responsibilities are changing, how training programs are currently structured, and what challenges and opportunities surface with the emergence of AI. The outcomes will include an updated synthesis of the literature, an overview of how teaching assistants are used at different institutions, a cross-institutional study of TA training practices, and recommendations for TA training. Together, these contributions aim to support understanding and developing the role of the teaching assistant in a contemporary computing education landscape.
