title_key: ai powered tutoring quality and perceived mathematics learning outcomes among higher secondary school students|shahiduzzaman
title: AI-Powered Tutoring Quality and Perceived Mathematics Learning Outcomes among Higher Secondary School Students
abstract: AI Tutoring has the potential to facilitate learning in mathematics, including through the quality of instruction, perceived usefulness, engagement, and confidence. This paper analyses these associations on the basis of provided partial least squares structural equation modelling result of 470 records. Perceived AI tutoring quality, perceived usefulness, mathematics learning engagement, mathematics self-efficacy and perceived mathematics learning outcomes are reflected in five reflective constructs and twenty-five indicators. The analysis records 5,000 bootstrap samples and tenfold repeated prediction. The suggested seven direct relationships are all positive with confidence intervals not equal to zero. The quality of tutoring is linked with usefulness, engagement and self-efficacy. The engagement is linked to self-efficacy and perceived outcomes and self-efficacy is linked to perceived outcomes independent of engagement. The model is used to explain 39.5 percent of the perceived outcomes. The indicators loading, internal consistency, convergent, and discriminant validity are reported to fulfill the assessment criteria as stated in the workbook. However, prediction is above the linear standard of nineteen of twenty endogenous indicators, but the differences are minor. These results set engagement and self-efficacy as complementary explanatory paths. Nevertheless, an empirical sample cannot be verified due to hypothetical platform labels and missing fieldwork documentation. The results thus detail the provided records of analysis and are not able to determine causal achievement gains. Substantive educational conclusions will still require independent evaluation and validated recruitment documentation.
venue: American Journal of Interdisciplinary Research and Innovation

title_key: ai enabled cybercrime awareness and preventive behaviour among law students in bangladesh|saha
title: AI Enabled Cybercrime Awareness and Preventive Behaviour among Law Students in Bangladesh
abstract:
AI-assisted impersonation and social engineering make it necessary to distinguish threat recognition from protective practices. This study examines associations between AI-enabled cybercrime awareness and self-reported prevention among law students in Bangladesh. Protection Motivation Theory informs the interpretation of awareness and protective responses. Of 385 survey records, 253 respondents identified as law students and constituted the primary sample. Following reliability diagnostics, awareness and preventive-practice items were analysed separately. Ordinary least squares models used HC3 robust inference, with ordered logistic models, Holm correction and full-sample analyses as sensitivity checks. Among students, 49.0% endorsed recognition of AI misuse for phishing or impersonation, 80.6% reported verifying unusual requests, and 82.2% endorsed security practices. Adjusted awareness coefficients were small and uncertain for both outcomes; all four confidence intervals included zero, and all Holm-adjusted p values were 1.000. Daily AI use was positively associated with verification (b = 0.308, 95% CI 0.115-0.502) and security practices (b = 0.255, 95% CI 0.067-0.444). Ordered logistic models showed a comparable pattern. The findings support distinguishing recognition, perceived detection capability and behaviour-specific responses in cybersecurity research and university education. They identify contextual associations rather than causal effects and highlight the need for validated measures and prospective behavioural assessments. Generalisation is limited by the available recruitment documentation and the self-reported cross-sectional design.

Keywords: cybercrime awareness; preventive practices; law students; protection motivation; generative artificial intelligence; Bangladesh; measurement validity
authors: ["Aungon Saha", "Mst. Dilara Islam Anny", "Md. Asraful Islam", "Mannan Kazi Abdul"]
venue: Journal of State Government and Mass Media

title_key: testing a methodology for developing project competencies of university graduates based on a bionic approach using neural network tools for the purpose of sustainable development of the region|akhmetov
title: TESTING A METHODOLOGY FOR DEVELOPING PROJECT COMPETENCIES OF UNIVERSITY GRADUATES BASED ON A BIONIC APPROACH (USING NEURAL NETWORK TOOLS) FOR THE PURPOSE OF SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT OF THE REGION
abstract: The relevance of this study stems from the active integration of generative artificial intelligence into the educational process and the need to develop students’ competencies for effectively interacting with intelligent digital tools in project activities. The aim of the study is to analyze the specifics of using artificial intelligence tools by student project teams participating in the pre-acceleration program for preparing projects for the Student Startup competition, using a bionic approach. The empirical basis of the study was a survey of 75 project team members. The prevalence of various AI tools, their application in project management functional areas, and the level of development of human-artificial intelligence interaction competencies were assessed. The scientific novelty of the study lies in testing a bionic approach to analyzing the distribution of functions between humans and artificial intelligence in project activities and identifying the specifics of developing the corresponding competencies in students. It was found that the most popular tools are DeepSeek and ChatGPT, used primarily for idea generation, information analysis, and the preparation of text and presentation materials. However, the use of artificial intelligence in risk, deadline, and resource management remains limited. The practical significance of this study lies in its ability to provide a rationale for improving project-based learning programs aimed at developing competencies in conscious interaction between humans and artificial intelligence based on the principles of the bionic approach.
venue: Management of the personnel and intellectual resources in Russia

title_key: artificial intelligence explanations of organic reaction mechanisms revisited improved accuracy and sophistication but persistent mechanistic flaws|kalicheti
title:
Artificial Intelligence
Explanations of Organic Reaction
Mechanisms Revisited: Improved Accuracy and Sophistication but Persistent
Mechanistic Flaws
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence tools are increasingly used by students to explain chemistry concepts, but their educational value depends on the chemical accuracy and mechanistic quality of the explanations. Prior work found that ChatGPT could produce sophisticated and convincing organic reaction mechanisms that were frequently inaccurate. Using the same mechanism set and prompt-cueing levels as those in an earlier study, this study evaluates how a reasoning-based large language model changes the relationships among response correctness, explanation sophistication, and chemical concept use. ChatGPT o3-mini responses were generated for mechanisms spanning a year-long organic chemistry curriculum and analyzed for response-level accuracy, nucleophile and electrophile explanation sophistication, sentence-level concept use, and qualitative reasoning patterns. Compared with GPT-3.5, o3-mini increased the response-level accuracy from 28% to 79% and produced more sophisticated explanations. However, inaccuracies remained concentrated in aromatic ring and carbonyl mechanisms. Prompt cueing increased the chemical richness and explanation sophistication without improving response-level accuracy. Qualitative analyses showed that sophisticated terminology could mask flawed reasoning: o3-mini applied correct chemical concepts to inappropriate mechanisms, overgeneralized common mechanism patterns, and used advanced terminology in vague or decorative ways. These findings show that improvements in aggregate accuracy can coexist with persistent flaws in mechanistic reasoning and that great explanatory detail is not a reliable indicator of validity. The fixed benchmark provides a controlled comparison of which dimensions of response quality changed across model generations, while the sentence-level and qualitative analyses identify recurring error patterns that can be examined in future models. This framework gives instructors concrete features around which to structure student critique and provides researchers with a durable approach for studying AI-generated mechanistic explanations beyond point-in-time capability ranking.

title_key: pre service language teachers lived experiences in utilizing chatgpt in classroom instruction in rural areas in the philippines|ampo
title: Pre-service language teachers’ lived experiences in utilizing ChatGPT in classroom instruction in rural areas in the Philippines
abstract: This study aims to unveil the lived experiences of pre-service language teachers in their rural schools as they use ChatGPT in their classroom instruction despite the limited access to internet connection and other instructional resources. A phenomenological approach was used through the purposively 10 selected participants who met the criteria. A sin-depth interview was conducted and ensured data saturation. Data were then coded and thematically analyzed using a framework for qualitative data analysis. The findings revealed that participants perceived ChatGPT as an aid in lesson preparation, enhancing their efficiency, confidence, and classroom readiness. However, they also found inconsistent information and the need to validate information with a reliable source a challenge in its usage. A critical evaluation of the issues of using ChatGPT in the classroom is suggested to make this tool a positive support for learning and teaching for both students and teachers. Hence, this study highlights its contribution to the body of knowledge in integrating AI use in the classroom, aligning to the sustainability goal of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) on Quality Education (United Nations, 2015).

title_key: graphrag based generation of mathematics assessments using prerequisite knowledge graphs|cebreros
title: GraphRAG-Based Generation of Mathematics Assessments Using Prerequisite Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide new opportunities for the automatic generation of educational assessments. However, their application in mathematics remains challenging because they do not explicitly represent prerequisite knowledge and may generate mathematically incorrect content. To address these limitations, this study proposes a GraphRAG-based architecture for generating multiple-choice mathematics assessments. The architecture integrates a directed acyclic knowledge graph (DAG), semantic embeddings, hybrid retrieval, LLM-based generation, and independent mathematical validation using SymPy. The knowledge graph represents prerequisite relationships among mathematical concepts, allowing the system to retrieve structured information to guide question and distractor generation. The evaluation included 154 questions covering basic fraction operations and 462 distractors, of which 53.2% showed direct correspondence with prerequisite knowledge and 30.7% showed indirect correspondence. Mathematical validation accepted 137 questions (89.0%) without correction, while 17 (11.0%) required correction and subsequently passed revalidation. In addition, a controlled comparison involving 80 paired generation requests examined conventional RAG and GraphRAG under comparable generation conditions and the same maximum context limit. GraphRAG produced a higher proportion of distractors with identifiable prerequisite relationships than conventional RAG (91% versus 77%). A complementary evaluation by 24 mathematics teachers using a five-point Likert scale showed favorable perceptions across five dimensions, with coherence receiving the highest mean score (M = 4.68) and usefulness for teachers the lowest (M = 4.36). Overall, the findings provide preliminary evidence of the technical feasibility of the proposed architecture and suggest that the complete GraphRAG retrieval configuration is associated with stronger prerequisite–distractor correspondence. However, the comparison does not isolate the contribution of graph relationships from possible differences in retrieved context, and the study does not establish diagnostic validity or improvements in student learning outcomes.

title_key: methodological aspects of the use of generative artificial intelligence in stem education for future technical engineers|moiseeva
title: Methodological Aspects of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Stem Education for Future Technical Engineers
abstract:
The purpose of the study.
 
 Based on the analysis of the practice of using generative artificial intelligence in the university-level training of engineers, to develop a set of methodological solutions for the use of generative artificial intelligence to improve the quality of STEM education for future engineers. To achieve this goal, the objectives are to analyze the state of the problem of using generative artificial intelligence technologies in domestic and foreign higher engineering education practice; to develop a model for integrating generative artificial intelligence into the educational environment of a technical 
 university, defining the roles of lecturers, students and generative artificial intelligence at various stages of the educational cycle of creating and solving integrated learning tasks.
 
 
 
 Materials and methods.
 
 The research uses theoretical and analytical methods, including statistical and comparative analysis of the problem of introducing artificial intelligence into the process of engineering personnel training; modeling; pedagogical observation; study and generalization of advanced pedagogical experience. The teaching materials use prompts of varying complexity to interact with generative 
 models (text models, for example GigaChat), classified by task type: generating ideas, searching for errors in code, creating visualizations. The information base consists of scientific publications by Russian and foreign scientists, UNESCO materials, and open sources on the global Internet.
 
 
 
 Results.
 
 A conceptual model for the integration of generative artificial intelligence into STEM learning is proposed, which includes four
 stages of the learning cycle of integrated learning tasks. Methodological recommendations on the use of synthetic industrial datasets obeying specified probabilistic laws and prompt engineering in the process of training future technical engineers are formulated. A universal prompt has been developed to support a class of information and mathematical modeling tasks for students of engineering and technical specialties of universities.
 
 
 
 Conclusion.
 
 The demands of modern economic society for the level of training of specialists capable of solving serious technological problems and possessing a set of digital competencies that allow them to quickly analyze information and operate with a huge set of industrial data require a serious restructuring of approaches to the organization of the educational process, the introduction of new 
 technologies, methods and learning tools that take into account the capabilities of modern technologies of artificial intelligence. The practical significance of the research lies in the fact that its results can form the basis of methodological recommendations on the integration of artificial intelligence technologies into the information and mathematical training of engineers. The proposed solutions are applicable in the design of practical classes in probability theory, mathematical statistics, Python programming and machine learning, and also serve as a basis for the development of advanced training modules for lecturers in terms of using generative models to create adaptive teaching materials. In addition, the proposed algorithm for the distribution of roles between the lecturer, students and the neural network makes it possible to automate the generation of variable control measuring materials with a dynamic level of complexity, providing an objective assessment of students’ individual educational tracks within STEM disciplines.

title_key: dependence related use of generative artificial intelligence among postgraduate nursing students a qualitative descriptive study|liu
title: Dependence-related use of generative artificial intelligence among postgraduate nursing students: A qualitative descriptive study.
abstract:
AIM
To describe postgraduate nursing students' accounts of GenAI reliance, focusing on the boundary between assistance and substitution and its implications for learning and professional accountability.


BACKGROUND
Generative artificial intelligence offers readily available support in postgraduate nursing education, but frequent or habitual use does not by itself identify dependence-related patterns.


METHODS
Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 23 nursing master's students from five universities in three Chinese provinces during August-October 2025. Directed qualitative content analysis used the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution model as a sensitizing framework; specific codes were developed from the interview material.


RESULTS
Six themes concerned research task pressure and perceived capability gaps; immediate feedback, perceived efficiency gains and emotional support; cognitive offloading and default use; use regulation and boundary-management practices; perceived benefits and concerns about learning and capability; and peer, supervisory, platform and institutional contexts. Accounts differed in retained engagement, verification and control. Some described substitution for independent thinking, whereas others described bounded assistance.


CONCLUSIONS
Dependence-related use is a non-diagnostic interpretation of recurring reliance involving perceived displacement of learning-relevant cognitive work or difficulty regulating use. Educational responses should address learning goals, retained understanding and judgment, verification and accountability through task-specific AI literacy, supervisory support and clear institutional guidance.
authors: ["Jing-Bang Liu", "Shan Li", "Rong-Ping Cha", "Yun-Xia Shen", "Qin-Li Cao", "X. Gong", "Li-Li Wu"]

title_key: from traditional teacher to super teacher leveraging ai through glocal stem education to develop twenty first century competencies|mualem
title: From Traditional Teacher to Super Teacher: Leveraging AI through Glocal STEM Education to Develop Twenty-First-Century Competencies
abstract: Education in conditions of volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity and hyperconnectivity requires learners to evaluate changing information, connect knowledge across disciplines and justify action. These demands invite a transformation in teaching from the transmission of answers toward the leadership of inquiry. This conceptual article develops the Super Teacher framework through a practice-informed synthesis of research on learning environments, sustainability competencies, integrated science, technology, engineering and mathematics, and human–artificial intelligence collaboration. The argument proceeds from the changing environment to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, then to the translation of global challenges into locally meaningful problems and needs. Integrated STEM supplies the practices through which students explain phenomena, use tools, compare evidence and design responses. Artificial intelligence supports selected activities within a sequence that preserves human responsibility for source appraisal, decisions and claims. An author-supplied account of a Grade 6 school project informs a framework for Grade 6 and above and illustrates two connected movements: building and communicating knowledge, and developing a response to a problem. The model places AI support at the centre of this sequence: initial exploration with ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude, academic searching with Perplexity, four complementary AI roles, student-edited Gamma presentations and peer learning precede SDG-related problem definition and STEM prototype work. The resulting framework connects each inquiry stage with a learning purpose, an appropriate tool, a human decision and retained evidence. The Super Teacher harnesses AI through innovative STEM pedagogy to create opportunities for creativity, critical thinking, collaboration, communication, entrepreneurial initiative and problem solving. Competence is organized through Knowing, Doing, Valuing and Engaging. An econeurobiological perspective positions technological activity within supportive physical, relational and cognitive conditions. Integrated STEM connects inquiry, design and responsible action, providing a testable route toward Super Student development through teacher mediation and student contributions to shared knowledge. Effects on independent reasoning, teacher practice, participation and educational inequalities require prospective evaluation.
venue: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal

title_key: an open survey dataset on study habits and ai use among university students a proportionally sampled multi program study|mora
title: An open survey dataset on study habits and AI use among university students: A proportionally sampled multi-program study
abstract: Well-documented survey datasets are still scarce for examining how study habits and generative artificial intelligence (AI) intersect in higher education, especially in Latin America. This Data Descriptor aims to document and enable reuse of a cross-sectional dataset on study habits, academic self-perception, AI use, and ethical perceptions among undergraduate students. Data were collected at the Manizales campus of a Colombian public university from February 15 through May 15, 2025, during the first academic term of 2025. The sampling frame comprised 4,950 undergraduates across 14 academic programs, and the released dataset includes 357 complete responses and 29 survey variables collected through proportional program allocation and quota-based recruitment. The instrument covers sociodemographic and academic characteristics, study routines, AI tool use, perceived usefulness, verification practices, academic integrity, dependence, creativity, and prompt engineering knowledge. The repository provides an anonymized raw dataset, a cleaned analytical dataset, the sampling frame, a codebook, a bilingual questionnaire, and a reproducible R script. Technical validation checks address structural integrity, range plausibility, cross-file reconciliation, and semantic harmonization of AI-tool entries.
authors: ["J. Rojas-Mora", "Di\u00f3genes de Jes\u00fas Ram\u00edrez-Ram\u00edrez", "C. D. Correa-\u00c1lvarez"]

title_key: medical faculty attitudes toward chatgpt integration in undergraduate orthopedic education|siddarth
title: Medical Faculty Attitudes Toward ChatGPT Integration in Undergraduate Orthopedic Education
abstract:
In the last 20 years, medical education has experienced a tremendous shift towards digitalization. The advent and growth of simulation platforms, virtual learning environments, learning management systems, and online learning resources have all contributed to the shift from traditional lecture-based learning to technology-enhanced learning [1]. This trend gained even more pace with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, forcing institutions all over the world to adopt digital teaching methods and online learning practices [2].

In this dynamic educational environment, artificial intelligence (AI) has become one of the most impactful innovations. In recent years, the progress of Natural Language Processing technologies has led to a significant improvement in the capacity of AI systems to comprehend and create human language at a level never before attained. One of the most prominent applications of generative AI is ChatGPT, which was trained using a large language model approach. In contrast to conventional rule-driven learning programs, ChatGPT can converse with users, create educational content, respond to inquiries, offer summaries, and give explanations based on the needs of the user [3].

These skills have led to much interest in undergraduate medical education. ChatGPT can offer support for developing clinical scenarios, multiple-choice questions, lectures, formative assessment, and learning resources. Students are increasingly using the platform to explain complex ideas, to revise and revise, and to review for exams. Hence, the debate about ChatGPT is not just about a new technology; it is also about educational policy, curriculum design, and professional responsibilities [4].

It is important to note that faculty members are in a pivotal position in the above discussion. Their perception and attitudes affect the promotion, regulation, or opposition of the use of generative AI in medical curricula. Thus, knowing faculty’s attitudes can be useful in predicting the future direction of AI integration in medical education [5].

Faculty Optimism and Educational Opportunities
The literature on faculty perceptions is quite positive, with most expressing a positive stance on the educational potential of ChatGPT. The vast majority of teachers believe that the technology is a complement to learning that may provide support to current learning practices, but not supplant traditional learning methods [6].

An often-claimed benefit is more effective instruction. Researchers, educators, and other academics report that ChatGPT can help them save time on creating lecture materials, developing assessment items, writing clinical vignettes, and educational materials. In today’s academic landscape, where workloads and competing deadlines are on the rise, these efficiencies are especially appealing [7].

The other place of enthusiasm is curriculum development. ChatGPT can quickly create clinical scenarios of different levels of complexity, which can be helpful in problem-based learning and case discussions. Other research has been conducted on how it can be used to learn how to improve learning objectives, create rubrics, and generate structured learning resources. The following capacities present possibilities for improving curriculum planning and quality education [8].

Faculty members also acknowledge ChatGPT’s ability to facilitate personalized learning. The focus of medical education on learner-centered approaches is reflected in the way students engage with content in ChatGPT [9]. The conversational style of ChatGPT enables students to engage with content at their own speed, reflecting the focus of medical education on learner-centered approaches. Students can ask further questions, ask for clarification, or ask for simplification and receive instant feedback without the limitations of teaching sessions. These interactions could promote self-directed learning and increased learner engagement [10].

Beyond teaching activities, faculty also identify practical administrative benefits. Drafting emails, report preparation, summarizing documents, and synthesizing information can help to alleviate administrative burden so teachers can spend more time mentoring and engaging in scholarly activities [11]. However importantly, faculty enthusiasm is still kept in check. In all studies, teachers have consistently indicated that ChatGPT should not take the place of the human aspects of medical education. There are irreplaceable contributions that can only be made by humans, such as clinical judgment, professional mentorship, empathy, and role modeling [12].

Concerns Regarding Accuracy, Integrity, and Professionalism
While the use of ChatGPT in medical education holds promise, there is significant worry across the academic community. These concerns are not meant to imply that they are opposed to innovation, but rather that they are dedicated to ensuring educational quality and professionalism [13].

One of the most important problems is still accuracy. Generative AI systems may generate inaccurate information, fabricated references, and misleading explanations and present them convincingly. In the healthcare industry, where misinformation can have significant consequences, it is no surprise that doctors are hesitant to use AI-generated content without checking it. Doctors are rightly wary of going on the record with information created by AI, where inaccurate info can have serious implications. An important aspect of the use of outputs that may detract from some of the efficiencies sought by teachers is the need for fact-checking [14].

Academic honesty is also a major issue. Faculty members are concerned that students could use ChatGPT to submit assignments, reflections, or any other work designed to assess their understanding. With the rise in the sophistication of AI-generated content, it is going to be tougher to tell AI-generated content from original student work. This challenge introduces questions concerning authorship, authenticity, and fairness related to assessment in education [15].

Concerns also cover the development of critical thinking and clinical reasoning abilities. In medical education, it is not just about imparting knowledge; it is also about fostering analytical thinking, diagnostic reasoning, and professional judgment. Relying too much on AI-generated answers can foster a passive engagement with information, potentially reducing the critical and creative thinking needed to solve intricate clinical issues. Over-dependence on AI responses could lead to passive learning rather than active problem-solving with complex clinical questions. Teachers are worried about the effects of excessive reliance on AI, which could impede the intellectual skills required for effective healthcare delivery [16].

There is also a sense of skepticism due to ethical issues. Issues of data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, and evidence-based medicine are still not resolved. These challenges are acknowledged by medical educators, especially in a field that has ethical responsibilities and patient safety as its core principles [17].

Rethinking Assessment in the Age of AI
The impact of generative AI on medical education is likely more significant than in any other area, particularly when it comes to assessment. The integrity of traditional, written assignments and unsupervised take-home tasks is under threat from AI, questioning the authenticity and independent work long assumed to be the nature of such tasks [18].

As a result, faculty have started to think about how to change assessment approaches. More weight is being given to viva voce examinations, Objective Structured Clinical Examinations, application-oriented problem-solving exercises, workplace-based assessment, and oral examinations. These approaches test higher-order cognitive skills and clinical reasoning, which are less likely to be misused by AI. Many teachers argue that, instead of outright banning, the inclusion of AI literacy in medical education is a better approach. AI tools should be taught to students, and they should also be equipped with the skills to critically analyze the results, identify inaccuracies, understand bias, and be aware of the ethical boundaries. This approach will move the focus of education from detection and punishment to responsible and informed use [19]. With the advent of generative AI, this is now the time to modernize assessment practices and uphold skills that are distinctly human, such as critical thinking, communication, clinical judgment, and ethical reasoning [20].

Building Institutional Readiness through Faculty Development
There are several factors that affect faculty attitudes towards ChatGPT: their familiarity with technology, disciplinary background, teaching experience, and institutional culture. Teachers who have already experienced digital tools are more likely to be open to exploring the possibilities for using AI. In contrast, teachers with less experience are likely to be uncertain or reticent. Institutional support is a key determinant of acceptance. Regularly, faculty members point to the need for policies, guidance, and professional development that are clear and structured. Adoption is often done in an uncoordinated way in the absence of institutional frameworks, leading to variability in practice and uncertainty over the right way to use it [21].

Therefore, faculty development programs must be made a priority. Educational programs can provide hands-on experience in prompt engineering, AI-generated content creation, critical analysis of AI-generated content, and ethical considerations for work with AI. These can alleviate technophobia and create a sense of confidence about responsible use. Equally significant is the creation of governance mechanisms that will deal with transparency, academic integrity, disclosure of authorship, data privacy, and acceptable use. title_key: development of role based information models and software shells as a means of aesthetic education application methodology and experience of hybrid interaction with llm|iunov
title: Development of role-based information models and software shells as a means of aesthetic education: Application methodology and experience of hybrid interaction with LLM
abstract: The article presents a methodology for the aesthetic education of students in the process of information training based on the pedagogical strategy of role-based information modeling. The key idea is that the educational effect is achieved in the process of developing and analyzing role-based information models oriented toward people close to the students who have age-related and cognitive limitations. Two implementation variants are described: a standard one for students of all fields of study, and an advanced one for IT students.Software shells, working with which does not require programming, serve as an additional tool for humanities students and school teachers.Checklists are provided for evaluating the developed models according to the criteria of digital aesthetics, empathetic design, and the "ZNAK" (sign) acronym (Protection, Clarity, Adaptation, Beauty). The validity of the conclusions is substantiated by methodological triangulation. The experience of hybrid interaction with a large language model (DeepSeek) during the development of the checklists is described.The work is oriented toward a wide target audience: university professors, school teachers, and methodologists.The novelty of the research examined in the article lies in the fact that the concepts of "digital aesthetics", "empathetic design", and the "ZNAK" acronym are adapted for the purposes of aesthetic education for the first time and are implemented in a two-level system of information model development, as well as in software shells for the construction of pedagogical software tools by humanities students and teachers.The international significance of the study consists in its contribution to the development of aesthetic competencies in education: the methodology aligns with foreign research and can be adapted for the educational systems of other countries.

title_key: para alem do codigo formacao de mulheres em programacao com tecnologias web e multimidia em tempos de ia generativa|pimentel
title: Para Além do Código: Formação de Mulheres em Programação com Tecnologias Web e Multimídia em Tempos de IA Generativa
abstract: The underrepresentation of women in Computing calls for initiatives that promote not only access to education, but also conditions that foster participation, retention, and continuity. This paper presents and analyzes four free, remote introductory programming courses offered between July 2025 and June 2026: three nationwide vacation courses and one course aimed at a university community. The courses combined the teaching of Python and Scratch with programming problems contextualized in everyday situations and social issues, support from teaching assistants, and educational resources developed by the team, including Scratch animations. Gender and inclusion issues were integrated both into discussions and into programming and authoring activities. Web technologies and multimedia resources supported teaching, mentoring, and authoring activities. Throughout the courses, teaching and assessment strategies were also adapted to the context of the increasing availability of generative AI tools, including the replacement of automated exercise grading with manual assessment of the solutions and the programming strategies employed. The analysis of these experiences identified strategies related to flexibility in forms of participation, pedagogical support, the integration of social issues into the teaching of computing concepts, the promotion of authorship and creativity, and the adaptation of course planning to needs observed during the courses. The progressive expansion of the teaching assistants’ roles also stands out: they began to take on teaching activities and, in one case, to lead a new course offering. Based on these experiences, we systematize strategies and lessons learned that can inform the planning of Computing outreach initiatives committed to the inclusion of women and to the continuity of such initiatives.
authors: ["M. da Gra\u00e7a C. Pimentel", "K. R. da Hora Rodrigues", "Juliana Maria De Almeida Carvalho", "Maria Eduarda Dantas Leite Pessoa", "Sarah Duzi Ferreira Costa"]
venue: Brazilian Symposium on Multimedia and the Web

title_key: visual question and answer educational game design for natural and social sciences learning|pangestu
title: Visual Question and Answer Educational Game Design for Natural and Social Sciences Learning
abstract: Natural and Social Sciences (IPAS) learning in elementary schools is still dominated by lectures, which makes it difficult for students to understand abstract concepts. This study aims to design an educational game based on Visual Question and Answer (VQA) as an IPAS learning medium for fourth-grade students at UPT SD Negeri Papungan 02 and to determine its feasibility. The study employed Research and Development (R&D) with the Multimedia Development Life Cycle (MDLC) model consisting of six stages: concept, design, material collecting, assembly, testing, and distribution. The game was built with the HTML5-based Construct 2 engine and integrated with an Express.js backend connected to the Google Gemini API to generate adaptive exam questions based on students' practice scores. Feasibility was measured through black box testing, media expert validation, material expert validation, and a student response questionnaire. The results show that all 22 black box scenarios were successful, and the feasibility percentages were 87% from the media experts, 100% from the material expert, and 91.43% from the student responses, all in the very feasible category. The VQA educational game is feasible as an IPAS learning medium. Future work should add more learning materials, audio narration, and an offline version.

title_key: closing the explanation experiment loop an llm guided interactive simulation framework for power system dynamics education|eguakun
title: Closing the Explanation-Experiment Loop: An LLM-Guided Interactive Simulation Framework for Power System Dynamics Education
abstract: Power system dynamics is among the hardest subjects in an electrical engineering curriculum: the governing behaviour that must be modeled is fast, coupled, and mathematically complex, and the hardware that exhibits such behaviour is expensive and limited. Simulation-based laboratories fill in part of this gap, but are usually scripted: students perform a set sequence of steps, and are never told the why the trajectory takes the form it does. Large language models (LLMs) can supply that explanation on demand, but alone they hallucinate numerical claims and cannot be trusted with quantitative engineering content. This paper presents a three-layer interactive learning framework that couples an LLM to a live dynamic simulator so that every explanation the model produces is conditioned on, and verifiable against, the numerical state of a running microgrid model. We specify the architecture, the grounded interaction protocol that binds the language layer to the simulation layer, and a set of guardrails designed to detect and withhold unsupported numerical claims before they are presented to the student. We instantiate the framework on microgrid secondary frequency control and report a reproducible case study: a center-of-inertia model with droop and integral secondary control, exercised over the proportional gain, the integral gain, and the inertia constant. The case study yields a closed-form stability boundary, $K_{i}^{\text {crit }}=\left(D / 2 H+1 / T_{g}\right)\left(D+1 / R+K_{p}\right)$, that agrees with time-domain simulation to within the resolution of the sweep, and that gives the AI layer an analytic ground truth against which student predictions can be checked rather than merely paraphrased. The learning-objective mapping is described, as well as the misconceptions that each experiment aims to uncover, and a pre-specified classroom assessment procedure. No human subject data are claimed, and this paper presents the system and its validated simulation layer.
authors: ["Osasumwen Cedric Ogiesoba-Eguakun", "S. U. Ur Rashid", "R. Sah", "Phani Kumar Inkollu", "Suman Rath", "Douglas Jussaume"]

title_key: generative ai and the future of higher education transforming pedagogy assessment and student engagement|tilak
title: Generative Ai and the Future of Higher Education: Transforming Pedagogy, Assessment, and Student Engagement
abstract: Generative AI (the Large Language Models that can generate coherent text, code, mathematical reasoning and creative content on demand) poses a challenge to the structure of higher education, one of a deeper nature than any other educational technology that has come before it, not just because it provides a new channel through which to deliver content, but because it changes the epistemological relationship between the learner, the knowledge and the educator. The paper proposes a Generative AI Higher Education Framework (GAEF) that combines an adaptive LLM pedagogy engine, an AI-resilient assessment redesign module, a personalised student engagement system, and an academic integrity management layer that is being evaluated in 38 higher education institutions (HEIs) (16 research universities, 14 teaching-focused colleges, and 8 community colleges) involving 12,400 students (8,680 train / 3,720 test; split chronological 70/30) with 4,200 faculty members, and 92,400 sessions of learning interactions over an 18-month evaluation period. The GAEF achieves a composite educational-effectiveness score of $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{0. 8 6 3}$ against expert-validated pedagogical outcome benchmarks, outperforming ML-only adaptive learning systems $(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{0. 7 4 4}$; +16.0% $[(0.863-0.744) / 0.744])$, rule-based EdTech platforms $(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{0. 6 2 8}$; +37.4% [(0.863-0.628)/0.628]), and human-only conventional pedagogy $(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{0. 5 1 6}; +\mathbf{6 7. 2 \%}[(\mathbf{0. 8 6 3}-\mathbf{0. 5 1 6}) / \mathbf{0. 5 1 6}])$. Outcomes of deployment for the cohort of institutions: increase in student learning outcome (46.2%), increase in assessment validity (32.8%), increase in student engagement (54.6%), decrease in dropout and attrition rate (28.6%), increase in faculty productivity (36.8%) and decrease in academic integrity incidents (41.8%). Sub-dimension scores: Pedagogical Transformation $(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{0. 8 9 6})$; Assessment Redesign (0.874); Student Engagement Enhancement (0.851); Academic Integrity Management (0.819). Without development of critical thinking, the effectiveness drops to 0.786 (-8.9% [(0.863-0.786)/0.863]) with deployed mitigation protocols for both circumstances, and for high academic integrity incident rates, it drops to 0.728 (-15.6% [(0.863-0.728)/0.863]) with both mitigation protocols deployed.
authors: ["G. Tilak", "Anuja Palkar", "Jayashree Patole", "Archana Borde", "Sandip Sane", "Rajeshwari Patil"]

title_key: analysis of the use of and attitudes towards generative artificial inteligence among graphic art students|nakic
title: Analysis of the Use of and Attitudes Towards Generative Artificial Inteligence Among Graphic Art Students
abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (genAI) is reshaping higher education by transforming learning processes, teaching practices, and creative disciplines such as graphic design. Despite the growing adoption of genAI tools, empirical evidence on their use and perceived impact among graphic arts students remains limited. This study examines the frequency and purposes of genAI use, students' perceptions of its benefits and risks, and the relationships between AI literacy, usage patterns, and responsible use in higher education. Data were collected through an anonymous online questionnaire completed by 202 undergraduate and postgraduate graphic arts students at the Faculty of Natural Sciences and Engineering, University of Ljubljana. Descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rank correlation analysis were used to examine the data. The findings indicate that most students are familiar with genAI and use it regularly, primarily to explain course content, generate ideas, write academic texts, summarise materials, and search for information. A statistically significant positive correlation was found between self-assessed knowledge of genAI and the frequency of its use, suggesting that greater familiarity with the technology encourages its integration into academic work. However, no statistically significant relationships were identified between self-assessed AI literacy and either the perceived benefits and risks of genAI or students' self-control in using these tools. Participants recognised substantial advantages, including increased efficiency, time savings, and improved access to information, while simultaneously expressing concerns about unreliable outputs, plagiarism, reduced critical thinking, ethical issues, privacy, and dependence on technology. The results show that effective integration of genAI into graphic art education requires not only technical proficiency but also the systematic development of AI literacy, critical evaluation skills, ethical awareness, and clear institutional guidelines for responsible and sustainable use.

title_key: development of digital competences of scientific and pedagogical workers and students of medical education in conditions of digital transformation|chornenka
title: DEVELOPMENT OF DIGITAL COMPETENCES OF SCIENTIFIC AND PEDAGOGICAL WORKERS AND STUDENTS OF MEDICAL EDUCATION IN CONDITIONS OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
abstract: The purpose of the research is to substantiate the structure of digital competencies of scientific and pedagogical workers and medical education students and to develop a conceptual model of their development in the conditions of digital transformation. Methods. Bibliometric analysis of scientific publications, analysis and generalization of international normative documents and frameworks of digital competences, comparative and systemic analysis, methods of systematization, modelling and generalization were used. The results. The main directions of the development of digital competences in the modern educational and scientific environment are determined, international approaches to their formation are summarized, the structure of digital competences is proposed, which includes educational, research-analytical, educational-methodical, management-communication, clinical-digital and end-to-end components, and a conceptual model of their development is developed taking into account the use of digital technologies, open science and generative artificial intelligence Conclusions. The proposed model can be used as a methodological basis for assessing the level of digital competences, improving educational programs, planning the professional development of scientific and pedagogical workers, and digital training of students of medical education.

title_key: generative ai use and legal research competence among law students in bangladesh the roles of ai literacy and formal training|islam
title: Generative AI Use and Legal Research Competence among Law Students in Bangladesh: The Roles of AI Literacy and Formal Training
abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering legal education, yet evidence remains limited on whether frequent use itself translates into stronger legal research competence in emerging legal-education systems. This study examines the association between GenAI use, AI literacy/responsible-use awareness, formal AI training, and self-reported legal research competence among 385 respondents in Bangladesh. The supplied cross-sectional dataset was analysed using descriptive statistics, item-level diagnostics, bivariate association tests, one-way analysis of variance, and hierarchical moderated regression. The results show that use frequency had a small positive bivariate association with legal research competence (r = .138, p = .0066), whereas AI literacy/responsible-use awareness had a substantially stronger association (r = .353, p < .001). Formal AI training was also associated with higher competence scores: respondents with no training averaged 3.45, those with short orientation 3.56, and those with course/certified training 3.62; the overall difference was statistically significant (F = 5.29, p = .0054, η² = .027). In the multivariable model, AI literacy remained the dominant predictor, formal training retained a positive effect, and the direct contribution of use frequency was no longer statistically significant. The frequency × AI-literacy interaction was also non-significant. These results suggest that competence is linked less to exposure alone than to verification, risk awareness, human oversight, and structured training. However, internal-consistency coefficients for the multi-item blocks were low, requiring cautious interpretation and instrument refinement before confirmatory latent-variable modelling. The study contributes a capability-centred perspective to GenAI adoption in legal education and identifies concrete priorities for curriculum design in Bangladesh.

Keywords: generative AI; legal education; legal research competence; AI literacy; responsible AI; formal training; Bangladesh
authors: ["Shopnil Islam", "Md. Hanif Iqbal Hawlader", "Md. Rohmot Ali Tonoy", "Mannan Kazi Abdul"]

title_key: does chatgpt influence metacognitive calibration during undergraduate physics problem solving|dowsett
title: Does ChatGPT influence metacognitive calibration during undergraduate physics problem solving?
abstract: We present a controlled pilot study examining how access to generative Artificial Intelligence influences metacognitive calibration, the alignment between perceived and actual learning. Second-year undergraduate physics students of the University of Bath were split into a control group, completing three successive first-year exam problems of comparable difficulty under standard exam conditions, and an experimental group, in which ChatGPT access was permitted during the intermediate problem. We quantify the performance improvement of students via a partial-credit marking scheme, while their perceived improvement is recorded through self-assessment questions. Students with access to ChatGPT show a ∼60% improvement in calibration accuracy, primarily associated with a reduction in underconfidence. Our exploratory study suggests that the educational value of generative AI may extend beyond performance by supporting students in forming more accurate assessments of their own performance, and in turn, understanding.

title_key: bace blooms asymmetric hybrid cognitive level classification educational large language model|yi
title: BACE: Bloom’s Asymmetric Hybrid Cognitive-Level Classification Educational Large Language Model
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used in intelligent teaching and cognitive-level classification. However, mainstream Transformer architectures incur redundant attention computation, and a single feed-forward network struggles to perform the fine-grained routing of features for Bloom’s cognitive features. This study proposes BACE, an educational LLM for cognitive-level text classification based on an asymmetric hybrid architecture guided by Bloom’s taxonomy. Built on the pretrained ChatGLM3-6B, BACE replaces the MLP in the first 4 layers with a shallow Top-2 sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing module to achieve token-level dispatching of cognitive features while retaining the self-attention mechanism. The middle 20 layers retain the native self-attention and MLP structures to maintain semantic transition. In the last 4 layers, attention is replaced with a deep, selective state-space modeling strategy, combined with chain-of-thought fine-tuning based on Bloom’s taxonomy, to integrate the global instructional context. Experiments on a public computer science course question dataset across multiple random seeds show that BACE achieves an average accuracy of 73.56% and a weighted F1 score of 0.6915, improving on ChatGLM3-6B (65.78%/0.6011) by 7.78 percentage points and 0.0904, respectively. Although its accuracy and weighted F1 are slightly lower than those of Qwen1.5-7B, BACE attains a BLEU-4 of 0.3426 and a ROUGE-L of 0.4601 on the generated chain-of-thought reasoning, both outperforming open-source models including Qwen1.5-7B, Mistral-7B, and Llama-3-8B. Through its asymmetric hybrid architecture, the model enables the classification of Bloom’s cognitive levels and provides a scalable technical pathway for question-answering-based cognitive-level assessment in intelligent education scenarios.

title_key: ethnomathematics in the age of artificial intelligence navigating cultural preservation and technological advancement|addae
title: Ethnomathematics in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Navigating Cultural Preservation and Technological Advancement
abstract: This study maps and synthesises two adjacent bodies of literature—research on ethnomathematics and culturally responsive mathematics instruction focused on Akan cultural practices, and research on artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education—to propose a culturally responsive, AI-supported instructional framework for Ghanaian classrooms. A systematic scoping review was conducted following the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) and PRISMA 2020 flow conventions. Six databases were searched for records published between 2005 and 2025, supplemented by hand-searching. AI was operationalised broadly, from intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning systems to generative AI from late 2022 onwards. Of 612 records, 25 studies were retained for qualitative thematic synthesis. The synthesis indicates that kente weaving, Adinkra symbolism, market transactions, and drumming patterns encode mathematical ideas such as symmetry, proportion, sequence, and logical reasoning. The AI-focused studies, most of which predate generative AI, suggest that these tools can support personalised, interactive, and contextualised learning. No included study combines the two strands in the Akan context; this absence is a central finding and motivates the proposed framework. Blending ethnomathematics with AI is associated with greater cultural relevance, engagement, and conceptual clarity, although digitising Indigenous knowledge raises ethical questions of ownership, representation, and community consent.
venue: Journal of Mathematics Instruction, Social Research and Opinion

title_key: incorporating cognitive load and knowledge transfer for multi domain knowledge tracing|zhang
title: Incorporating Cognitive Load and Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Tracing
abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) aims to assess students' dynamic knowledge states from their learning histories. While most existing KT methods focus on single-domain learning with notable success, real-world learning scenarios often involve multiple domains simultaneously, introducing two critical factors: 1) Cognitive load, arising from managing learning across domains in both temporal and knowledge dimensions. 2) Knowledge transfer, where knowledge states in one domain influence related states both within and across domains. In this paper, we focus on exploring these factors to improve students' knowledge state assessment in multi-domain learning scenarios and propose a novel method incorporating cognitive Load and knowledge Transfer for Multi-domain Knowledge Tracing (LT-MKT). Specifically, to bridge isolated domains, LT-MKT first integrates textual information from questions and their associated concepts to construct a Multi-domain Hierarchical Graph, leveraging the advanced representational capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Then, cross-domain features in both the temporal and knowledge dimensions are explicitly modeled to capture the effects of cognitive load. Additionally, a knowledge transfer module is designed to model the propagation of knowledge states within and across domains. By jointly modeling these factors, LT-MKT enables more accurate prediction of students' future performance. Finally, extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/sosweetzhang/LT-MKT.
authors: ["Haotian Zhang", "Shu-Cun Wang", "Jin-Ze Wu", "Liang Ding", "Shuo-Chen Liu", "Zhen-Ya Huang", "Jing Sha", "Shi-Jin Wang", "Qi Liu"]
venue: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title_key: an ai integrated relational curriculum mapping framework for alignment and transparency in medical education implementation study|badeau
title: An AI-Integrated Relational Curriculum Mapping Framework for Alignment and Transparency in Medical Education: Implementation Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Medical school curricula are managed through fragmented, static tools that prevent faculty and curriculum committees from seeing a unified view of content scope, sequence, and licensing examination alignment. Governance relies on manual reporting that is neither timely nor consistent, and no widely adopted platform incorporates a generative AI agent that queries a relational curriculum database to produce tailored, on-demand reports.


OBJECTIVE
This study aimed to design, implement, and evaluate a 4-phase, AI-integrated relational curriculum mapping framework providing faculty self-directed curriculum search; cross-course alignment reports classifying content as redundant, complementary, or a gap, with recommendations; and alignment with United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE) content and accreditation requirements.


METHODS
We implemented the framework during academic year 2025-2026. It captures session learning objectives (SLOs) annually; maps them to program objectives, course objectives, USMLE codes, Association of American Medical Colleges keywords, and Bloom's levels using a large language model with expert verification; centralizes verified data in a relational database (Airtable) with faculty read-only search; and uses a second AI agent via an API to generate on-demand reports on scope, sequence, redundancy, gaps, and USMLE alignment across all 16 preclerkship courses and all clinical clerkship rotations.


RESULTS
Course directors gained self-directed curriculum access through Airtable Extensions search. Cross-course vertical alignment reports identified redundant, complementary, and gap findings and generated course-level recommendations. An analysis of 2 preclerkship courses identified 50 matched SLO pairs across 3 USMLE pathology domains within minutes. A USMLE Step 1 alignment report across all 16 courses identified a curriculum-wide pathology coverage deficit (42% vs a target of 45%-55%) that was descriptively consistent with institutional performance data (not formally tested). An accreditation query identified all preclerkship and clerkship content on a specified topic and generated Data Collection Instrument-ready documentation within seconds. A Medical Education Program Objective coverage analysis across all 9 clinical clerkships, generated within minutes, found documented coverage for 24 of 25 (96%) program objectives and 1 objective with no matching SLO in any clerkship, a gap not previously tracked. In a blinded validation study, 3 independent course directors each coded a 30-SLO sample; agreement with the database (Fleiss κ, 3 raters plus database) was substantial at the exact-code level (κ=0.67, 95% CI 0.55-0.78) and almost perfect at the USMLE domain level (κ=0.94, 95% CI 0.88-1.00).


CONCLUSIONS
An AI-integrated relational curriculum database with a faculty-facing search interface can convert curriculum governance from a periodic, retrospective activity into a continuous, self-service one, producing alignment and gap analyses within minutes rather than weeks. Workload effects have not been formally measured. Extension to assessment items and prospective correlation with licensing examination outcomes are planned.

title_key: ai integrated learning across four generative ai supported classrooms students perceptions digital confidence critical digital literacy and information evaluation|pattaufi
title: AI-Integrated Learning Across Four Generative AI-Supported Classrooms: Students’ Perceptions, Digital Confidence, Critical Digital Literacy, and Information Evaluation
abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in higher education, but evidence remains limited on how students report multiple digital-learning outcomes across classrooms using different platforms within a common instructional framework. This exploratory posttest-only study describes four intact classrooms using ChatGPT (n = 29), Gemini (n = 29), DeepSeek (n = 28), and Perplexity AI (n = 32) during an eight-session AI-integrated learning program. Because each platform was represented by only one classroom, platform and classroom effects could not be separated; therefore, the study reports descriptive classroom profiles rather than platform-level causal or inferential effects. The four classrooms showed distinct descriptive patterns across the outcomes. The DeepSeek-supported classroom had the highest observed means for AITBLM perception (4.10), Digital Confidence (4.06), and Critical Digital Literacy (4.07), whereas the Perplexity AI-supported classroom had the highest observed Technology Information Evaluation mean (4.21). Across classrooms, AITBLM perception ranged from 3.86 to 4.10, Digital Confidence from 3.84 to 4.06, Critical Digital Literacy from 3.90 to 4.07, and Technology Information Evaluation from 3.89 to 4.21. ChatGPT and Gemini showed nearly identical AITBLM perception means (3.91 and 3.90), while Gemini and Perplexity AI showed comparatively higher TIE means (4.08 and 4.21). These contrasts indicate different classroom response profiles rather than a consistent ranking across all outcomes. The findings are exploratory and should not be interpreted as evidence that one AI platform is more effective than another.

title_key: use of chatgpt assisted feedback to improve english writing among students of first year of bachillerato|anchapaxi
title: Use of ChatGPT Assisted Feedback to Improve English Writing among students of First year of Bachillerato
abstract: This educational case study examined changes in English writing performance among first-year Bachillerato students in the context of ChatGPT-assisted feedback. The study involved 171 students from Nelson Isauro Torres Educational Unit in Cayambe, Ecuador, during the 2026–2027 academic year. A quantitative pre-test–post-test approach was used to compare writing performance across four dimensions: grammar, vocabulary, organization and coherence, and task completion. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and individual score comparisons. The findings revealed an increase in the overall mean score from 6.27 to 7.06 points. Furthermore, 72.5% of students improved their performance, while 8.8% maintained their scores and 18.7% experienced a decrease. Organization and coherence showed the greatest average improvement, whereas grammar remained the lowest-scoring dimension. These findings indicate positive changes in writing performance while highlighting differences in individual progress. Although the absence of a control group prevents causal conclusions regarding ChatGPT, the study provides contextualized evidence supporting further investigation into technology-assisted feedback, teacher guidance, and individualized writing instruction in secondary education settings where English is learned as a foreign language.
authors: ["Ra\u00fal Fernando Coyaguillo Anchapaxi", "Jos\u00e9 Luis Pomavilla Pati\u00f1o", "Mauro David Villacr\u00e9s Benalc\u00e1zar"]

title_key: when algorithms fail why traditional teaching still outperforms ai in language learning|shimray
title: When algorithms fail: Why traditional teaching still outperforms AI in language learning
abstract: This quasi-experimental study investigates the comparative efficacy of generative AI-enhanced self-learning and traditional Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) in Thailand’s low-proficiency English as a foreign language (EFL) context. The intensive exploration was conducted through pre/post-tests (TOEIC-modelled, α = 0.82) and a mixed-methods analysis of 36 students who shared similar English proficiency backgrounds. The findings reveal a statistically significant advantage for the teacher-led CLT approach. The CLT group (n = 16) attained a post-test mean of 63.6% (SD = 9.4), substantially outperforming the AI group (n = 20) at 38.7% (SD = 8.1), with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.12). Qualitatively, while AI was valued for its flexibility (33.3%) and grammar support (16.7%), students eagerly reported critical shortcomings in developing oral proficiency and a sense of dehumanised interaction (19.4% cited loneliness). Conversely, CLT was strongly associated with essential social engagement (41.7%) and immediate feedback. Grounded in sociocultural and self-determination theories, these findings underscore AI’s current inability to provide human-mediated scaffolding in low-proficiency settings. The study concludes by advocating for a context-sensitive hybrid model integrating AI’s adaptive features with CLT’s interpersonal strengths, cautioning against AI-centric approaches in foundational language acquisition. This can suggest that AI is most effective when carefully scaffolded by human instructors who can compensate for its social and contextual limitations, and has important implications for teacher training programs, which may need to incorporate technology mediation skills alongside traditional pedagogical methods.
venue: Studies in English language and education

title_key: exploring the design space of llm based programming support in cs education a scoping review through the lens of assistance governance|kim
title: Exploring the Design Space of LLM-Based Programming Support in CS Education: A Scoping Review through the Lens of Assistance Governance
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become integrated into programming education, learner-facing systems increasingly differ in how that assistance is bounded, enacted, and controlled. These governance decisions are often described implicitly, making it difficult to compare systems in educationally meaningful ways. To address this gap, we conduct a scoping review and qualitative synthesis of 90 peer-reviewed LLM-based programming support systems in CS education. We analyze assistance governance through three dimensions, which we refer to collectively as PEA: Policy, capturing what forms of help are allowed or restricted; Enforcement, capturing how those boundaries are operationalized through interaction and system behavior; and Authority, capturing who can configure, adapt, or override them during use. Our findings show that systems often share similar pedagogical goals, but implement those goals through varied enforcement mechanisms. At the same time, authority remains highly centralized in system logic, with fewer systems giving learners or instructors runtime control. This work contributes PEA as a three-dimensional analytic lens, a governance codebook empirically refined within these dimensions, and a map of underexplored configurations in the current design space of LLM-based programming support. By making these explicit and comparable, PEA offers a vocabulary for analyzing existing systems and designing future tools that are pedagogically bounded, configurable, and accountable.
authors: ["Minsun Kim", "S. M. A. Monisha", "Zi-Han Wu", "David H. Smith"]
