title_key: the integration of generative artificial intelligence into tertiary health education a scoping review|cheung
title: The integration of generative artificial intelligence into tertiary health education: A scoping review
abstract: This scoping review aims to provide an overview of the integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in tertiary health education, including its practical applications in tertiary health education programs and how these applications are perceived by stakeholders. A literature search was conducted in five databases, including Ovid Medline, Ovid Emcare, Scopus, CINAHL, and ERIC. Articles integrating GenAI in tertiary health disciplines were included. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews checklist was followed in the reporting of results. Overall, 20 studies were included and three categories were identified: 1) application of GenAI in tertiary health education, 2) perceptions of GenAI use in health education, and 3) ethical and responsible use of GenAI in health education. Currently, GenAI is being integrated as a complementary tool to automate academic tasks and improve the critical thinking skills of tertiary health students through optimizing class designs. Although GenAI applications were well-received by students due to high accessibility, concerns over misinformation, over-reliance, and data confidentiality were consistently flagged. The review identified a lack of formal AI literacy training, highlighting the need for structured AI literacy training modules and clear ethical guidelines to support tertiary health students in using GenAI. GenAI applications are being rapidly integrated into tertiary health education, primarily for automated grading/feedback and improvement of learning outcomes. Future research is recommended to investigate the long-term impacts of GenAI and how to implement AI literacy training in current tertiary health education programs.

title_key: an international students meaning making in calculus across languages a longitudinal case study in indonesia|zulfa
title: An International Student’s Meaning-Making in Calculus across Languages: A Longitudinal Case Study in Indonesia
abstract: Although research has examined language in mathematics education and international students’ academic experiences, less is known about how international students construct mathematical meaning in calculus across languages over time. This study examined an international student’s learning of Differential and Integral Calculus in Indonesia. Data were collected through interviews, classroom observations, assignments, examination responses, and learning documents across two semesters in a longitudinal qualitative single-case study. Thematic analysis used four predetermined dimensions, organized into three groups: language use and mathematical representations; prior mathematical knowledge and independent practice; and learning support and practice. Linguistic differences primarily affected the participant’s access to verbal explanations and mathematical terminology, while familiar symbols and graphs provided additional entry points to calculus. His work documented engagement with derivative procedures, graphical information, and integral techniques through prior knowledge and independent practice, although consistent improvement in conceptual understanding was not established. The participant found lecturer support and assignments helpful and used generative artificial intelligence (AI) to identify topics, access explanations, and obtain practice examples. However, AI explanations were not always sufficient. This case highlights the need to examine mathematical work alongside linguistic challenges and learning strategies in multilingual calculus learning.

title_key: toward industry aligned flexible computing undergraduate programs in the ai era|zohar
title: Toward Industry-Aligned, Flexible, Computing Undergraduate Programs in the AI Era
abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the technology labor market and raising fundamental questions regarding the adequacy of traditional Computing Undergraduate Programs (CUPs) in preparing graduates for evolving software development practices. Historically, entry level software development roles have served as a critical transition between academic study and professional practice. However, the increasing integration of GenAI-based tools automates routine coding tasks, thereby reducing the relative importance of basic programming. At the same time, it elevates the need for higher-order competencies, including system level reasoning, architectural design, system integration, and the critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs, as well as concerns of security and reliability. Correspondingly, graduates face increasing difficulty in securing initial positions. These developments raise the question of whether existing CUP structures provide an adequate foundation for early-career competencies. In response, this spotlight proposes a staged modular structure organized into coherent packs, each pack includes courses, defined learning outcomes and competences alongside integrative projects. In addition, the proposed modular structure identifies the appropriate point, recognized by the institutions that will grant professional certificates, with which students can begin engaging in entry-level professional roles while continuing their academic studies. Such parallel engagement may create a feedback loop between academic learning and professional practice: practical experience can deepen the relevance and value of academic study, while continued coursework can support more reflective, informed, and theoretically grounded professional development.
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.2

title_key: effects of generative artificial intelligence gai utilization in social science education guidelines for developing a reference primer|cabuyadao
title: Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) Utilization In Social Science Education: Guidelines for Developing a Reference Primer
abstract: This descriptive-correlational research explored the effects of the utilization of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in social science education as a basis for the development of guidelines for a reference primer for social science educators. It aimed to present the respondent’s profile in terms of age, sex, year/level taught, and used AI tools; determine the contribution of GAI to lesson planning, teaching, and learning assessment; and identify the significant differences in the use of GAI grouped according to profiles. The study utilized a descriptive-correlational design, which answered by 30 social science educators. The data were analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, t-test, and F-test. The results showed that most of the respondents were aged 21-30 years with 6-10 years of teaching experience. The tools used were common and facilitated content creation, presentation, and assessment tasks. The results showed that GAI significantly improved the efficiency of lesson preparation, student engagement during teaching, and timely and diverse assessment approaches. Significant differences in the use of GAI were found across the selected demographic and professional variables. The study concludes that GAI has a positive impact on teaching effectiveness when provided with systematic support like the recommendation to develop a GAI reference primer like Panangipablaak SocsAI, as well as ensuring continuous teacher training in the effective integration of AI in teaching.

title_key: teaching ux design to engineers in the age of artificial intelligence the double diamond as a framework for reskilling|chaima
title: Teaching UX Design to Engineers in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: The Double Diamond as a Framework for Reskilling
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence transforms software development and digital design practices, engineering education must address the interplay between technical expertise, an understanding of user needs, and critical judgment. This article examines the contribution of UX Design education to this evolution, using the Double Diamond model as a framework for structuring the design process. The research is based on a pedagogical experiment conducted at the École Supérieure Privée d’Ingénierie et de Technologies (ESPRIT) in Tunisia, as part of a 21-hour module for fourth-year students in web and mobile development during the 2025–2026 academic year. The methodological approach is based on the observation of teaching practices and the analysis of student work, including user interviews, personas, usage scenarios, and prototypes. The Double Diamond framework organizes the process into four phases: discover, define, develop, and deliver. It allows for an examination of how students explore usage scenarios, reframe problems, develop solutions, and subject their proposals to evaluation. The article also proposes a cross-cutting examination of the role of generative artificial intelligence in these phases, distinguishing between assisted production and the validation of design choices. It advances the hypothesis that teaching UX design can help broaden the skill set of future engineers, provided that technical mastery is integrated with human understanding, experimentation, and decision-making responsibility. This exploratory research proposes an analytical framework for studying this integration without presupposing the effects of the approach prior to the analysis of empirical data
venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology

title_key: instructor developed web based chemistry games design classroom implementation and student perceptions|tonami
title:
Instructor-Developed
Web-Based Chemistry Games: Design,
Classroom Implementation, and Student Perceptions
abstract: Course-specific digital learning materials can support engagement with chemical concepts, but their development may require programming expertise and external resources. This Technology Report describes the design, classroom implementation, and preliminary evaluation of two instructor-developed browser-based chemistry games used in an undergraduate analytical chemistry course. A central design principle was to make selected chemical information relevant to decisions during play rather than use chemistry only as quiz content. In Carbon Chain Puzzle, molecular names and formulas can help players anticipate simplified block geometry and plan spatial moves; in Titration Rush, stoichiometry, acid identity, and pKa can inform a coarse-to-fine titrant-addition strategy under a time–accuracy trade-off. Generative-AI-assisted coding supported implementation, while the instructor retained responsibility for chemical validity, instructional aims, gameplay, and final design decisions. A voluntary anonymous survey yielded 27 responses from 72 enrolled students. On a five-point rating scale, mean enjoyment scores were 4.59 and 4.67, and mean perceived-value scores as chemistry learning materials were 4.15 and 4.33 for Carbon Chain Puzzle and Titration Rush, respectively. Auxiliary web analytics documented use but were not treated as measures of conceptual understanding. The study addresses feasibility, student perceptions, and design considerations rather than learning gains, and documents an instructor-led case of developing chemistry games with generative-AI-assisted coding.

title_key: i check it when it feels wrong computer science student usage and perspectives on ai chatbots|rea
title: “I check it when it feels wrong” – Computer Science Student Usage and Perspectives on AI Chatbots
abstract: We present a qualitative interview study with 17 Canadian computer science and software engineering undergraduates exploring their self-initiated, unsupervised AI chatbot use. We find that most participants, despite being CS students often assumed to have stronger technical intuitions, lacked an accurate understanding of how generative AI produces output. This miscalibration was associated with plausibility-based fact-checking: participants who described genAI as a retrieval or database system had no reliable trigger for verifying confidently-stated misinformation. We discuss implications for AI literacy education and human-AI interaction design.
venue: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title_key: designer identity in the context of artificial intelligence a qualitative typology study on graphic design students|ozmutlu
title: Designer identity in the context of artificial intelligence: A qualitative typology study on graphic design students
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is changing design practice and raising questions about what it means to become a designer. This study examines how undergraduate graphic design students construct designer identities through professional positioning, creativity, control, and expectations for the future. A basic qualitative research design was employed with 18 students who had completed at least one comprehensive design project. Data were collected using a structured written form containing 16 open-ended questions, developed through a literature review and evaluation by a subject specialist and a qualitative research methods specialist. A five-stage hybrid thematic analysis combined deductive overarching categories with inductively generated codes and subcategories across five dimensions: designer identity, professional positioning, relationships with artificial intelligence, control, value and creativity, and perceptions of the future. Four subcategories were identified within each overarching category. Cross-category comparisons yielded four ideal-typical profiles: Technology-Integrated, Innovative, and Proactive; Traditional, Emotion/Art-Oriented, and Protective; Process/Development-Oriented and Cautious Student/Aspiring Designer; and Pragmatic, Functional, and Solution-Oriented. These profiles represent analytical configurations of meaning, not fixed participant groups; statements from the same participant could align with different profiles. Designer identity emerged as dynamic and context-sensitive, involving professional values, originality, perceived control, and technological change. Design education should recognize differing orientations toward artificial intelligence and support reflection on authorship, autonomy, and professional futures. Longitudinal and multi-institutional research could examine how these orientations develop across educational settings and stages.

title_key: world language teachers deliberative engagement with generative ai for designing meaningbased l2 reading instruction|ahnell
title: World language teachers' deliberative engagement with generative AI for designing meaning‐based L2 reading instruction
abstract: This interpretive qualitative case study examines how in‐service world language teachers deliberatively used, selectively adopted, or avoided generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools (e.g., ChatGPT, MagicSchool) while designing meaning‐based L2 reading instruction with authentic texts. Grounded in a sociocultural view of teacher learning and informed by an interactive approach to reading, teachers' engagement with GenAI is interpreted as a socioculturally mediated process situated within a shared pedagogical framework. Eight in‐service teachers enrolled in a graduate‐level literacy methods course designed L2 reading lessons using PreGAP, a meaning‐based framework for designing L2 literacy instruction. Analysis of whole‐group discussions revealed substantial variability in GenAI engagement, ranging from deliberate adoption to principled avoidance. Teachers' decisions reflected framework‐mediated pedagogical reasoning grounded in pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) and technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK). Across participants, GenAI was most often positioned as a bounded thought partner rather than a lesson generator within the constraints of meaning‐based instructional design. Findings suggest that teacher preparation programs should prioritize rigorous, sustained engagement with interactive, meaning‐based frameworks for L2 reading instruction with authentic texts before introducing GenAI as a tool to assist with lesson design.

title_key: editorial osotl 5 2|barr
title: Editorial: oSoTL 5(2)
abstract: In this bumper issue, we bring together eleven articles by authors from across the UK, Europe, and the USA. Six of these articles fall under two broad themes. The first is generative AI (GenAI): two articles consider what GenAI means for assessment, while two others put it to work, reimagining the course syllabus and auditing the curriculum. The second is mathematics and statistics anxiety, explored by two articles from psychology and the wider social sciences. The issue is rounded off by five articles on a broader range of topics, from professional services scholarship and shared reading to collaborative learning, open pedagogy, and the dual identity of artist and teacher-educator.
venue: Open Scholarship of Teaching and Learning

title_key: factors influencing the adoption of generative ai tools among university students a structured literature review|vats
title: Factors influencing the adoption of generative AI tools among university students: A structured literature review
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT are changing how university students access information, write, solve problems, write code and receive personalised academic support. Their rapid uptake has also raised concerns about accuracy, trust, privacy, academic integrity and overdependence. This paper presents a structured literature review of 20 scholarly publications from 2023 to 2026 that examine what influences students’ adoption of GenAI tools. The review draws on empirical, systematic and meta analytic studies, mainly those based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and UTAUT2. A thematic synthesis groups the determinants of adoption into four dimensions: technological, individual, social and contextual, and trust and risk. Perceived usefulness and performance expectancy are the most consistent positive predictors. Self efficacy, habit, facilitating conditions, social influence and academic value also support adoption. Trust, anxiety, perceived risk and AI literacy show effects that depend on context. The review argues that conventional acceptance models do not fully capture the features of GenAI, including output reliability, ethical use, academic integrity and the need for critical evaluation. It therefore proposes a multidimensional view that moves from simple acceptance toward effective and responsible adoption. The findings suggest that universities should pair access to AI tools with AI literacy training, clear institutional policies and faculty guidance. Future research should develop AI specific extensions of existing models, use longitudinal and cross cultural designs, and link GenAI use to measurable learning outcomes.

title_key: lead unsupervised fine grained visual representation learning with multi context enhanced entropy based adaptive distillation|dong
title: LEAD++: Unsupervised Fine-Grained Visual Representation Learning with Multi-context Enhanced Entropy-Based Adaptive Distillation

title_key: artificial intelligence in higher education transformations empirical evidence and challenges for student centred university learning|martinez
title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Transformations, Empirical Evidence and Challenges for Student-Centred University Learning
abstract: The rapid evolution and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, particularly following the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI (GenAI), have profoundly transformed teaching, learning and management practices in higher education worldwide. This paper aims to synthesise the empirical evidence available between 2020 and 2026 regarding the impact of AI in higher education, examining the prevalent technologies, pedagogical mediation, levels of human–AI collaboration, adoption patterns and ethical-normative implications. A systematic literature review was conducted in rigorous accordance with the PRISMA 2020 Statement. Six international scientific databases were consulted: Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, SciELO, PubMed and IEEE Xplore, identifying an initial corpus of 1,247 records. After the screening process for duplicates, title/abstract and full-text reading, 45 primary studies focused on university educational impact were selected, analytically complemented by global bibliometric and meta-systematic reviews of the period. Methodological quality was assessed using the MMAT (2018) tool and the certainty of the evidence via the GRADE approach. It is concluded that the predominant AI technologies in the literature are large language models (75.6 %), intelligent tutoring systems (31.1 %) and learning analytics tools (24.4 %). The principal applications concentrate on personalised learning (53.3 %), student motivation and engagement (46.7 %) and academic performance (42.2 %). However, evaluation of the autonomy continuum reveals a severe implementation gap: 45.56 % of integrations correspond to Substitution modalities (where AI replaces teaching functions), 39.05 % to Augmentation, 10.65 % to Toolification and only 4.73 % achieve genuine Human–AI Synergy. Longitudinally, student adoption reached near-universal levels (95 % in 2026), although gaps in ethical literacy and tensions surrounding academic integrity persist. The methodological quality of the corpus was high in 62.2 % of the studies, yet the global GRADE certainty was classified as low owing to the predominance of cross-sectional designs and heterogeneity of metrics. It may further be concluded that AI possesses a proven transformative potential to optimise university learning, yet its effectiveness does not reside in mere technological adoption, but rather in intentional pedagogical mediation (the PMAISE model), the evolution of teaching practice towards the AI-TPACK framework and the establishment of executable governance policies (Policy-as-Code). A human-centred integration framework based on four pillars and a five-phase operational strategy with a detailed matrix of success indicators for institutional scalability is proposed.
authors: ["D. L. La Red Mart\u00ednez", "J. Acosta", "S. Gerzel"]

title_key: epistemic framing in ai mediated university physics problem solving a qualitative multiple case study|tuveri
title: Epistemic framing in AI-mediated university physics problem solving: a qualitative multiple-case study
abstract: Research on large language model (LLM)-based generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in physics education has examined model performance, students’ evaluations of generated responses, and learning outcomes. Less is known about how generated explanations and calculations enter students’ observable physics problem-solving activity. This qualitative multiple-case study examines epistemic-frame sequences and their relation to solution quality, alongside students’ interactions with ChatGPT and their subsequent use of generated contributions. It analyses 30 submissions from 73 students across five university courses: 22 using ChatGPT and eight without it. ChatGPT was selected because its free version was students’ most frequently reported GenAI tool for independent study. Written artefacts and interaction records were analysed using Nguyen et al.’s problem framing framework, with solution quality assessed independently. Activity recurrently moved between conceptual and algorithmic physics, but frame-sequence length did not distinguish solution quality. Challenges and reformulations made students’ evaluation of ChatGPT responses visible, whereas incorporation without documented evaluation sometimes carried generated errors into final submissions. The heterogeneous dataset confines interpretation to qualitative patterns and precludes causal comparison. The findings identify students’ observable evaluation and use of generated responses as a key link between GenAI output and documented physics reasoning.

title_key: beyond the tool what a course aligned ai assistant reveals about student learning in microbiology|sun
title: Beyond the tool: what a course-aligned AI assistant reveals about student learning in microbiology
abstract: Course-aligned artificial intelligence (AI) tutors are increasingly offered as learning support in higher education. Beyond providing practice and feedback, they may also help teachers identify gaps in understanding across a cohort. In a second-year medical microbiology and immunology unit of 500 to 800 students, a course-aligned AI assistant built on The University of Sydney’s Cogniti platform gave students scenario-based short-answer practice with rubric-referenced feedback. Its conversation logs turned out to be a diagnostic instrument. Across more than 1300 conversations, the logs revealed cohort-level knowledge gaps and recurring terminology errors mid-semester. An exploratory analysis also found small positive correlations between practice-oriented use of the assistant and final short-answer marks, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously. The gaps were fed back to the class through an interactive revision resource used in lectures. These insights could be obtained through three approaches requiring different levels of technical expertise: the platform’s own no-code summaries, method-led coding with basic programming, and specialist computational analysis. We also discuss how the approach can be adapted where no equivalent platform exists. The project highlights that a course-aligned AI assistant can provide valuable insight into cohort-level understanding of the subject.

title_key: the influence of artificial intelligence ai chatbots on learning independence and mathematical critical thinking skills|layn
title: THE INFLUENCE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) CHATBOTS ON LEARNING INDEPENDENCE AND MATHEMATICAL CRITICAL THINKING SKILLS
abstract: The puprpose of this study to examine how students’ learning independence and mathematical critical thinking abilities are affected by artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, particularly ChatGPT and Hemini AI though there is now little empirical data on AI’s dual efects on the affective and cognitive domains of mathematics its integration into education seems unavoidable. This study used a pretest-posttest control group in a quasi-experimental design. Purposive sampling was used to choose the 60 eleventh-grade students (30 in the experimental class and 30 in the control class) from a senior high school in Sorong, Indonesia. The tools included a 5-item mathematics critical thinking essay test based on Facione's indicators (validity 0.82, reliability 0.84) and a 20-item learning independence questionnaire (Likert scale, Cronbach's Alpha = 0.86). Using SPSS 26.0, the normality test (Shapiro-Wilk), homogeneity test (Levene), independent sample t-test, and N-Gain score were used to analyse the data. The experimental and control groups differed significantly, according to the data. With p <.001, the experimental class's learning independence posttest mean (M=85.40, SD=5.12) was higher than the control class's (M=72.15, SD=6.03). In a similar vein, the experimental class did better in mathematical critical thinking (M=82.67, SD=6.21) than the control class (M=68.90, SD=7.11). The experimental group's N-Gain score was 0.72 (high category), but the control group's score was 0.38 (middle category). This study offers empirical proof that, when combined with appropriate instructional design and ethical supervision, AI chatbots can be a useful pedagogical tool to promote self-directed learning and critical thinking. The results suggest that rather than using AI chatbots to replace critical thinking, math teachers should use them as a scaffolding tool.

title_key: a proposal for a student centred framework for critical thinking with generative ai in mathematics education|zangmo
title: A proposal for a student-centred framework for critical thinking with Generative AI in mathematics education
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping mathematics education by providing students with immediate access to explanations, worked examples, and problem-solving support. While these capabilities offering opportunities to enrich learning, they also raise concerns about how students develop critical thinking when AI-generated solutions are readily available. The use of GenAI is increasing in Bhutanese schools but little is known about how teachers and students currently use these technologies in mathematics classrooms or what pedagogical challenges limit their effective integration. This conceptual paper proposes a mixed-methods study to identify the opportunities, challenges, and pedagogical gaps associated with the use of GenAI in mathematics education, using Bhutanese secondary schools as the study context. Guided by a pragmatic paradigm, the study will employ questionnaires with quantitative and qualitative components to explore current practices, perceptions, and experiences of teachers and students. The findings will inform the development of a contextually relevant pedagogical framework that positions GenAI as a cognitive scaffold for analysing mathematical problems, evaluating alternative solution strategies, and strengthening critical thinking. By establishing an evidence base before framework design, the proposed study aims to support the responsible integration of GenAI into mathematics education and provide direction for future research, curriculum development, and classroom practice.

title_key: a balanced approach to artificial intelligence integration in student presentation skills a study of undergraduate engineering learners|thammineni
title: A Balanced Approach to Artificial Intelligence Integration in Student Presentation Skills: A Study of Undergraduate Engineering Learners
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming part of the everyday preparation of academic and professional presentations. Generative AI systems and AI-enabled presentation platforms can support brainstorming, content organisation, slide design, visual selection, language refinement and rehearsal. Yet the convenience of these systems creates a pedagogical tension: a technically polished presentation may not necessarily indicate that the student understands the content or can communicate it confidently in real time. This study examines the relationship between AI-assisted preparation and undergraduate students’ presentation performance, with particular attention to content ownership, confidence, creativity, audience engagement and spontaneous communication. A descriptive qualitative design was used with 40 first-year engineering students. Data were gathered through a structured Google Form survey and classroom video observations. The study focused on students’ use of tools such as ChatGPT, Canva and PowerPoint Designer, their degree of personalisation of AI-generated material, and their self-perceived confidence during live presentation. The findings indicate widespread use of AI during preparation, but also a noticeable gap between efficient slide production and effective oral delivery. Students who relied heavily on AI-generated material often found it difficult to explain ideas fluently, sustain audience engagement and respond spontaneously to questions. Students who revised AI-assisted content, added their own examples and rehearsed their presentations demonstrated stronger signs of confidence, eye contact and clarity. The study therefore argues for a human-centred, balanced model in which AI functions as a scaffold rather than a substitute for thinking and speaking. The paper proposes a practical AI–Presentation Balance Framework that integrates topic understanding, responsible prompting, personalisation, visual design, rehearsal and human delivery. The framework has implications for English language teaching, engineering education and employability-oriented communication training.
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science

title_key: scratch and claude to articulate computational thinking and mathematical reasoning|estarita
title: Scratch and Claude to Articulate Computational Thinking and Mathematical Reasoning
abstract: This paper reports on an initial experience with visual programming in Scratch, with the support of Claude, amongst 8th grade students at the interface of technology education and school mathematics. The study involved 15 students (aged 13 and 14) from a private bilingual school in the department of Atlántico, Colombia, selected by convenience. The aim was to describe and analyze this experience and to explore its potential for integration with mathematical reasoning. The intervention comprised a single session of approximately one hour with a conceptual introduction, the guided construction of a baseball video game in Scratch and project sharing. A descriptive qualitative approach was used, drawing on classroom observation and the documentary analysis of narrative and photographic pedagogical records, partial screenshots of the interaction with the conversational assistant Claude and a screenshot of a Scratch project, analyzed through four categories defined from the theoretical framework. The findings indicate initial interest, some initial difficulty in finding the blocks, and a greater ease of use, observed at group level, as the activity was guided. The mismatch in the color of a block shown in Claude's diagram became a relevant point for discussing the need to verify the help provided. The code itself revealed mathematical relationships, identified by the researchers (e.g. a linear rule for the change in the size of the ball), which could be used to support tasks of prediction and justification. The findings describe the organization of teaching and the nature of group participation; they do not document individual mathematical reasoning or autonomy, which are proposed as the focus of a subsequent phase. The experience offers a basis for the design of further interventions which would make the mathematical content explicit, document the reasoning processes and assess student autonomy through progressively more complex tasks, individual explanations and shared criteria for the formative monitoring of mathematical reasoning.
venue: International journal of research and scientific innovation

title_key: student perceptions of generative ai use and project participation in an advanced programming course a case study|lee
title: Student Perceptions of Generative AI Use and Project Participation in an Advanced Programming Course: A Case Study
abstract: This study empirically analyzed learner perceptions and collaboration patterns in a university programming course where the use of Generative AI (GenAI) was formalized. The survey results indicated that while students highly valued the efficacy of GenAI during project execution, they simultaneously expressed concerns regarding dependency and fairness in traditional assessment contexts. Furthermore, an analysis of team project data over two years revealed that the variance in team contribution ( V g ) decreased by 11.4% following the introduction of GenAI. Notably, a top-down normalization of collaboration was observed, as students previously in the free-rider range migrated into the moderate participation group. Based on these findings, this study discussed the necessity of foundational concept learning, strategic project design, multi-faceted PBL assessment frameworks, and the enhancement of learners' self-regulatory capabilities in the GenAI era. However, as a small-scale case study of a specific course, there are limitations to generalize the findings. Future research involving diverse learner groups and objective log data is required to further refine the analytical model.
venue: The Journal of Korean Association of Computer Education

title_key: large language model generation of plausible semantic distractors for data science parsons problems|zou
title: Large language model generation of plausible semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems
abstract: Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.
authors: ["Leying Zou", "Eduardo Ara\u00fajo de Oliveira", "Geela Venise Fabic Chee"]

title_key: development of an educational program to cultivate elementary school students generative ai ethics awareness and critical thinking|
title: Development of an Educational Program to Cultivate Elementary School Students' Generative AI Ethics Awareness and Critical Thinking
abstract: 본 연구는 생성형 AI의 확산에 따른 개인정보 유출, 저작권 분쟁, 환각 현상 등 새로운 윤리적 역기능에 대응하여, 초등학생들이 인공지능 결과물을 맹목적으로 수용하지 않고 스스로 판단하며 책임 있게 활용할 수 있도록 비판적 사고 함양 중심의 생성형 AI 윤리교육 프로그램을 개발하고 그 적용 가능성을 탐색하였다. 교육 프로그램은 문헌 조사 및 AI 윤리 가이드라인을 분석하여 ‘AI 및 생성형 AI 이해', ‘환각 현상', ‘저작권(책임성)', ‘개인정보 보호와 허위조작정보', ‘편향성', ‘연대성'의 6가지 내용 요소를 도출하고 총 12차시로 설계하였다. 특히 학습자가 비판적 사고 과정을 내재화하고 인지적 성찰과 윤리적 실천을 연계할 수 있도록 자체 개발한 ‘SOSAI 교수학습 모델(의심하기-확인하기-수정하기-만들기-책임지기)'을 적용하였다. 초등학교 5학년 학생 12명을 대상으로 단일집단 사전-사후 설계를 적용하고 윌콕슨 부호순위검정을 실시한 결과, 생성형 AI 윤리의식은 전체 영역에서 통계적으로 유의한 향상이 관찰되었다(p < .001). 비판적 사고성향은 전체 점수에서 유의한 변화가 나타나지 않았으며, 하위요인 중 ‘체계성'과 ‘건전한 회의성'은 보정 전 기준으로 유의한 상승을 보였으나 다중비교 보정 후에는 유의성이 유지되지 않았다. 다만 두 요인은 큰 효과크기를 나타냈다(r = .68, .62). 이러한 결과는 SOSAI 모델 기반 윤리교육이 초등학생의 생성형 AI 윤리의식 함양에 기여할 수 있는 가능성을 시사하며, 통제집단을 포함한 후속 연구를 통한 검증이 필요하다.
venue: Intelligent Information Convergence and Future Education

title_key: a escola na era pos chatgpt revisao sistematica sobre as interacoes com ia aprendizagem e agencia no ensino de ciencias|travitzki
title: A escola na era pós-ChatGPT: revisão sistemática sobre as interações com IA, aprendizagem e agência no Ensino de Ciências
abstract: O lançamento do ChatGPT no final de 2022 inaugura uma nova era de incertezas e possibilidades na educação. Este artigo apresenta uma revisão sistemática sobre as interações de alunos e professores com ferramentas de Inteligência Artificial Generativa (IAG) no Ensino de Ciências na Educação Básica, seguindo as diretrizes do PRISMA. Analisamos 17 estudos publicados desde 2023. Os resultados mostram que a qualidade das interações depende de capacidades prévias do usuário (sobretudo conhecimento disciplinar), que são condições para que ele mantenha a agência. Quando o usuário preserva sua agência, os resultados tendem a ser melhores do que quando a agência é delegada à ferramenta. A mesma redução de esforço que pode liberar o aluno para pensar com maior profundidade pode, em outras condições, simplesmente dispensá-lo de pensar. Destacamos alguns riscos: pensamento superficial; dependência acrítica; aprofundamento de desigualdades educacionais. Os achados têm implicações para o ensino, como a importância do uso pedagógico e intencional da IAG para a aprendizagem, buscando manter a agência de alunos e professores. Sobre a pesquisa na área, identificamos algumas lacunas no recorte analisado: a ausência de estudos sobre efeitos de médio e longo prazo sobre aprendizagem; a escassez de investigações sobre efeitos potencialmente prejudiciais.

title_key: generative ai enhanced stem education investigating teachers experiences from implementation in primary school settings|walan
title: Generative AI-Enhanced STEM-Education: Investigating Teachers’ Experiences from Implementation in Primary School Settings
abstract: This pilot study explores the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into primary STEM education in Sweden through a structured Teacher Professional Development (TPD) model. While GenAI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot have rapidly entered educational contexts, empirical research on their pedagogical use in primary schools remains limited. Eleven teachers participated in a six-month TPD programme comprising workshops, collaborative discussions, and classroom implementations. The empirical material consisted primarily of audio-recorded workshop discussions, which were transcribed and analysed, supplemented by a post-intervention questionnaire. Data were analysed using thematic coding informed by the Refined Consensus Model (RCM) and the Digital Promise AI Literacy Framework. Findings indicate that GenAI served primarily as an idea generator, supporting lesson planning and interdisciplinary integration across mathematics and science. Teachers reported opportunities for timesaving, differentiated instruction, and enhanced creativity, alongside challenges related to mathematical inaccuracies, unrealistic time estimates, and the need for contextual adaptation. The TPD model facilitated growth in pedagogical content knowledge and AI literacy, fostering confidence and critical engagement with GenAI tools. These results underscore the potential of structured professional development to bridge the gap between emerging technologies and classroom practice. Future research should extend implementation duration, include student perspectives, and address ethical and equity considerations in AI integration.
venue: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

title_key: perceived ai shaming and its relationship with students adoption of generative ai for personalized learning in mathematics|caubalejo
title: Perceived AI Shaming and Its Relationship with Students’ Adoption of Generative AI for Personalized Learning in Mathematics
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can support personalized mathematics learning, while students who use it may anticipate negative judgments. This descriptive-correlational study examined the relationship between perceived AI shaming and generative AI adoption among 301 first-year Mathematics in the Modern World students at a private university in Quezon City, Philippines, during the first term of Academic Year 2026–2027. Students recruited through proportionate quota sampling completed a researcher-developed questionnaire grounded in stigma theory and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology. The analysis used descriptive statistics, group difference tests, and Spearman’s rank-order correlation. Respondents agreed with statements measuring perceived AI shaming (M = 3.43), with stereotyping and labeling receiving the highest ratings. They also agreed with statements measuring adoption (M = 3.71), with performance expectancy rated highest. Perceived AI shaming did not differ significantly by age, sex, or academic program. Adoption differed significantly by sex and academic program, with no significant difference by age. The association between perceived AI shaming and adoption was very weak and statistically nonsignificant (ρ = .029, p = .619). The results informed the Stigma-Free Responsible Generative AI Framework for Mathematics Learning, which proposes governance, pedagogy, and support strategies to promote open, guided, and responsible use.
venue: QualiSearch Journal of Educational Research and Practice

title_key: a generative aisupported instructional model for statistical modeling in undergraduate probability and statistics|
title: A Generative AI–Supported Instructional Model for Statistical Modeling in Undergraduate Probability and Statistics
abstract: This instructional design article proposes a six-stage model for undergraduate probability and statistics. It asks how a modeling unit can connect calculations under a specified model with statistical decisions when data definitions change, and how instructors can adjust support using students’ initial responses and explanations of revisions. For each stage, the model specifies what students submit, what instructors check, and when students revisit an earlier decision. Instructors use generative AI (GenAI) only to draft follow-up questions for their review. Students respond to those questions without interacting with GenAI. A worked example shows how students move from a Poisson probability calculation to an order-level comparison using constructed logistics complaint records. The example also shows how instructors use students’ explanations to decide whether to reduce prompts or revisit an earlier stage. Classroom feasibility and effects on student learning remain to be evaluated.
venue: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications

title_key: generative artificial intelligence among business management engineering students academic uses learning and responsible practices|oran
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Among Business Management Engineering Students: Academic Uses, Learning, and Responsible Practices
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is already part of many students’ academic activities, but it remains necessary to understand what they use it for, how they learned to use it, and what responsible practices they follow. This study described these aspects among Business Management Engineering students at the Pachuca Institute of Technology and gathered their recommendations for the institution. A cross-sectional, non-experimental, descriptive study was conducted, with a predominantly quantitative approach and exploratory analysis of one open-ended question. All 410 students in the program were invited to participate. Of the 397 questionnaires received, nine were excluded because of inconsistencies. Of the remaining 388 records, 386 included consent and formed the analytical sample. A total of 85.5% reported currently using GenAI. ChatGPT was the most frequently selected primary tool (52.8%), followed by Google Gemini (29.8%). The most common use was searching for information and clarifying questions (82.6%), while the main way students learned to use these tools was by exploring and practicing on their own (58.0%). In their self-assessments, 62.0% considered themselves moderately capable of writing prompts, and 58.7% of identifying errors. Regarding responsible practices, 53.6% reported checking information against reliable sources frequently or always, and 50.0% reported disclosing their use when required by the rules. In response to the question, “What recommendation would you make to the Pachuca Institute of Technology to promote the academic, ethical, and responsible use of AI?”, the most common suggestion was to offer practical courses or workshops. Participants also proposed clarifying when and how AI may be used, including the topic in courses, and providing guidance for instructors. Overall, the findings point to the value of practical training and clear rules to support responsible GenAI use.

venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science

title: Middle School Students’ Performance and Critical Engagement in LLM-Supported Differentiated Learning: An Exploratory Study
