title_key: generative artificial intelligence in physics education a systematic mapping review|athanasopoulou
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Physics Education: A Systematic Mapping Review
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being adopted in education, yet its application to physics remains challenging because of the discipline’s reliance on mathematical, symbolic, and multimodal reasoning. This paper presents a PRISMA-based systematic mapping review of 146 studies published between January 2023 and June 2026 on the use of GenAI in physics education. The review examines the research landscape, approaches for supporting students and teachers, and methods for benchmarking and improving GenAI systems. The findings reveal rapid growth in research activity with widespread but uneven geographic distribution, with most studies focusing on higher education and relying heavily on third-party GenAI services. Student-support research primarily addresses conversational tutoring and personalized guidance, while teacher-support studies focus on lesson planning and teaching material development, professional development and teacher perceptions. A substantial body of work also benchmarks GenAI performance on physics-related tasks or proposes methods for improving it. Overall, the reviewed literature demonstrates considerable potential for GenAI in physics education while highlighting the need for further research on multilingual and inclusive systems, specialized educational uses, privacy-preserving approaches, improved multimodal support, and integration with complementary educational technologies.

title_key: useful but not always right engineering students use of chatgpt for english language learning in a non major classroom in bangladesh|ferdous
title: Useful but Not Always Right: Engineering Students’ Use of ChatGPT for English Language Learning in a Non-Major Classroom in Bangladesh
abstract: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT are now part of how many university students study, but we still know little about how students outside English departments use them to learn English. This exploratory survey looked at engineering students taking a non-major English course at a technical university in northern Bangladesh. Sixty-three students answered an online questionnaire with closed and open-ended items on how they use ChatGPT, what benefits they see and what problems they face. Use was very common: 96.8% had used ChatGPT, 55.6% used it daily and 54.0% used it often or always for English-related tasks, mainly for writing help, assignment preparation and generating ideas. Most students agreed that ChatGPT is easy to use (76.2%), gives useful explanations (73.0%) and saves time (71.4%). At the same time, 76.2% said its answers are not always accurate or relevant, 74.6% wanted more guidance on using it, and 66.7% reported that poor internet access limits regular use. More than half (57.1%) held both views together, finding the explanations useful and the answers unreliable. Students who used ChatGPT more often for English reported greater benefits (ρ = .41) and more over-reliance (ρ = .38), but they were no more likely to notice unreliable output (ρ = −.14). Only 39.7% preferred asking ChatGPT to asking a teacher. Open-ended answers pointed to wrong answers, language that is too advanced, and difficulty writing prompts. Because the sample is small, drawn from one institution and based on self-report, the findings describe students’ experience and not measured gains in proficiency. They suggest that these students need help in judging ChatGPT’s output more than they need encouragement to use it.
venue: International Journal of Arts and Humanities

title_key: motivators and demotivators of integrating large language models in software engineering education an exploratory familiarity allocation framework|khan
title: Motivators and Demotivators of Integrating Large Language Models in Software Engineering Education: An Exploratory Familiarity Allocation Framework
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly influencing software engineering practice and education. However, limited research has examined their systematic integration using stakeholder evidence and quantitative decision-support models. This study presents an exploratory familiarity–allocation framework for analyzing motivating and demotivating factors associated with LLM integration in software engineering education. Building on our previously developed literature-based taxonomy, we evaluated 19 factors, comprising nine motivators and ten demotivators, through a structured survey of 126 stakeholders from multiple countries. Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression were used to examine associations between the factor ratings and high self-reported LLM familiarity. Both models achieved an accuracy of 0.461, below the majority-class baseline, indicating limited ability to distinguish respondents with higher and lower familiarity. Their estimated probabilities were therefore used as exploratory relative scoring functions rather than reliable individual-level predictions. These estimates were incorporated into a Genetic Algorithm using a defined allocation score to support Global Factor Allocation (GC), Local Factor Allocation (LC), and category-level \(\Delta\) Fitness analyses. The descriptive results identified Programming Assistance and Debugging Support , Personalized and Adaptive Learning , and AI as a Learning Partner as the most highly rated motivators. The most highly rated demotivators were Plagiarism and Intellectual Property Concerns , Over-Reliance on AI in Learning , and Reduced Critical Thinking and Problem-Solving . Under the fitted probability models and allocation assumptions, GC assigned relatively higher levels to integrity- and governance-related factors, while LC revealed additional pedagogical and risk-related patterns within individual categories. The resulting configurations represent exploratory familiarity–allocation scenarios rather than validated implementation priorities, institutional costs, or evidence of educational effectiveness. Classroom and institutional validation is required before the framework can guide LLM integration in practice.

title_key: quasi experimental evaluation of a human centric ai tutoring and human in the loop assessment system in advanced stem education|jianxin
title: Quasi-experimental evaluation of a human-centric AI tutoring and human-in-the-loop assessment system in advanced STEM education
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping higher education, yet most deployments of large-language-model tutoring and automated grading target introductory courses and pay limited attention to the transparency, trust, and equity concerns that become acute in advanced, safety-critical technical domains. This paper presents a human-centric AI-assisted instructional system and evaluates it in a postgraduate hardware-security course on electromagnetic protection and side-channel analysis. The system couples three human-centric components: (i) a retrieval-augmented tutoring assistant whose answers are grounded in citable course materials to curb hallucination and preserve traceability; (ii) a human-in-the-loop assessment pipeline in which a language model drafts rubric-based feedback that instructors verify item by item; and (iii) an adaptive, tiered project-based learning path that offers differentiated entry points. We evaluated the system in a quasi-experiment with 47 postgraduates (24 experimental, 23 control) taught concurrently by the same instructors in parallel class sections. The experimental group’s competency score rose from 62.4 to 84.7, against 61.8 to 70.2 for the control group, a difference in gains that was statistically significant and associated with a large effect size ( \(t(41.2)=4.55\) , \(p<0.001\) , Cohen’s \(d=1.32\) ), while its score dispersion contracted from a standard deviation of 14.5 to 7.2. A baseline-by-group interaction indicated significantly stronger differential improvement among initially lower-scoring students in the experimental section, although this distributional finding is interpreted cautiously given the non-randomised design. Human-in-the-loop grading was associated with a 35.7% reduction in marking time while reaching an AI–instructor agreement of quadratic-weighted Cohen’s \(\kappa =0.95\) ; because this agreement measures consistency rather than correctness, we interpret it accordingly. We examine how human oversight, citation grounding, and adaptivity may have jointly contributed to these outcomes, treating the intervention as an integrated bundle whose individual components remain to be isolated, and we set out the responsible-AI safeguards that such deployments require.

title_key: error awareness in algorithm learning with ai chatbots and online judges among elementary software gifted students an analysis of reflective learning records|kimg
title: Error Awareness in Algorithm Learning with AI Chatbots and Online Judges among Elementary Software-Gifted Students: An Analysis of Reflective Learning Records
abstract: This study analysed how elementary school software-gifted students' error awareness appeared and changed in Python algorithm learning supported by AI chatbots and online judges. The data consisted of 658 online-judge-based reflective learning records written by 20 students; 185 records explicitly mentioning AI use were examined in depth, and 430 records suitable for student-level change analysis were used for the student-level analysis. The results showed that students checked not only errors in their code but also whether they had asked AI appropriate questions, whether AI-generated answers worked in the online judge, and whether they could explain the solutions in their own words. Debugging appeared as a process of rereading the problem, checking execution results, and reflecting on one's own understanding. These findings suggest that AI-chatbot-supported algorithm education should emphasise clarifying problem conditions, checking execution results, critically evaluating AI-generated answers, and explaining solutions in students' own words.
venue: The Journal of Korean Association of Computer Education

title_key: teachers professional fulfillment in stem education sources enablers and constraints among chinese primary and secondary stem teachers|xue
title: Teachers’ Professional Fulfillment in STEM Education: Sources, Enablers, and Constraints among Chinese Primary and Secondary STEM Teachers
abstract: Teachers’ professional fulfillment in STEM education remains underexplored, particularly regarding the experiences teachers find rewarding and the conditions that support or constrain them. Guided by the meaningful work framework, this study examined responses to two open-ended questions from a survey of 3,959 Chinese primary and secondary teachers. Following data screening, 2,953 teachers were included in a deductive–inductive qualitative content analysis supported by large language model–assisted coding and independent human reliability checks. Five sources of professional fulfillment were identified: student growth and learning, teachers’ professional growth, recognition and relational affirmation, meaning and social value, and intrinsic rewards of STEM teaching. Student-related experiences were perceived as both sources of fulfillment and enabling or constraining factors. Insufficient instructional resources, limited professional learning opportunities, workload, and examination-oriented evaluation emerged as prominent constraints, whereas institutional support and recognition were more frequently described as enabling. A small subset of teachers also described how these conditions restricted, sustained, or expanded their STEM teaching practices. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing professionally rewarding experiences from the conditions that enable or constrain opportunities to realize them.

title_key: technology enhanced calligraphy education a systematic review and bibliometric analysis of research trends|tang
title: Technology-enhanced calligraphy education: A systematic review and bibliometric analysis of research trends
abstract: Calligraphy is simultaneously an academic subject, a cultural practice inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and a skill increasingly mediated by digital technology. Research on technology-enhanced calligraphy education has grown quickly, yet remains scattered across engineering, computing and education venues and has rarely been examined through a science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics (STEAM) lens. This study systematically reviews international research published between 2015 and 2025. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guideline, 753 records were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure; after deduplication and dual independent screening, 62 studies met the eligibility criteria. Bibliometric analysis, keyword co-occurrence mapping, appraisal with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and thematic coding were applied. Annual output remained modest until 2019, expanded after 2020 and peaked in 2024, with 82.3% of studies carrying mainland-China or Taiwan affiliations—a concentration replicated across the international and Chinese-language databases. Five themes organize the field: AI-based assessment of calligraphy quality; online and web-based learning; intelligent tutoring, generative AI and pedagogy; immersive learning environments; and robotics and haptic skill training. System-development studies dominate, classroom-based effect evidence is scarce, methodological quality is mostly low to moderate, and only one study operationalizes an explicit STEAM framework. The field is technology-rich but pedagogy-poor. A STEAM integration framework is proposed in which calligraphy functions as the arts component, with science and mathematics made explicit in instructional design.
venue: Journal of Pedagogical Sociology and Psychology

title_key: making learning visible in the age of generative ai reported assessment practices for cognitive engagement and self regulated learning and the development and external appraisal of a higher education assessment framework|lasekan
title: Making learning visible in the age of generative AI: reported assessment practices for cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning, and the development and external appraisal of a higher education assessment framework
abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents?
 
 
 
 Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction.
 
 
 
 Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency.
 
 
 
 Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

title_key: frictionless by design creating space for productive discomfort in interdisciplinary teaching|warren
title: Frictionless by design? Creating space for productive discomfort in interdisciplinary teaching
abstract:
Working across disciplines requires educators and students to hold conflicting perspectives in tension, negotiate contested meaning, and integrate knowledge in ways no single discipline allows (Mansilla & Duraising, 2007). Such work is cognitively, emotionally, and socially demanding (Manathunga et al., 2006). Yet this difficulty reflects a well-established finding in education research: that struggle, effort, and a degree of discomfort are not obstacles to learning but conditions for it, provided learners feel safe enough to stay with them (Bjork & Bjork, 2011).
As generative AI becomes embedded in higher education, it reshapes not only how knowledge is accessed, but the learning experience itself. This technology holds real value, yet its orientation towards fluent, instantly agreeable output can run counter to this. In practice, it smooths over the uncertainty, disagreement, and difficulty through which interdisciplinary understanding is built, narrowing the epistemic diversity such work depends on (McInnes & Airey, 2025). The question, then, is not whether to use digital tools but when – understanding where they enhance learning, and where they erode this difficulty, is a central design question for technology-enhanced learning.
A key challenge for interdisciplinary educators, therefore, is how to design learning that creates space for this discomfort to thrive. While toolkits for interdisciplinary research are now plentiful, resources for teaching it remain scarce (Laursen et al., 2024). Drawing on an extensive review of the literature, we present a seven-stage model for interdisciplinary learning and teaching, spanning reflexivity, teamwork, visioning, wicked problems, disciplinary integration, creative play, and interdisciplinary assessment. The model is grounded in constructive alignment (Biggs, 1996) and draws on transition-based approaches to teaching complex, real-world challenges (Bertolini et al., 2024).
Originally designed around a multi-day, face-to-face interactive workshop, the model has since been translated into more practical formats: a board game version, currently being trialled, and a Canvas course in development. Across all formats, the seven stages are not about engineering discomfort but about creating a supportive, structured space in which the tensions intrinsic to interdisciplinary work can be explored directly rather than avoided or bypassed: space for sitting with not-knowing, for productive disagreement, and for the slow work of finding common ground (Colwill & Boyd, 2008). It leans on digital tools where they extend what educators can do, while keeping the work of integration and productive disagreement deliberately analogue.
The purpose of this poster is to share the seven-stage model with educators and to sharpen it against the realities of interdisciplinary teaching across different disciplines and institutions. Preparing educators to teach across disciplines, not merely within them, remains an under-served challenge, and this model is a deliberate response to it. In prioritising the relational, embodied, and sometimes uncomfortable work of learning together, it offers a human-centred response to interdisciplinary teaching in an increasingly digital society – where designing for the productive difficulty that interdisciplinary work depends on is not a constraint to be managed but a capacity worth protecting.

title_key: beyond the pretty graph human centred assessment design for evaluative judgement|korolkiewicz
title: Beyond the pretty graph: Human-centred assessment design for evaluative judgement
abstract: Assessment in data visualisation courses too often rewards technical output over communicating substance. When visualisation is taught as a tool rather than a discipline, students learn to produce work that meets the brief but has little to say. This paper reports on a course redesign that addresses this gap through a human-centred assessment design grounded in evaluative judgement theory, treating evaluative judgement as a capability exercised by both students and markers. The redesign is structured around five elements addressing student ownership of project topics, portfolio assessment, descriptive capability levels, practitioner modelling, and creative freedom within a structured framework, implemented in a required course within a Master of Data Science program. Practitioner inquiry into the operation of this design in the presence of generative AI revealed that AI functioned not as a threat to academic integrity but as a mechanism that raised creative ambition, shifting the limiting factor from technical skill to evaluative judgement. Although situated in a data visualisation course, the contribution is broader. As generative AI makes technical production easier, helping students develop the capacity to recognise, justify, and communicate insight becomes the central challenge across higher education, and this paper suggests one way to address it.

title_key: pemanfaatan artificial intelligence ai dalam penyusunan dan validasi asesmen pembelajaran di ma muhammadiyah 1 malang|hafiizh
title: Pemanfaatan Artificial Intelligence (AI) dalam Penyusunan dan Validasi Asesmen Pembelajaran di MA Muhammadiyah 1 Malang
abstract: This community service program assisted teachers in using generative artificial intelligence (AI) to develop and review learning assessments at MA Muhammadiyah 1 Malang. Twenty-two teachers from different subjects participated in a face-to-face workshop and online mentoring from 24 April to 1 May 2026. Participants practised developing assessment items with ChatGPT, designing visual presentations using Canva AI, checking AI-generated outputs for alignment with learning objectives and cognitive demands, and revising their assessment products. Evaluation included 20-item pre- and post-tests, a product assessment rubric, and a 20-item participant response questionnaire. The mean test score increased descriptively from 15.95 to 18.41 out of 20. The mean product score was 86.08, with 11 products rated Good and 11 rated Very Good, while the questionnaire score reached 79.27% of the maximum possible score. Based on these evaluations, the mentoring program achieved its intended objectives during the training period. However, some assessment products still require greater cognitive depth in higher-order thinking tasks. These findings reflect outcomes observed during the program and do not establish the empirical validity of the assessments in classroom use or the long-term sustainability of teachers' skills.
authors: ["Mochammad Hafiizh", "V. Kusumasari", "E. T. D. Cahyowati", "S. Sudirman", "Fazrina Saumi", "Nourma Pramestie Wulandari", "Rosmariyadi Rosmariyadi"]

title_key: designed not delegated human centred prompt engineering as a promising approach to ai supported learning design|mair
title: Designed, not delegated: Human-centred prompt engineering as a promising approach to AI-supported learning design
abstract: Generative AI can improve students’ immediate performance while reducing the cognitive and metacognitive work required for durable learning. Although recent work on AI learning companions offers a promising response, these systems remain largely beyond the resources available to individual educators. This paper argues that educators can adopt a more modest form of human-centred AI design by encoding pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) into prompt design and sustaining student partnership throughout iterative development. Drawing on human-centred design, PCK, technological pedagogical content knowledge, and Students as Partners, the paper develops a conceptual account of how pedagogical, content, technical, and contextual knowledge can shape what a large language model (LLM) provides, withholds, and asks students to do. An illustrative case of an AI peer tutor for identifying and evaluating peer-reviewed sources demonstrates how this approach was enacted through five major prompt iterations and progressively deeper forms of student involvement. The case shows how educator knowledge of recurring student difficulties can be translated into pedagogical pathways, while student partnership can contribute contextual knowledge and complementary expertise that further develops the educator’s technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK). Evaluation indicated substantial improvement in peer-tutoring behaviour and favourable student perceptions, while highlighting the need for continued iteration and research examining effects on student learning.

title_key: epistemological vigilance and instructional design in the age of generative ai aligning evidence based inquiry spatial historical thinking and process assessment in the century of turkiye maarif model and the c3 framework|avc
title: Epistemological Vigilance and Instructional Design in the Age of Generative AI: Aligning Evidence-Based Inquiry, Spatial-Historical Thinking, and Process Assessment in the Century of Türkiye Maarif Model and the C3 Framework
abstract:
The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) in K–12 and teacher education poses a fundamental epistemological challenge to Social Studies instruction. Whereas disciplinary thinking in History, Geography, Civics, and Economics relies on provenance (sourcing), contextual friction between competing records, spatial scale analysis, and deliberative trade-offs, probabilistic language models synthesize fluent, single-voiced prose that erases source boundaries and invites cognitive offloading. Existing practitioner literature largely addresses classroom AI through generic prompt-engineering tips or binary bans. By contrast, this study develops a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary instructional design architecture that operationalizes AI governance across the 2024–2026 Century of Türkiye Maarif Model (TYMM) Social Studies Curriculum (Grades 4–7) and the United States National Council for the Social Studies (NCSS) C3 Framework Inquiry Arc.
Employing qualitative document analysis and normative instructional design synthesis across official curriculum and ethics mandates (MEB, 2025a, 2025b, 2026a, 2026b; NCSS, 2013), cognitive architecture theory (Mayer, 2009; Mayer & Moreno, 2003; Sweller, van Merriënboer, & Paas, 2019), and disciplinary literacy scholarship (Ashby & Lee, 1987; Gersmehl, 2014; Hess, 2009; Wineburg, 1991, 2001; Wineburg & McGrew, 2019), the article advances five original contributions: (1) a Comparative Inquiry-Governance Matrix demonstrating how TYMM’s sixth learning area ('Technology and Social Sciences'), Systems Thinking, nine literacies (OB1–OB9), and Virtue–Value–Action (EDE) framework extend the C3 Inquiry Arc for the AI era; (2) a Taxonomic Verb-Alignment and Scaffolding Withdrawal Model (across Revised Bloom’s and SOLO taxonomies) that prevents 'cognitive verb drift' during the gradual release of responsibility (Modeling -> Guided Practice -> Independent Practice); (3) Domain-Specific AI Verification Protocols across all four core Social Studies disciplines—including contradiction-margin source packages in History (SBAB2, SBAB3, SBAB4), five-component spatial reasoning in Geography (SBAB7, SBAB8, SBAB10), institutional receptor verification and deliberative steel-manning in Civics (SBAB5), and the tripartite statistical rule plus assumption-testing in Economics/Entrepreneurship (SBAB6, SBAB11); (4) a Subtractive Material Engineering Protocol incorporating three rapid pre-classroom tests (Self-Completion, Subtraction, and Blind Peer tests); and (5) a Two-Tier Psychometric Rubric pairing comment-first formative feedback (Butler, 1988) with process-authentication criteria that replace biased AI detectors (Liang et al., 2023).
Keywords: Social Studies instructional design, generative artificial intelligence, Century of Türkiye Maarif Model (TYMM), C3 Framework Inquiry Arc, constructive alignment, gradual release of responsibility, spatial and historical thinking.

title_key: algorithmic global value chains and higher education transformation re engineering international business pedagogy in the era of autonomous intelligence|he
title: ALGORITHMIC GLOBAL VALUE CHAINS AND HIGHER EDUCATION TRANSFORMATION: RE-ENGINEERING INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS PEDAGOGY IN THE ERA OF AUTONOMOUS INTELLIGENCE
abstract: The rapid emergence of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive supply chain orchestration, and real-time cross-border regulatory analytics is fundamentally transforming how multinational enterprises (MNEs) govern global value chains (GVCs) and enter foreign markets. Yet International Business (IB) higher education remains largely tethered to twentieth-century pedagogical paradigms—relying on static international trade models, retrospective written case studies, and essentialist cultural heuristics that fail to prepare graduates for algorithmically mediated global commerce. Moving beyond surface-level classroom adoption of generative chatbots, this study develops a comprehensive theoretical and operational framework for re-engineering International Business education through the lenses of Global Value Chain Governance Theory, Activity Theory, and Metacognitive Scaffolding. We argue that the defining competency for next-generation IB professionals is Algorithmic Value-Chain Orchestration—the ability to align predictive and generative AI systems with cross-jurisdictional institutional realities, geopolitical risks, and culturally grounded human judgment. To operationalize this capability, the paper introduces a Three-Horizon Curricular Transformation Architecture alongside a Synthetic Global Commerce Laboratory that immerses students in dynamic multi-tier supply chain disruptions, automated customs and rules-of-origin auditing, and cross-cultural digital platform governance. Drawing upon longitudinal pedagogical implementations across undergraduate and postgraduate IB cohorts, we demonstrate significant gains in students' systemic risk reasoning, critical verification of algorithmic outputs, and cross-border strategic adaptability. Finally, the study examines structural challenges—including cognitive atrophy, Western-centric training data biases, and cross-border data compliance—and establishes an institutional governance charter for sustainable business school transformation.

title_key: tools at the tempo of teaching vibe engineering an lms embedded fishbowl tool|zhang
title: Tools at the tempo of teaching: Vibe engineering an LMS-embedded Fishbowl tool
abstract:
Background
The Fishbowl is a discussion format: an inner ring discusses a prompt while an outer ring observes and swaps in (Bermudez, n.d.). When it runs well, the interaction reaches the interactive tier of Chi and Wylie’s (2014) ICAP framework, most strongly linked to deep learning. Novice teachers struggle to orchestrate so complex a discussion and often avoid it or run it as procedural theatre (Dillenbourg, 2002), while students lack the scaffolding to grasp what good discussion looks like or to notice their participation in real time. Fixed-seat rooms make the concentric-ring layout harder to set up.
The shift
An LMS-embedded learning tool can address these problems by scaffolding through the interface itself: built-in phase sequencing and role-specific views support teachers as drivers rather than executors (Dillenbourg, 2013), while giving students concrete moves for good discussion and cues to notice their participation. Such a tool was never technically impossible, only unjustifiable, requiring a software team and budget cycle for one learning activity. Generative AI now lets a single learning designer (LD) author and revise a version between deliveries, so refinement moves at the tempo of teaching rather than procurement. However, unmediated “vibe coding” is fragile across accessibility, security, and pedagogical validity. Vibe engineering (Willison, 2025) is the discipline that makes the speed safe.
Development snapshot
Vibe engineering can be brought to education by drawing on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) orchestration and collaboration-script theory (Fischer et al., 2013; Kollar et al., 2006): balancing under- and over-scripting (Dillenbourg, 2002), preserving intrinsic script constraints (Dillenbourg & Tchounikine, 2007), and scaffolding transactive discourse (Fischer et al., 2013). Each version is audited in a separate AI session against accessibility and security checklists, while pedagogical validity is judged by the LD through CSCL orchestration principles and classroom observation. Every update ships as one small static HTML file, stored centrally with no student data and no runtime AI, so it propagates automatically to every unit that uses it.
Poster experience 

Live demonstration on two adjacent devices: the projected Fishbowl discussion phase (teacher-facing) alongside the private ideas phase (student-facing).
Annotated walkthrough of core design elements with their theoretical warrants.
A few major versions showing how the tool evolved, with a QR link to selected prompt history.
The accessibility and security checklists, with a QR link to the open-source versions.

Relevance to the theme: Human-centred learning design
The Fishbowl builds connection through structured dialogue, and the tool preserves that priority. It orchestrates the room without mediating the conversation, and the interface directs student attention to peers rather than screens. The approach is not specific to one activity: in principle, any collaboration script an LD can specify pedagogically could be authored at teaching tempo (cf. Holstein et al., 2019).
Next steps
The tool will run across teaching periods in 2026, with observations of orchestration load, participation, and facilitator experience feeding back into design rationales, checklists, and successive versions. The two checklists will be released as open-source, citable Markdown artefacts for the LD community.

title_key: making programming learning visible students perceptions of an authentic process oriented assessment design|hendry
title: Making programming learning visible: Students’ perceptions of an authentic, process-oriented assessment design
abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has increased questions about whether a final code artefact alone can constitute sufficient evidence of student learning in programming education. This poster presents a practice-based evaluation of a redesigned second-year programming unit that incorporated multiple forms of evidence of learning. The assessment design is informed by authentic assessment (Boud & Molloy, 2013), feedback for learning (Carless & Boud, 2018) and self-explanation theory (Chi et al., 1989). It responded to current calls for assessment reform in the age of AI by shifting attention from the final artefact to the processes through which students design, explain, test and improve code (Lodge et al., 2023).
Across three progressively sequenced assessments, students produced working Python programs, submitted WakaTime development records, recorded video explanations of design decisions, declared and justified GenAI use where permitted, and revisited prior code to improve exception handling and pytest testing. GenAI was allowed under accountable-use conditions, during which students were required to identify GenAI-assisted code, ensure that their submissions used concepts taught in the unit, and demonstrate that they understood and could explain the code they submitted. Assessment 1 established foundational object-oriented programming practices. Assessment 2 asked students to build a weather-data bot using CSV data, web scraping, datetime, logging, collections and pandas analysis. Assessment 3 required students to return to their Assessment 2 codebase and use feedback from Assessment 2 to strengthen its robustness through built-in exceptions, custom exceptions and tests. The design operationalised process-oriented assessment at task level. Code provided product evidence; WakaTime provided process evidence; video explanation provided conceptual evidence; and feedback with staged task design supported iterative development. Together, these tasks created an evidentiary architecture that made programming processes, conceptual reasoning and judgement more visible than final code alone.
The evaluation drew on 68 anonymous unit feedback responses. Open-ended feedback was examined using thematic analysis (Clarke & Braun, 2017). Three student-perception themes were emergent. First, authentic tasks positioned programming as professional practice: students valued project-based tasks such as CSV analysis, web scraping and data-processing bots because they resembled meaningful programming work. Second, explanation and process evidence made computational thinking visible: students described shifts from writing code to thinking in terms of modularity, validation, debugging and engineering practice. Third, feedback supported iterative improvement and confidence: students reported that feedback helped them identify errors, revise code and progress more independently.
The poster argues that process-oriented programming assessment should not rely only on restricting AI use. Instead, assessment can require multiple forms of evidence to validate student learning (Dawson et al., 2024) such as working code, development traces, self-explanatory video, feedback uptake, accountable AI-use declarations and testing artefacts. Video explanation is especially important because it prompts students to justify programing structures, methods, strategies and data-analysis approaches (Lai & Niblock, 2024). The study is limited by its reliance on one unit, one teaching period and self-reported student feedback. Further analysis of WakaTime data, video explanations, code revisions and pytest artefacts will examine how process evidence relates to conceptual understanding, reasoning and feedback uptake.

title_key: generative ai dependency and its eff ects on introductory programming learning an experimental study|coutinho
title: Generative AI Dependency and its Eff ects on Introductory Programming Learning: An Experimental Study
abstract: This study investigated the impact of the dependence on Generative Artificial Intelligence, specifically ChatGPT, on learning retention in Introduction to Programming students. A controlled experiment was conducted with 18 students, divided into an experimental group and a control group. The experimental group used ChatGPT to solve exercises and was subsequently deprived of the tool, while the control group had no access to the AI. The results showed that, although the use of AI increased initial performance, students who depended on it showed a drop in performance when deprived of the resource. In contrast, the control group demonstrated improvement in knowledge retention and application. The findings suggest that excessive use of GenAI can foster dependence and hinder learning consolidation, reinforcing the need for its balanced pedagogical use.
authors: ["Vin\u00edcius Castro Coutinho", "Diana Maria da Camara Gorayeb", "O. Viana"]
venue: Anais do XXIII Encontro Nacional de Inteligência Artificial e Computacional (ENIAC 2026)

title_key: generative artificial intelligence as a pedagogical agent for education for sustainable development a scoping review|gutierrez
title: Generative artificial intelligence as a pedagogical agent for education for sustainable development: a scoping review
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being rapidly adopted in education, prompting growing interest in its application to Education for Sustainable Development (ESD). This scoping review examines studies in which a generative system acts as a pedagogical agent that directly mediates learning about sustainability. Following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported under PRISMA-ScR, searches in Scopus, Web of Science and ERIC retrieved 172 records, of which 25 studies, reported in 26 publications and published between 2024 and 2026, met the eligibility criteria. Charting combined descriptive variables with reviewer-assigned interpretive codes governed by explicit decision rules. The corpus is close to evenly distributed between Global North and Global South settings, concentrated in higher education, and pedagogically well embedded: 20 of the 21 implemented interventions are integrated into instruction rather than running alongside it, although only 11 frame the generative activity with briefing, debriefing or guided reflection. Generative systems are deployed most frequently as dialogic tutors and instructional co-designers, and all studies target cognitive outcomes, although measured change in learners is evidenced in ten and against a comparison condition in only five. The review also identifies where the field can consolidate: explicit operationalisation of sustainability competency frameworks, designs able to isolate the generative component, delayed measurement of outcomes, deliberative configurations that keep normative judgement with the learner, and attention to the environmental footprint of the tools themselves. Four evidence-informed design principles are proposed to guide this consolidation.

title_key: mining what matters concept level preference learning for proactive task selection under humanagent interaction scarcity|huang
title: Mining What Matters: Concept-Level Preference Learning for Proactive Task Selection Under Human–Agent Interaction Scarcity
abstract: Learning individual preferences through proactive interaction is constrained by limited user attention and feedback. We present Proactive Dual-Value Task Mining, which estimates task preferences with a dynamic concept graph and selects candidate tasks by combining this estimate with frequency-based novelty and graph centrality. The InteractMine dataset contains 1000 sampled tasks with independent ratings from four student volunteers and four LLM-simulated profiles. A scenario-disjoint offline evaluation compares the method with simple predictors, active selection strategies, and ablations under matched feedback budgets. At 90 observations, its human-rating MAE is 0.2150 and its deployment reward 0.7308, on par with kNN (0.2143 and 0.7302); with ten observations its human-rating MAE is 0.2207, against 0.2309 for kNN, lower in all four human columns. No difference from the baselines is statistically significant, and the centrality term rarely changes the selected task. With the same estimator, the dual-value rule performs like ε-greedy selection, so these results reflect the estimator rather than the selection rule. The concept-level representation thus matches strong simple baselines, is more accurate on human ratings when feedback is scarce, and is designed to keep preferences interpretable and editable. A wearable prototype with a WeChat Mini Program implements the sensing and monitoring steps.

title_key: evaluating speech to text models for brazilian portuguese in egua assist supporting programming learning for people with visual impairments|santos
title: Evaluating Speech-to-Text Models for Brazilian Portuguese in Égua Assist: Supporting Programming Learning for People with Visual Impairments
abstract: This paper presents a comparative evaluation of nine Speech-to-Text model configurations — including the Web Speech API, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and seven OpenAI Whisper variants — for Brazilian Portuguese in Égua Assist, an assistive tool supporting visually impaired students in early programming learning. Using 200 audio samples (100 synthetic, 100 real) from 20 participants under varied acoustic conditions, models were evaluated in terms of accuracy (WER, CER, BLEU), efficiency (RTF), and stability (error distribution and outlier analysis). Whisper via API achieved the best trade-off among accuracy, latency, and robustness, while compact local models showed high instability and hallucination-like failures on real audio. These findings provide empirical guidance for real-time ASR model selection in voice-driven assistive educational applications for Brazilian Portuguese.
authors: ["Daniel dos Santos", "P. C. F. Cardoso", "V. H. Pinto"]
venue: Anais do XXIII Encontro Nacional de Inteligência Artificial e Computacional (ENIAC 2026)

title_key: exploring ai mediated justice and fairness in collaborative learning|kuutti
title: Exploring AI-mediated justice and fairness in collaborative learning
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly entering educational practice, yet its implications for justice and fairness in group work remain underexplored. This exploratory qualitative study examines 28 anonymous written responses collected from a Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) on AI pedagogy and well-being involving higher-education students from five European universities. Participants responded to an open-ended question about how AI affects justice or fairness in education and group work. Using inductive thematic analysis and multi-label coding, the study identified recurring concerns around access, learning support, group-work support, contribution visibility, bias, agency, transparency and assessment. The findings should be read as a pilot mapping of fairness-related perceptions within this specific educational context rather than as representative evidence. We synthesise these perceptions into six preliminary dimensions of AI-mediated collaborative justice: access, contribution, assessment, epistemic and linguistic, agency, and transparency justice. The framework provides a starting point for future research and for the design of fairer AI-supported collaborative learning.

title_key: exploring the relationship between chatgpt use and vocabulary mastery among indonesian efl secondary school students|wahidatin
title: Exploring the Relationship between ChatGPT Use and Vocabulary Mastery among Indonesian EFL Secondary School Students
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded opportunities for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, particularly through ChatGPT as an accessible language-learning tool. Although previous studies have reported generally positive perceptions of ChatGPT among language learners, empirical evidence concerning its relationship with measurable language proficiency remains limited. This study examined the relationship between ChatGPT use and vocabulary mastery among eleventh-grade students at MAN 1 Kota Palu, Indonesia. Using a quantitative correlational design, the study involved 54 students selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using a 20-item ChatGPT Usage Questionnaire measuring frequency of use and perceived usefulness, along with a 30-item Vocabulary Mastery Test assessing lexical knowledge. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the Kolmogorov–Smirnov normality test, and Pearson's product-moment correlation. The findings showed that students generally reported moderate to high levels of ChatGPT use and perceived it as useful for vocabulary learning. However, the correlation analysis revealed a negligible positive and statistically nonsignificant relationship between ChatGPT use and vocabulary mastery (r = .020, p = .886). These findings suggest that frequent use and positive perceptions of ChatGPT do not necessarily correspond to higher vocabulary achievement. Other learner-related and contextual factors, which were not directly examined in this study, may contribute to differences in vocabulary mastery. Therefore, ChatGPT may be more appropriately viewed as a supplementary resource whose educational value depends on how it is used and integrated into meaningful language-learning activities.
venue: FOSTER Journal of English Language Teaching

title_key: whose appraisal a freire informed think aloud study of allied health students use of generative ai in evidence appraisal|ribeiro
title: Whose appraisal? A Freire-informed, think-aloud study of allied health students’ use of Generative AI in evidence appraisal
abstract:
Background 
Generative AI (GenAI) can now produce artefacts such as essays, literature reviews, and worked rationales which challenge assessment designs that reward the products of thinking over the practice of it (Bearman et al., 2024; Corbin et al., 2025; Dawson et al., 2024). In evidence-based practice (EBP) education, students are required to appraise study quality, interpret effect sizes, and integrate findings into clinical decisions (Lehane et al., 2019). GenAI can now generate convincing outputs for each of these tasks. Observational data on what students do cognitively when they use GenAI in EBP tasks are scarce. Depending on how students use it, GenAI may scaffold the reasoning that EBP education is designed to develop or may bypass it (Vendrell & Johnston, 2026).
Aim
This study explores how allied health students engage with GenAI, how much they rely on it, and how they reason about its use when completing an EBP evidence-appraisal task.
Methods
This is an exploratory qualitative study using a concurrent think-aloud protocol with allied health students who have completed an EBP unit. The unit must have included critical reasoning as a learning outcome. Participants complete a structured 60-minute EBP task involving a clinical scenario. During this task, participants verbalise their reasoning and rationale for using or declining GenAI. A researcher facilitates this process through non-directive questions.
Sessions are audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed in two stages. In the first stage, transcripts are coded deductively and inductively against the six critical thinking processes in Vendrell and Johnston’s (2026) framework: conceptual interpretation, inferential reasoning, evaluative judgement, metacognitive regulation, intellectual curiosity, and epistemic integrity. This stage identifies whether and how reasoning is handed over to GenAI.
In the second stage, an interpretive analysis informed by critical pedagogy (Freire, 2005) examines how students position themselves in relation to AI-generated knowledge. Freire described a banking model of education, in which an authority deposits knowledge into passive students. This model offers a lens for examining uncritical acceptance of GenAI output, should that be present (Freire, 2005). Freire located authority in the school system and in the teacher who deposits knowledge into students (Freire, 2005). GenAI is a further candidate for that position in higher education. Unlike a teacher or an institution, it is designed by companies whose incentive is engagement and commercial return rather than student learning (Bartsch et al., 2025).
Findings 
Data collection is in progress. This study will generate think-aloud data on how allied health students engage cognitively with GenAI during EBP appraisal tasks, mapping where GenAI use aligns with or diverges from the reasoning processes EBP education is designed to develop. The interpretive analysis will explore the degrees of agency students exercise over AI-generated knowledge and the conditions in which they exercise or relinquish it, which process-level coding alone cannot capture.
Conclusion
Findings may inform teaching and assessment design in EBP units and provide a think-aloud protocol that can be adapted to examine GenAI use in reasoning tasks across health professions education.

title_key: when technical is easy using capability level rubric data to surface the gap between production and judgement|young
title: When technical is easy: Using capability-level rubric data to surface the gap between production and judgement
abstract:
Generative AI has not changed the need for assessment, but it has changed what certain forms of assessment can reliably tell us about student performance. When students can access AI support for idea generation and technical implementation, what assessment should measure becomes an open question (Perkins et al., 2024) and aggregate course grades may provide little insight to distinguish strong conceptual work from competent production. We report on a preliminary analysis of rubric data from a postgraduate data visualisation course (n =175) where AI use for idea generation and coding support was explicitly permitted and treated as a normal part of the workflow. The course assessment was redesigned around capability-level rubrics to capture what matters most when technical production can be AI-assisted.
The assessment design was informed by evaluative judgement theory (Bearman et al., 2024; Tai et al., 2018), where the capacity to recognise and justify quality is positioned as a graduate capability developed through repeated engagement with standards. The course used descriptive capability rubrics with five levels from Foundation to Exceptional, applied across multiple assessments and a final project portfolio. As Gyamfi et al. (2022) demonstrate, descriptive levels preserve the interpretive work that evaluative judgement requires rather than orienting students toward compliance. A separate competency review assessed critique, interpretation, and application of visualisation principles under exam conditions without AI access.
The final grade distribution looked similar to previous iterations of the course, but the capability-level rubric data had a more interesting story to tell. Distinct student profiles emerged, including those whose technical implementation capability exceeded their ability to communicate a coherent data story, suggesting a gap between procedural and deeper conceptual capability (Biggs & Tang, 2011). A similar pattern was visible in a dedicated storytelling assessment, where strong visuals were not consistently matched by strong narrative performance. These within-student differences were largely invisible in aggregate grades. The competency review provided an independent measure of evaluative judgement: what students could do without AI assistance or visualisation making tools. Competency review performance showed the strongest though modest association with the portfolio data story criterion, suggesting that the ability to interpret and communicate was the more reliable indicator of independent judgement (Bearman et al., 2024).
We argue that rubric data, already generated through normal marking processes in most LMS environments, constitutes an under-utilised source of learning analytics. Examined at the level of capability profiles rather than aggregate scores, this approach can surface distinctions between production and judgement that grades conceal across many discipline contexts, providing actionable insights that connect assessment evidence to teaching decisions (Kennedy et al., 2025). Rather than framing AI as a threat to assessment integrity, we ask a different question: if technical production is increasingly supported, which capabilities remain the most trustworthy evidence of what students know? As argued by Corbin et al. (2026), deciding which forms of evidence deserve the greatest trust may matter more than detecting whether AI was used. We show that capability-based rubric data may be one such form of trustworthy evidence.

title_key: keeping humans in the loop ai assisted curriculum at program scale|frost
title: Keeping humans in the loop: AI-assisted curriculum at program scale
abstract:
As universities adopt generative AI for curriculum development, a central risk is that efficiency gains may come at the expense of educational judgement, disciplinary expertise and human connection. Yet the same technology, used selectively, can free academics to focus on how students think and solve problems (Truu, 2026).
 
This poster presents a programmatic, human-led method for AI-assisted course development used across UNSW College’s new Applied Degrees: industry co-designed, work-blended bachelor programs in business and information technology. It addresses two questions: how can generative AI support curriculum development at program scale while preserving human educational judgement; and where must that judgement be structurally embedded? The method is grounded in constructive alignment (Biggs & Tang, 2011) and human-centred AI (Le Dinh et al., 2025), applied at program rather than course level.
The main focus is programmatic coherence. Rather than building courses one at a time, the method applies shared design patterns across an entire program. Even with different subject matter experts (SMEs) and program leads contributing to different courses, these design principles remain consistent from first year to capstone. AI generates content within this architecture, but functions as a structured design assistant rather than an autonomous author. Different workflow stages route to different AI models suited to each context. This preserves checkpoints where human framing and contextual judgement re-enter the process, consistent with calls to keep human control central to AI in education (Alfredo et al., 2024; Bearman et al., 2023; Hau, 2025; Islam, 2026).
The human-led, AI-supported workflow moves from industry and academic SME input and course overview revision through curriculum blueprinting, assessment critique, rubric development, Canvas-ready asynchronous content, workshop planning, and student-facing resources. The assessment-critique stage is especially significant as generative AI reshapes what assessment must do, with recent scoping evidence showing AI is driving a re-examination of assessment design across student, teacher and institutional levels (Chiu et al., 2024).
Human judgement remains decisive throughout: SMEs establish disciplinary intent; program leads review coherence and progression; learning designers evaluate scaffolding, accessibility and learner experience; and final quality assurance confirms alignment before publication. The ASCILITE Technology Enhanced Learning Accreditation Standards (TELAS, 2022) informed the design from the outset and now provide the basis for review, making quality auditable. This matters for Applied Degrees, where quality depends on integrating academic standards, industry relevance, work-integrated learning and inclusive learning design. Outputs are structured for continuous improvement in Canvas, keeping pedagogical authority close to the point of delivery rather than locked inside opaque AI outputs (UNESCO, 2023).
Critically, automating the repetitive build frees human effort for the work most often skipped under time pressure: the programmatic view, gathering student feedback, time with industry to collect current case studies and simulations, and targeted employability development so graduates are work ready. AI can accelerate curriculum production while strengthening human-centred design, provided the architecture and its checkpoints are designed first. The contribution is that architecture. The design patterns, curriculum blueprinting and checkpoints where human judgement re-enters are transferable to other program-scale builds regardless of which AI tools are used.

title_key: scientific mapping of problem based and project based learning for environmental literacy education a bibliometric and content analysis|mellyzar
title: Scientific Mapping of Problem-Based and Project-Based Learning for Environmental Literacy Education: A Bibliometric and Content Analysis
abstract: Background Problem-Based Learning (PBL) and Project-Based Learning (PjBL) have emerged as strategic pedagogies for cultivating environmental literacy (EL) and sustainability competencies within the Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) agenda. Yet the intellectual structure, thematic evolution, and conceptual integration of this body of scholarship remain insufficiently mapped, particularly in relation to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and to disciplinary contexts such as chemistry and environmental chemistry education. Methods This study combines bibliometric science mapping with systematic content analysis in a two-tier design. All 48 records retrieved from Scopus (2011–2026) through a Boolean query were mapped with VOSviewer and the Bibliometrix R package (co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, and thematic evolution). For the content analysis, the 45 records with available full texts were screened against PRISMA 2020-based eligibility criteria, and the 21 eligible journal studies were coded for educational level, learning approach, learning outcomes, SDG alignment (distinguishing goals named by the original authors from goals assigned by the coders), and research methodology. Coding was performed in two independent AI-assisted coding runs (Claude, Anthropic) using the same codebook (Cohen’s κ = 0.87–0.97 across categories); disagreements were resolved with documented rationales and all codes were verified manually by two authors. Results Publication output accelerated after 2021, a period that coincides with the ESD for 2030 framework; the field is anchored by Indonesian and North American institutional clusters and organized around four thematic clusters. Among the 21 eligible studies, undergraduate education predominates (43%), PjBL (52%) and PBL (48%) are used in roughly equal measure, EL is measured in 57% of studies, and only two studies (10%) explicitly name specific SDGs, whereas most (71%) are only thematically aligned. Persistent gaps include limited integration of chemistry education, short-term designs, and heterogeneous EL measures. Conclusion Within Scopus-indexed, English-language scholarship, PBL and PjBL are positioned mainly as delivery vehicles for measurable EL outcomes, whereas their role as enabling pedagogies for transformative sustainability education remains largely asserted rather than empirically demonstrated. We propose longitudinal designs, validated instruments, explicit testing of the differentiated affordances of PBL and PjBL, deliberate SDG-oriented design, and multi-database, multilingual mappings.
authors: ["M. Mellyzar", "N. Nahadi", "H. Hernani", "Asep Supriatna", "Oktariani Oktariani", "M. Marhami", "Desi Aryanti Nabuasa"]

title_key: teachers use of artificial intelligence in life studies and social studies education a systematic review|topcubas
title: Teachers' Use of Artificial Intelligence in Life Studies and Social Studies Education: A Systematic Review
abstract: Research on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching practice has focused predominantly on science, mathematics and language education, whereas social studies remains comparatively underexplored. This systematic review synthesises empirical research on in-service and pre-service teachers' use of AI in Life Studies and Social Studies education. Following PRISMA 2020 and the SPIDER framework, Web of Science, Scopus, OpenAlex, TR Dizin and the YÖK National Thesis Centre were searched for Turkish- and English-language studies published between 2020 and 2026. Of 360 unique records, 43 studies met the criteria; quality was appraised with the MMAT and findings were synthesised thematically. All studies were published in 2024–2026; 28 came from Türkiye (ten of them graduate theses), 13 from the Philippines, Nigeria and Indonesia, and none from North America or Europe. No study addressed Life Studies or primary classroom teachers. Teachers used AI—overwhelmingly ChatGPT—primarily to produce materials and content (24 studies), for assessment and feedback (21) and for lesson planning (19), and rarely for classroom management; where measured, acceptance ran well ahead of actual use. Perceived contributions were time saving, concretisation of historical and geographical content, and content diversity; barriers clustered into epistemic risk (inaccuracy, dependence, eroded critical thinking), infrastructural and training deficits, and professional–ethical concern. Subject-specific findings were distinctive: teachers positioned values education as the limit of AI's usefulness, reported culturally mismatched AI output, and treated historical and spatial accuracy as a subject-particular risk. Implications are drawn for subject-specific professional development, AI-TPACK-based teacher education and research on the unstudied primary grades.

title_key: ai driven instructional task differentiation and support for sustainable education a systematic literature review|iliska
title: AI-Driven Instructional Task Differentiation and Support for Sustainable Education: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to individualise instruction in secondary technology-enhanced learning environments, yet evidence remains fragmented across modelling approaches and learner outcomes. This systematic review synthesises empirical studies of learner-facing AI-enabled or data-driven technologies that diagnose learner needs and translate them into differentiated feedback, scaffolding, task sequencing, recommendation, assessment, or personalised learning pathways. Searches in Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC identified 3709 records; after filtering and deduplication, 744 records were screened, 84 full texts were assessed, and 46 studies met the eligibility criteria. Evidence was grouped by AI modelling family, differentiated instructional function, learner outcome, and design-based strength. The studies covered six AI modelling families: generative AI and large language models; intelligent tutoring and adaptive systems; recommender systems and learning analytics; automated assessment and diagnostic modelling; agent-based and companion systems; and multimodal, game-based, or AI-XR environments. Twelve studies provided higher-strength comparative or experimental evidence, 17 moderate-strength evidence, and 17 contextual or exploratory evidence. Reported outcomes covered achievement, computational thinking, motivation, engagement, self-regulated learning, cognitive-load management, retention, and system use, with favourable findings alongside mixed or limited evidence. However, unconstrained generative support could reduce productive effort and later learning. The reviewed evidence suggests that timely, interpretable, and pedagogically constrained AI support may contribute to responsive instruction while preserving learner agency. Its long-term sustainability and equity implications remain insufficiently established.

title_key: discalculai a computational approach for the identification of dyscalculia in educational contexts|pinhata
title: DISCALCULAI: A Computational Approach for the Identification of Dyscalculia in Educational Contexts
abstract: Dyscalculia is a specific learning disorder that affects numerical processing and mathematical reasoning. It remains underrecognized in educational contexts due to limited teacher training and restricted access to specialized knowledge. This scenario contributes to the misinterpretation of students’ difficulties, delaying appropriate pedagogical interventions and exacerbating educational inequalities. This study presents DISCALCULAI, a system designed to support teachers’ literacy regarding dyscalculia and assist in identifying its indicators within educational environments. Its approach is grounded in Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, particularly Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), to provide reliable and contextually relevant responses based on previously selected scientific literature. The system integrates text processing, semantic representation generation, vector indexing, and the use of Large Language Models (LLMs), enabling interaction through natural language queries. Unlike approaches based solely on generative models, the proposed architecture delivers evidence-based responses supported by retrieved information, reducing the occurrence of inaccurate outputs. To evaluate the system’s effectiveness, an experiment was conducted comparing the RAG-based approach with a standalone language model using a set of 31 domain-specific queries. The results indicate statistically significant improvements in semantic similarity, groundedness, and error rate (p = 0.0226), demonstrating that the integration of retrieval mechanisms substantially enhances the relevance and contextual quality of the responses. By contributing to the recognition of dyscalculia indicators, DISCALCULAI promotes more inclusive educational environments and highlights the role of technology in reducing barriers to access specialized knowledge.

title_key: cognitive offloading with large language model agents in cybersecurity education perceived burden and engagement in a single cohort study with ten year institutional context|kim
title: Cognitive Offloading with Large Language Model Agents in Cybersecurity Education: Perceived Burden and Engagement in a Single-Cohort Study with Ten-Year Institutional Context
abstract: Practice-oriented cybersecurity education often requires novice learners to build target web systems by hand before security analysis begins, imposing extraneous cognitive load. An earlier study introduced a Red/Blue teaming model in which a large language model (LLM) agent builds the target systems (vibe coding) under Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) control, so that learners audit, attack, and defend. This single-cohort study examines learner-level evidence from the 2026 cohort (n = 34) of a university web-security course, set against institutional Course-Quality-Improvement (CQI) satisfaction records for nine of the ten academic years 2017–2026. Evidence comprised self-reported coding-effort logs (n = 25), single-item final-course survey measures (n = 27), and peer cross-evaluation scores (71 ratings). Logged total coding effort had a median of 3.8 h. In the final-course survey, 96% agreed implementation burden had decreased and 93% that deeper engagement in vulnerability analysis and defense design was possible (raw means 4.67 and 4.44 of 5; Wilcoxon p < 0.001). The 2026 CQI score (91.55) ranked second among the nine records (descriptive). In this single-institution context, delegating system construction to an LLM agent was associated with lower perceived implementation burden, greater reported security-analysis engagement, and high satisfaction; multi-site replication is required.

title_key: pemanfaatan ai dan hasil belajar rasio siswa kelas 6 sd mi studi pra eksperimen|rahmayani
title: Pemanfaatan AI dan Hasil Belajar Rasio Siswa Kelas 6 SD/MI: Studi Pra-Eksperimen
abstract: Ratio requires students to understand the relationship between two quantities rather than merely calculate with them, and many sixth graders still find it difficult. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence (AI) is entering classrooms, yet evidence from primary school mathematics, especially on ratio, remains limited. This study examined the difference in ratio learning outcomes between sixth-grade students who learned with a teacher-guided AI tutor and a historical comparison group that learned conventionally. A pre-experimental static-group comparison design was used, in which the comparison group was the sixth-grade cohort of the previous academic year (2025/2026; archived scores, n = 24), not a concurrent control class. The AI group was one sixth-grade class (n = 20) at MI Mas'udi Pontianak in the 2026/2027 academic year, which learned over four meetings with an AI assistant acting as a tutor under the teacher's guidance. Learning outcomes were measured by a 20-item multiple-choice test and analysed with an independent-samples t-test and Cohen's d. The AI group obtained a higher mean ratio score (M = 87.00, SD = 8.18) than the comparison group (M = 66.67, SD = 11.20), t(42) = 6.75, p < .001, d = 2.04. Because there was no pretest, no randomisation, and no concurrent control group, the difference may partly reflect differences between cohorts and cannot be attributed to AI alone; it is an initial indication that needs to be tested in a design with a concurrent control group.Keyword: AI-assisted learning, artificial intelligence, learning outcomes, ratio
authors: ["R. Rahmayani", "Sri Nurlailah Saputri", "Irfan Bahri", "A. Yani T", "Nurfadilah Siregar"]

title_key: ai based quality control of examination questions detecting flawed items through a human supervised feedback approach|dogan
title: AI-Based Quality Control of Examination Questions: Detecting Flawed Items Through a Human-Supervised Feedback Approach
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) have introduced new opportunities for quality control in educational assessment. This study presents a human-supervised approach for detecting potentially flawed multiple-choice examination items before administration within the Distance Education Programs in Turkish (TÜRTEP) of Ahmet Yesevi University. Institutional records covering six academic years from 2020-2021 to 2025-2026 were analyzed using a period-based comparative descriptive design. Among 77,300 items used during the four years before AI-assisted checking, 395 items (0.511%) were cancelled after examinations. During the two years in which AI-assisted quality control was used, 70 of 37,080 items (0.189%) were cancelled. This corresponds to an absolute decrease of 0.322 percentage points and a relative reduction of approximately 63.1%. The AI tools were not used as final decision makers; instead, they independently solved each item, identified possible inconsistencies between the stem, options, and answer key, and generated reasoned warnings for review by the course instructor. At every stage, the final decision is left to the human course advisor. The findings indicate that combining AI-based error detection with human-supervised feedback may provide a useful additional quality-control layer for large-scale distance-education examinations.

title_key: when genai helps and when it hurts testing expertise reversal within a cognitive load framework across different guidance task complexity and genai access conditions|yusuf
title: When GenAI helps and when it hurts: testing expertise reversal within a cognitive load framework across different guidance, task complexity, and GenAI access conditions
abstract: Studies have examined the impact of Generative AI (GenAI) on students’ learning outcomes, revealing a wide range of effects on performance, cognitive load, and learning processes. However, little is known about whether these effects change with learner expertise and the conditions under which GenAI support is provided. This study examined expertise reversal in GenAI-supported programming education across four eight-week experiments involving Year 3 computer science students from research universities in Saudi Arabia. Drawing on cognitive load theory, the experiments investigated GenAI support, guidance level, task complexity, and access condition in relation to intrinsic cognitive load, extraneous cognitive load, mental effort, and independent programming performance. The findings showed that GenAI support produced greater reductions in extraneous load and stronger independent performance among lower-expertise learners, while higher-expertise learners retained smaller benefits. Detailed guidance produced a crossover expertise reversal, benefiting lower-expertise learners while increasing extraneous load and weakening performance among higher-expertise learners. Higher task complexity increased cognitive demands and reduced performance across expertise levels, with greater effects among lower-expertise learners. Personalised access also benefited lower-expertise learners more strongly without disadvantaging higher-expertise learners. Overall, the findings distinguish a crossover expertise reversal under detailed GenAI guidance from diminishing benefits as learner expertise increases under other support and access conditions. The effects of task complexity further demonstrate that expertise-dependent differences do not necessarily constitute a reversal in instructional effectiveness. We recommend that effective GenAI support requires careful calibration to learners’ existing knowledge and the cognitive demands of learning.
