title_key: beyond permission mapping generative ai policy approaches across australian universities|zhu
title: Beyond permission: Mapping generative AI policy approaches across Australian universities
abstract: Australian universities are revising generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) guidance under strong pressure to assure learning, academic integrity and assessment quality. This concise paper reports a public-source mapping of GenAI policy, assessment guidance and student AI-literacy preparation across the 38 Universities Australia member universities. Using six TEQSA sources as contextual material, 100 university sources were coded by authority level, dominant public guidance approach, assessment model and student-facing literacy support. The public evidence shows diverse policy configurations: 18 universities used a structured framework, scale, tier or lane model, while eight relied mainly on assessment-specific rules. Student preparation was also prominent: 19 universities provided formal AI-specific learning opportunities, and 12 provided structured student hubs or toolkits. The findings suggest that GenAI policy can function as curriculum infrastructure rather than only academic-integrity compliance. The paper contributes to Human-Centred Learning Design by treating GenAI policy as learning design infrastructure that connects assessment authority, student trust, feedback expectations and AI literacy.

title_key: learning with ai to prepare for working alongside ai|khosravi
title: Learning with AI to prepare for working alongside AI
abstract: Generative AI is now woven into students’ everyday learning, supporting tasks such as writing, coding, reasoning and analysis. Yet its educational value remains uncertain, because systems built to improve immediate task performance may weaken the cognitive and metacognitive processes on which durable learning depends. At the same time, there are strong calls for education to better prepare students for an AI-rich future of work and the capabilities it demands. This paper tackles this double challenge through the design of AI tools that prioritise learning over performance while developing the capabilities that matter for working with AI: creating original work, exercising sound judgement and achieving disciplinary mastery. We first outline the design framework we adapt for building such tools, in which AI learning companions are embedded within authentic learning environments. We then present RiPPLE, a co-creation platform used by more than 100,000 students, where AI companions support learners as they create learning resources, evaluate the work of peers, and engage in personalised practice, with each activity targeting one of the three capabilities. We conclude with reflections and selected empirical findings from the development and deployment of RiPPLE, drawing out lessons for designing AI tools that put learning first.

title_key: a hybrid multi agent framework for the early prediction of sepsis utilizing ensemble learning and explainable artificial intelligence|elakiya
title: A Hybrid Multi-Agent Framework for the Early Prediction of Sepsis Utilizing Ensemble Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence
abstract: It is important to identify sepsis early in order to reduce death rates and improve patient outcomes in intensive care units. Even though independent ML models can attain a high degree of accuracy, they often act as “black boxes”, which hampers their interpretability and prevents them from capturing the complex, changing course of a patient's condition factors that reduce clinicians' confidence and hinder practical use. The present paper introduces an innovative MultiAgent Explainable AI (XAI) Framework which enables early prediction of sepsis by means of the cooperative work of specialised intelligent agents. The framework includes four key elements: a Perception Agent that carries out preprocessing of clinical data; a Prediction Agent that uses XGBoost to evaluate the risk of sepsis from multi-modal electronic health records (EHRs); an Explanation Agent that obtains mathematical feature importances by means of SHAP and LIME; and an Action Agent that generates proactive alerts and evidence-based recommendations. Crucially, the Explanation Agent makes use of a Large Language Model (LLM) to turn the quantitative SHAP/LIME feature weights into clear, easily understandable clinical narratives. In this study, XGBoost and the SHAP pathway are computationally validated on the PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2019 dataset; LIME, the LLM narrative module and the Action Agent are implemented and demonstrated qualitatively in a prototype dashboard, with quantitative benchmarking held in reserve for future work. This approach successfully links the results of complex algorithms to practical medical insights. The whole process ends with the availability of a Doctor Dashboard that includes a human-in-the-loop component for clinical validation. By combining powerful predictive abilities with dual-layer explainability and collaborative agent autonomy, our framework promotes clinician trust and provides a scalable structure for rapid and transparent sepsis intervention in high-acuity healthcare environments.

title_key: from expert feedback to ai assisted course review scaling educational judgement in paair|chanane
title: From expert feedback to AI-assisted course review: Scaling educational judgement in PAAIR
abstract:
Monash University has embarked on an ambitious Assessment Advancement project seeing the review of over 500 courses and areas of study redesigned programmatically with intentional integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to prepare students for an ever-changing world. The Programmatic Assessment and AI Review (PAAIR) project at Monash University is generating rich, expert feedback on course design, assessment regimes, learning outcome alignment, and AI integration across coursework programs (Baartman et al., 2022; Fawns et al., 2026; Heeneman et al., 2021; Sotiriadou et al., 2020). GenAI is intensifying the need for scalable but trustworthy curriculum review practices that preserve human agency, accountability and professional judgement. AI governance guidance emphasises that AI should augment, not displace, human agency, with human oversight, accountability and risk management built into system design (Miao & Holmes, 2023). This poster presents emerging work to use feedback from the PAAIR Panel, a cross-faculty group of Monash education experts, to train an AI agent that can support education teams in reviewing Course Design Spreadsheets as part of course reaccreditation and continuous review. 
The proposed AI agent is deliberately positioned as an assistant, not a decision-maker. Its role is to highlight areas within a course that may warrant closer human attention, such as unclear alignment between course learning outcomes, unit learning outcomes and assessment tasks; limited evidence of progression across a course; unclear rationale for AI use or restriction; over-reliance on particular assessment types; or places where assessment security may depend too heavily on final products rather than visible evidence of learning. The AI does not replace educational judgement, approve course design, or provide final feedback to course teams. Instead, it prompts reviewers to look more closely, ask better questions, and provide contextualised human feedback.
The work responds to a key institutional challenge and a sector-wide response to enacting assessment reform in a time of AI: how to scale educative feedback across large numbers of courses while maintaining the professional judgement, disciplinary sensitivity and care that meaningful course review requires (Lodge et al., 2025). By training the agent on feedback authored by Monash education experts, the project seeks to preserve and amplify local educational expertise rather than outsource it. The AI is being designed to support consistency, reduce reviewer workload, and make recurring patterns visible across submissions, while keeping humans responsible for interpretation, dialogue and decision-making. Achieving these aims without compromising feedback quality is a high priority in our testing.
This approach contributes to broader conversations about responsible AI in higher education by exploring a human-in-the-loop model where AI assists educational teams to review complex curriculum data. The AI supports the review while decisions stay with educators. The model could transfer to institutions following a similar review process, though their policy, curriculum templates and staffing will shape feasibility. The poster will share the emerging design principles, potential workflow, and early opportunities for using expert-informed AI to support programmatic assessment and AI integration.

title_key: rethinking the engineering workforce pipeline preparing engineers for 2035|wade
title: Rethinking the Engineering Workforce Pipeline: Preparing Engineers for 2035
abstract: Contemporary engineering practice increasingly involves interconnected, evolving systems whose boundaries cross technical disciplines, organizations, and societal contexts. Yet engineering education remains largely organized around disciplinary specialization, sequential courses, and knowledge transmission. This article argues that the resulting structural misalignment cannot be resolved simply by adding new subjects or technologies to existing curricula. Preparing engineers for 2035 requires an educational architecture that develops systems literacy, lifecycle reasoning, integrative judgment, and the capacity for continuous learning. Drawing on experience with a professional systems engineering program at the University of California, San Diego, the article describes an alternative architecture built around persistent enterprise projects, experiential learning, and continuous integration of engineering foundations. Generative artificial intelligence supports this approach by enabling depth‐on‐demand learning while increasing the importance of durable fundamentals, critical evaluation, and professional responsibility. The article further proposes replacing the traditional linear workforce pipeline with an adaptive professional learning ecosystem in which universities, employers, engineers, and intelligent learning systems remain connected through ongoing feedback. The central challenge is not to predict every capability engineers will need in 2035, but to create systems that sustain and evolve engineering capability throughout professional careers.

title_key: prompt literacy of future computer science teachers in solving and debugging programming tasks with chatgpt perceptions practices and academic performance patterns|rakhmetov
title: Prompt literacy of future computer science teachers in solving and debugging programming tasks with ChatGPT: perceptions, practices, and academic performance patterns
abstract: This study examines prompt literacy among future computer science teachers in the context of solving and debugging programming tasks with ChatGPT. It focuses on students' perceptions of prompt literacy, their understanding of responsible AI use, documented practices of verifying and modifying AI-assisted solutions, and patterns of academic performance. A descriptive multi-method study was conducted during a 16-week programming course involving 113 future computer science teachers at Kh. Dosmukhamedov Atyrau University, Kazakhstan. Data were collected through questionnaires, student programming submissions, ChatGPT-use disclosure notes, reflective comments, code-similarity screening, and course-grade records. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative content analysis was used to identify recurring patterns in students' reported use, verification, and revision of AI-generated solutions. The findings were compared across data sources to address the research questions without testing causal effects or participant-level associations. The 20-item Prompt-Literacy Perceptions Questionnaire demonstrated high overall internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.94). Students generally reported positive perceptions of ChatGPT for code generation, debugging, and explaining programming logic. They also recognized the importance of verifying AI-generated outputs and disclosing substantial AI assistance. However, students' documentation of verification and modification practices was frequently general rather than detailed. Pairwise code-similarity screening identified relatively few submission pairs exceeding the predefined 50% similarity threshold. Mean academic scores were numerically close across practical assignments and independent control tasks, although differences in assessment conditions and grading criteria limited direct comparisons. The findings highlight the importance of integrating prompt literacy, critical verification, and transparent documentation of AI use into computer science teacher education. Positive perceptions of responsible ChatGPT use did not necessarily correspond to detailed documentation of verification and revision practices. Code-similarity results cannot independently establish whether students modified AI-generated solutions. Furthermore, the descriptive single-cohort design does not support conclusions about causal effects or improvements in prompt-literacy competence. The study emphasizes the pedagogical value of making students' reasoning, verification, and responsible AI-use practices explicit during programming instruction.
authors: ["M. Rakhmetov", "B. Kenzhegulov", "Turkmenbayev Asset", "Berdyguzhin Leskaliy", "G. Saltanova", "K. Turebayeva", "Aliya Muratkaliyeva"]

title_key: a study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading cognitive load allocation and academic engagement in ai empowered curriculum environments|jia
title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments
abstract:
While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy.
 
 
 
 
 A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences (
 n
  = 368) and STEM (
 n
  = 465) cohorts.
 
 
 
 
 The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts.
 
 
 
 Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

title_key: sensed a voice driven ai tutor for visually impaired engineering students|chaduvula
title: SensED: A Voice-Driven AI Tutor for Visually Impaired Engineering Students
abstract: Education for visually impaired engineering students remains profoundly challenging due to the pervasive reliance of existing learning platforms on visual content delivery. Screen readers and basic assistive tools provide limited support, offering content narration without interactive doubt clarification, conversational tutoring, or adaptive curriculum engagement. This paper presents SensEd, a voice-driven intelligent tutoring application designed specifically for visually impaired engineering students. SensEd enables fully hands-free interaction through natural speech, allowing students to explore hierarchically organized engineering curricula spanning eight-plus disciplines, receive AI-generated explanations comparable to human tutoring, resolve doubts conversationally, and practice through voice-navigated multiple-choice quizzes. The system integrates Google Gemini 2.5 Flash for natural language understanding and content generation, speech-to-text and text-to-speech services for bidirectional voice interaction, and a structured SQLite database for offline curriculum access and response caching. A multi-key API rotation mechanism ensures service continuity under free-tier rate limits. Additional wellness features include a configurable study timer with voice-alert break notifications to reduce cognitive fatigue. The SensEd mobile app developed with Flutter to provide platform independence is fully usable through voice in all activities without any need for visuals. The prototype testing conducted with the involvement of 120 engineering students resulted in a SUS score of 81.2, an accuracy rate of commands processed by the STT of 92.8%, success rate of quizzes at 88.5%, and a user satisfaction score of 4.2 (scale from 1 to 5). Potential areas for future investigation could involve offline STT and LMS capability.

title_key: a century of u s fluids engineering education tradition transformation and turbulence in an age of ai|milanovic
title: A Century of U.S. Fluids Engineering Education: Tradition, Transformation, and Turbulence in an Age of AI
abstract:
This centennial paper offers the first synthetic history of U.S. fluids engineering education as a distinct site of pedagogical development within the broader evolution of engineering education. Spanning from 19th-century hydraulic practice and polytechnic laboratory traditions through the engineering science revolution, the rise of computation, and the present age of generative artificial intelligence, we trace how fluids education has repeatedly reorganized the ways flow is made visible, interpretable, and teachable. In doing so, we show that the history of fluids instruction reveals transformations in engineering education, professional identity, and national priorities. The field has often mirrored, and at times anticipated, wider curricular and pedagogical changes.
 Situated within broader international lineages, we connect U.S. developments to European hydraulic laboratories, Russian and Soviet scientific traditions, Japanese and Chinese statetechnical formations, and the broader restructuring of engineering education under ABET and Bologna. Across these settings, educational change expressed evolving assumptions about what engineers are for, what forms of knowledge count, and how institutions understand their responsibilities. Within this larger arc, fluids education retained a central commitment: the effort to make fluid behavior intelligible across changing forms of representation and analysis.
 We show how thermo-fluids convergence, learning-science insights, outcomes-based reform, and simulation-integrated pedagogy reshaped both curriculum and professional identity. By enabling the integration of analysis, experiment, and computation within a single learning sequence, simulation made fluids education especially receptive to exploratory and digitally enhanced forms of instruction. At the same time, these developments exposed new fractures in continuity, conceptual depth, and student readiness. In many cases, visual fluency and automation began to outpace understanding.
 Generative AI signals a Sixth Shift in which reasoning becomes increasingly distributed across human and machine systems. As tools begin to participate in inference and authorship, the pedagogical challenge is to preserve discernment and agency.

title_key: from psychological needs to knowledge practices individual inquiry and shared learning in generative ai supported vocational education|liu
title: From psychological needs to knowledge practices: individual inquiry and shared learning in generative AI-supported vocational education
abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provides rapid access to explanations and examples, but information access does not necessarily become effective learning. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study examined associations among autonomy, competence, and relatedness need satisfaction, knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing, and perceived learning effectiveness.
 
 
 
 A cross-sectional survey included 300 adult students in computing-related programs at seven vocational colleges in Nanchang, China. The common reference was learning in web design and development during the preceding 4 weeks. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were complemented by fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA).
 
 
 
 All three psychological needs were positively associated with knowledge acquisition. Autonomy and competence were significantly associated with knowledge sharing; the relatedness coefficient was positive but did not reach the 0.05 significance level. Acquisition and sharing were both positively associated with perceived learning effectiveness. Autonomy and competence had significant statistical indirect associations through both practices, whereas relatedness had a significant indirect association only through acquisition. These separate significance tests do not establish differences between coefficients. Three configurations were associated with high perceived effectiveness, two of which included relatedness. Low-outcome configurations remained exploratory because their proportional reduction in inconsistency values fell below the specified threshold.
 
 
 
 GenAI was the contextual framing rather than an independently measured exposure, and the knowledge practices were not exclusive to GenAI. The outcome was subjective, and neither the indirect paths nor the configurations establish causality or objective learning gains.

title_key: standard anchored delegation in teachers use of generative ai|farooq
title: Standard-Anchored Delegation in Teachers'Use of Generative AI
abstract: Teachers who use generative AI must decide which parts of their work to hand over, while they remain accountable for what reaches students. We studied these decisions in Punjab, Pakistan, through a qualitatively driven mixed-methods study. We interviewed 13 teachers from government, private, NGO and vocational institutions, four administrators and one student, and coded each teacher's position on twelve educational tasks. Nine teachers accepted AI drafts or substantial assistance with lesson planning, but none accepted AI-drafted learning objectives, and eleven did not use AI to encourage or emotionally support students. Teachers who would accept AI marking required that the model be given a rubric or marking criteria. Building on assessment research and HCI work on verifiability, we call this pattern standard-anchored delegation: teachers handed a component of a task to AI when a standard outside the model, such as a textbook or rubric, defined a correct output and the teacher could apply that standard to the result. Having a standard was not always enough. Several government-school teachers did not use AI to mark quizzes even though the quizzes had answer keys, because they expected students to look for evidence of the teacher's effort. Checking AI output required subject knowledge and time, and private schools gave teachers more support for this than government schools did. Participants also read disclosure of AI use as a statement about whether the teacher had reviewed the work. We propose that teacher-facing AI tools ask for the relevant standard before generating and show each output beside it, and that schools account for the time that checking takes.

title_key: inteligencia artificial generativa en el aprendizaje autonomo del idioma ingles estudio piloto en la universidad tecnica latinoamericana|osorio
title: Inteligencia artificial generativa en el aprendizaje autónomo del idioma inglés: estudio piloto en la Universidad Técnica Latinoamericana
abstract: English language proficiency constitutes a relevant competence in higher education; however, many university students experience limitations in their language skills, which may affect their academic performance and access to specialized information. In this context, the present study aimed to explore the use of generative artificial intelligence as a support resource for autonomous English language learning, with emphasis on reading comprehension and written production. An applied mixed-methods study with a descriptive-exploratory scope was conducted using a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design without a control group. The sample was non-probabilistic and convenience-based, comprising 17 university students from Universidad Técnica Latinoamericana who voluntarily participated in a six-week pilot program based on autonomous activities mediated by generative artificial intelligence tools. A diagnostic test, a final test, perception surveys, and an analysis of written products were administered. The results showed favorable changes in the indicators related to the use of grammatical structures, vocabulary, and textual coherence among the three students who completed the intervention. Participants also reported positive perceptions of the tools, particularly regarding immediate feedback, ease of use, and flexibility. However, participation progressively declined, reaching three students at the end of the program, equivalent to 17.65% of the initial sample. Difficulties related to time management, consistency, and follow-up complemented the description of this pattern. It is concluded that generative artificial intelligence constitutes a support resource with potential for language practice, whose integration requires pedagogical strategies that articulate learner autonomy, digital competencies, guidance, and follow-up. The findings are limited to the specific conditions of the study and cannot be generalized to other populations.

title_key: development and initial validation of the genai stress scale for chinese k 12 teachers t genaiss|zhao
title: Development and Initial Validation of the GenAI Stress Scale for Chinese K-12 Teachers (T-GenAISS)
abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in K-12 education poses distinctive psycho-social challenges for teachers that are not fully captured by traditional technostress frameworks. However, existing technostress measurements, developed for direct human–computer interactions, are inadequate to capture the multifaceted stressors stemming from GenAI’s generative and opaque characteristics. This study reports the development and initial validation of a GenAI stress scale tailored to Chinese K-12 teachers (T-GenAISS). Drawing on the transactional stress-appraisal perspective, GenAI stress is defined as teachers’ cognitive appraisals that GenAI-related demands and conditions in their professional work exceed their resources or threaten valued goals. Exploratory analysis on a randomly split half of 612 teachers (174 pre-service and 438 in-service) affiliated with an Alliance of Thinking Schools professional learning community (n = 306) suggested seven dimensions: Privacy Violation, Job Replacement, Professional Development, Against Ethics, Lack of Transparency, Technological Dependence, and Bias Behavior. The 33-item instrument showed high internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.947). Confirmatory factor analysis on the other half (n = 306) yielded a mixed pattern: most indices were acceptable (CFI = 0.924, IFI = 0.925, TLI = 0.914, RMSEA = 0.066), whereas GFI (0.832) and NFI (0.875) remained below the conventional 0.90 benchmark, and acceptable fit was reached only after eight post hoc residual covariances had been specified. Discriminant validity was supported by the heterotrait–monotrait ratio but not fully by the Fornell–Larcker criterion, and scalar invariance across gender was supported on the baseline structure, so the reported gender comparisons are interpretable as latent-mean comparisons. The study provides initial psychometric evidence for a seven-factor structure in this ATS-affiliated sample and identifies the substantive refinements that independent replication must address before the instrument is used for diagnostic or evaluative purposes.

title_key: editorial issue 2 2026 water heritage a view from paris|hein
title: Editorial Issue 2/2026 Water Heritage: A View from Paris
abstract:
Since the 1990s, policy making, water and heritage management and cultural activities along the Seine in Paris and in the Île-de-France region have offered exemplary models of innovative, long-term action and of the successful reactivation of historical places and practices for sustainable living. The riverbanks, quays, monuments and urban vistas of the World Heritage property, together with the imaginary of the Seine, play an important role in this context as demonstrated by the 2024 Olympic Games. In an era of climate change, there is an urgent need to rethink the relationship between people, built heritage and rivers and other bodies of water. Approaches that include socio-ecosystemic thinking and nature-based solutions can help (re)create habitable, sustainable and just spaces that draw on historical practices, while protecting and adapting heritage and learning from history. The narratives we weave, the projects we realize and the heritage we preserve to live with water, both today and in the future, require careful attention. Exploring natural and cultural heritage, as well as intangible practices, can help build new narratives for cities, including riverside World Heritage cities. In these cities, citizens’ growing interest in water and aquatic activities challenges paradigms of the modern and industrial era, paving the way for better heritage protection and encouraging the design of a sustainable future. 
Central Paris, with the Seine and its quays at the core, offers a valuable case study for exploring both the challenges and opportunities of living with water in a World Heritage site, as argued by Carola Hein, Professor of History of Architecture and Urban Planning at Delft University of Technology, UNESCO Chair “Water, Ports and Historic Cities” and Researcher-in-Residence at the IEA Paris (Sorbonne University Chair) in 2024–2025. In collaboration with Laurence Lestel from Sorbonne University, head of the CNRS’ Zone Atelier Seine, with researchers of the PIREN-Seine program and the OPUS institute of Sorbonne University, Hein’s research in Paris tested the value case approach she developed as UNESCO Chair Water, Ports and Historic Cities, focusing on multiple and potentially conflicting uses of the Seine. During her stay in Paris, she explored the role of different water values in the transformation of the center of Paris and explored how these different water forms and functions intersect and how a shift in values can lead to a transformation of urban forms, functions and imaginaries. Several research and educational activities complemented Hein’s research at the IEA in Paris. Notably, Yvonne van Mil and Léa Kayrouz led research on the UNESCO Urban Heritage Atlas, with Kayrouz also contributing through literature review and cartographic analysis. In collaboration with van Mil and Lukas Hoeller, research for the River Port City Atlas extended the inquiry to regional and metropolitan scales, examining the Seine River as a structuring element of the wider territory. Zuzanna Sliwinska focused on mapping water museums, centers and cultural waterscapes across the Seine basin, while students in the Adaptive Design course developed design projects for Bercy Port. 
Based on her research, with support from Sorbonne University, IEA Paris and the UNESCO World Heritage Center, Hein organized a major conference, “(Re)Connecting River and City – The Seine in Paris and the Île-de-France: A Model for Nature Positive Approaches in World Heritage Cities for Climate Resilience,” at the IEA Paris in March 2025, engaging academic and professional participants from Paris and the world. The conference received support from several academic and professional partners, notably UNESCO, the IEA and the City of Paris, as well as the LDE PortCityFutures Center. This special issue of Blue Papers captures key arguments from the conference in revised and reviewed format. Sincere thanks to all institutions, colleagues and students who contributed their time, expertise and creativity to these research and educational activities. Their contributions enriched the research and fostered a collaborative exchange of ideas across different scales and perspectives. The goal of this issue is to share the debates and to contribute to broader discussions on multiple uses of a shared resource, the Seine. 
The articles compiled in this issue of Blue Papers provide background information on the historical and contemporary development of Paris from various disciplinary perspectives – including anthropology, archaeology, history, planning, heritage management and more. The first group of papers explores the broader context of the Seine and its multiple uses and the second speaks to the four themes selected for the conference: Swimming, Sewage, Shipping and Safety. 
Carola Hein begins by setting the context in Part I, describing various coexisting values associated with water in Paris and how these values can be used to improve river governance in Paris. Laurence Lestel shows how Parisians’ relationship with the Seine has evolved since the nineteenth century and why drawing on this historical perspective can restore meaning to that relationship. Hélène Noizet describes the evolution of the Seine in Paris since the Middle Ages, breathing new life into its ancient channels, which must regain their rightful place in shaping the relationship between the Seine and Parisians. Raphaël Morera reminds us how the bond between Paris and its river has shaped both the river and the city. Emmanuelle Lallement explores three initiatives to reclaim the banks of the Seine since the 1990s (Paris-Plage, the Voies sur Berge and the redevelopment of the area around Notre-Dame de Paris), each reflecting a different approach, thereby illustrating the potential diversity of efforts to rebuild the connection between residents and their river. Olivier Aïm takes us into the world of the guinguettes, once places of leisure outside the city limits (beyond the city toll gates) and today a symbol of a joyful approach to the riverbanks. Sahima Hamlaoui and Maria Cellamare remind us that the Seine is not merely a backdrop that enhances Paris, but is also the setting for a rich ecosystem, observed here through its phytoplankton. 
All decision-makers must take different spatial scales and functions into account. Yvonne van Mil, Carola Hein and Lukas Höller broaden the perspective with a study of the Parisian port city territory, which situates Paris within its river basin and connects the city to international trade. Olivier Burel illustrates this international dimension of the Seine in Paris using the example of energy, and Jean Debrie explains in detail what this port dimension means for the City of Paris. From a public health perspective, Anita Ravlic reminds us that the Seine, like so many other rivers, once served as an outlet for Paris’s sewers and explains how the management of this wastewater has led to a reclaiming of the Seine by city residents. Thomas Thiebault, Catherine Carré and Jérémy Jacob examine the wastewater in greater detail and what it reveals about Parisians’ dietary habits and health. Jean-Pierre Tabuchi, Catherine Carré and Jean-Claude Deutsch draw conclusions from this regarding the system’s ability to adapt to future global changes. Bruno Gouyette emphasizes that three approaches are necessary for a sustainable river: considering the entire Seine basin, viewing the Seine as a system to be considered as a whole and granting rights to the Seine to make it a visible issue in political debates. Finally, Clément Brun, Léonard Bertrand and Annabelle Nantier explore how the public health challenges associated with swimming have transformed the City of Paris’s vision and management of the river.

title_key: teaching students to verify generative ai using the trace ai framework|arinze
title: Teaching Students to Verify Generative AI Using the TRACE-AI Framework
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce polished mathematical solutions, executable code, persuasive media, and professional recommendations, yet fluency does not establish correctness, provenance, security, or contextual fitness. Existing AI-literacy frameworks appropriately describe broad competencies, while emerging studies in mathematics, programming, and health professions education show the value of domain-specific validation. What remains underdeveloped is a portable instructional process that makes verification, uncertainty, and reliance observable across disciplines. This conceptual article introduces TRACE-AI: Translate the task and stakes; Represent the problem, assumptions, and constraints; Audit the AI's reasoning and output; Corroborate pivotal claims through independent evidence, tests, or tools; Estimate uncertainty and warranted reliance; Act proportionately by accepting, revising, rejecting, or escalating; and Internalize learning through reflection and unaided transfer. The framework was developed through a theory-informed critical synthesis of AI literacy, mathematical problem solving, computational thinking and debugging, epistemic cognition, self-regulated learning, and trust calibration. Each stage produces an assessable artefact, and a risk gate increases verification and human oversight as uncertainty, irreversibility, or potential harm rises. Worked applications in mathematics, programming/cybersecurity, and health-professional reasoning demonstrate invariant functions with discipline-specific standards of proof. An assessment architecture distinguishes final-answer quality from process quality, appropriate reliance, confidence calibration, verification quality, and delayed unaided transfer. Six propositions define a research programme for comparative and randomized evaluation. TRACE-AI is not presented as an effectiveness-tested intervention; it is a transdisciplinary curriculum and research architecture requiring contextual adaptation and empirical validation. Its contribution is to move GenAI education beyond prompt production toward disciplined human judgment about when AI output deserves trust.

title: СТРУКТУРНІ СКЛАДОВІ ГОТОВНОСТІ МАЙБУТНІХ УЧИТЕЛІВ ІНФОРМАТИКИ ДО ПРОЄКТУВАННЯ ЦИФРОВОГО ОСВІТНЬОГО КОНТЕНТУ З ВИКОРИСТАННЯМ ГЕНЕРАТИВНОГО ШТУЧНОГО ІНТЕЛЕКТУ
abstract:
The article substantiates the structural components of future computer science teachers' readiness to design digital educational content using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). The relevance of the study is determined by the rapid integration of GenAI into education and the lag between the content of professional training and the development of these technologies. The analysis of publications has shown that the problems of computer science teachers' readiness for professional activity and the use of GenAI in education are mostly studied separately. The expediency of shifting from a mathematical to a technological and didactic approach to studying artificial intelligence in the course of professional training is substantiated. It has been established that designing digital educational content using GenAI encompasses two interrelated types of activity of future computer science teachers. The first is creating educational content intended to teach students the basics of GenAI, its capabilities, limitations and rules of responsible use. The second is using GenAI tools as pedagogical means for developing, adapting and improving computer science learning materials, such as explanations, tasks, tests, program code examples and multimedia resources. It is the specificity of these types of activity that determined the content of the structural components of the readiness under study.
The concept of "future computer science teachers' readiness to design digital educational content using GenAI" is considered as an integrative professional quality of personality that determines the ability to apply GenAI tools consciously, critically and responsibly to create learning materials. Four structural components of readiness have been identified and characterized. The motivational component involves a positive yet critical attitude towards GenAI and responsibility for the quality of content. The cognitive component encompasses subject knowledge in computer science, knowledge of the principles of operation and limitations of GenAI, and didactic and methodological knowledge. The activity component reflects the skills to set didactic goals, compose prompts, and verify, edit and integrate generated materials. The reflective component ensures self-control, self-correction and self-assessment in compliance with academic integrity. Prospects for further research lie in developing criteria and indicators of the formation of future computer science teachers' readiness to design digital educational content using GenAI.

title_key: mapping publicly shared nursing education applications a descriptive repository audit based on a structured github search|chang
title: Mapping publicly shared nursing education applications: A descriptive repository audit based on a structured GitHub search.
abstract:
AIM
To identify publicly shared nursing education applications on GitHub and audit what their public artefacts allow educators to establish before classroom use.


BACKGROUND
Public repositories make applications, including tools developed with generative artificial intelligence (AI), widely accessible, yet their documentation may not support appraisal of educational fit, clinical content accountability, learner-data practices, or conditions for use.


DESIGN
Descriptive audit of GitHub repositories.


METHODS
The GitHub repository search API was queried on 1-5 August 2026 using 34 free-text and 12 topic-label queries. Of 551 unique repositories screened by two independent reviewers, 76 underwent full inspection and 52 were included. Rule-based coding of public artefacts captured educational purpose and disclosure indicators.


RESULTS
Knowledge acquisition and recall was the most common purpose (19/52, 37%), followed by psychomotor or procedural preparation (8/52, 15%) and simulation, debriefing and reflection (7/52, 13%). All repositories stated the tool's function, but only 23 (44%) stated reuse terms, 18 (35%) learning objectives, 15 (29%) a clinical source, 13 (25%) a teacher role, 7 (13%) a learner-facing disclaimer and 3 (6%) a learner-data statement; none publicly documented clinical validation. Public evidence of AI-assisted development appeared in 13 (25%) repositories, and 17 (33%) contained reader-visible information about AI. These categories could overlap, and learner-facing AI functionality was not coded or quantified.


CONCLUSIONS
Findings describe what public artefacts made observable and do not establish learning effectiveness, clinical validity, software quality or safety. Before local adoption, educators should appraise educational purpose, content provenance, learner-data practices, reuse conditions, AI involvement and use boundaries.

title_key: program distillation transferring llm capability from system 2 to system 0|zheng
title: Program Distillation: Transferring LLM Capability from System 2 to System 0
abstract: Recent studies leverage large language models (LLMs) to construct executable programs through environment interaction, feedback analysis, and code revision. However, prior work has mainly treated LLMs as optimizers, overlooking their ability to transfer knowledge across system levels. We propose Program Distillation (PD), a framework that formalizes the transfer of abilities from System 2 to System 0. During learning, the LLM provides task knowledge and draft strategies; at deployment, a student program executes the resulting policy. We show that this approach can improve performance while reducing inference time. We introduce PDBench, a benchmark comprising 27 discrete- and continuous-control tasks with fixed initial policies, and PDMetaHarness, a model-harness-independent meta-system for monitoring and guiding the learning process. The strongest model achieves a normalized mean score of 0.728, surpassing PPO (0.656) and Jev-like decision models (0.239), while running exclusively on CPUs and reducing inference costs. Our analysis shows that performance is largely driven by the first breakthrough during learning, and structural modifications have a slightly lower success rate than parameter modifications but typically yield larger gains. We further introduce style distillation, which enables interpretable stylistic control over the learning process. Overall, we present an analytical framework for PD and demonstrate its practical viability.

title_key: evaluating the effectiveness of chatgpt as an ai assisted learning tool a quasi experimental study|uzma
title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of ChatGPT as an AI-Assisted Learning Tool: A Quasi-Experimental Study
abstract: This study evaluates the effectiveness of a structured generative-artificial-intelligence (GenAI)-assisted learning workflow for preparing students to perform a monologue speaking task. The monologue, a report text about animals, serves as the application scenario for evaluating the AI-assisted preparation mechanism. A quantitative quasiexperimental nonequivalent control group design involved 40 ninth-grade students from two Madrasah Tsanawiyah in Bekasi, with 20 students in the experimental group and 20 in the control group. The experimental group received a 15-minute ChatGPT-assisted preparation session to support idea organization, vocabulary selection, and monologue structuring, whereas the control group prepared independently using a physical dictionary for the same duration. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, N-Gain, Shapiro-Wilk normality testing, Welch’s t-test, and the Mann-Whitney U test. The experimental group improved from M = 8.85 to M = 12.60, compared with an increase from M = 8.80 to M = 9.60 in the control group. The post-test comparison was significant (Welch’s t = -3.146, df = 31.02, p = .004, |d| = .995), and the N-Gain comparison was also significant (U = 18.00, p < .001, r = .910). The findings indicate that a short, structured GenAI-assisted preparation workflow is feasible and associated with substantially greater performance improvement than non-AI preparation in this setting. Because participants were drawn from naturally formed classes in different schools, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of an association rather than definitive causal proof.
authors: ["Fadliyah Uzma", "D. Hidayat", "Ratna Sari Dewi", "D. Nugraha", "Rokhishotul Amaliyah"]

title_key: artificial intelligence and critical thinking in basic education students|arellano
title: Artificial intelligence and critical thinking in basic education students
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has introduced new challenges for checking information and explaining academic decisions in basic education. The objective was to understand the perceptions and educational practices reported by 38 teachers at private schools in Quito regarding artificial intelligence and critical thinking. A qualitative, descriptive-interpretive study examined responses to 14 questions from a semi-structured interview guide. The resulting corpus comprised 532 responses, which were coded and organized through reflexive thematic analysis. Five themes were identified: pedagogical boundaries for using artificial intelligence, verification of generated information, evidence of reasoning, tensions between autonomy and dependence, and institutional conditions. Teachers described checking sources, correcting fabricated quotations or inaccurate data, and requiring oral explanations and demonstrations of student work. They also reported differences in classroom rules and a need for subject-specific training. It was concluded that, in the teachers’ accounts, critical engagement with artificial intelligence depended on checking answers, justifying decisions, and pedagogical guidance. The interview data did not allow direct assessment of students’ critical-thinking performance.
authors: ["Coraima Micaela Valdiviezo-Arellano", "Jeferson Marcelo Grijalva Rosero", "Mar\u00eda Fernanda Grijalva Rosero", "Alvaro Alexander Viteri Teran", "Danny Javier Vinueza Pillajo", "Nelson Fernando Ram\u00f3n Calvache"]

title_key: construcao de serious game sobre feridas cronicas com suporte da inteligencia artificial estudo metodologico|oliveira
title: Construção de serious game sobre feridas crônicas com suporte da inteligência artificial: estudo metodológico
abstract: Objective: To describe the construction of a serious game aimed at nursing education in the care of people with chronic wounds, developed with the support of generative artificial intelligence, under the supervision and scientific responsibility of the authors. Method: A methodological study focusing on the technological construction phase, grounded in the Analysis, Design, and Development stages of the ADDIE model and Design Thinking. Code engineering in React.js was performed by the research team with the support of generative artificial intelligence in the CodeSandbox environment, with storage on Firebase. The design included ethical approval in Brazil and Portugal for the subsequent validation stage by expert judges and evaluation by nursing students. Results: The simulator was consolidated into a single-screen architecture structured into four operational modules. The system integrates interactive keys for cross-cultural adaptation between Brazil and Portugal, management of chromatic stimuli (in Dark/Light modes) and sound stimuli, scenario randomization mechanics, and immediate evidence-based feedback for each correct or incorrect action. Conclusion: The study demonstrates that nurses can lead the production of digital technologies, delivering a practical, autonomous, and cross-cultural tool aimed at nursing education.
authors: ["Raphael Monteiro de Oliveira", "J\u00falia Queiroz de Morais", "P. Parreira", "V. R. D. Coutinho", "Bruna Maiara Ferreira Barreto Pires"]

title_key: generative ai and assessment redesign in chemical engineering education a conceptual framework for learning evidence|liu
title: Generative AI and Assessment Redesign in Chemical Engineering Education: A Conceptual Framework for Learning Evidence
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) complicates the interpretation of assessment in chemical engineering education: a correct calculation, coherent report or plausible design may not reveal the student’s own reasoning. This narrative review brings together research on chemical engineering education, related disciplines, assessment validity and academic integrity. It distinguishes model capability, stakeholder perceptions and observed learning outcomes, then identifies four threats to assessment evidence: answer substitution, compression of reasoning into final products, smoothing of design rationales, and loss of individual attribution. Detection, prohibition, disclosure and authentic tasks address these problems only partially. We propose the Authenticity, Process Visibility, Verification, Reflection and Transparency (APVRT) framework to connect these vulnerabilities with complementary evidence functions and the conditions under which observations can support individual judgements. APVRT remains a conceptual proposal; its effects on judgement validity, fairness and workload require empirical evaluation.

title_key: an ai based commentary function with estimated state rating framework for student learning support in java programming learning assistant system|jing
title: An AI-Based Commentary Function with Estimated State Rating Framework for Student Learning Support in Java Programming Learning Assistant System
abstract: As Java remains a widely used object-oriented programming language in various application systems, we have developed the Java Programming Learning Assistant System (JPLAS) to support novice learners in their self-studies. JPLAS provides a variety of exercise problems that have different learning goals and difficulties. Among them, Grammar-Concept Understanding Problems (GUP) is designed as the first step problem where key grammar concepts appearing in a given source code are questioned. In this paper, we propose a commentary function supported by generative AI for GUP to study challenging concepts of Java programming such as generics and lambda expressions. This function provides AI-generated four-level hints to help students solve given questions. Besides, the Estimated State Rating (ESR) framework is presented to numerically describe the learning stagnation of a student. ESR is calculated using the time interval elapsed from the previous hint access and the current answer accuracy. For evaluations, we assigned the 10 GUP instances with the commentary function to 33 students in Okayama University, Japan, and calculated ESR from their log data. The evaluation examines the ESR values associated with the first recorded access to each commentary function and derives the corresponding 75th percentile as a reasonable reference threshold to allow the next-level hint. In future work, we will apply the proposal to other students and examine the effects on their problem solving and learning outcomes.
authors: ["Yan-Hui Jing", "N. Funabiki", "Hui-Yu Qi", "M. Mentari", "Htoo Htoo Sandi Kyaw"]

title_key: generative ai feedback in college students english argumentative writing effects dilemmas and pedagogical implications|tian
title: Generative AI Feedback in College Students’ English Argumentative Writing: Effects, Dilemmas, and Pedagogical Implications
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is gradually entering college students’ English argumentative writing instruction. This paper systematically reviews the effects, main dilemmas, and pedagogical implications of generative AI feedback in college students’ English argumentative writing. Existing studies show that generative AI feedback provides notable immediate support at lower-order linguistic levels such as grammar, spelling, punctuation, lexical substitution, language fluency, and lexical diversity, and can enhance writing motivation, self-efficacy, and some aspects of learning engagement. However, in higher-order dimensions such as argument development, argumentation quality, discourse organization, coherence and cohesion, cultural context, and authorial voice, the effect of AI feedback used alone is limited; teacher feedback and human–AI hybrid feedback are better able to compensate for these shortcomings. At the same time, generative AI feedback also brings problems such as lengthy and difficult-to-understand feedback, insufficient specificity, over-reliance, weakened critical thinking, academic integrity concerns, authorial voice issues, cultural bias, assessment validity, and insufficient AI literacy. On this basis, this paper proposes that generative AI feedback should be positioned as “supplementary rather than substitutive”; that a human–AI division of labor should be implemented in which AI handles lower-order language feedback and teachers lead higher-order argumentative feedback; that the timing of AI intervention should be arranged in stages; that collaborative processing of feedback, revision logs, prompt engineering, and AI feedback literacy training should be carried out; and that academic integrity and data-use regulations should be established, thereby improving the quality of college students’ English argumentative writing instruction.
venue: International Journal of Education and Humanities

title_key: genai and novice programmers conceptual understanding a systematic review|wangmo
title: GenAI and novice programmers’ conceptual understanding: A systematic review
abstract: Programming education remains challenging for novice learners, and the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has introduced new opportunities and challenges for learning programming. While existing research reports a range of potential benefits, the influence of GenAI on conceptual understanding remains underexplored. This systematic literature review investigates the role of GenAI in influencing novice programmers’ conceptual understanding in higher education programming contexts. Guided by the PRISMA framework, empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026 were reviewed and synthesised using a conceptual understanding framework comprising three dimensions: understanding programming constructs, reasoning about program behaviour, and developing mental models of program execution. The findings indicate that GenAI primarily functions as a learning support tool that may enhance understanding of programming constructs. However, evidence is less conclusive regarding reasoning about program behaviour and is extremely limited in relation to mental models of program execution. The review suggests that the effects of GenAI are concentrated in more surface-level dimensions of understanding and do not consistently translate into deeper conceptual understanding. The study identifies important gaps in current research and outlines directions for further investigation.

title_key: professionally oriented digital tasks in developing information and communication competence of future masters students in agricultural engineering|kramarenko
title: Professionally oriented digital tasks in developing information and communication competence of future master’s students in agricultural engineering
abstract: The article addresses the design of professionally oriented digital tasks for future master’s students in agricultural engineering. Its aim is to substantiate a task structure that connects engineering data analysis, digital modelling, verification of a proposed solution, and communication with a professional audience within one learning cycle. The study uses conceptual analysis of digital competence frameworks, alignment of learning outcomes with learning activities and assessment, and methodological modelling of agricultural engineering situations. A task specification is proposed that identifies a professional problem and its intended recipient, the provenance and limitations of data, available tools, the procedure for independent verification, and the required digital and communicative outputs. Observable evidence is mapped to four components of information and communication competence: information analysis, practical digital work, professional communication, and reflective and ethical judgement. A teaching case on selecting a machinery operating mode illustrates how students check input data, compare alternatives, test assumptions, prepare a technical recommendation, and defend it. Two additional task types concern variable-rate application and equipment condition monitoring. The paper further explains how an analytic rubric, a versioned electronic portfolio, and actionable feedback can support assessment and revision. Accessibility, responsible use of generative AI, and protection of personal and operational data are treated as design requirements. The outcome is a methodological model that may be adapted to courses in an agricultural engineering programme. The paper does not report an implemented intervention or empirical evidence of effectiveness; such evidence requires a separate, documented evaluation.

title_key: digital governance of generative ai in higher education authentic assessment as a pathway to student engagement and educational equity|jiang
title: Digital governance of generative AI in higher education: authentic assessment as a pathway to student engagement and educational equity
abstract: Universities worldwide are struggling to govern students’ use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), yet it remains unclear whether institutional governance actually shapes meaningful learning. Existing student-level evidence is largely descriptive, and the little inferential work available suggests that mere awareness of AI policies has no effect on student conduct—leaving the effects of governance quality untested. Drawing on procedural justice, self-determination, and digital divide perspectives, this study develops and tests a model in which perceived GenAI governance quality shapes students’ perceptions of authentic assessment, which in turn relate to student engagement and perceived educational equity. Two-wave survey data were collected from 644 undergraduate and postgraduate students across research-intensive, teaching-oriented, and vocational-applied universities in eastern, central, and western China, and were supplemented by objective coding of institutional AI policies. Estimated with institution-clustered standard errors, governance quality was positively associated with perceived authentic assessment well beyond mere policy awareness, more than doubling the explained variance. Authentic assessment fully mediated the relationship between governance quality and student engagement and partially mediated its relationship with perceived educational equity, while digital access remained an independent predictor of equity. Findings indicate that AI governance becomes educationally meaningful primarily when students experience it as authentic assessment, whereas equity additionally requires attention to procedural and resource conditions. Implications for institutional AI policy design are discussed.

title_key: hopd historical on policy distillation for sar mllm continual learning|li
title: HOPD: Historical On-Policy Distillation for SAR MLLM Continual Learning
abstract: Continual SAR interpretation requires multimodal large language models to learn incoming sources while retaining earlier task abilities. This is difficult when acquisition and geographic shifts alter visual evidence, regionally concentrated categories bias answers, and historical images are scarce. We address this problem with Historical On-Policy Distillation (HOPD), which reuses source-acquisition LoRA states as persistent teachers for one evolving student. Archiving each state before consolidation preserves a stable source reference. The teachers supervise student-generated prefixes, transferring historical behavior to the student's changing generation contexts. To enrich sparse replay, original-view teachers guide augmented historical student views while preserving spatial coordinates. This knowledge is consolidated into a single deployed adapter that requires no source identity. On SARVQA-CL, our source-incremental evaluation protocol, HOPD achieves the highest final mean score of 54.51 among the compared methods, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.96 points. It also improves the final source-macro score in every evaluated task over shared-memory Replay-SFT, with gains across source orders. These results support source-acquisition history as supervision for retaining earlier task performance during continual SAR adaptation. Code and data: https://github.com/zcablii/HOPD.

title_key: strategi metakognitif untuk mitigasi halusinasi logik kecerdasan buatan generatif dalam pendidikan sekolah menengah|manaf
title: Strategi Metakognitif untuk Mitigasi Halusinasi Logik Kecerdasan Buatan Generatif dalam Pendidikan Sekolah Menengah
abstract:
ABSTRAK 
  
Penggunaan Kecerdasan Buatan Generatif (GenAI) dalam pendidikan sekolah menengah di Malaysia semakin meluas, khususnya dalam menyokong pembelajaran dan pentaksiran akademik. Walau bagaimanapun, perkembangan ini turut membawa risiko kognitif tersembunyi yang dikenali sebagai halusinasi logik. Fenomena ini merujuk kepada situasi di mana Model Bahasa Skala Besar (LLM) menjana langkah penaakulan yang salah atau tidak koheren walaupun jawapan tersebut kelihatan meyakinkan dari segi fakta. Risiko ini berpotensi memesongkan pemahaman konsep murid, terutamanya dalam bidang Sains, Teknologi, Kejuruteraan dan Matematik (STEM). Kertas konseptual ini bertujuan menangani jurang literasi AI sedia ada melalui dua objektif utama, iaitu: (1) menganalisis limitasi keupayaan penaakulan algoritma LLM berdasarkan sorotan literatur terkini, dan (2) mencadangkan satu intervensi pedagogi berasaskan metakognisi yang dinamakan Teknik Semakan Logik Berstruktur. Dari segi metodologi, kajian ini menggunakan pendekatan Analisis Logik dan Sintesis Teoretikal dengan mengintegrasikan aras kelima Taksonomi Bloom (penilaian) serta Teori Bias Automasi bagi membentuk satu kerangka mitigasi yang praktikal. Analisis konseptual mendapati bahawa kerentanan murid terhadap ralat AI bukan berpunca daripada kekurangan kemahiran teknikal, sebaliknya disebabkan ketiadaan rutin metakognitif yang sistematik untuk mengesahkan maklumat. Sehubungan itu, kajian ini mencadangkan satu protokol semakan kendiri tiga langkah yang merangkumi Semakan Kesinambungan, Semakan Percanggahan dan Semakan Konteks sebagai rutin pemikiran kritis di dalam bilik darjah. Secara keseluruhan, intervensi kognitif ini menawarkan satu solusi yang mampan dan kos efektif untuk mengubah peranan murid daripada pengguna pasif kepada penilai aktif terhadap output AI, selaras dengan hasrat Dasar Pendidikan Digital negara. 
  
Kata kunci: Kecerdasan Buatan Generatif; Halusinasi Logik; Metakognisi; Literasi AI; Pendidikan Sekolah Menengah 
  
ABSTRACT 
  
The rapid adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in Malaysian secondary school education has introduced new possibilities for learning and assessment practices. However, this development also presents a hidden cognitive risk known as logical hallucination. Logical hallucination occurs when Large Language Models (LLMs) generate reasoning steps that are incorrect or incoherent, despite appearing factually plausible. This phenomenon poses a significant threat to students’ conceptual understanding, particularly in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) education. This conceptual paper addresses an existing gap in AI literacy by pursuing two main objectives: (1) to critically examine the limitations of algorithmic reasoning capacity in LLMs based on recent literature, and (2) to propose a metacognitively driven pedagogical intervention termed the Structured Logic Checking Technique. Methodologically, the study employs Logical Analysis and Theoretical Synthesis by integrating the fifth level of Bloom’s Taxonomy (evaluation) with Automation Bias Theory to construct a practical mitigation framework. The analysis reveals that students’ vulnerability to AI-generated errors is not primarily due to a lack of technical skills, but rather the absence of systematic metacognitive routines for verifying information. In response, the study proposes a three-step self-checking protocol comprising Consistency Check, Contradiction Check, and Contextual Relevance Check to be embedded as a critical thinking routine in classroom practice. Overall, this cognitive intervention offers a sustainable and cost-effective approach to transform students from passive users into active evaluators of AI output, in alignment with the first thrust of Malaysia’s Digital Education Policy aimed at cultivating ethically responsible and digitally competent learners. 
  
Keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence; Logical Hallucination; Metacognition; AI Literacy; Secondary Education
authors: ["Nurulhafizah Abdul Manaf", "M. E. M. Mohd Matore"]

title_key: examining pre service teachers ai integrated lesson planning through the tpack framework|hur
title: Examining Pre-service Teachers’ AI-Integrated Lesson Planning: Through the TPACK Framework
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly gained attention as a tool to support teachers in lesson planning, yet pre-service teachers often lack the knowledge and prompting skills necessary to integrate it effectively into their practice. This study employed a formative research design to investigate how pre-service teachers used GenAI for lesson plan development through the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework and to identify instructional guidance that fosters more meaningful interactions. Across two semesters in an introductory educational technology course at a large US university, 137 pre-service teachers engaged in lesson planning activities with GenAI tools. Data sources included student-AI chatlogs, reflective blog journals, and instructors’ reflective notes. In the first phase, pre-service teachers primarily used GenAI superficially, requesting complete lesson plans with minimal refinement. Based on these findings, instructional guidelines were developed and introduced in the second phase. PSTs subsequently demonstrated more robust use of GenAI, such as brainstorming, seeking pedagogical advice, and iterative refinement, with prompts reflecting greater attention to technological, pedagogical, and content-related considerations. Findings highlight both the potential and challenges of leveraging GenAI in teacher preparation, including the need for explicit guidance in prompt engineering, iterative collaborations with GenAI, and critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs. This study contributes to practical guidelines for scaffolding pre-service teachers’ AI use through the lens of TPACK and AI competencies.
authors: ["Jaesung Hur", "Idam Kim", "Nuo-Di Zhang", "Shi-Yao Wei", "Hui Shi", "V. Dennen"]

title_key: sir ben tagalog science ai teacher and study buddy on students perceived usability and learning outcomes|cuvinar
title: SIR BEN: TAGALOG SCIENCE AI TEACHER AND STUDY BUDDY ON STUDENTS PERCEIVED USABILITY AND LEARNING OUTCOMES
abstract: This action research aimed to determine the effectiveness of Sir Ben , a Tagalog-speaking AI chatbot, in improving Grade 10 students’ science learning outcomes at Dayap National High School. Using a quasi-experimental research design, four sections were involved: two experimental groups (Dao, n = 41; Mahogany, n = 41) exposed to the chatbot, and two control groups (Acacia, n = 42; Apitong, n = 41) taught using traditional methods. Data was collected through pretest and posttest assessments and perception surveys, and analyzed using mean gain scores, t-test for independent samples, and Cohen’s d for effect size. Findings revealed that the experimental group achieved a significantly higher mean gain of 43.56% compared to 32.52% in the control group, with results showing strong statistical significance, t(160) = –15.74, p < .001, and a very large effect size (d = 2.21). Survey results further indicated high levels of student acceptance, with ratings in ease of use (M = 4.51), engagement (M = 4.47), clarity (M = 4.49), and satisfaction (M = 4.46), and over 90% of learners expressing positive feedback. The study concludes that localized AI tools like Sir Ben significantly enhance student comprehension and engagement in science. It is recommended that schools consider integrating similar AI-supported interventions to promote inclusive, scalable, and technology-driven learning environments.
authors: ["Ben Mark Joy A. Cuvinar", "Department of Education"]

title_key: digital society and educational inequality exploring the impact of social media and artificial intelligence on university students in pakistan|khan
title: Digital Society and Educational Inequality: Exploring the Impact of Social Media and Artificial Intelligence on University Students in Pakistan
abstract: This study examines the relationships between social media use, generative artificial intelligence (AI), digital access, digital literacy, and educational inequality among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was employed, using a structured questionnaire to collect data from 350 students enrolled in public and private universities through convenience sampling. Data were analysed using SPSS version 27, applying descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple linear regression, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), and chi-square analysis. The findings indicate that students reported relatively high social media use (M = 3.86, SD = 0.74) and moderate-to-high generative AI use (M = 3.62, SD = 0.81). Digital access and digital literacy were negatively associated with perceived educational inequality (r = −.42 and r = −.36, respectively, p < .01), while generative AI use also showed a negative association (r = −.21, p < .01). In contrast, social media use had a positive association with educational inequality (r = .18, p < .05). Multiple regression analysis showed that digital access, digital literacy, generative AI use, socioeconomic status, social media use, and area of residence jointly explained 46% of the variance in perceived educational inequality (R² = .46, p < .001). Significant differences in digital access were also observed across income groups and between urban and rural students. The study concludes that digital technologies may provide academic opportunities, but their educational benefits are associated with differences in access, skills, and socioeconomic circumstances. It highlights the importance of equitable digital infrastructure, digital literacy development, and responsible AI use in higher education.
