title_key: enhancing serious games through robotic embodiment in education|suciu
title: Enhancing Serious Games through Robotic Embodiment in Education
abstract: This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of an educational system that combines serious games with a low-cost robotic teaching assistant to enhance student engagement and learning experiences. Unlike most existing gamebased learning approaches, which are primarily screen-based, the proposed system integrates digital gameplay with physical interaction through an affordable ESP32-driven robot equipped with a mobile phone interface. The system was developed following a needs analysis conducted with more than 200 university students, high school students, and teachers, which highlighted a strong demand for more interactive and engaging learning tools. Based on these findings, we designed a set of educational games targeting: (1) French language learning for high school students and (2) Graph theory concepts for both secondary and higher education students. During gameplay, the robot acts as an embodied teaching assistant, interacting with learners and providing guidance through a Large Language Model (LLM) constrained via prompt engineering to deliver hints rather than direct answers. This interaction aims to increase motivation, sustain attention, and reduce the anxiety associated with making mistakes. The system was evaluated in classroom studies with 52 high school students. Results indicate improved engagement and reduced anxiety compared to traditional computer-based educational games. To support reproducibility and adoption, the full implementation is publicly available, enabling educators to use, adapt, and extend the system.

title_key: learning video foresight reasoning from unlabeled videos via on policy self distillation|sun
title: Learning Video Foresight Reasoning from Unlabeled Videos via On-Policy Self-Distillation
abstract: Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video pairs into a natural self-supervised signal without extra annotations or LLM supervision. Second, they treat the whole future clip as equally valuable, although most of it is irrelevant context information. We address this by defining a foresight score, from which we obtain a contrastive privilege advantage that drives the model to learn the most valuable future information. Since the score is intractable, we optimize a tractable lower-bound surrogate that interpolates this advantage, computed between the true and a random reference future, with a teacher-student distillation advantage; together, they amplify decision-relevant content information and suppress irrelevant context information. We call the resulting framework Future-OPSD. On open-ended prediction and closed-ended planning, Future-OPSD improves base models by up to 14.2 and 15.9 points without compromising general video understanding. Code will be available at https://jingchensun.github.io/future-opsd/
authors: ["Jing-Chen Sun", "Jia-Xing Zhang", "Qing-Qiao Hu", "Ding-Qiang Ye", "Yu-Qi Jia", "Yi-Jun Liang", "Di Fu", "Yun-Jie Tian", "Dong-Di Zhao", "Chang-You Chen"]

title_key: chatgpt based generative ai scaffolding experiential learning styles and technical writing skills among industrial technology students|aler
title: ChatGPT-based generative AI scaffolding, experiential learning styles, and technical writing skills among industrial technology students
abstract: This study examined the relationships among ChatGPT-based generative AI scaffolding, experiential learning styles, and technical writing skills of Industrial Technology students at the University of Camarines Norte, providing the basis for a proposed English language program. A quantitative, descriptive-correlational design was employed, with a sample of 450 respondents determined using the Raosoft Sample Size Calculator at a 95% confidence level and a 5% margin of error, allocated through proportionate stratified random sampling across the College of Engineering (CoEng), College of Computing and Multimedia Studies (CCMS), and College of Technology (CoTT). Findings revealed that most respondents were male students enrolled in the College of Engineering and were almost evenly distributed across the four-year levels. Students agreed that they use ChatGPT-based generative AI as a scaffolding tool, with familiarity rated highest and frequency of use rated lowest. However, they strongly agreed on their experiential learning styles, with the reflector learning style rated highest and the activist learning style rated lowest, and agreed on their technical writing skills, with objectivity rated highest and functionality rated lowest. Meanwhile, ChatGPT-based generative AI scaffolding varied significantly by sex, college, and year level; experiential learning styles varied only by sex and college; and technical writing skills varied only by year level. The three major variables were highly and positively correlated, with experiential learning styles most closely associated with technical writing skills, while ChatGPT-based generative AI scaffolding was associated with better technical writing skills as a supporting mechanism. These findings formed the basis for a proposed program, E-CRAFT (Experiential and ChatGPT-Responsive Approach to Functional Technical Writing), that addresses underutilized ChatGPT scaffolding, underdeveloped active and practical learning-style experiences, and identified gaps in functionality, clarity, and precision in technical writing.
venue: International Journal of Research Studies in Education

title_key: designing an ai companion preservice teachers learning to teach stem with robotics|jamani
title: Designing an AI Companion: Preservice Teachers Learning to Teach STEM with Robotics
abstract: Research shows that preservice teachers’ self-efficacy to teach with technology impacts how they implement technology in teaching practice. In many countries, elementary teachers are expected to teach all STEM subjects, even though they have no undergraduate preparation in STEM. Therefore, an important goal of Teacher Education is to enhance elementary preservice teachers’ confidence to teach STEM subjects with technology such as Educational Robotics (ER). This conceptual paper reports on the theoretical foundations and structural design features of an artificial learning companion (ALC) designed to support preservice teachers learning how to teach STEM with ER. While ALCs have been reported to enhance students’ learning, motivation, and self-regulation, this paper responds to calls to explore ALCs as facilitators of learning by negotiation. The ALC design is therefore explained in terms of Vygotsky’s Sociocultural Learning Theory, specifically the Zone of Proximal Development, instructional scaffolding, and prompt engineering design. Generative AI (GenAI) will serve as an ALC to scaffold learning tasks such as coding. The ALC will function as a responsive scaffold by offering task-specific support through questions, hints, feedback, and reflection with gradual reduction in support as preservice teachers’ competence and confidence increase. This work illustrates how a GenAI ALC can simultaneously support preservice teachers as learners of STEM and as future STEM instructors. The paper provides STEM teacher educators with a concrete, adaptable model for embedding AI scaffolds into robotics-based learning to foster reflective and pedagogical thinking.

title_key: fostering professional vision in clinical ward rounds through digital simulation based learning with eye movement modelling examples and personalised feedback study protocol for four experimental studies|gartmeier
title: Fostering professional vision in clinical ward rounds through digital simulation-based learning with eye-movement modelling examples and personalised feedback: study protocol for four experimental studies
abstract: Abstract Introduction Clinical ward round communication is a core competency in medicine. Advanced professional vision (aPV)—comprising visual noticing and knowledge-based reasoning—is foundational to effective ward round performance. Eye movement modelling examples (EMMEs) represent a promising simulation-based approach to training aPV in medical students. This protocol describes four randomised experiments embedded within the EMMA learning environment examining design features of EMME-based training. Methods and analysis Four pre-registered randomised controlled experiments with pre-test/intervention/post-test design. Studies 2a and 2b (October 2026–January 2027): parallel screening experiments; Study 2a: EMME-based learning with raw fixation visualisation versus attention map visualisation versus minimal control (same ward round videos without gaze visualisation) (pre-post design). Study 2b: video-based learning without EMME gaze visualisation, with textual versus graphical versus combined large language model (LLM)-generated feedback versus minimal control (pre-post design). Study 3 (Q2–Q3 2027): confirmatory 2×2 factorial (4 cells, n≈55 per cell) crossing the best visualisation (Study 2a) with the best LLM feedback (Study 2b). Study 4 (Q1-Q2 2028): EMME-based simulation with embedded prompts versus a priori prompts versus no prompts. Participants are randomly assigned via computerised allocation and are medical students in the clinical phase of their studies (third year onwards) at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) with no prior clinical ward round leadership experience. Study 2a: n=96; Study 2b: n=88; Study 3: n=220; Study 4: n=190 (all studies f=0.25, α=0.05, power=0.80, mixed split-plot Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)). Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval was obtained from the Munich Technical University ethics committee (03/2026; grant code 2025-702 S-CT). Dissemination is planned in peer-reviewed journals in the areas of education psychology and medical education. Data of studies 2–4 will be made available following the findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability (FAIR) principles () in the TUM Open Data Repository or OSF including metadata and persistent identifier (PID)/digital object identifier (DOI) assignment. Trial registration number The four studies will be pre-registered separately prior to participant enrolment at the Open Science Foundation (OSF) Registries (https://osf.io/registries). Registration numbers and dates will be inserted here upon receipt. Each study will be registered as a separate pre-registration entry, given their distinct hypotheses and designs.
authors: ["M. Gartmeier", "T. Seidel", "P. Berberat", "C. Kosel", "G. Kahraman", "K. Vogt", "A. Frenzel", "Mario Gollwitzer", "Enkelejda Kasneci"]

title_key: exploring multimodal llm engagement on prompt engineering competency among non tech students in india|yildiz
title: Exploring Multimodal LLM Engagement on Prompt Engineering Competency Among Non-Tech Students in India
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly prevalent in the daily use of university students’ educational contexts, yet the specific perceptual LLM engagement patterns that contribute to effective LLM usage remain weakly understood. This exploratory cross-sectional study (N = 75) examines which factors of LLM engagement most strongly predict self-perceived prompt engineering competency among non-tech university students in India. Academic participants completed a survey measuring: Self-Perceived Prompt Engineering Competency (dependent variable), Basic Modality Use of LLM Input (text, images, audio, video, code), Strategic Integration & Application (purposeful combination of modalities), Depth of Use (usage of basic queries vs complex multi-modal tasks), and Self-Readiness & Access to AI tools, Primary Adoption Barrier to use AI. Non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, multiple regression, and barrier analyses through Chi-square tests were conducted. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests determined whether scores significantly exceeded the theoretical scale midpoint of 3.0. Three of five constructs were significantly above the midpoint: Self-Readiness & Access (W = 1323, p < .001, r = .782, large), Prompt Engineering Competency (W = 2197, p < .001, r = .768, large), and Integration & Application (W = 1008, p = .002, r = .463, medium). Basic Modality Use (W = 516, p = .997) and Depth of Use (W = 496, p = .963) did not exceed the midpoint. These results indicate that despite high perceived competency, multimodal and complex LLM engagement remains limited. Results of the multiple regression analysis show that the four-predictor regression model explains 41.6% of the variance in competency (F(4, 70) = 12.5, p < .001). Integration & Application was the strongest unique predictor (B = 0.51, p < .001), followed by Self-Readiness & Access (B = 0.34, p = .006). Neither Basic Modality Use nor Depth of Use contributed unique variance. A Chi-square goodness-of-fit test revealed a significantly unequal barrier distribution (χ²(5, N = 75) = 37.6, p < .001, w = 0.708). Lack of knowledge was the most prevalent Adoption Barrier to use AI (37.3%) and scored significantly lower on competency than students reporting privacy concern (U = 158, p = .034, r = .373). This study demonstrates that Prompt Engineering Competency is driven specifically by the purposeful integration of LLMs into academic workflows, rather than frequent exposure or access alone. Implications for AI literacy curriculum design are further discussed.
authors: ["Meltem Alkoyak-Yildiz", "Sandrapuri Aswin Tejasvi", "Venkatesh Viswanathan", "Luis Felipe Hernandez Mora"]

title_key: genai adoption in heis as a curriculum and pedagogical practice a case study|pereira
title: GenAI adoption in HEIs as a curriculum and pedagogical practice: a case study
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) became widely accessible with the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, rapidly transforming expectations regarding the competencies required of graduates. While higher education institutions continue to debate its pedagogical and ethical implications, some have already embedded GenAI into undergraduate curricula. This study presents a qualitative case study of bachelor's degree programs that integrated GenAI as a transversal competency during the first semester of the first year. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with professors from different courses and with varying levels of experience using GenAI. Interview data were analyzed through thematic analysis to explore faculty perceptions of GenAI integration, implementation strategies, enabling conditions, and perceived challenges. The findings reveal interconnected themes: opportunities to enhance feedback, content creation, and personalized learning; risks related to academic integrity, student overreliance, and AI bias; and contextual factors influencing adoption, including institutional policies, faculty training, technological infrastructure, and peer culture. Although participants expressed a generally positive attitude toward GenAI's educational potential, its implementation remained cautious, experimental, and uneven due to limited institutional guidance and professional development opportunities. The study also identifies the professional competencies considered essential for graduates and examines how these were embedded across the curriculum. These findings highlight the importance of institution-wide strategies, faculty capacity building, and clear ethical governance to support the sustainable integration of GenAI into higher education. The proposed framework contributes to the development of GenAI as a transversal graduate competency and offers guidance for universities seeking to align teaching and learning with the evolving demands of the digital workforce.

title_key: beyond prompting an epistemic agency framework for generative ai literacy|han
title: Beyond prompting: An epistemic agency framework for generative AI literacy
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has fundamentally altered how learners access, construct, and engage with knowledge. Existing discussions of GenAI literacy have largely emphasised operational competencies, such as prompt engineering, understanding AI capabilities, and ethical use. While these competencies remain important, they do not fully address the epistemic challenges arising from AI-mediated knowledge production. This paper proposes reframing GenAI literacy through the lens of epistemic agency; that is, learners’ capacity to critically evaluate, regulate, justify, and take responsibility for knowledge generated in collaboration with intelligent systems. Rather than viewing GenAI literacy as a collection of technical skills, this conceptual paper argues that its primary educational purpose is to cultivate learners who can exercise informed judgement in increasingly AI-mediated learning environments. Building on existing AI literacy scholarship and theories of epistemic agency, the paper introduces a conceptual framework comprising four interrelated dimensions: epistemic evaluation, epistemic regulation, epistemic responsibility, and epistemic autonomy. The framework provides a theoretically grounded perspective for understanding how GenAI literacy can move beyond operational competence towards fostering independent, reflective, and responsible knowledge construction.

title_key: the rise of multi agent ai in strategic human resource management exploring how collaborative ai agents transform talent management workforce coordination and hr decision authority|shoukat
title: The Rise of Multi-Agent AI in Strategic Human Resource Management: Exploring How Collaborative AI Agents Transform Talent Management, Workforce Coordination, and HR Decision Authority
abstract:
This study examined how professionals in Pakistan understood the role of collaborative artificial intelligence (AI) agents in talent management, workforce coordination and HR decision authority. Guided by Socio-Technical Systems Theory and Organizational Information Processing Theory, the study used reflexive thematic analysis to interpret 20 online interviews with HR, operations and technology professionals. Six themes captured participants’ accounts of recruitment, career development, workforce planning, decision authority, procedural fairness and organizational readiness. Participants located a critical point of recruiter oversight at initial screening, when historical hiring preferences could exclude qualified applicants before human review. In development and scheduling, they identified employee aspirations, skills and personal circumstances as information that could change an otherwise plausible recommendation. They assigned responsibility for pay adjustments to compensation committees and staffing reductions to executives. Across functions, participants connected fairness with understandable reasons and access to a reviewer empowered to correct an outcome. The findings show that, in participants’ judgments, the value of collaborative agents depends on whether decision owners can inspect underlying evidence, exercise judgment and intervene when recommendations affect employment opportunities.

title_key: from consumers to designers building rule based chatbots to reinforce chemistry learning and foster critical ai literacy|makaridze
title:
From Consumers
to Designers: Building Rule-Based Chatbots
to Reinforce Chemistry Learning and Foster Critical AI Literacy
abstract: This article describes an instructional approach that shifts secondary school participants from passive consumers of artificial intelligence to active designers by engaging them in building a closed-loop, rule-based chatbot. Implemented with 62 students (grades 8–12) in Georgia, the project required collaborative curation of chemistry content and programming of deterministic conversational logic. Unlike generative AI, this rule-based approach aligns with the rule-governed nature of core chemistry concepts such as stoichiometry and the mole concept. Pre- and post-test comparisons demonstrated substantial conceptual gains, particularly in abstract domains (+28% to +30%). Incorporating a social-contextual layer containing class-specific “insider knowledge”-triggered cognitive conflict that reduced uncritical trust in chatbot outputs from 70% to 15%. This approach offers secondary chemistry educators a practical strategy to simultaneously reinforce disciplinary understanding and foster critical digital literacy.

title_key: sentiment analysis of learner feedback in distance education in vietnam using machine learning models|nguyen
title: Sentiment Analysis of Learner Feedback in Distance Education in Vietnam Using Machine Learning Models
abstract: In the context of the rapidly accelerating digital transformation of education, distance learning has become an indispensable part of higher education in Vietnam. To improve teaching quality, educational institutions typically rely on periodic surveys to collect student opinions; however, this approach reflects only the views of a small group at a particular point in time and lags behind reality, whereas discussions and reviews on social media platforms such as Facebook, Threads and TikTok are updated continuously and express learners' opinions objectively. To leverage this resource, the research team collected and constructed the V-LearnerSentiment dataset comprising 6,366 valid observations, filtered and manually annotated from these platforms, to support sentiment analysis and aspect-based sentiment classification. The study compares the performance of traditional machine learning models (Support Vector Machine - SVM, Decision Tree - DT, Random Forest - RF), a deep learning model (Transformer) and large language models (LLMs) based on Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1-score, using macro and weighted averages to reflect sentiment classification effectiveness under imbalanced data conditions. Experimental results show that Gemini 2.5 achieves the highest Accuracy (86.22%), demonstrating its ability to effectively handle diverse and context-dependent feedback, while the specialized fine-tuned Transformer PhoBERT achieves an Accuracy of 82.6% and better identifies negative feedback belonging to the minority class. In addition to overall sentiment analysis, the team implemented aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) through a two-step procedure: the LDA model was used as a data exploration tool to extract and propose an Aspect Schema consisting of 5 main groups (Tuition & Costs, Degree & Value, Program & Quality, Schedule & Learning Mode, Counseling & Procedures), and a large language model was then employed to extract the context and classify the corresponding sentiment polarity for each aspect, transforming unstructured text data into measurable quantitative indicators. This approach not only enhances the interpretability of the results but also clearly identifies learners' main concerns, thereby providing a practical basis for improving the quality of distance education in Vietnam.

title_key: pedagogical aspects of using an adaptive mathematics teaching strategy as a means of implementing individual educational routes for schoolchildren|rodionov
title: Pedagogical aspects of using an adaptive mathematics teaching strategy as a means of implementing individual educational routes for schoolchildren
abstract: The article presents a model of personalized mathematics education based on adaptive educational technology, which is based on the joint activities of teachers and students, and is based on the appropriate use of traditional and adaptive automated methodological approaches. As part of the research, the study identified the educational and methodological framework that ensures the automatic functioning of the adaptive learning system in accordance with the specified functionality, and selected adaptive content that takes into account the level of students’ subject-specific mathematical training and development. A learning management system has been developed, including one based on artificial intelligence, which allows for automatic assessment of the level of «lagging» components of students’ mathematical training and ensures that this level is leveled. A prototype of an instrumental environment based on the LMS Moodle platform has been proposed, which provides for the variable deployment of educational materials using external information resources, including an AI assistant, when building and solving a chain of research-related tasks, as well as the generation of various types and formats of reports for the integral assessment of students’ success in implementing their individual educational routes. The results obtained allow us to state that in order to form an effective adaptive educational environment, it is advisable to select an adaptive platform for multi-user interaction that ensures adequate interaction between the three key participants in the educational process: the teacher, the student, and the system that acts as a mediator in this process. This model can be integrated into the learning management system, providing a personalized approach to learning content.

title_key: egs a complementary safety framework for educational llms|fei
title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. We introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that complements intrinsic alignment through query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance, and response moderation. EGS triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific educational interventions, and audits outputs before delivery. Experiments across general and education-specific benchmarks show that EGS improves moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs. These findings suggest that defense-in-depth guardrails can strengthen safety while preserving the pedagogical utility required in educational LLMs. Our code and model weights will be publicly available to support community adoption.

title_key: comparing human ai collaboration and teacher student collaboration in developing pre service teachers instructional design competence an experimental study|wang
title: Comparing human-AI collaboration and teacher-student collaboration in developing pre-service teachers' instructional design competence: an experimental study
abstract:
The application of generative artificial intelligence in learning has become increasingly prominent, and how it can complement and augment teachers' roles has become a key topic of discussion.
 
 
 
 This study adopted an experimental research paradigm to examine the effects of human-AI collaboration and teacher-student collaboration on the improvement of pre-service teachers' instructional design ability from the perspectives of information feedback and theory of mind.
 
 
 
 The results showed that both human-AI collaboration and teacher-student collaboration could enhance pre-service teachers' instructional design ability. However, at different time points, pre-service teachers' instructional design ability after eight weeks of training was significantly higher than that before training and after four weeks of training. Under different learning strategies, no statistically significant difference was detected between teacher-student collaboration and human-AI collaboration in the overall instructional design competence score, although the two strategies showed distinct advantages at the dimensional level and in learning experience. However, the subject-specific analysis revealed a significant interaction between learning strategy and subject discipline: the difference in the effects of the two learning strategies was more pronounced in the Chinese language subject than in the mathematics subject. Moreover, both the flow experience measurement and self-reports indicated significant differences in the learning process between teacher-student collaboration and human-AI collaboration.
 
 
 
 Based on these findings, it is recommended to establish an interactive dual-feedback loop of information, enhance feedback interactivity and emotional experience, and focus on subject-specific knowledge logic for guidance and feedback.

title_key: relating demographic factors with skills benefits and ethical use of artificial intelligence a survey of research students|khalil
title: Relating demographic factors with skills, benefits and ethical use of artificial intelligence: A survey of research students
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly entering the writing and research practices of postgraduate students, yet little is known about how research students in Pakistan judge their own AI skills, the benefits they gain, and their understanding of ethical and responsible use, or whether these perceptions differ across demographic groups. This study examined research students’ perceptions of AI skills for academic writing, the benefits of AI for evidence and writing, and the ethical and responsible use of AI, and related these constructs to age, research experience, university type, gender and level of study. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was used. Data were collected from 164 MS/MPhil and PhD students enrolled in public and private universities in Pakistan through an online structured questionnaire, using convenience sampling. The instrument measured three constructs on a five-point Likert scale; Cronbach’s alpha values ranged from .74 to .83. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and independent-samples t-tests. Research students reported high levels of AI skills for academic writing (M = 4.10), strong perceived benefits of AI for evidence and writing (M = 4.15) and high awareness of ethical and responsible use (M = 4.13). The strongest agreement was that over-dependence on AI could reduce critical thinking (M = 4.31), while awareness that AI output could be wrong, biased or incomplete was comparatively lower (M = 3.80). The three constructs were moderately and positively correlated (r = .35 to .44, p < .01). Age (r = −.349, p < .001) and research experience (r = −.162, p = .039) were negatively related to perceived benefits, but not to skills or ethical use. Students from private universities scored higher in all three constructs compared to their counterparts from government institutions, while there was no gender distinction. The research presents a unique analytical insight into AI skills and advantages and ethical issues regarding its application among students in Pakistan. The results indicate that institutional context has a greater impact than gender and education level, with young researchers set to derive more benefits from using AI technologies. The outcomes of the research support the necessity of the elaboration and implementation of structured education programs related to AI literacy together with the development of institutional policies concerning AI technologies.

title_key: a reflection grounded framework for ai workflows and assessment in design education|liu
title: A Reflection-Grounded Framework for AI Workflows and Assessment in Design Education
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) can rapidly produce polished personas, visual concepts, interface layouts, and design outputs, making final artefacts an increasingly unreliable indicator of students’ design understanding and contribution. This paper examines how assessment in design education can move beyond visual outcomes to evaluate the capabilities students exercise when working with generative AI. The study analyses 80 beginning-of-semester concept submissions and 79 end-of-semester reflections from an undergraduate design course, including 77 matched student pairs. Crucially, this setup allowed us to trace how workflows evolved as students transitioned from a mandated-AI conceptual phase to a free-choice prototyping phase. Through inductive coding and cross-stage qualitative comparison, findings show that students valued AI as a cognitive partner for early divergent exploration. However, many deliberately abandoned it during high-fidelity execution due to limited directability, generic outputs, cultural misrepresentation, and inefficiency. Based on these trajectories, we propose an assessment framework mapped to the Double Diamond design process. This framework derives seven assessable AI-era capabilities, enabling educators to evaluate design judgment, verification, and ethical responsibility rather than generated outputs alone.

title_key: changing attitudes towards academic integrity with language students practitioner insights|dewart
title: Changing attitudes towards academic integrity with language students: Practitioner insights
abstract: Teaching a language has changed considerably in the last decade due to advances in AI and GenAI. In some ways, Google Translate and ChatGPT have simplified using an additional language for many people. However, these tools have also complicated language learning with myriad crutches and supports. At a university in Montreal, Quebec, Canada,undergraduate students and professionals register in English as a second language (ESL) courses for varied reasons. They may have personal motivations, professional motivations, or low motivation when simply fulfilling a program requirement. Likewise, the students’ former academic experience may vary greatly, but they also have something in common: research has indicated that students functioning in an additional language are at an increased risk of suspected academic infractions. A student may be accused of plagiarism or unauthorized assistance when a submitted assignment doesn’t reflect the student’s previously demonstrated linguistic level. With a sensitivity to the context of language learners, two teachers initially set out to prevent plagiarism by providing information to students in English programs, and this objective shifted over time to promoting academic integrity. This paper details the evolution of a 10-year project, including the impetus for creating a learning module integrated into the university’s learning management system (LMS); the conception of the original module; its implementation and impact; and its complete redesign to reflect insights from contemporary scholars in academic integrity and to address concerns with emerging technology. Theoretical underpinnings, the relevant literature, and methods precede the discussion of practical applications.

title_key: ctrl concurrent training and rollout for llm reinforcement learning via gpu co residency|yang
title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.

title_key: explainable generative ai x genai in adaptive e learning a methodology for interpretable generation of personalized educational trajectories|oleynikova
title: Explainable Generative AI (X-GenAI) in Adaptive E-Learning: A Methodology for Interpretable Generation of Personalized Educational Trajectories
abstract: The integration of Generative AI (GenAI) into e-learning systems opens up unprecedented opportunities for the automated personalization of educational trajectories; however, it creates a critical “trust” deficit, as educators and instructional designers cannot easily verify the logic of the AI’s “black box” decision-making. This lack of transparency introduces risks of reinforcing cognitive biases, algorithmic bias, and suboptimal learning scenarios. This paper presents an X-GenAI (Explainable Generative AI) framework that ensures the interpretable generation of personalized learning paths based on Large Language Models enhanced with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) mechanisms. A key component is the explainability module, which builds a real-time semantic knowledge graph of the learner for the instructor, visualizes the weight coefficients of each learning element’s influence, and provides textual justification for the selection of the next educational activity. A pilot study involving 214 engineering university students over one semester was conducted. Results demonstrated that utilizing X-GenAI improves academic performance by 17.3% compared to traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS), reduces course adaptation time for instructors by 62%, and, according to the System Usability Scale (SUS), increases the level of trust in AI recommendations from 3.1 to 4.6 points. Finally, a taxonomy of explainability levels for educational AI systems is proposed, alongside ethical principles for their deployment. Author Contributions: O.O.O. conceptualized the X-GenAI framework, designed the explainability mechanisms, and wrote the main manuscript; M.N.S. supervised the pilot study, designed the experimental protocol and controls, and managed data collection; E.V.S. developed the semantic knowledge graph module, implemented the Chain-of-Thought integration, and conducted the statistical analysis of the results. All authors reviewed and approved the final manuscript.
