title_key: pengembangan learning management system berbasis web terintegrasi ai untuk pendidikan matematika|agusti
title: Pengembangan Learning Management System Berbasis Web Terintegrasi AI untuk Pendidikan Matematika
abstract: This study aims to develop a web-based Learning Management System (LMS) integrated with artificial intelligence (AI) to support mathematics education. The study employed the Design and Development Research (DDR) method, which involved system design, development, and functional testing. Matiku LMS was developed using ReactJS, Vite, TypeScript, Supabase, and the Gemini API. The system features include learning material and assignment management, digital assessment, learning analytics, AI-based learning recommendations, an AI-powered mathematics assistant, and GeoGebra 2D and 3D integration for mathematical visualization. Functional testing results indicated that the tested features operated according to the established indicators and specifications in a localhost environment. These findings demonstrate the system’s initial functional feasibility but do not establish its effectiveness in improving mathematics teaching or learning outcomes. Further evaluation is required to assess usability, system security, AI accuracy, and implementation by teachers and students in authentic learning environments..Keyword: Learning Management System, Artificial Intelligence, Mathematics Education, GeoGebra, Personalized Learning

title_key: prompting evaluating and adapting ai generated mathematical tasks secondary preservice teachers curricular decision making with chatgpt|sapkota
title: Prompting, evaluating, and adapting AI-generated mathematical tasks: Secondary preservice teachers’ curricular decision-making with ChatGPT
abstract: Despite emerging research on Artificial Intelligence in mathematics education, studies on how secondary preservice mathematics teachers make curricular decisions when using Artificial Intelligence tools (e.g., ChatGPT) to generate mathematical tasks are underdeveloped. Building on prior research that shows how teachers consider factors related to students’ needs, valid mathematics disciplinary ideas, contextual and institutional factors, and their own characteristics, we unpack how these factors interacted when secondary preservice mathematics teachers reflected on their prompts used to generate mathematical tasks using ChatGPT and their evaluation of ChatGPT-generated tasks. We also examined the potentials and challenges teachers identified in using ChatGPT for generating tasks. Preservice mathematics teachers highlighted the need for adjusting the difficulty level of ChatGPT-generated tasks, expressing concerns that the tasks at times did not (a) appropriately address students’ comprehension, (b) align with given standards/goals, and (c) present mathematics ideas coherently. They also shared formulating right prompts to generate appropriately challenging tasks was more time-consuming than writing their own tasks. By presenting examples of the factors that secondary preservice mathematics teachers considered when evaluating ChatGPT-generated mathematical tasks, we suggest strategies to help teacher and educators use Artificial Intelligence tools more efficiently in their curricular decision-making. We discuss how teachers’ engagement with Artificial Intelligence in curating curricular resources repositions teachers' curricular-decision making.
venue: International Electronic Journal of Mathematics Education

title_key: deep learning for physicists from linear regression to reasoning models|hanada
title: Deep Learning for Physicists: From Linear Regression to Reasoning Models
abstract: These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly. The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students. The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, but the basic ideas emphasized here are unlikely to go out of date soon.

title_key: a cobit 2019 based governance by design model for an llm powered scholarship pathway platform|awallaisal
title: A COBIT 2019-Based Governance-by-Design Model for an LLM-Powered Scholarship Pathway Platform
abstract: Preparing for international scholarships requires careful planning. LLMs provide personalized assistance in interpreting and executing the rules, but LLMs also bring new types of vulnerabilities such as prompt bugs introduced, hallucinated outputs, and clouded accountability by abstracting away how far reasoning has run. All, this article proposes a COBIT 2019-based governance model to mitigate against those. We constructed LINGKUP, a web platform that suggest individualized route to scholarship for Indonesian students by using Design Science Research (DSR). Built with Laravel 12. The system combines Gemini AI, user profiling, and prompt engineering with x and MySQL. Schema constrained JSON output; six classes of error handling taxonomy ensure reliability. With the Global Korea Scholarship (GKS) profile evaluation, AI latency revealed that a 60-second API timeout was needed. Our main contribution is a 'deep traceable control model' connecting abstract COBIT objectives with tangible AI engineering artifacts. The study further describes a risk-control-evidence matrix and governance roadmap that delineates technical feasibility, ability to implement effective governance mechanisms, and capacity to assess the impact of research education.
venue: 2026 14th International Conference on Cyber and IT Service Management (CITSM)

title_key: assessment integrity in the age of artificial intelligence redesigning learning evaluation for authentic human competency|adams
title: Assessment Integrity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Redesigning Learning Evaluation for Authentic Human Competency
abstract:
Widely accessible generative artificial intelligence has unsettled long held assumptions about how
learning can be measured and trusted. Tools capable of producing fluent essays, functional code,
and plausible solutions on demand have exposed the fragility of evaluation models that reward the
unsupervised production of polished artifacts. This paper argues that the appropriate institutional
response is not an escalating contest between detection software and evasion techniques, but a
deliberate redesign of evaluation around authentic human competency. Drawing on established
scholarship in authentic assessment, constructive alignment, and formative feedback, the paper
develops a five-principle framework for evaluation that remains meaningful when capable AI is
freely available. The framework shifts emphasis from the finished product toward the reasoning
process, foregrounds contextual judgment that machines cannot convincingly simulate, distributes
evidence of competency across a program rather than isolated high stakes events, treats AI as a
declared and scrutinized instrument rather than prohibited contraband, and grounds security in
thoughtful design rather than pervasive surveillance. Common assessment formats are appraised
for their resilience, and implementation challenges relating to staff workload, equity of access,
and institutional policy are examined. The paper concludes that the disruption introduced by
generative AI, although genuinely destabilizing, presents an overdue opportunity to align
evaluation with the competencies that human learners must actually develop, and to recover the
formative purpose of assessment that narrow integrity policing has long obscured.
venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY

title_key: the effect of ai hint transparency on user retention in an educational platform|zinchenko
title: The Effect of AI Hint Transparency on User Retention in an Educational Platform
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly embedded in coding courses, but their educational value depends on how this assistance is delivered to the student (Brown et al., 2025). This study tests whether revealing that clues are generated by AI - indicating their origin, naming their limitations, and requiring verification - affects the early retention of teenagers in an online course on coding. Developed a dedicated web platform providing a two-week self-paced Python introductory course, and conducted a supervised field experiment involving 93 high school and college students which were divided into three transparency conditions by means of a fixed alternating sequence: clues without mentioning that they are generated by AI (A), indicated clues with the verification instruction (B) and indicated clues with the verification instruction and the mandatory microphlexy (C) Four behavioral metrics were also calculated: week-2 retention, module-1 completion rate, stuck rate, and hint-to-progress time. The more transparent formats were associated with significantly higher retention and completion rates, as well as lower trapping frequency and faster progress after the hint, with the most complete C format having the strongest effect. The results suggest that the tooltip design, which combines source disclosure, information about AI failure, test queries and microflexy, is associated with lower early drop-off without changing the content of the course. This can be seen as a component of the measurable design mechanism.

title_key: aesthetic education in the information training of students gaps in the federal state educational standards for higher education a new conceptual framework and experience of interaction with large language models|iunov
title: Aesthetic education in the information training of students: Gaps in the Federal State Educational Standards for Higher Education, a new conceptual framework, and experience of interaction with large language models
abstract: The article analyzes the problem of the absence of aesthetic and empathetic competencies in the current Federal State Educational Standards of Higher Education (FSES HE) for fields of study 09.03.03, 01.03.02, 45.03.01, 45.03.03, and 44.03.05.The purpose of the article is to identify gaps in the FSES HE across various fields of study regarding aesthetic training, propose a new conceptual framework, and justify the necessity of its inclusion in educational standards.The methodology includes the analysis of regulatory documents, the synthesis of the authors’ long-term pedagogical experience, and the use of the DeepSeek large language model in a hybrid authorship mode to structure and formalize the conceptual framework.It is demonstrated that the technocratic model of information training leads to the “digital blindness” of specialists. As a solution, three original concepts are justified and introduced into the higher education system: “digital aesthetics” (with core criteria of composition, typography, and coloristics), “empathetic design” (through the “Grandmother” role model), and “ZNAK” (sign) — an acronym that expands a triplex study of role-based information models (previously developed by one of the authors) by adding Beauty to Protection, Clarity, and Adaptation. A formulation of the competence to supplement the FSES HE is proposed.The practical significance of the study lies in the fact that the developed concepts and criteria can be applied in designing educational programs and courses in informatics and IT for various fields of study in higher education, as well as in the teacher professional development system.The work is oriented toward a large target group: developers of educational standards (to improve the FSES of higher education), university professors and informatics teachers (for practical use in the educational process), and methodologists (to integrate the conceptual framework into professional development courses for teaching staff).The novelty of the results consists in: 1) justifying the need to supplement the FSES HE with aesthetic and empathetic competencies and developing specific formulations for such competencies; 2) the systematic introduction of three original concepts — “digital aesthetics”, “empathetic design”, and “ZNAK” — providing concrete recommendations for competence development; 3) the use of a large language model in a hybrid interaction mode to structure the conceptual framework and generate criteria.The international significance of the work is determined by its contribution to the development of the theory of empathetic design in education: the proposed conceptual framework aligns with modern foreign research and can be used to modernize educational standards in other countries.

title_key: evaluating the effectiveness of chatgpt voice for improving english speaking skills in vocational efl classrooms|saputra
title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of ChatGPT Voice for Improving English Speaking Skills in Vocational EFL Classrooms
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English language teaching has created new opportunities to enhance students' speaking skills through interactive and personalized learning experiences. However, empirical evidence regarding the effectiveness of ChatGPT Voice in vocational high school settings remains limited. This study aimed to examine the effectiveness of ChatGPT Voice in improving the English speaking skills of tenth-grade students in the Accounting and Finance Program at SMKN 1 Kota Besi, Indonesia. A pre-experimental one-group pretest–posttest design was employed involving 24 students selected through total sampling. Data were collected using speaking performance tests administered before and after three instructional meetings integrating ChatGPT Voice into speaking activities. Students' speaking performances were assessed using Brown's analytical speaking rubric, covering pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the Shapiro–Wilk normality test, a paired-samples t-test, and Cohen's d effect size. The findings revealed that the mean speaking score increased from 57.71 in the pre-test to 75.21 in the post-test. The paired-samples t-test indicated a statistically significant improvement (t(23) = 7.840, p < .001), while the effect size analysis demonstrated a large educational effect (d = 1.60). These findings suggest that ChatGPT Voice can serve as an effective supplementary instructional tool for enhancing English speaking skills in vocational EFL classrooms. Future studies are recommended to involve larger samples, longer intervention periods, and experimental designs with comparison groups to further validate these findings.
venue: Jadila: Journal of Development and Innovation in Language and Literature Education

title_key: negotiating identity and relationality an ai enhanced polylogue on human centred learning design practices|fernandez
title: Negotiating identity and relationality: An AI-enhanced polylogue on human-centred learning design practices
abstract:
This poster presents a developing AI-enhanced polylogue methodology and conceptual framing to understand how third-space professionals in higher education are negotiating their shifting roles and identities while designing human-centred learning and assessment.
Recent technological disruptions (e.g., widespread proliferation, advancement and use of generative AI, focus on cybersecurity, adoption of data-enabled technologies and ecosystems) have intensified tensions around higher education assessment structures and practices, exposing the limitations of isolated, task-based evaluation of student learning (Boud et al., 2020; Corbin et al., 2025). In response to the challenges posed to learning and assessment in the contemporary higher education landscape, emerging scholarship has foregrounded relationality and human connection alongside a shift to more program-wide approaches to assessment and assurance of learning (Lodge et al., 2023; Nicola-Richmond et al., 2025). This has highlighted questions about how educators can sustain meaningful relationships with each other and with students amidst these disruptions (Maldon et al., 2025).
In this work-in-progress project, we focus on these relational questions and explore how technological disruptions are reshaping the roles and identities of educators, specifically curriculum designers working in third-space roles at the boundary of academic and professional domains (Whitchurch, 2012). We build on work that positions teaching and learning as fundamentally relational, emphasising connection, trust, care, and dialogue between educators, students, and third-space professionals (Riddle & Hickey, 2023). Our aim is to understand how relationality may be conceptualised in the context of transforming curriculum to support human flourishing and critical engagement with generative AI in our everyday learning design practice, particularly in the design of program-level assessment, feedback, mentorship, and collaborative sense-making structures.
The project employs an AI-enhanced polylogue methodology inspired by Markauskaite et al. (2022). The AI-enhanced polylogue is a structured, multi-voiced inquiry, where participants engage in iterative cycles of individual reflection and collaborative dialogue, involving AI as a reflective interlocutor to surface gaps, alternative perspectives, and assumptions. Over several months, three curriculum designers independently responded to targeted questions in reflective logbooks, then engaged in semi-structured conversations about connection in higher education, program-level learning design, evolving educator roles, and the contributions of third-space professionals. This was complemented by a collaborative chat with a generative AI tool, in which participants used AI to probe gaps, tensions, and alternative perspectives arising from the conversations. These strands are then brought together in collaborative critical reflection sessions to identify emerging patterns in relational practice and their significance in program-level curriculum design.
This poster shares early themes from the logbooks and conversations. Early analysis highlights how participants experience and navigate tensions between increasing technological mediation alongside their third-space roles and their commitment to relational practice. The importance of human-centred learning design and its implications will also be examined and shared. The project contributes to contemporary discussions on inter-collegial practices that keep connection, trust, and dialogue central in increasingly AI-mediated educational environments. As part of this project, participants treat disruption as an invitation to remake educator identities and practices in more relational, collaborative, and inclusive ways.

title_key: automated question generation and assessment using the gemini large language model with indobert based semantic similarity|muharram
title: Automated Question Generation and Assessment Using the Gemini Large Language Model with IndoBERT-Based Semantic Similarity
abstract: Manually creating questions and assessments is still a problem and burden for teachers, especially in terms of time efficiency, consistency, and objectivity in learning evaluation. While AI-driven automated generation and grading offer a potential solution, existing studies tend to address these aspects in isolation rather than fully integrating them. This research proposes an integrated approach combining the Gemini 1.5 Flash Large Language Model (LLM) for question generation with an IndoBERT-based semantic similarity model to provide an interpretable alternative grading mechanism. The methodology used to implement the AI Project Cycle includes problem definition, data acquisition, model development, and model evaluation. The Gemini LLM was trained on question-and-answer datasets to generate multiple-choice and essay questions, while automated assessment utilized prompt engineering with Gemini 1.5 Flash alongside a Cosine Similarity model trained using IndoBERT vector representations. Evaluation is carried out by adjusting the semantic similarity threshold value in the range of 0,1 to 1,0. The experimental results show that the optimal threshold of 0.6 produces an accuracy of 87.76%, an F1-Score of 0.8929, a recall of 0.9615, and a precision of 0.8333, which indicates the best results in classifying the relevance of students' answers. Explainable AI analysis was conducted using SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) methods; these helped elucidate the factors influencing similarity predictions, thereby enhancing the transparency of the model's decision-making process. This research contributes by presenting a combined approach of LLM gemini and semantic-similarity interpretable models to improve the efficiency and consistency of the learning evaluation process.
authors: ["A. T. Muharram", "Bambang Warsuta", "Chandra Wirawan", "Rizki Elisa Nalawati", "Agus Setiawan", "Raden Roro Afifah Ramadhani"]
venue: 2026 14th International Conference on Cyber and IT Service Management (CITSM)

title_key: cultivating mathematics classroom practices to support reasoning and proof in the era of genai|sears
title:
Cultivating Mathematics Classroom Practices to Support Reasoning and Proof in the Era of
 GenAI
abstract:
This editorial invites the mathematics education community to examine strategies for promoting reasoning and proof by leveraging the capabilities of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), and to consider classroom practices that facilitate these processes. Drawing on Sears and Buchbinder,
 AI Integration in K‐12 Mathematics: A Framework Linking Curriculum, Classroom Enactment, and Student Learning (AIM‐CEL Framework)
 , we discuss practices that consider the interplay among teachers, students, mathematical content, and the GenAI tool to promote reasoning and proof. We also identify research areas that can further explore classroom practices that attend to reasoning and proof in the era of GenAI.

title_key: when brain outsourcing becomes habit governmentality dilemmas and learning alienation in agentic workflows|chen
title: When "brain outsourcing" becomes habit: governmentality dilemmas and learning alienation in agentic workflows
abstract: The spread of generative AI has made "brain outsourcing"—delegating cognitive tasks to AI—a common phenomenon in higher education, especially in low-tier private undergraduate colleges. Existing studies explain it mainly at the individual level, neglecting the institutional consequences of the technologies used to govern it. Drawing on design-based research principles, this study conducted a three-group quasi-experiment in a Data Structures course at such a college: an adversarial workflow (Group A, n = 36), a negotiative workflow (Group B, n = 40), and a traditional control group (n = 44), triangulated across five chains of evidence. Results show that Group A's direct-dumping rate fell to 11.1% (vs. 57.5% and 75.0%), yet concealed forms—cosmetic modification and division-of-labor outsourcing—rose compensatorily, leaving the composite outsourcing index unchanged across groups (p = 0.864). Process engagement rose sharply while output authenticity stayed low (comment–code matching 3.62/5; only 27.8% of difficulty tags authentic), indicating "performative engagement". Only 1 of 120 students adopted a self-regulated strategy. In Group A, perceived control rose (+2.17) and negotiation space fell (−0.91) without meaningful growth in autonomy; the 18.3-point advantage over the control group in comprehension depth shrank to 6.8 points in transfer application. The "non-outsourceable" workflow thus changed outsourcing's form, not its deep structure, alienating learning into an adversarial game of evading detection—a new hidden curriculum. Agent design should shift from adversarial surveillance to dialogic support.
venue: Journal of Education and Educational Policy Studies

title_key: navigating curricular complexity programmatic assessment and ai in a business context|azouz
title: Navigating curricular complexity: Programmatic assessment and AI in a business context
abstract:
Traditional models of programmatic assessment are historically rooted in highly structured, linear disciplines such as medicine (Heeneman et al., 2015; Torre et al., 2021). Translating these principles to a diverse, modular Business and Economics faculty presents profound curricular, structural, and governance challenges. Business courses within Monash University operate within a flexible architecture designed to support highly personalized student pathways, where over 90% of students have unique pathways via diverse combinations of majors, minors, and electives. Consequently, units are highly interconnected—sometimes contributing to up to 20 distinct programs—so that an assessment alteration in one unit ripples across multiple independent degree structures. This structural friction is compounded by distributed governance split across separate academic departments, departmental Directors of Education (DOEs), Course Directors, and Chief Examiners.
To navigate this complex landscape, the Senior Educational Designer and the Associate Dean of Learning and Teaching (ADLT) collaborated on a university-wide initiative entitled Programmatic Assessment and Artificial Intelligence Review (PAAIR) spurred by TEQSA requirements (Lodge et al., 2023). We adapted established theory around programmatic assessment to synthesize a tailored five-principle framework, designating “Collaborative and Transparent Culture” as Principle 1. To address modular friction, we drew on Dawson’s (2020) concept of programmatic assessment security, shifting the unit of analysis from hardening every individual, isolated module to strategically securing key programmatic assessment moments across the entire course. Cultivating this shared-accountability mindset was critical because curriculum reviews occurred by course, where a single unit could feed into multiple programs with diverse departmental oversight. It was difficult to have a unified, static “full picture” of a complete course at any one stage of a review, as some units may have been completed as part of other reviews, or they may be dual-coded with a postgraduate course, requiring complex cross-referencing across courses, departments, year levels, and campuses.
To bridge this diagnostic gap, we collaborated with the faculty’s data analytics team to develop the PAAIR Dashboard in PowerBI. Serving as an interactive visual analytics platform, the dashboard empowers DOEs, Course Leaders, and Educational Designers to see beyond disciplinary silos, map competency coverage across shared pathways, monitor assessment distributions, and facilitate data-informed co-design conversations in real time. It helps flag structural gaps—such as when a core graduate competency is not assessed under secure conditions at least twice per year level—ensuring curriculum resilience across highly complex student pathways.
At the launch of the project, we developed a comprehensive suite of guidelines to support Unit Learning Outcome (ULO) refinement, Course Learning Outcome (CLO) mapping, and balanced assessment design. These guidelines have been instrumental in improving our course designs by scaffolding competencies progressively and designing assessment tasks with and without generative AI (Lodge et al., 2023; Matheis & John, 2024). This dual approach balances the educative, values-driven framework of academic integrity with the adversarial, hardening requirements of assessment security (Dawson, 2020).
As the initiative now enters the initial transition to Business-As-Usual (BAU) operations, we are actively developing a future governance strategy to manage subsequent curriculum changes sustainably. This Pecha Kucha presentation delivers a transparent roadmap and strategic recommendations for other modular higher education faculties seeking to operationalize programmatic assessment and AI review within highly complex, non-linear educational ecosystems.

title_key: development of research competence of undergraduates through training in text linguistics based on artificial intelligence|kudasbekova
title: Development of research competence of undergraduates through training in text linguistics based on artificial intelligence
abstract:
This study addresses the development of undergraduates' research competence through teaching Text Linguistics by integrating artificial intelligence tools. The study aims to develop a scientific and methodological model and experimentally evaluate its effectiveness.
 
 
 
 A mixed-methods quasi-experimental design was employed involving 58 first-year undergraduates enrolled in the Kazakh Language and Literature educational program. The experimental group consisted of 30 students, while the control group included 28 students. ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity AI, Elicit, Consensus, and Scite.ai were integrated into tasks involving scientific text analysis, academic writing, literature review, evaluation of scientific evidence, and research reflection. Research competence was assessed using a 100-point test, scientific text analysis tasks, a Likert-scale questionnaire, and an expert assessment rubric. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, the Shapiro-Wilk test, paired and independent t-tests, Cohen's d, and Cronbach's alpha.
 
 
 
 
 The experimental group's research competence score increased from 58.43 ± 6.87 to 84.27 ± 5.94 points. The improvement was statistically significant (
 p
  < 0.001), with a large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.92).
 
 
 
 
 The findings indicate that the systematic pedagogical integration of artificial intelligence tools into Text Linguistics instruction can support the development of undergraduates' scientific text analysis, academic writing, critical thinking, evidence-based reasoning, and research independence.

title_key: feedback guidance from large language model chatbots to physical education teachers an exploratory cross model and cross language content analysis|romdhani
title: Feedback Guidance from Large Language Model Chatbots to Physical Education Teachers: An Exploratory Cross-Model and Cross-Language Content Analysis
abstract: Teachers increasingly consult large language model (LLM) chatbots, yet little is known about the feedback guidance these conversational interfaces give physical education (PE) teachers, or whether it depends on the chatbot or the language. We submitted one prompt, describing a low-skilled child who repeatedly fails a forward roll and a teacher tempted to reprimand him publicly, to ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and DeepSeek in English, French, and Arabic. In this exploratory single-run study, a directed content analysis of the 12 responses (109 scripted feedback statements) described and compared chatbots and languages. All chatbots rejected the public reprimand and prescribed a chin tuck and a simpler task. However, only half explained the cause of the error, two-thirds of the technical cues combined several points, 95% of the technical cues directed attention to the body, and six responses contradicted their own guidance to give one cue at a time. Praise was often unspecific, one statement invited the student’s view, and several responses flattered the teacher. Descriptively, the chatbot accounted for 58% of the dissimilarity between coded responses and the language for 12%, and these shares cannot be separated from run-to-run variation. Within these limits, teachers may wish to check diagnosis, cue load, and autonomy support.

title_key: kurdishmcq a multiple choice question dataset for the kurdish language sorani dialect|ahmed
title: KurdishMCQ: A multiple-choice question dataset for the Kurdish language (Sorani dialect).
abstract: This article presents a large-scale multiple-choice question (MCQ) dataset for the Kurdish language (Sorani dialect), designed to support research in natural language processing (NLP) and low-resource language modeling. The dataset was constructed from authentic educational materials, including middle and high school textbooks, end-of-chapter exercises, and official examination questions prepared by educational authorities. As these resources were not available in digital format, the questions were digitized using an optical character recognition (OCR) pipeline specialized for Sorani Kurdish and verified by native Kurdish speakers. Each instance includes the question text, multiple-choice options, the correct answer, and metadata such as subject and grade level. Only text-based questions were included; items requiring external context such as images or tables were excluded. The dataset comprises 17,221 questions spanning biology, chemistry, mathematics, physics, natural science, history, geography, economics, Kurdish grammar and literature, and religion studies. The questions primarily correspond to grades 9-12, with additional categories such as driving tests. A multi-stage quality-control process was applied, including duplicate removal, manual review, and external validation by native speakers. The dataset can be used for multiple NLP tasks, including question answering, knowledge probing, reasoning evaluation, and multilingual model assessment, and is suitable for training, fine-tuning, and benchmarking large language models, particularly in zero-shot and few-shot settings. By offering a comprehensive and culturally grounded collection of Kurdish-language questions, this resource contributes to expanding data availability for underrepresented languages and facilitates research in multilingual and low-resource NLP.

title_key: where did that student risk model come from hidden inference in agentic ai generated teacher facing dashboards|bakharia
title: Where did that student risk model come from? Hidden inference in agentic AI-generated teacher-facing dashboards
abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) coding tools have the potential to democratise the development of teacher-facing learning analytics dashboards by enabling educators to generate complete applications from natural language specifications. In this study we evaluate Claude Code (Fable) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.5 High) across three dashboard specifications of increasing complexity using realistic educational datasets typically available to educators. Both AI systems successfully generated functional dashboards that accurately implemented the required visualisations and interactions. However, they also independently introduced additional analytical functionality, including student risk classifications and AI-generated insights, despite these features not being requested. These implicit inferences raise important concerns regarding transparency, bias and student data privacy, particularly where educators may be unaware of the analytical models or external AI services embedded within generated applications. The findings suggest that while agentic AI can significantly reduce the technical barriers for end user educators developing learning analytics tools, careful review of generated analytical logic and data flows is essential to support responsible and trustworthy use in educational settings.

title_key: engineering visible thinking evt a human centred assessment framework for the generative ai era|hatem
title: Engineering Visible Thinking (EVT): A human-centred assessment framework for the Generative AI era
abstract: Generative AI is changing how students complete assessments and demonstrate what they know. As AI tools become part of everyday study, final assessment submissions alone may not provide sufficient evidence of how students think, solve problems, or develop understanding throughout the learning process. This paper introduces Engineering Visible Thinking (EVT), a human-centred assessment framework designed for the AI era. Rather than focusing on whether students use AI, EVT focuses on designing assessments that generate multiple forms of evidence to support judgements about student learning. The framework is built around three connected elements: visible thinking, process evidence, and capability validation. The paper draws on the design of a new Applied IT degree and includes a detailed example from the first-year Networking Fundamentals course to illustrate the application of the EVT framework in practice. The paper argues that the real challenge is not detecting AI use but designing assessments that provide evidence to support judgements about students’ learning and capability. By extending assessment beyond final products to include evidence of thinking, process and demonstrated competence, EVT offers a practical approach to assessment design that keeps people, not technology, at the centre of learning.

title_key: comparing the positive and negative impacts of ai a large scale study of student perspectives|walton
title: Comparing the positive and negative impacts of AI: A large-scale study of student perspectives
abstract: Higher education students are incorporating generative artificial intelligence into many aspects of their studies, yet the ways they judge its positive and negative impacts remain poorly understood. Using qualitative content analysis supported by code-frequency analysis, this paper examines open-ended comments from 2,802 participants drawn from a survey of 8,021 students across four Australian universities. Reported impacts clustered around four themes: study practices, quality, efficiency, and institutional practices. Positive impacts were more frequently coded overall, particularly when students described using AI to support their own study practices and efficiency. Negative responses centred on the inaccuracy of AI outputs. Although relatively few participants commented on institutional teaching and assessment practices, these responses were predominantly negative. The findings suggest that students value AI not only for the quality of its outputs, but also for its role in helping them begin, continue, refine, and complete academic work. Rather than uncritically accepting or categorically rejecting AI, students appeared to make situated judgements about its usefulness and limitations, shaped by concerns about accuracy and trust, as well as by the agency and control they retained over its use. Institutional responses should therefore engage with the complexity of students’ practices and the conditions under which they perceive AI to be useful or problematic.
authors: ["J. Walton", "S. Hosseini", "Michael Henderson", "T. Corbin", "Christine Slade", "Jennifer Chung", "Yi-Fei Liang"]

title_key: relato de experiencia e potencial interdisciplinar de um produto tecnico tecnologico voltado ao ensino de com arte assistido por inteligencia artificial generativa|silva
title: RELATO DE EXPERIÊNCIA E POTENCIAL INTERDISCIPLINAR DE UM PRODUTO TÉCNICO-TECNOLÓGICO VOLTADO AO ENSINO DE/COM ARTE ASSISTIDO POR INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL GENERATIVA
abstract: Digital technologies have transformed contemporary educational contexts in profound ways, pressing educators toward more informed pedagogical approaches. This article analyzes the interdisciplinary potential of a Technical-Technological Product (TTP) focused on the teaching of and with art through generative artificial intelligence, developed within a Professional Master's Degree in School Education. The methodology consisted of qualitative, participatory action research carried out through workshops offered to early-years Elementary students at a municipal public school. Findings show that the TTP's pedagogical planning organically activates competencies from Brazil's National Common Curricular Base across Portuguese Language, Mathematics, Sciences, and the Computing complement. The study concludes that a critical and poetic engagement with artificial intelligence in schools goes beyond instrumental use, functioning as a cross-disciplinary catalyst for digital literacy across multiple fields of knowledge.
venue: Revista de Estudos Aplicados em Educação

title_key: the impact of artificial intelligence ai on the teaching and learning of english language and literature in english language a case of level 200 language students of wesley college of education|stephen
title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the Teaching and Learning of English Language and Literature in English Language: A Case of Level 200 Language Students of Wesley College of Education
abstract:
The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming education globally, especially in language teaching and learning. In Ghanaian Colleges of Education, AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, Duolingo, QuillBot, and AI-powered literature analysis platforms are increasingly being accessed by teacher trainees. However, there is limited research on how these tools specifically influence the teaching and learning of English Language and Literature-in-English at the tertiary level. 
This study investigated the impact of AI on the teaching and learning of English Language and Literature-in-English among Level 200 Language students of Wesley College of Education, Kumasi. The study sought to: 
 
Examine the extent of AI usage among students and facilitators, 
Identify the benefits and challenges of AI in English and Literature classes, and 
Suggest strategies for effective integration of AI in language teacher education. 
 
The study adopted a descriptive survey design. A sample of 150 Level 200 Language students and 10 English/Literature facilitators was selected using purposive and simple random sampling techniques. Data were collected using questionnaires, semi-structured interviews, and classroom observation. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics with SPSS, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically. 
The findings revealed that the majority of the students are aware of AI tools and use them mainly for grammar correction, essay writing, paraphrasing, and literature summary. Facilitators use AI for lesson planning, generating comprehension questions, and providing instant feedback. The study identified several benefits: improved writing skills, personalized learning, increased engagement, access to literary analysis, and time savings for facilitators. However, key challenges were also found. These include over-reliance on AI that can lead to plagiarism and reduced critical thinking, inaccurate literary interpretations by AI, limited internet access and data costs, and a lack of training for facilitators on ethical AI use. 
It was concluded that AI has both positive and negative impacts on the teaching and learning of English Language and Literature-in-English. While AI can enhance proficiency and make literature more accessible, its misuse can undermine creativity and academic integrity. 
The study recommends that Wesley College of Education organize training workshops on the ethical and pedagogical use of AI, integrate AI literacy into the curriculum, provide reliable internet facilities, and develop a college policy to guide responsible AI use among students and facilitators. This will ensure that AI serves as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for human instruction in language and literature education.
venue: The International Journal of  Humanities & Social Studies

title_key: prototype effects and implicit models in llm responses to geometry tasks|kratka
title: Prototype Effects and Implicit Models in LLM Responses to Geometry Tasks
abstract: This paper investigates the role of implicit models in large language model (LLM) responses to geometry questions, with a particular focus on the phenomenon of prototype effects (Rosch, 1975). Building on Fischbein’s account of tacit and implicit models in mathematical thinking (Fischbein, 1987; 1989), together with his later theory of figural concepts (Fischbein, 1993), we analyze how LLMs reproduce and reinforce such models in their explanations. The study draws on a large dataset of elementary geometry tasks in Czech language, as a case of less dominant language. The theoretical framework combines Fischbein’s theory of figural concepts (Fischbein, 1993), emphasizing the dual conceptual–figurative nature of geometric objects, with research on prototype effects in geometry education. These effects manifest, for example, when angles are interpreted primarily as convex regions or when geometric figures are associated with dominant visual prototypes rather than formal definitions (Brunheira and da Ponte, 2019). We consider that LLMs can tend to systematically privilege such prototypical representations. Methodologically, we conduct a qualitative content analysis of LLM responses (ChatGPT and Claude) to geometry prompts. Unlike previous analyses focused on correctness, richness, or errors within Czech and English prompts’ responses, this study codes for the presence, type, and didactical role of implicit models. Particular attention is paid to how these models align with or diverge from local curricular norms and classroom expectations. Results show recurring prototype-based representations, some of which may conflict with local curricular standards despite being mathematically valid. This creates a new layer of didactical tension: not merely between correct and incorrect answers, but between formally valid explanations and those aligned with classroom practice. We discuss this tension in relation to the didactical contract, where AI systems become co-constructors of mathematical meaning. The paper contributes to research on AI in education by showing that LLMs may reproduce and reinforce representations that could influence learners’ implicit conceptual frameworks. This has significant implications for teaching: rather than treating AI outputs as neutral resources, educators must address their underlying implicit models and integrate them into reflective classroom practice.

title_key: large language modelpowered ai assisted simulated patient for nursing education quasi experimental study|chan
title: Large Language Model–Powered AI-Assisted Simulated Patient for Nursing Education: Quasi-Experimental Study
abstract: Abstract Background Large language model (LLM)–powered virtual patient systems are gaining popularity in nursing education but also face persistent challenges, such as hallucinations and role inconsistency. Objective This paper reports the model architecture design, technical considerations, implementation challenges, and evaluation of an LLM-powered AI-assisted simulated-patient system integrated into a nursing triage simulation game. Methods The system integrated a Unity-based game client, with GPT-4o hosted through Microsoft AI Foundry to support real-time simulated-patient dialogue in Traditional Chinese using Cantonese syntax. This developmental study comprised exploratory model selection, formative student feedback–informed enhancement from Version 1 to Version 2, development-stage script-fidelity evaluation, and evaluation of system usability and the Net Promoter Score in 2 tutorial cohorts of nursing students. Results Key technical contributions include a layered hallucination mitigation architecture that combines grounded prompt inclusion, few-shot conversational exemplars, negative role constraints, and calibrated model parameters. In the predefined script-fidelity evaluation, script-inconsistent responses occurred in 78 of 125 (62.4%) Version 1 outputs and 21 of 125 (16.8%) Version 2 outputs—an absolute difference of 45.6 percentage points. The implementation process also addresses stateless API memory management, cloud-based safety filter calibration for domain-specific clinical prompts, and prompt engineering strategies to prevent role drift and hidden scenario information leakage. GPT-4o was selected as the production model through exploratory development testing that considered script consistency, Cantonese-language suitability, response latency, technical reliability, deployment feasibility, cost considerations, and Unity integration compatibility; 45 of 50 (90%) assessed GPT-4o responses were rated fully script-consistent. Conclusions This study demonstrates the development and real-world tutorial deployment of a Cantonese-language, LLM-powered simulated-patient system for nursing triage education. Integrating formative student feedback with structured technical debugging enabled iterative refinement of dialogue fidelity, role consistency, protected-information handling, and game interaction functions. The resulting Version 2 system provides a practical, contextually tailored approach to supporting scalable simulated-patient dialogue in nursing education.
authors: ["Max Chun Ming Chan", "Danny Chun Kit Hung", "T. Kwok", "Janet Yuen-Ha Wong"]

title_key: pemanfaatan chatgpt dalam pembelajaran matematika untuk mengembangkan literasi numerasi materi peluang|syaifuddin
title: Pemanfaatan ChatGPT dalam Pembelajaran Matematika untuk Mengembangkan Literasi Numerasi Materi Peluang
abstract: Numeracy literacy is an important competency in mathematics learning to equip students to understand, analyze, and solve contextual problems. Along with digital technology development, Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, has emerged as a tool supporting interactive and student-centered learning. This study aims to analyze the use of ChatGPT as a supporter of mathematics learning on probability in developing the numeracy literacy of eighth-grade students at Muhammadiyah 1 Ponorogo Junior High School. This study employed a qualitative approach with a descriptive research design. The participants were 18 eighth-grade students. Data were collected through observation, interviews, documentation, and analysis of students’ work. Data were analyzed using the Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña model, consisting of data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The results showed that ChatGPT facilitated interactive learning through concept understanding, discussion, problem-solving, problem creation, and answer evaluation. It encouraged active student engagement and supported numeracy literacy by improving students’ ability to understand concepts and explain problem-solving processes. However, challenges included limited internet access, difficulties developing prompts, lengthy responses, and students’ tendency to rely on AI. Therefore, teacher guidance is essential to ensure critical, effective, and responsible use of ChatGPT in mathematics learning.

title_key: generative artificial intelligence ai policy in higher education a content analysis of ethical themes in the qs top 200 university policies 2026|lund
title: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) policy in higher education: A content analysis of ethical themes in the QS Top 200 university policies (2026)
abstract: The rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities worldwide to develop institutional policies governing its ethical, pedagogical, and administrative use. While global organizations such as UNESCO and national consortia like the Russell Group have issued high-level principles, universities have responded unevenly, producing policies that vary widely in scope, depth, and ethical coverage. Existing studies have examined subsets of institutions—such as the top 50 global universities, U.S. universities, or leading Asian universities—and consistently report gaps in transparency, data governance, academic integrity guidance, and algorithmic literacy. However, no study, to the researchers’ knowledge, has systematically analyzed AI policies across the world’s top 200 universities. This research addresses that gap in policy awareness by conducting a comprehensive content analysis of 197 publicly available AI policies from the 2025 QS Top 200 universities. Using a 16-theme AI ethics coding framework and statistical comparisons across region, size, public/private status, and ranking quartile, the study identifies dominant themes (e.g., data bias, privacy, security), underrepresented areas (e.g., explainability, misinformation, deepfakes), and structural differences in policy emphasis across institutional types. The findings reveal a global policy landscape that is expanding rapidly but remains fragmented, with significant inconsistencies in ethical coverage, documentation expectations, and support for instructors and students. This report contributes a global, data-driven understanding of how universities are governing GenAI and highlights critical gaps that must be addressed to ensure responsible and equitable AI integration in higher education.

title_key: verimath human in the loop generation and verification of curriculum aligned mathematics assessment items|nguyen
title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
abstract: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.
authors: ["Q. Nguyen", "Duong Q. Nguyen", "Dinh P. T. Nguyen", "Truong-Giang T. Le", "Truong A. Bui", "Vi H. Vo", "Quang-Thinh Bui", "My-Phuong Ngo", "Trong N. Do", "Thao P. Le", "Phuc M. Nguyen", "H. Nguyen-Xuan"]

title_key: bridging the gap health professions students preferences for ai curriculum integration and perceived barriers|hua
title: Bridging the gap: health professions students’ preferences for AI curriculum integration and perceived barriers
abstract:
Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into health professions curricula poses significant pedagogical challenges. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this study examined how undergraduate health professions students perceive AI educational modalities, evaluated tool effectiveness, and identified barriers to acceptance.
 
 
 
 Between January and February 2026, 713 students from three institutions in eastern China completed a validated online survey. Stratified random sampling ensured representation across academic years (1–5) and disciplines (clinical medicine, medical laboratory science, and allied health programs). The instrument assessed preferences for four instructional formats and three AI tool categories. Analyses included descriptive statistics, Cochran’s Q tests, paired t-tests, mixed-effects logistic regression, and thematic analysis of 412 open-ended responses.
 
 
 
 
 Integration into existing coursework was the dominant preference across all tool types (41.65–44.74%), whereas standalone modules attracted limited support (16.69–21.74%). Mixed-effects logistic regression showed that senior students (Years 4–5: OR 1.79, 95% CI 1.23–2.60,
 p
 = .002) and those reporting high perceived usefulness (OR 2.44, 95% CI 1.71–3.48,
 p
 < .001) and ease of use (OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.04–2.19,
 p
 = .031) were significantly more likely to favour the integrated approach. A usability paradox was observed: specialized medical AI tools were rated marginally more useful than general large language models (mean 4.43 vs. 4.12; Cohen’s d = 0.24), yet less easy to use (mean 3.89 vs. 4.35; Cohen’s d = 0.31). Given the limited clinical exposure reported by many respondents, these ease-of-use ratings likely reflect perceived rather than experienced usability. Key adoption barriers were data privacy concerns (30.0%) and ethical uncertainty (21.9%). Participants valued clinical applicability over breadth of coverage (4.67 vs. 4.38,
 p
 < .001).
 
 
 
 
 Findings support moving away from isolated AI courses toward clinically embedded training. Curricular reform should prioritise hands-on relevance and ethical governance while addressing the usability barriers of specialised platforms, thereby preparing future health professionals to direct AI applications critically rather than rely on them passively.

title_key: competition shapes students use of generative ai in creative problem solving behavioral distancing and its individual and collective changes|cheng
title: Competition Shapes Students’ Use of Generative AI in Creative Problem-Solving: Behavioral Distancing and Its Individual and Collective Changes
abstract: Generative AI can support students’ learning and problem-solving, yet little is known about whether and how human–AI collaboration changes across social contexts. This study introduces competition as an important social context and examines how it shapes students’ use of AI-generated content in creative problem-solving. A total of 92 undergraduates were randomly assigned to competition or no-competition conditions and completed three creative problem-solving tasks with GenAI support, yielding 276 student-task observations. Semantic similarity analysis, behavioral coding, regression analysis, and permutation tests were used to examine changes in AI-content use and their individual- and collective-level changes. Results showed that competition reduced students’ semantic overlap with AI-generated content and increased almost full rejection of AI suggestions, without a corresponding statistically detectable increase in self-directed improvement. Competition was associated with greater idea fluency and flexibility, but lower fluency-normalized flexibility, and neither individual semantic distinctiveness nor collective semantic diversity consistently increased. Together, these findings distinguish behavioral distancing from constructive human agency in AI-supported problem-solving: using less AI-generated content does not necessarily mean engaging with AI more independently or achieving greater relative diversity. The study therefore highlights human–AI collaboration as a socially situated process and shifts attention from the amount of AI use to the performance of students’ engagement with AI-generated content. Supporting effective AI-assisted learning may require fostering students’ capacity to critically evaluate, transform, and extend AI-generated ideas rather than simply encouraging greater or lesser reliance on GenAI.

title_key: sophistication without clarity student writing versus unedited genai delegation|guo
title: Sophistication without clarity: Student writing versus unedited GenAI delegation
abstract: Writing is central to how students develop and demonstrate communicative competence, yet that development is increasingly difficult to observe as GenAI enters the writing process. This paper establishes a pre-GenAI stylistic baseline of student academic writing and characterises how unedited GenAI responses to the same assessment prompts differ from it. Using stylometric and writing analytics techniques, we analysed over 118,000 words collected in 2021 from 18 higher education students in a software engineering subject. Study 1 used the seven students who completed all four tasks to establish a within-cohort reference: the size and direction of stylistic change in the same students’ writing across two semesters and two rhetorical genres. Study 2 paired each of 59 authentic submissions with a length-matched, zero-shot response to the identical prompt from three large language models. Student writing moved toward shorter words, fewer rare terms and markedly higher readability. Unedited model outputs moved in the opposite direction on each measure, gaining lexical sophistication through a narrower working vocabulary at substantial cost to readability; the human–GenAI gap in readability exceeded the students’ own shift between semesters.
authors: ["Zi-Xuan Guo", "K. Misiejuk", "Sonsoles L\u00f3pez-Pernas", "Mohammed Saqr", "Guan-Liang Chen", "Eduardo Oliveira"]

title_key: a bibliometric analysis of software development in higher education and its role in educational quality and industry innovation|batoon
title: A bibliometric analysis of software development in higher education and its role in educational quality and industry innovation
abstract: This study maps the development, intellectual structure, conceptual themes, and international collaboration patterns of research on software development in higher education. A bibliometric analysis was conducted using publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection from 2020 to 2024. Following relevance screening and metadata assessment, 375 publications constituted the final analytical corpus. Bibliometric performance analysis was used to identify prominent documents, publication sources, authors, institutions, and countries, while country-level co-authorship, co-citation, and keyword co-occurrence analyses were conducted using VOSviewer. The findings reveal an interdisciplinary research landscape connecting software engineering education, programming pedagogy, artificial intelligence, technology-enhanced learning, assessment, software quality, and industry alignment. China and the United States were the leading contributors by publication output, whereas Finland demonstrated the strongest international collaboration based on total link strength. Co-citation analysis identified seven intellectual clusters encompassing software engineering education foundations, artificial intelligence and machine learning, programming-learning challenges, AI-supported programming education, technology-enhanced pedagogies, industry-relevant assessment, and methodological quality assurance. Co-word analysis further identified five major conceptual themes centered on formal software education, student-centered instructional design, empirical software engineering and AI, project-based and industry-aligned education, and AI-augmented programming instruction. Comparison with related contemporary research indicates increasing convergence among software engineering education, generative AI, digital learning, authentic assessment, and university–industry collaboration. The findings provide a structured basis for curriculum review, faculty development, responsible AI integration, assessment redesign, and international and industry collaboration. However, the results represent patterns of scholarly activity and intellectual relationships rather than direct evidence of improvements in educational quality, employability, or industry innovation. The study is limited by its reliance on English-language Web of Science records and the exclusion of records with incomplete metadata.
authors: ["Jayson Batoon", "Digna S. Evale", "Rosemarie Bautista", "Reylan M. Evale", "W. Wider"]

title_key: design thinking scaffolds for learner agency preserving ai use effects on creative self efficacy cognitive flexibility and engagement|wang
title: Design-thinking scaffolds for learner-agency-preserving AI use: effects on creative self-efficacy, cognitive flexibility, and engagement
abstract:
Generative AI can facilitate the production of student work but may also displace learners' responsibility for problem framing, evaluation, and revision. This study examined whether design-thinking scaffolds were associated with creative self-efficacy, cognitive flexibility, and problem-solving engagement during AI-supported project learning.
 
 
 
 A three-condition, four-wave quasi-experimental study included 162 undergraduates in six intact class sections (54 per condition). Non-AI project learning, ordinary GenAI use, and design-thinking-scaffolded GenAI use were compared across a four-week educational design task. Baseline-adjusted models assessed self-reported outcomes, human-coded AI-use logs, and independently rated products from 54 teams. Cluster-bootstrap analyses examined temporally ordered indirect associations and moderation by pre-intervention AI over-reliance.
 
 
 
 
 Compared with ordinary GenAI, the scaffolded condition showed higher T2 creative self-efficacy (adjusted difference = 0.33,
 p
 = 0.006), T3 cognitive flexibility (0.35,
 p
 = 0.003), and T4 engagement (0.35,
 p
 = 0.004). Mean team product quality was 20.14 in the scaffolded condition, compared with 17.62 under ordinary GenAI and 16.76 without AI. Coded prompts showed fewer answer-completion requests and more comparison, critique, and reflection. Indirect estimates via creative self-efficacy (0.07), cognitive flexibility (0.09), and their sequential pathway (0.04) had bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. Higher initial AI over-reliance weakened the overall engagement contrast and the two single-mediator indirect pathways, whereas the moderated-sequential index had a confidence interval including zero.
 
 
 
 
 The findings are consistent with agency-preserving cognitive offloading when instructional scaffolds retain student responsibility for higher-order decisions. Intact-section allocation, task-specific self-reports, and limited section-level replication preclude strong causal or general-transfer claims.

title_key: students perception on the use of generative artificial intelligence tools in essay writing|tsin
title: STUDENTS’ PERCEPTION ON THE USE OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS IN ESSAY WRITING
abstract: The role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has evolved from automated systems to Generative AI (GenAI), now seen as collaborative partners for students in academic writing. This study employs a quantitative cross-sectional survey design to investigate the use of GenAI tools by English as a Second Language (ESL) tertiary students in Kota Kinabalu, Sabah, and their perceptions of these tools. An online questionnaire was administered to 136 diploma students, and the responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Results indicate widespread awareness and integration of GenAI tools, with students reporting the strongest use of GenAI for content summaries (79.4% agreement) and context-specific word and phrase suggestions (70.6%), suggesting that the technology serves as a linguistic scaffold for second language (L2) learners. Students perceived improvements in error identification (73.5%), clarity and coherence (64.7%) and organization of ideas (64.0%), although agreement regarding gains in self-editing (48.6%) and confidence in their own knowledge of GenAI tools (47.1%) was more modest. Students also expressed a strong desire to maintain autonomy in decision-making during writing, with 77.9% agreeing that human authors should make the final decisions on grammar and spelling corrections. The findings suggest that assessment practices may need to attend to the writing process rather than only the product, and that frameworks promoting a balance of collaboration between humans and AI systems can help students maintain their originality and human voice when producing written work.

title_key: students perceptions of using artificial intelligence in mathematics education|khan
title: Students’ Perceptions of Using Artificial Intelligence in Mathematics Education
abstract: AI is transforming education by providing immediate clarifications, tailored guidance, feedback and self-learning. This study has evaluated the awareness, use and perception of AI in mathematics education by students and compared the perception of male and female students. A descriptive survey was conducted by convenience sampling of participants. The data were collected both online and offline using a researcher-developed questionnaire, which had eight questions regarding students’ engagement with AI in mathematics education. Data were analysed by proportions. The results showed that the students knew about AI and valued its benefits in Mathematics education. Many students used AI for their learning, but a small portion of students used regularly for Mathematics, although many reported using it occasionally. Most of the students opted for AI platforms like Google Gemini, ChatGPT and others. Students primarily used AI for problem solving, exam preparation, and conceptual understanding. They also thought AI could make learning math easier and supported its use in their schools. Mathematics: Male students used AI more than female students. The findings show that AI is a powerful learning tool for students, but its educational use needs to be properly directed, responsibly used and critically verified for AI-generated mathematical answers.
venue: International Journal of Educational Analysis and Global Research (IJEAGR)
